title: MechReason: Benchmarking Multi-Image Multi-Hop Reasoning in Mechanical Engineering
summary: Despite significant progress in general visual question answering and cross-modal understanding, multimodal large language models still face a pronounced gap in evaluation for complex reasoning within the mechanical engineering domain. Existing benchmarks predominantly focus on rudimentary tasks such as drawing recognition, CAD interpretation, or single-chart querying, falling short of assessing whether models can integrate multiple images, textual conditions, physical principles, and engineering constraints to perform multi-step reasoning when confronted with authentic, intricate mechanical problems. To address this, we introduce MechReason, a benchmark derived from real mechanical engineering papers, comprising 12k question-answer pairs with explicit reasoning-chain annotations and 21k visual materials spanning nine evidence types, including statistical charts, parameter tables, engineering drawings, microscopic images, simulation images, system architectures, real mechanical scene photos, CAD model images and manufacturing flowcharts. MechReason covers eight task types across four reasoning dimensions: explanation, prediction, design, and diagnosis. We devise a four-stage construction pipeline: we first extract core engineering claims and decompose their supporting evidence into premises, reasoning processes, conclusions, and corroborative evidence; we then generate shortcut-preventing questions by masking posterior verification information; finally, we apply multimodal quality validation to ensure task quality and multi-hop nature. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that MechReason is highly challenging, with even the most advanced models achieving only 62.89\% accuracy.

AI.tldr: MechReason is a benchmark for evaluating multimodal large language models on complex mechanical engineering reasoning tasks, containing 12k QA pairs with explicit reasoning chains and 21k visual materials across 9 evidence types. Even state-of-the-art models achieve only 62.89% accuracy, highlighting significant challenges in this domain.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for multimodal LLMs focus on basic tasks (drawing recognition, CAD interpretation, single-chart querying) and fail to assess whether models can integrate multiple images, textual conditions, physical principles, and engineering constraints for multi-step reasoning on authentic mechanical problems.
AI.method: Four-stage construction pipeline: (1) Extract core engineering claims and decompose supporting evidence into premises, reasoning processes, conclusions, and corroborative evidence; (2) Generate shortcut-preventing questions by masking posterior verification information; (3) Apply multimodal quality validation to ensure task quality and multi-hop nature.
AI.result: MechReason is highly challenging - even the most advanced models achieve only 62.89% accuracy. The benchmark covers 8 task types across 4 reasoning dimensions (explanation, prediction, design, diagnosis) with 9 evidence types (statistical charts, parameter tables, engineering drawings, microscopic images, simulation images, system architectures, real mechanical scene photos, CAD model images, manufacturing flowcharts).
AI.conclusion: The benchmark addresses a critical gap in evaluating multimodal reasoning in mechanical engineering, providing a comprehensive testbed that requires integration of multiple modalities and multi-step reasoning. The low accuracy of current models indicates substantial room for improvement in complex engineering reasoning.

title: DenseFace: Bias Mitigation in Face Recognition via Density-Aware Probabilistic Matching
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures. Accepted at IEEE/IAPR International Joint Conference on Biometrics (IJCB) 2026
summary: Despite steady progress in face recognition, current face recognition models still suffer from significant demographic biases. While approaches for bias mitigation have been proposed, existing methods often impose constraints on the training procedure and result in the degradation of recognition accuracy. To address this issue, we here introduce a method that reduces racial bias in pre-trained face recognition models without compromising their accuracy. To this end, we model face embeddings of each person by von Mises-Fisher (MF) distribution. We next observe the dependency between demographic attributes and the density of MF distributions, and propose DenseFace, a probabilistic face matching procedure that accounts for differences in MF distributions. Our extensive experiments demonstrate DenseFace to consistently reduce racial bias in strong face recognition models varying in network architectures, training datasets and loss functions. Notably, DenseFace preserves recognition accuracy and requires no retraining of the underlying face recognition model. Our work also investigates previously adopted bias measures and makes suggestions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces DenseFace, a method to reduce racial bias in pre-trained face recognition models without compromising accuracy. The approach models face embeddings using von Mises-Fisher distributions and accounts for demographic-dependent density differences during matching.
AI.motivation: Current face recognition models suffer from significant demographic biases, and existing bias mitigation methods often require training constraints and degrade recognition accuracy. The authors aim to address this tradeoff.
AI.method: The method models face embeddings as von Mises-Fisher (vMF) distributions, observes the dependency between demographic attributes and vMF distribution density, and proposes a probabilistic face matching procedure called DenseFace that accounts for these distribution differences.
AI.result: DenseFace consistently reduces racial bias across strong face recognition models with varying architectures, training datasets, and loss functions. It preserves recognition accuracy and requires no retraining of the underlying model.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DenseFace method effectively reduces racial bias in face recognition without accuracy degradation. It works as a post-processing technique requiring no model retraining. The paper also reviews and provides suggestions on previously adopted bias measures.

title: Hyperbolic Contrastive Learning with Entailment for Spatial Transcriptomics
summary: Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) has transformed biomedical research by enabling the spatial mapping of gene expression across tissue sections. However, high operational costs, specialized equipment requirements, and sensitivity to experimental noise limit the accessibility and scalability of ST. Recent computer vision approaches aim to overcome these limitations by predicting spatial gene expression directly from histopathology images. While effective, current approaches often suffer from gene expression over-smoothing and overly uniform predictions across tissue regions, suggesting that further progress depends on learning representations that reflect the hierarchical and asymmetric structure of gene regulation and tissue morphology. To address these issues, we propose Hyperbolic Contrastive Learning with Entailment for Spatial Transcriptomics (HyCLoST), a hyperbolic contrastive learning model that captures the intrinsic hierarchical relationships within ST data. By leveraging hyperbolic geometry and a gene-to-image entailment loss, HyCLoST learns structured, biologically grounded representations that improve gene expression prediction accuracy, achieving a 6% reduction in MSE and an 8% increase in PCC across 26 ST datasets, over previous methods. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/BCV-Uniandes/HyCLoST

AI.tldr: HyCLoST is a hyperbolic contrastive learning model that predicts spatial gene expression from histopathology images by leveraging hyperbolic geometry and gene-to-image entailment loss, achieving 6% MSE reduction and 8% PCC improvement across 26 ST datasets.
AI.motivation: Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) faces limitations including high operational costs, specialized equipment requirements, and sensitivity to experimental noise. Current computer vision approaches for predicting spatial gene expression from histopathology images suffer from gene expression over-smoothing and overly uniform predictions across tissue regions, failing to capture the hierarchical and asymmetric structure of gene regulation and tissue morphology.
AI.method: HyCLoST uses hyperbolic contrastive learning to capture intrinsic hierarchical relationships within ST data. The model leverages hyperbolic geometry (which naturally represents hierarchical structures) combined with a gene-to-image entailment loss to learn structured, biologically grounded representations that better reflect the hierarchical nature of gene regulation and tissue morphology.
AI.result: HyCLoST achieves a 6% reduction in Mean Squared Error (MSE) and an 8% increase in Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) across 26 ST datasets compared to previous methods.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic geometry combined with contrastive learning and entailment losses can effectively address the over-smoothing and uniform prediction issues in spatial gene expression prediction, enabling more accurate and biologically grounded representations for spatial transcriptomics analysis.

title: SceneBench: A Hierarchical Benchmark for Vision-Language Understanding of 3D Scenes
summary:
Vision-language models excel at 2D image understanding but remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning. Progress is hindered by limitations in current benchmarks. First, 3D datasets often rely on point clouds that capture geometry but discard rich visual features like texture, text, and materials. Second, annotations treat objects in isolation while ignoring real-world hierarchical organization (scenes, rooms, functional areas, object groups). Third, evaluation tasks focus narrowly on basic recognition rather than multi-step spatial reasoning.
  In this context, we introduce SceneBench, a benchmark of 966 photorealistic 3D scenes reconstructed with Gaussian Splatting and densely annotated with hierarchical semantics spanning scenes, rooms, functional areas, object groups, and individual objects. These annotations are produced through a human-in-the-loop pipeline combining vision-language models with roughly 1,500 human-hours of iterative refinement and verification, producing over 183K annotated nodes with textual descriptions and 3D bounding boxes. Building on this representation, we define three evaluation tasks: Existence-Based Questions probing object attributes, Spatial Intelligence Questions covering counting, size comparison, distance, and directional relations, and Grounded Question-Reasoning-Answer (QRA) triplets requiring multi-step reasoning across semantic levels. Experiments with state-of-the-art vision-language models show that while models perform well on basic recognition tasks (e.g., up to 85% accuracy for detection), performance drops substantially on hierarchical and compositional reasoning (e.g., down to 60% for counting), revealing limitations not captured by existing benchmarks. SceneBench provides a realistic testbed for developing and evaluating models capable of fine-grained spatial reasoning in photorealistic 3D environments.

AI.tldr: SceneBench is a new benchmark for evaluating vision-language models' 3D spatial reasoning capabilities, consisting of 966 photorealistic 3D scenes with hierarchical annotations (183K nodes) spanning scenes, rooms, functional areas, object groups, and individual objects. Three evaluation tasks are defined: Existence-Based Questions, Spatial Intelligence Questions, and Grounded QRA triplets. Experiments reveal performance gaps between basic recognition (85% accuracy) and hierarchical reasoning (60% for counting).
AI.motivation: Current vision-language models excel at 2D image understanding but struggle with 3D spatial reasoning due to three key benchmark limitations: (1) 3D datasets use point clouds that discard rich visual features (texture, text, materials), (2) annotations treat objects in isolation ignoring real-world hierarchical organization, and (3) evaluation tasks focus on basic recognition rather than multi-step spatial reasoning.
AI.method: SceneBench was built through a human-in-the-loop pipeline combining vision-language models with approximately 1,500 human-hours of iterative refinement and verification, producing 966 photorealistic 3D scenes reconstructed with Gaussian Splatting and densely annotated with hierarchical semantics. The dataset contains over 183K annotated nodes with textual descriptions and 3D bounding boxes spanning five semantic levels: scenes, rooms, functional areas, object groups, and individual objects.
AI.result: Experiments with state-of-the-art vision-language models show that while models perform well on basic recognition tasks (up to 85% accuracy for detection), performance drops substantially on hierarchical and compositional reasoning (down to 60% for counting). This reveals limitations in current models that are not captured by existing benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: SceneBench provides a realistic testbed for developing and evaluating models capable of fine-grained spatial reasoning in photorealistic 3D environments. The benchmark reveals significant gaps in current vision-language models' hierarchical and compositional reasoning capabilities, highlighting the need for more sophisticated 3D spatial reasoning approaches.

title: EMODY Flow: Emotion-Aware Audio-Driven Full-Body Motion Generation
summary: Embodied conversational agents require synchronized full-body motion (body gestures and facial expressions) that aligns with speech and emotional state. Omni-modal large language models excel at multimodal understanding but produce only linguistic outputs, leaving a critical gap in embodied response generation. We identify and address a failure of emotion conditioning: like other conditional generators that under-use weak conditioning signals, a flow-matching model given both a rich audio embedding and a discrete emotion label suppresses the emotion, generating near-identical motion regardless of the specified emotion. We present EMODY Flow, a lightweight (around 35M parameters) flow-matching framework that attaches to a frozen Qwen-3 Omni model and reuses its internal Mimi audio-codecs to condition two parallel DiT generators - one for SMPL-X body pose, one for FLAME facial expressions. A training-time auxiliary emotion classifier restores emotion sensitivity by forcing generated motion to be emotion-identifiable. EMODY Flow sets a new state of the art on BEAT2 gesture quality, with FGD 0.302, Beat Correlation 0.853, and Diversity 24.62 - improving over the best prior results by 26%, 5%, and 62% respectively - and transfers to zero-shot facial animation on TFHP without domain-specific fine-tuning. Beyond these quantitative gains, the classifier yields clearly emotion-separated motion, which we demonstrate qualitatively through a multidimensional-scaling analysis of the generated gestures.

AI.tldr: EMODY Flow is a lightweight (35M parameters) flow-matching framework that generates synchronized full-body motion (body gestures and facial expressions) conditioned on audio and emotion labels, addressing a critical gap in embodied conversational agents where omni-modal LLMs produce only linguistic outputs. A training-time auxiliary emotion classifier restores emotion sensitivity that typical conditional generators suppress.
AI.motivation: Embodied conversational agents require synchronized full-body motion (body gestures and facial expressions) aligned with speech and emotional state. While omni-modal large language models excel at multimodal understanding, they produce only linguistic outputs, leaving a critical gap in embodied response generation. The authors identified a specific failure mode: flow-matching models given both audio embeddings and discrete emotion labels suppress the emotion signal, generating near-identical motion regardless of the specified emotion.
AI.method: EMODY Flow attaches to a frozen Qwen-3 Omni model and reuses its internal Mimi audio-codecs to condition two parallel DiT (Diffusion Transformer) generators—one for SMPL-X body pose and one for FLAME facial expressions. A training-time auxiliary emotion classifier forces generated motion to be emotion-identifiable, restoring emotion sensitivity that would otherwise be suppressed.
AI.result: EMODY Flow sets a new state of the art on BEAT2 gesture quality with FGD 0.302 (26% improvement), Beat Correlation 0.853 (5% improvement), and Diversity 24.62 (62% improvement). It also transfers to zero-shot facial animation on TFHP without domain-specific fine-tuning. Qualitative analysis through multidimensional scaling demonstrates clearly emotion-separated motion.
AI.conclusion: The proposed EMODY Flow successfully generates emotionally-expressive synchronized body gestures and facial expressions from audio and emotion conditioning. The auxiliary emotion classifier training mechanism effectively addresses the emotion suppression problem. The lightweight architecture (35M parameters) achieves significant quantitative improvements while maintaining zero-shot transfer capability to unseen domains.

title: MUUNRiver-Bench: Diagnosing Relation-Dependent Music Retrieval with Multimodal Instructions
summary: Music retrieval is relation-dependent: given a reference track, a listener may seek its style with a new theme, a cover, or a comparable voice, and these intents demand contradictory rankings. We present MUUNRiver-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark whose reference-audio queries use natural-language instructions to define relevance. A pipeline combining expert genre priors, LLM-generated prompts and lyrics, synthesis, and expert review yields 3,440 tracks spanning 13 genres and 116 sub-genres, and seven tasks: similar-music, style-preserving lyric-rewriting, lyric-preserving style-rewriting, cover, vocal-timbre, isolated-vocal, and segment retrieval. Across six models in eight configurations, task-wise rank reversals reveal complementary biases: acoustic encoders favour local identity, whereas text-aligned encoders favour semantic relations. Frozen encoders diagnose default similarity preferences; instruction-aware and audio-text fusion systems provide exploratory tests of textual conditioning, with neither simple fusion scheme consistently improving its backbone

AI.tldr: MUUNRiver-Bench is a diagnostic benchmark for music retrieval that uses natural-language instructions to define relevance. It addresses the fundamental challenge that music retrieval intents are contradictory - finding style with new theme, covers, or comparable voices require different rankings. The benchmark contains 3,440 tracks across 13 genres and 116 sub-genres, with seven retrieval tasks.
AI.motivation: Music retrieval is relation-dependent: given a reference track, listeners may seek style with new theme, cover versions, or comparable voices - but these intents demand contradictory rankings. Existing benchmarks lack natural-language instructions to define relevance, making it difficult to diagnose model biases across different retrieval intents.
AI.method: The pipeline combines expert genre priors, LLM-generated prompts and lyrics, synthesis, and expert review to create 3,440 tracks spanning 13 genres and 116 sub-genres. Seven tasks are defined: similar-music, style-preserving lyric-rewriting, lyric-preserving style-rewriting, cover, vocal-timbre, isolated-vocal, and segment retrieval. Six models in eight configurations were evaluated.
AI.result: Task-wise rank reversals reveal complementary biases: acoustic encoders favor local identity (audio-specific features), whereas text-aligned encoders favor semantic relations (lyrics/semantic content). Frozen encoders can diagnose default similarity preferences, while instruction-aware and audio-text fusion systems provide exploratory tests of textual conditioning.
AI.conclusion: Neither simple fusion scheme consistently improves its backbone encoder. The benchmark reveals that different encoder architectures have fundamentally different similarity preferences - acoustic encoders prioritize local audio identity while text-aligned encoders prioritize semantic relations. This suggests the need for more sophisticated fusion approaches that can flexibly handle contradictory retrieval intents.

title: Multimodal Emergency Vehicle Classification via Audio-Visual Transformers and Knowledge Distillation
summary: Emergency vehicle detection in autonomous driving is a safety-critical perception task that demands robustness under diverse and adverse real-world conditions. Existing approaches rely on a single modality, either audio or video, which leads to systematic failure when that modality is degraded: microphone-based systems fail in noisy urban environments, and camera-based systems fail at night or under occlusion. This report presents AVNet, a multimodal audio-visual transformer that classifies emergency vehicles (ambulance, fire engine, police car) and road background using both audio and video, while gracefully handling the absence of either modality at inference time. AVNet introduces three key contributions: (1) a temporally aligned cross-modal fusion module that performs second-level cross-attention between audio spectrogram tokens and video frame tokens, exploiting their exact temporal correspondence without any learned alignment mechanism; (2) learned null embeddings that substitute for missing modality tokens, enabling a single unified model to operate in audio-only, video-only, or joint audio-visual mode without retraining; and (3) a knowledge distillation training strategy in which specialist unimodal teacher models transfer inter-class dark knowledge into the multimodal student fusion branch via soft probability targets. Evaluated on 281 clips from the Google AudioSet dataset, AVNet achieves 66.6% overall accuracy in audio-visual mode, outperforming the audio-only branch by +10.4% and the video-only branch by +15.0%. The largest per-class gain is observed for the hardest class, Ambulance, where fusion achieves +29.5% over either unimodal branch alone, demonstrating that the two modalities provide complementary information that the aligned cross attention mechanism successfully exploits.

AI.tldr: AVNet is a multimodal audio-visual transformer for emergency vehicle detection in autonomous driving that handles audio-only, video-only, or joint audio-visual modes using learned null embeddings and cross-modal attention, achieving 66.6% accuracy on Google AudioSet.
AI.motivation: Existing emergency vehicle detection approaches rely on a single modality (audio or video), leading to systematic failures when that modality is degraded - microphone-based systems fail in noisy environments, camera-based systems fail at night or under occlusion. Robust perception under diverse real-world conditions is safety-critical for autonomous driving.
AI.method: The paper proposes three key technical contributions: (1) A temporally aligned cross-modal fusion module performing second-level cross-attention between audio spectrogram tokens and video frame tokens using exact temporal correspondence without learned alignment; (2) Learned null embeddings that substitute for missing modality tokens, enabling unified operation across audio-only, video-only, or joint modes without retraining; (3) A knowledge distillation training strategy where specialist unimodal teacher models transfer inter-class dark knowledge to the multimodal student fusion branch via soft probability targets.
AI.result: Evaluated on 281 clips from Google AudioSet, AVNet achieves 66.6% overall accuracy in audio-visual mode, outperforming the audio-only branch by +10.4% and the video-only branch by +15.0%. The hardest class (Ambulance) shows the largest per-class gain with +29.5% improvement over either unimodal branch, demonstrating successful exploitation of complementary information from both modalities.
AI.conclusion: The temporally aligned cross-attention mechanism successfully exploits complementary audio-visual information, with the fusion approach providing substantial gains over unimodal baselines. The learned null embeddings enable graceful degradation when either modality is unavailable, addressing real-world robustness requirements for safety-critical autonomous driving perception.

title: Coaching Qwen3 Coder 30B to Think Like a CodeClash Arena Agent
summary: Large language model coding agents have recently become useful for software tasks, but weaker or open-weight agents still struggle to reliably interpret user intent and execute complex multi-step workflows. This gap is especially visible in long-horizon settings, where an agent must repeatedly inspect prior outcomes, diagnose failure, and choose the next code edit under interaction constraints. It motivates a natural question: what can we do to improve the thinking process of a weak code agent? We study this question in CodeClash, a code-arena benchmark where the original work evaluates 8 commercial coding agents across 6 arenas through multi-round tournaments. Since Qwen3 Coder Plus ranks last among them, we take the open-weight Qwen3-Coder-30B as a case study and investigate how to improve it with distilled knowledge from stronger agents. Our analysis shows that Qwen3-Coder-30B is not well optimized for arena-style interaction: it frequently produces syntax and protocol-breaking errors and exhibits weak strategic adaptation across rounds. These failures are difficult to correct with vanilla instruction tuning alone, since offline SFT cannot directly verify whether a generated action is valid or beneficial. To address this, we propose ReAct SFT, which rewrites teacher trajectories into explicit [obs][thought][act] chains, and trajectoryquality weighted SFT, which reweights samples to encourage post-edit checking. ReAct SFT substantially improves strategic behavior, and our fine-tuned model outperforms the original Qwen3 Coder Plus in tournament evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses how to improve weak open-weight code agents by distilling knowledge from stronger agents. The authors propose ReAct SFT, which converts teacher trajectories into explicit reasoning chains, and trajectory-quality weighted SFT to encourage post-edit checking. The fine-tuned model outperforms the original Qwen3 Coder Plus in tournament evaluation.
AI.motivation: Weak or open-weight code agents struggle to reliably interpret user intent and execute complex multi-step workflows, especially in long-horizon settings where agents must repeatedly inspect prior outcomes, diagnose failures, and choose next actions. This gap is particularly visible in CodeClash benchmark where Qwen3 Coder Plus ranks last among 8 commercial coding agents.
AI.method: The authors take Qwen3-Coder-30B as a case study and analyze its failure modes: syntax/protocol-breaking errors and weak strategic adaptation across rounds. They propose two solutions: (1) ReAct SFT, which rewrites teacher trajectories into explicit [obs][thought][act] chains to improve strategic reasoning; (2) Trajectory-quality weighted SFT, which reweights samples to encourage post-edit checking behavior.
AI.result: ReAct SFT substantially improves strategic behavior. The fine-tuned model outperforms the original Qwen3 Coder Plus in tournament evaluation on the CodeClash benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge distillation from stronger agents combined with structured reasoning chain formats (ReAct SFT) can significantly improve weak code agents' performance in multi-round coding tasks. The approach addresses both technical errors and strategic adaptation problems that vanilla instruction tuning alone cannot fix.

title: Causal neural set filtering for online multi-target tracking
summary: Transformer-based multi-target tracking (MTT) jointly learns data association and state estimation, but MT3/Track-MT3-style trackers repeatedly re-encode measurement windows, incurring redundant computation. We propose Causal Neural Set Filtering (CNSF)\footnote{\href{https://github.com/daihuangyu/CNSF}{Code: https://github.com/daihuangyu/CNSF}}, a neural set filter that encodes only current measurements while carrying past evidence in a structured recursive track state. CNSF combines exclusive Sinkhorn association, association-conditioned Kalman-shaped updates with moment matching, and recurrent Bernoulli lifecycle modeling with measurement-driven birth. These mechanisms impose soft one-to-one constraints, propagate association-induced state uncertainty, and support existence estimation under missed detections and birth--death transitions. On a held-out three-regime simulated test set, CNSF reduces mean GOSPA and T-GOSPA relative to Track-MT3 by 19.3\% and 30.4\%, with 55.9\% fewer parameters and a $3.76\times$ speedup in single-thread CPU inference.

AI.tldr: CNSF is a neural set filter for multi-target tracking that addresses redundant computation in transformer-based trackers by encoding only current measurements while carrying past evidence in a recursive track state. It combines exclusive Sinkhorn association, association-conditioned Kalman updates with moment matching, and recurrent Bernoulli lifecycle modeling.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based MTT trackers (like MT3/Track-MT3) suffer from redundant computation by repeatedly re-encoding measurement windows. The authors seek a more efficient approach that maintains accuracy while reducing computational burden.
AI.method: The proposed CNSF uses three key mechanisms: (1) Exclusive Sinkhorn association for soft one-to-one constraints, (2) Association-conditioned Kalman-shaped updates with moment matching to propagate association-induced state uncertainty, (3) Recurrent Bernoulli lifecycle modeling with measurement-driven birth for existence estimation under missed detections and birth-death transitions.
AI.result: On a held-out three-regime simulated test set, CNSF reduces mean GOSPA by 19.3% and T-GOSPA by 30.4% compared to Track-MT3, while using 55.9% fewer parameters and achieving 3.76× speedup in single-thread CPU inference.
AI.conclusion: CNSF successfully addresses the computational redundancy issue in transformer-based MTT while improving tracking accuracy. The combination of structured recursive state, Sinkhorn association, and Bernoulli lifecycle modeling provides both efficiency and robust performance across different tracking regimes.

title: Optimal Pruning for Neural Architectures using Fisher Information Distances
summary: A new scheme for parameter pruning is introduced, derived from the differential-geometric distance in model space. Pruning a parameter sets its value to zero, representing a displacement of the model to the hypersurface on which that parameter vanishes. The minimal distance from the unpruned model to this hypersurface is naturally computed via the geodesic distance in the model space as determined by the Fisher information metric. This distance determines the true change in the model, and its performance, under pruning. By analysing progressively more faithful approximations of this geodesic distance a natural hierarchy of optimality for pruning methods is determined. This starts with the traditional magnitude pruning, then develops into new more sophisticated and effective pruning schemes. The method is demonstrated for both fully-connected networks and vision transformers, on MNIST and CIFAR-10, over the complete $0$-$100\%$ pruning range and across five random seeds. It outperforms pruning by parameter magnitude and by the local Fisher information alone in every architecture and dataset combination considered, on both accuracy and the Matthews correlation coefficient. Additionally, analysis of different levels of geodesic approximation produces intermediate pruning schemes that are computationally efficient and maintain near-optimal performance. This geometric picture supplies not only a state-of-the-art pruning methodology for AI models, but also a verified and mathematically-motivated justification for pruning schemes.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a differential-geometric framework for neural network parameter pruning, using the Fisher information metric to compute geodesic distances between unpruned models and pruning hypersurfaces. The method provides a mathematically rigorous justification for pruning and establishes a hierarchy of optimality from magnitude pruning to full geodesic approximation. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 with fully-connected networks and vision transformers demonstrate state-of-the-art performance.
AI.motivation: Traditional pruning methods (e.g., magnitude pruning) lack theoretical justification. This work aims to provide a mathematically principled approach by viewing pruning as geodesic displacement in model space, where the Fisher information metric provides a natural distance measure that reflects true model changes.
AI.method: The method treats parameter pruning as displacement to a hypersurface where pruned parameters vanish. The minimal distance to this hypersurface is computed using geodesic distance determined by the Fisher information metric. Progressive approximations of this geodesic distance yield a hierarchy of pruning methods: (1) magnitude pruning, (2) local Fisher information, (3) full geodesic approximation.
AI.result: The proposed geodesic-based pruning outperforms magnitude pruning and local Fisher information pruning on all architecture-dataset combinations (FC networks and Vision Transformers on MNIST and CIFAR-10), across the full 0-100% pruning range, in both accuracy and Matthews correlation coefficient. Intermediate approximations provide computationally efficient near-optimal performance.
AI.conclusion: The geometric framework provides both a state-of-the-art pruning methodology and a mathematically rigorous justification for pruning. The hierarchy of optimality connects existing methods (magnitude, Fisher) within a unified theoretical foundation, while the full geodesic approach achieves superior practical performance.

title: ProtoLIP: From Sentence-Level to Object-Level Evidence Disentanglement
summary: Query-conditioned vision--language models enable fine-grained interpretation by revealing how visual evidence changes with textual queries. However, evidence conditioned on complete descriptions does not necessarily resolve into object-specific evidence, nor does an exposed evidence map necessarily identify the evidence that constitutes the model's prediction. Across multiple VLM architectures and independent benchmarks, we find that object-level queries often retain evidence from co-occurring objects and shared context. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{ProtoLIP}, a lightweight prototype-mediated evidence layer that organizes reusable visual prototypes into text-derived semantic families and uses query-dependent family routing to constrain which prototypes may provide evidence. Without spatial annotations or backbone retraining, ProtoLIP improves evidence localization and separation across query granularities, with localization gains transferring to independently pretrained VLMs with well-aligned patch--text representations. Despite using only text-derived weak supervision, ProtoLIP remains competitive with a spatially supervised grounding model while maintaining strong matching and competitive image--text retrieval. Crucially, ProtoLIP constructs its matching score directly from localized prototype evidence, enabling the score to be exactly decomposed into semantic-family and prototype contributions.

AI.tldr: ProtoLIP introduces a lightweight prototype-mediated evidence layer for vision-language models that organizes visual prototypes into text-derived semantic families and uses query-dependent routing to constrain evidence to object-specific prototypes, improving localization without spatial annotations or backbone retraining.
AI.motivation: Current vision-language models often retain evidence from co-occurring objects and shared context when conditioned on complete descriptions, failing to resolve into object-specific evidence. Even exposed evidence maps may not identify the actual evidence constituting the model's prediction.
AI.method: ProtoLIP organizes reusable visual prototypes into text-derived semantic families and uses query-dependent family routing to constrain which prototypes may provide evidence. It requires no spatial annotations or backbone retraining, and constructs matching scores directly from localized prototype evidence, decomposable into semantic-family and prototype contributions.
AI.result: ProtoLIP improves evidence localization and separation across query granularities. Localization gains transfer to independently pretrained VLMs with well-aligned patch-text representations. It remains competitive with spatially supervised grounding models while maintaining strong matching and competitive image-text retrieval.
AI.conclusion: ProtoLIP achieves improved object-specific evidence localization through prototype-based semantic family routing without requiring spatial supervision or backbone retraining, enabling exact decomposition of matching scores into semantic-family and prototype contributions.

title: Cascaded Non-Line-of-Sight Imaging
summary: Time-of-flight non-line-of-sight (NLOS) imaging recovers information from hidden objects by analyzing the time of flight of indirect photons scattered on a visible (relay) wall. Most methods make the simplifying assumption that photons travel exclusively three-bounce paths, thus ignoring other useful information encoded in higher-order photons (with, e.g., four- or five-bounce paths). We present a novel cascaded NLOS imaging approach that leverages higher-order information and allows imaging a broader range of single- and multi-corner scenarios. We combine ultra-fast laser scanning with recent time-gated 2D sensor arrays to capture the scene's impulse response on a visible relay wall. From the captured impulse response, our method computes an analogous virtual impulse response at any other hidden wall. This effectively allows us to concatenate a second, virtual NLOS imaging system that leverages higher-order illumination. We validate our cascaded imaging method both in simulation and with a real prototype, demonstrating NLOS imaging with fourth- and fifth-bounce illumination of objects in challenging orientations and hidden around two corners. We also analyze how wave-based NLOS imaging interacts with rough hidden walls, which explains and helps overcome existing visibility limitations. We further illustrate how to image hidden objects from different perspectives, thus observing previously unseen features, by relying on multiple hidden walls.

AI.tldr: A novel cascaded NLOS imaging approach that leverages higher-order photon paths (4-bounce, 5-bounce) by combining ultra-fast laser scanning with time-gated 2D sensor arrays, computing virtual impulse responses at hidden walls to enable imaging around corners and from multiple perspectives.
AI.motivation: Traditional NLOS imaging methods assume photons travel exclusively three-bounce paths, ignoring useful information encoded in higher-order photons (four- or five-bounce paths). This limits the range of scenarios that can be imaged, particularly multi-corner and challenging orientations.
AI.method: The method combines ultra-fast laser scanning with time-gated 2D sensor arrays to capture the scene's impulse response on a visible relay wall. From this captured impulse response, the method computes an analogous virtual impulse response at any other hidden wall, effectively concatenating a second virtual NLOS imaging system that leverages higher-order illumination. The approach also analyzes wave-based NLOS imaging interactions with rough hidden walls.
AI.result: Validated both in simulation and with a real prototype. Demonstrated NLOS imaging with fourth- and fifth-bounce illumination of objects in challenging orientations and hidden around two corners. Successfully imaged hidden objects from different perspectives using multiple hidden walls, revealing previously unseen features.
AI.conclusion: The cascaded NLOS imaging approach enables imaging a broader range of single- and multi-corner scenarios by leveraging higher-order photon information. This method overcomes existing visibility limitations and provides multiple viewing angles for hidden objects, significantly expanding the capabilities of NLOS imaging technology.

title: SongCraft: Unified Song Generation and Editing with Reconstructive Learning
summary: Song generation and editing have mostly been treated as separate tasks. Existing editing methods often require noise injection and regeneration or curated paired training data. We propose a unified approach for song generation and editing based on reconstructive pretraining, in which a model is trained to reconstruct audio from varying numbers of interpretable conditions. With conditions such as text and lyrics, the model learns to generate diverse songs. With dense conditions specifying fine-grained music attributes, the model learns to reconstruct the target and enables editing by modifying any single attribute while keeping others fixed. This leads to SongCraft, a latent flow matching based model trained for both generation and fine-grained editing. To improve song generation quality, we further introduce word-level phoneme alignment that improves pronunciation learning and accelerates convergence, beat conditioning that improves general musicality, and representation alignment on VAE latent space that produces semantically meaningful latents for improved generation quality. Experiments show that SongCraft achieves the lowest word error rate among evaluated song generation baselines while maintaining competitive audio quality. We further show that a single model can support editing of lyrics, vocal melody, beats, and singer identity, and we also study the trade-off between reconstruction quality and editability.

AI.tldr: SongCraft is a unified latent flow matching model for both song generation and fine-grained editing, trained using reconstructive pretraining with interpretable conditions. It achieves the lowest word error rate among baselines while supporting editing of lyrics, vocal melody, beats, and singer identity.
AI.motivation: Existing song generation and editing methods treat these as separate tasks, with editing methods often requiring noise injection/regeneration or curated paired training data. This creates a need for a unified approach that can handle both generation and precise editing capabilities.
AI.method:
1) Reconstructive pretraining - model trained to reconstruct audio from varying numbers of interpretable conditions
2) Word-level phoneme alignment for improved pronunciation learning and faster convergence
3) Beat conditioning for improved musicality
4) Representation alignment on VAE latent space for semantically meaningful latents
5) Latent flow matching architecture
AI.result: Achieves lowest word error rate among evaluated song generation baselines while maintaining competitive audio quality. Single model supports editing of lyrics, vocal melody, beats, and singer identity. Trade-off between reconstruction quality and editability is studied.
AI.conclusion: The unified approach using reconstructive pretraining enables both high-quality song generation and fine-grained editing capabilities in a single model, with the conditioning techniques (phoneme alignment, beat conditioning, VAE latent alignment) further improving generation quality and convergence.

title: Mechanism-Level Evaluation for Vision-Language Models: Controlled Activation-Replacement Diagnosis of Gender Bias
summary: Behavioral benchmarking reveals \emph{what} biases exist in vision-language models but not \emph{which internal components} are most sensitive to targeted intervention, precluding principled intervention. We argue for mechanism-level evaluation as a necessary complement, demonstrating causal mediation analysis as a diagnostic instrument for gender bias. We decompose gender-cue effects into controlled indirect effects attributable to specific-layer activations and direct effects through all other pathways, producing layer-by-layer mechanistic signatures. Across six models spanning three architectural families (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, InstructBLIP at 7B/13B) and two 8B-scale architectures, three findings emerge: language-layer activations exhibit the greatest output sensitivity under controlled intervention, with the direct component often carrying the opposite sign; architectural choices redistribute layer-wise sensitivity to activation replacement; and counterfactual scores diverge from surface-level scores, exposing implicit associations. Systematic ablation validates internal consistency. An intervention experiment finds that the average indirect effect (AIE) and downstream intervention effectiveness are only weakly correlated (Pearson $r = 0.33$), and the layer with the second-largest AIE produces near-zero bias change---indicating that mechanistic diagnosis captures activation-replacement sensitivity but does not, by itself, identify optimal intervention targets. These results show mechanism-level evaluation captures architecture-specific sensitivity patterns that behavioral benchmarks cannot; pairing both should become standard NLP practice. Code: https://github.com/zhaozhipeng1997/CARD-GenderBias.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using causal mediation analysis as a diagnostic tool to identify which internal components of vision-language models are most sensitive to gender bias intervention. The method decomposes gender-cue effects into indirect effects (through specific layer activations) and direct effects (through other pathways), producing layer-by-layer mechanistic signatures across six models.
AI.motivation: Behavioral benchmarks reveal what biases exist in vision-language models but fail to identify which internal components are most sensitive to targeted intervention, hindering principled bias mitigation efforts.
AI.method: The authors apply causal mediation analysis to decompose gender-cue effects into controlled indirect effects (attributable to specific-layer activations) and direct effects through all other pathways. They test six models across three architectural families (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, InstructBLIP at 7B/13B) and two 8B-scale architectures, generating layer-by-layer mechanistic signatures.
AI.result: Three key findings emerge: (1) Language-layer activations exhibit the greatest output sensitivity under controlled intervention, with the direct component often carrying the opposite sign; (2) Architectural choices redistribute layer-wise sensitivity to activation replacement; (3) Counterfactual scores diverge from surface-level scores, exposing implicit associations. The intervention experiment reveals that average indirect effect (AIE) and downstream intervention effectiveness are only weakly correlated (Pearson r = 0.33), and the layer with the second-largest AIE produces near-zero bias change.
AI.conclusion: Mechanism-level evaluation captures architecture-specific sensitivity patterns that behavioral benchmarks cannot detect. Pairing mechanistic diagnosis with behavioral evaluation should become standard NLP practice. However, mechanistic diagnosis alone does not identify optimal intervention targets—AIE does not strongly predict intervention effectiveness.

title: Docker Containers vs. Virtual Machines: A Comparative Study of Architecture, Performance, Configuration, and Security
summary: Modern application platforms must isolate workloads while preserving deployment speed, portability, resource efficiency, and security. Virtual machines (VMs) and Docker containers address this requirement at different abstraction layers: VMs virtualize hardware and run independent guest operating systems, whereas containers isolate processes while sharing the host kernel. This paper presents a comparative, literature-based analysis of the two approaches across architecture, configuration and lifecycle management, performance, scalability, and security. Published studies generally associate containers with shorter startup times, smaller images, higher workload density, and near-native execution for many workloads. These benefits depend on workload characteristics, storage and network drivers, resource controls, and experimental design. VMs introduce greater overhead but offer independent kernels, heterogeneous guest operating systems, and a stronger isolation boundary. The comparison therefore treats efficiency and isolation as a design trade-off rather than declaring one technology universally superior. A hybrid architecture, in which containers run inside hardened VMs, often provides a practical balance for cloud and multi-tenant systems.

AI.tldr: A literature-based comparative analysis of Virtual Machines (VMs) and Docker containers across architecture, configuration, performance, scalability, and security dimensions, examining the trade-off between efficiency and isolation.
AI.motivation: Modern application platforms require workload isolation while maintaining deployment speed, portability, resource efficiency, and security. The need to compare VM and container approaches at different abstraction layers to determine optimal deployment strategies.
AI.method: Literature-based comparative analysis examining architecture differences, configuration/lifecycle management, performance benchmarks, scalability characteristics, and security profiles of VMs versus containers.
AI.result: Containers offer shorter startup times, smaller images, higher workload density, and near-native execution for many workloads. VMs provide stronger isolation with independent kernels and heterogeneous OS support but with greater overhead. Results depend on workload characteristics, storage/network drivers, resource controls, and experimental design.
AI.conclusion: Efficiency and isolation represent a design trade-off rather than universal superiority of either technology. A hybrid architecture combining containers running inside hardened VMs provides practical balance for cloud and multi-tenant systems.

title: Managing Action Preconditions in Neuro-Symbolic RL: Three Placement Strategies for Embodied Agents
summary: Humans carry behaviour knowledge of how to act in familiar situations into every new task rather than relearning it from scratch. There is no reason a Reinforcement Learning (RL) agent shouldn't do the same: known behaviour patterns need not be learned, only applied. Neuro-symbolic RL bridges prior knowledge and RL by injecting symbolic knowledge alongside a learned policy. The point at which this knowledge is integrated is critical: a poor choice can produce, for instance, hallucinated preconditions, which surface as safety and reliability problems in agents acting in changing environments. We formalise this behavioural knowledge as a precondition Bayesian network (BN) over the agent's \emph{structural actions} - the actions whose legality depends on preconditions, such as picking up a key, grasping a block, toggling a door, or dropping an object. The BN restricts when these actions may fire, and we inject it into the RL loop at three placements: (1) a \emph{symbolic verifier}, consulted only at inference, that fires a structural action once its preconditions hold; (2) a \emph{symbolic enforcer}, active during both training and inference, that governs structural-action use throughout learning; and (3) a \emph{symbolic learner}, which folds the knowledge into the network and learns the restriction and use of structural actions itself. To test the three variants we run experiments on two benchmarks with opposite regimes: one built on long, ordered planning chains, the other on continuous manipulation. We compare against strong baselines on solution quality, sample efficiency, and traceability. The payoff is substantial. On MiniGrid, all three placements improve the \emph{solution quality} over the PPO+RND baseline, the symbolic enforcer leading at $98.2\%$ against the baseline's $88.8\%$. On Fetch, $\dots$

AI.tldr: This paper proposes integrating prior behavioral knowledge into reinforcement learning agents via precondition Bayesian networks over structural actions, comparing three integration placements: symbolic verifier, symbolic enforcer, and symbolic learner.
AI.motivation: Humans carry behavioral knowledge into new tasks rather than relearning from scratch; RL agents should do the same. However, poor integration of symbolic knowledge can cause hallucinated preconditions, leading to safety and reliability issues in changing environments.
AI.method: The authors formalize behavioral knowledge as a precondition Bayesian network (BN) over structural actions (actions whose legality depends on preconditions, e.g., picking up a key, toggling a door). They test three integration placements: (1) symbolic verifier - consulted only at inference; (2) symbolic enforcer - active during both training and inference; (3) symbolic learner - folds knowledge into the network itself.
AI.result: On MiniGrid (long ordered planning chains), all three placements improve solution quality over PPO+RND baseline, with symbolic enforcer leading at 98.2% vs baseline's 88.8%. On Fetch (continuous manipulation), substantial improvements were also observed.
AI.conclusion: The placement of symbolic knowledge integration in the RL loop is critical. The symbolic enforcer placement achieves the best performance, demonstrating substantial improvements in solution quality, sample efficiency, and traceability across different task regimes.

title: Safe Error Correction for Language Models: Frozen-Base Adjustment with Capability Preservation
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables. Code, weights, and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/eulogik/prajna and https://huggingface.co/eulogik/Prajna-CRNv2
summary: We study a practical question: can a small correction module fix errors in a frozen language model's outputs without degrading its base capabilities? We propose CRN v2, a lightweight logit-level correction module (~34M trainable parameters, 0.73% of the 4.65B text module) that sits atop a fully frozen Gemma 4 E2B model. The base model is never updated; only the correction module learns, via supervised fine-tuning followed by reference-free DPO on 83,400 error-correction pairs. On a 60-question domain exam (CEHRI: Certified Human-Robot Intelligence, covering facts, arithmetic, and implicit-goal reasoning), CRN v2 corrects 53.3% of base-model errors (reworded variant: 43.3%) while showing no degradation on tested capability benchmarks (MMLU/BoolQ N=200; car-wash N=8). A LoRA baseline at the matched CRN v1 budget (6.6M params, rank 19) achieves 83.3% correction but suffers 30-75% capability loss on the same benchmarks -- the correction-capability tradeoff. An ablation shows that the KL preservation term (lambda=0.1) is critical: lowering it to 0.01 degrades correction to 35.0%. A hidden-state injection variant at earlier layers (1.6M params, SFT-only) reaches 50.0%/55.8% but does not exceed logit correction; shallower injection (layer 4) drops to 30.0%/28.3%; multi-depth logit correction (~35M) reaches only 40%; and longer training (5,000 SFT + 2,000 DPO) stays at 53.3% -- none of the alternative configurations we tested exceeded the rank-128 logit result, consistent with a best-achieved result of ~53% rather than a floor. This is a study of a design principle (frozen base + logit correction + KL anchoring), not a claim of architectural novelty. All code, main-result weights, and evaluation scripts are released (deep variant as code only -- no trained deep checkpoints).

AI.tldr: CRN v2 is a lightweight logit-level correction module (~34M params, 0.73% of base model) that fixes errors in a frozen Gemma 4 E2B model without degrading its base capabilities. It uses SFT + reference-free DPO on 83,400 error-correction pairs, achieving 53.3% error correction while maintaining performance on capability benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses a practical question: can a small correction module fix errors in a frozen language model's outputs without degrading its base capabilities? This tackles the "correction-capability tradeoff" where methods like LoRA can achieve high correction (83.3%) but suffer significant capability loss (30-75%).
AI.method: CRN v2 uses a logit-level correction module sitting atop a fully frozen Gemma 4 E2B model. Training involves supervised fine-tuning followed by reference-free DPO on 83,400 error-correction pairs. The KL preservation term (lambda=0.1) is critical for anchoring to the base model distribution. Compared against LoRA baseline (6.6M params, rank 19) and various ablation configurations (hidden-state injection, multi-depth logit correction, longer training).
AI.result: CRN v2 corrects 53.3% of base-model errors (reworded variant: 43.3%) while showing no degradation on MMLU/BoolQ (N=200) and car-wash (N=8) benchmarks. LoRA baseline achieves 83.3% correction but suffers 30-75% capability loss. Ablations show: KL term at 0.01 degrades correction to 35.0%; hidden-state injection reaches 50.0%/55.8%; shallower injection drops to 30.0%/28.3%; multi-depth logit correction reaches only 40%; longer training stays at 53.3%.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that logit-level correction with KL anchoring (frozen base + logit correction + KL preservation) can fix errors without degrading base capabilities, avoiding the correction-capability tradeoff seen in LoRA. The best result (~53% correction) is not a floor but represents optimal performance for this design principle. All code and main-result weights are released.

title: Sequence Recognition in Bharatnatyam dance
comment: Accepted at 7th International Conference on Computer Vision and Image Processing (CVIP), 2022
summary: Bharatanatyam is the oldest Indian Classical Dance (ICD) which is learned and practiced across India and the world. Adavu is the core of this dance form. There exist 15 Adavus and 58 variations. Each Adavu variation comprises a well-defined set of motions and postures (called dance steps) that occur in a particular order. So, while learning Adavus, students not only learn the dance steps but also take care of its sequence of occurrences. This paper proposed a method to recognize these sequences. In this work, firstly, we recognize the involved Key Postures (KPs) and motions in the Adavu using Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Support Vector Machine (SVM), respectively. In this, CNN achieves 99% and SVM's recognition accuracy becomes 84%. Next, we compare these KP and motion sequences with the ground truth to find the best match using the Edit Distance algorithm with an accuracy of 98%. The paper contributes hugely to the state-of-the-art in the form of digital heritage, dance tutoring system, and many more. The paper addresses three novelties; (a) Recognizing the sequences based on the KPs and motions rather than only KPs as reported in the earlier works. (b) The performance of the proposed work is measured by analyzing the prediction time per sequence. We also compare our proposed approach with the previous works that deal with the same problem statement. (c) It tests the scalability of the proposed approach by including all the Adavu variations, unlike the earlier literature, which uses only one/two variations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method to recognize Bharatanatyam dance sequences (Adavus) using computer vision and machine learning. It combines CNN for Key Posture recognition (99% accuracy) and SVM for motion recognition (84% accuracy), then uses Edit Distance algorithm to match sequences against ground truth, achieving 98% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Bharatanatyam is a classical Indian dance with 15 Adavus and 58 variations. Students learning this dance must master both individual dance steps and their correct sequences. There existed a need for an automated system to recognize these sequences for digital heritage preservation and dance tutoring applications.
AI.method: The proposed method uses: (1) Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for recognizing Key Postures (KPs); (2) Support Vector Machine (SVM) for motion recognition; (3) Edit Distance algorithm to compare predicted KP and motion sequences with ground truth for best match identification.
AI.result: CNN achieved 99% accuracy for Key Posture recognition, SVM achieved 84% for motion recognition, and the overall sequence matching using Edit Distance achieved 98% accuracy. The method was tested on all 58 Adavu variations to verify scalability.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes to digital heritage and dance tutoring systems by providing a sequence-based recognition approach (rather than only Key Postures). The three novelties include: (a) recognizing sequences based on both KPs and motions; (b) analyzing prediction time per sequence and comparing with prior works; (c) testing scalability across all Adavu variations.

title: 3D Field Data Reduction with Adaptive Sample-Based Gaussian-Encoded Reconstruction
summary: In scientific simulation, regular grids, unstructured meshes, and particle-based formats are chosen to represent field data for computational efficiency, geometry/adaptive flexibility, and following motion/deformation, respectively. Each of these field data formats is often handled through separate data-specific processing pipelines. We present a unified sample-based Gaussian encoding method that represents these data forms under a single fixed-budget formulation. The method initializes and refines Gaussian primitives directly from the input samples while preserving a prescribed primitive count and encoded size to achieve a desired level of data reduction. Across structured, unstructured, and particle data, the sample-based formulation improves reconstruction accuracy with measurably fewer primitives in comparison to prior formulations, achieving up to 4.8 dB higher PSNR with an approximate 44x reduction in primitive count. For time-varying data, warm-starting from the previous timestep reduces the optimization required to reach independently trained reconstruction quality. Together, these results demonstrate a unified fixed-budget Gaussian encoding framework for structured, particle, unstructured, and time-varying scientific data with predictable storage, higher reconstruction accuracy, and improved temporal encoding efficiency.

AI.tldr: A unified sample-based Gaussian encoding method that represents structured, unstructured, and particle-based field data under a single fixed-budget formulation, preserving prescribed primitive count and encoded size for data reduction.
AI.motivation: Scientific simulation uses different data formats (regular grids, unstructured meshes, particle-based) that require separate processing pipelines. This creates a need for a unified approach that can handle all three data types under a single framework.
AI.method: The method initializes and refines Gaussian primitives directly from input samples while preserving a prescribed primitive count and encoded size. For time-varying data, warm-starting from the previous timestep is used to reduce optimization required.
AI.result: The sample-based formulation improves reconstruction accuracy with fewer primitives compared to prior methods—achieving up to 4.8 dB higher PSNR with approximately 44x reduction in primitive count. Warm-starting also reduces optimization needed to reach independently trained reconstruction quality.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates a unified fixed-budget Gaussian encoding framework for structured, particle, unstructured, and time-varying scientific data, offering predictable storage, higher reconstruction accuracy, and improved temporal encoding efficiency.

title: CLASH: Counterfactual Auditing of Lexical and Prosodic Reliance in Spoken Sarcasm Detection
summary: Spoken sarcasm detectors may exploit lexical content, prosody, or their interaction, yet conventional evaluation cannot reveal which cues drive their predictions. We introduce CLASH (Controlled Lexical-Acoustic Separation Harness), a bilingual counterfactual diagnostic framework that evaluates each utterance under original, lexical-preserving, prosody-preserving, and approximately neutralised conditions. We evaluate handcrafted acoustic-feature systems, self-supervised learning (SSL) probes, and large audio language models (LALMs) on CMMA and MUStARD. For target-only Qwen3-Omni, lexical-preserving speech retains a 0.135--0.148 AUROC advantage over prosody-preserving speech after duration balancing, with cluster-bootstrap intervals above zero; alternative lexical resynthesis preserves this advantage. Acoustic interventions shift scores without consistently improving discrimination or changing binary predictions under the evaluated conditions. Context and interaction estimates vary across corpora. These findings distinguish acoustic sensitivity from sarcasm discrimination while exposing duration, identity, and transformation effects.

AI.tldr: CLASH is a bilingual counterfactual diagnostic framework introduced to evaluate spoken sarcasm detection systems by testing utterances under original, lexical-preserving, prosody-preserving, and neutralized conditions. The framework distinguishes acoustic sensitivity from sarcasm discrimination while exposing duration, identity, and transformation effects.
AI.motivation: Conventional evaluation methods for spoken sarcasm detectors cannot reveal which cues (lexical content, prosody, or their interaction) drive predictions. The authors introduce CLASH to address this gap by providing a controlled framework to diagnose what sarcasm detection systems actually learn.
AI.method: The CLASH framework evaluates utterances under four conditions: original, lexical-preserving (preserves words but not prosody), prosody-preserving (preserves prosody but not words), and approximately neutralized. Handcrafted acoustic-feature systems, self-supervised learning (SSL) probes, and large audio language models (LALMs) were evaluated on CMMA and MUStARD datasets. Duration balancing and cluster-bootstrap intervals were used for analysis.
AI.result: For target-only Qwen3-Omni, lexical-preserving speech retains a 0.135-0.148 AUROC advantage over prosody-preserving speech after duration balancing, with cluster-bootstrap intervals above zero. Alternative lexical resynthesis preserves this advantage. Acoustic interventions shift scores without consistently improving discrimination or changing binary predictions. Context and interaction estimates vary across corpora.
AI.conclusion: The findings distinguish acoustic sensitivity from sarcasm discrimination, exposing duration, identity, and transformation effects. Lexical content is the primary driver of sarcasm detection performance, while prosody alone provides limited discriminative power. The framework reveals the need to carefully separate and evaluate different cues in sarcasm detection.

title: CTAN: Cycle-Temporal Attention Network for Embodied Audio-Visual Navigation
comment: Main paper (6 pages). Accepted for publication by IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics 2026 (IEEE SMC 2026)
summary: Audio-visual embodied navigation equips robots with the capability to infer the locations of sound sources by integrating visual inputs and acoustic information (e.g., depth observations and binaural audio cues). The core challenge lies in establishing effective semantic interactions across heterogeneous modalities (which exhibit distinct feature distributions). Existing feature fusion strategies, however, often rely on simple multimodal aggregation and therefore fail to capture the underlying geometric and semantic relationships, leading to information degradation in complex environments. To overcome these limitations, this work presents the Cycle-Temporal Attention Network (CTAN), a framework designed for active semantic-enhanced fusion (rather than straightforward multimodal combination). Specifically, the proposed Audio-Visual Reconstruction Cross-Attention (AVRCA) module employs a bidirectional cycle-consistency constraint (between visual and acoustic representations) to reinforce the spatial semantic attributes of both modalities, thereby facilitating more robust cross-modal interaction. Additionally, we design a Temporal Cross-Modal Memory (TCMM) mechanism to dynamically integrate real-time enhanced multimodal features with historical context, reducing performance drops caused by auditory dead zones. Experimental results obtained on the Replica and Matterport3D benchmarks indicate that the proposed approach achieves superior performance over previous audio-visual navigation methods in terms of success rate (SR), success weighted by path length (SPL), and scene navigation accuracy (SNA).

AI.tldr: This paper proposes CTAN (Cycle-Temporal Attention Network), a framework for audio-visual embodied navigation that addresses semantic heterogeneity across visual and acoustic modalities. The approach introduces bidirectional cycle-consistency constraints and temporal memory mechanisms to enhance cross-modal interactions and handle auditory dead zones.
AI.motivation: The core motivation is to overcome limitations in existing audio-visual navigation methods that rely on simple multimodal aggregation, which fails to capture geometric and semantic relationships across heterogeneous modalities (visual and acoustic), leading to information degradation in complex environments.
AI.method: The paper proposes two key components: (1) Audio-Visual Reconstruction Cross-Attention (AVRCA) module using bidirectional cycle-consistency constraint between visual and acoustic representations to reinforce spatial semantic attributes; (2) Temporal Cross-Modal Memory (TCMM) mechanism to dynamically integrate real-time enhanced multimodal features with historical context to handle auditory dead zones.
AI.result: Experimental results on Replica and Matterport3D benchmarks show superior performance over previous audio-visual navigation methods in terms of success rate (SR), success weighted by path length (SPL), and scene navigation accuracy (SNA).
AI.conclusion: The proposed CTAN framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in audio-visual embodied navigation by effectively addressing cross-modal semantic heterogeneity and temporal continuity challenges through cycle-consistency constraints and memory mechanisms.

title: Models as Governed Interfaces for AI-Native MBSE: Read-Side Adequacy and Write-Side Admissibility
comment: Accepted by the 29th International Conference on Model Driven Engineering Languages and Systems (MODELS), 4-9 October 2026, Malaga, Spain, as a New Ideas and Emerging Results (NIER) paper
summary: Machine-readable models such as SysML v2 are now programmatically accessible, and a growing body of work treats that access as the enabling condition for AI participation in systems engineering. Access is necessary, but not sufficient. The remaining work lies not in the modelling language but in the data architecture around it. An AI reader that queries a structurally complete model for a derivation still runs into absent derivation chains, untagged epistemic status, missing provenance, and evidence that the model cannot resolve. Faced with these gaps, it does not abstain; it fills them from training data, a source that is neither verifiable nor governed. To make the case on a model that is exemplary by current practice rather than deficient, we probe the public Apollo 11 SysML v2 reconstruction. We name the missing property epistemic adequacy and offer it as a candidate data-architecture pattern in two halves. Read-side adequacy lets derivation, status, and provenance answer a query rather than invite a guess; write-side admissibility gates an AI contribution before it enters the record. The property is broken down into five criteria. Four sit on the read side, evidenced by the case and convergent literature; the fifth sits on the participation side, advanced as a hypothesis this paper does not yet test. The architecture space runs from an inline metadata extension up to a substrate-native multi-model store, and over it, we propose the Governed-Query Architecture Framework, which governs agent participation through the viewpoint conventions that engineers already use. We commit the reframing to falsification: the epistemic layer counts as refuted if it cannot beat a retrieval-augmented baseline on the same model, tested first on the Apollo chain and then in an industrial pilot.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the gap between programmatic access to SysML v2 models and meaningful AI participation in systems engineering. The authors argue that AI systems often fill knowledge gaps with unverifiable training data rather than abstain, and propose "epistemic adequacy" as a data architecture pattern to govern AI contributions. The framework is tested against the Apollo 11 SysML v2 reconstruction using a falsification approach.
AI.motivation: While machine-readable models like SysML v2 enable programmatic access, AI readers still encounter absent derivation chains, untagged epistemic status, missing provenance, and unresolved evidence. Rather than abstaining from these gaps, AI fills them from training data—a source that is neither verifiable nor governed. This poses a fundamental challenge to trustworthy AI participation in systems engineering.
AI.method: The authors use the Apollo 11 SysML v2 reconstruction as a case study to demonstrate the problem. They propose "epistemic adequacy" as a candidate data-architecture pattern with two components: read-side adequacy (derivation, status, and provenance answering queries) and write-side admissibility (gating AI contributions before entering the record). The property is broken into five criteria—four evidenced by the case and convergent literature, and one on the participation side advanced as a hypothesis. The research uses a falsification approach: the epistemic layer is considered refuted if it cannot beat a retrieval-augmented baseline on the same model.
AI.result: The paper identifies five criteria for epistemic adequacy: four on the read side (derivation chains, epistemic status tagging, provenance tracking, and evidence resolution) and one on the participation/write side (admissibility gating). The architecture space ranges from inline metadata extension to substrate-native multi-model store. The authors propose the Governed-Query Architecture Framework (GQAF) to govern agent participation through existing viewpoint conventions.
AI.conclusion: The paper commits to falsification: the epistemic layer will be considered refuted if it cannot outperform a retrieval-augmented baseline on the Apollo 11 model, with testing planned first on the Apollo chain and then in an industrial pilot. The work reframes AI participation in systems engineering as a data architecture problem rather than a modeling language problem.

title: OmniHarness: Harnessing Generalizable Visual Generation via Symbolic Policy Learning
summary: Unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and multi-agent systems have advanced visual generation. However, three limitations remain. (1) Existing methods often distill task-specific experience with limited generalizability. (2) Reflection is often deferred until task completion. (3) Knowledge is often acquired only in response to downstream task demands. To address these limitations, we introduce OmniHarness, a framework for generalizable visual generation via symbolic policy learning. OmniHarness abstracts verified executions into symbolic policies for visual generation task families, capturing shared procedures and applicability conditions while removing instance-specific inputs. The harness instantiates, adapts, and composes these policies for new tasks. Intermediate verification guides refinement and failure recovery during execution. Through self-directed inquiry, OmniHarness autonomously generates and executes practice tasks near its capability limits before downstream objectives are specified. Execution feedback continually refines the policies while model parameters remain fixed. Experiments across six benchmarks, three MLLM backbones, and three visual agent frameworks demonstrate strong performance and continual capability expansion. On ComfyBench's Creative tasks, OmniHarness achieves a 95.0% resolve rate, exceeding the strongest baseline by 27.5 percentage points. Frozen policy snapshots improve existing visual agent systems through plug-and-play reuse.

AI.tldr: OmniHarness is a framework for generalizable visual generation via symbolic policy learning. It abstracts verified executions into reusable symbolic policies for task families, enabling instantiation, adaptation, and composition for new tasks with intermediate verification for failure recovery.
AI.motivation: Unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and multi-agent systems for visual generation have three key limitations: (1) task-specific experience with limited generalizability, (2) deferred reflection until task completion, and (3) knowledge acquisition only in response to downstream task demands.
AI.method: OmniHarness abstracts verified executions into symbolic policies that capture shared procedures and applicability conditions while removing instance-specific inputs. The harness instantiates, adapts, and composes these policies for new tasks. Intermediate verification guides refinement and failure recovery during execution. Self-directed inquiry generates practice tasks near capability limits before downstream objectives are specified. Execution feedback continually refines policies while model parameters remain fixed.
AI.result: Experiments across six benchmarks, three MLLM backbones, and three visual agent frameworks demonstrate strong performance and continual capability expansion. On ComfyBench's Creative tasks, OmniHarness achieves a 95.0% resolve rate, exceeding the strongest baseline by 27.5 percentage points. Frozen policy snapshots improve existing visual agent systems through plug-and-play reuse.
AI.conclusion: OmniHarness effectively addresses the limitations of existing visual generation systems through symbolic policy learning, achieving state-of-the-art performance and enabling continual capability expansion. The approach demonstrates that reusable symbolic policies can significantly improve generalizability and efficiency in visual generation tasks.

title: GPEvac: GNN-Based PPO for Adaptive Evacuation Routing During Shooting Events
summary: The sharp increase in mass shootings underscores an urgent need for systems that guide victims to safety in real time. An effective evacuation system must minimize threat exposure while also accounting for adversarial uncertainty and crowding dynamics. Current methods in the literature are rigidly constrained to layout-specific policies and computationally intractable in large-scale layouts, while practical guidelines simply advise victims to "run", "hide", or "fight". We propose GPEvac: a GNN-based PPO framework that computes adaptive evacuation routes during shooting events. To capture both local and long-distance dependencies, we introduce an edge-first sequential message-passing scheme with a learnable virtual global node.
