The resulting graph embeddings are integrated into a permutation-invariant scoring mechanism that allows a single learned policy to operate across building layouts of diverse topologies and sizes. Through extensive simulation, we show that GPEvac outperforms intelligent baselines across distinct architectural layouts, significantly reducing total threat exposure. Crucially, the system computes global evacuation routes in just 14.73 ms on local CPU hardware, enabling seamless integration with live surveillance systems. In addition to saving lives during shooting events, the methodologies developed are transferable to other graph-structured decision-making domains, including critical infrastructure, intelligent transportation systems, and adaptive sensor networks.

AI.tldr: GPEvac is a GNN-based PPO framework that computes adaptive evacuation routes during shooting events, using edge-first sequential message-passing with a learnable virtual global node to generate graph embeddings integrated into a permutation-invariant scoring mechanism. It operates across diverse building layouts and computes routes in 14.73 ms on CPU.
AI.motivation: The sharp increase in mass shootings creates an urgent need for real-time evacuation systems that minimize threat exposure while accounting for adversarial uncertainty and crowding dynamics. Current methods are layout-specific and computationally intractable, while practical guidelines are overly simplistic (run, hide, fight).
AI.method: GPEvac uses a Graph Neural Network (GNN) combined with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). It introduces an edge-first sequential message-passing scheme with a learnable virtual global node to capture both local and long-distance dependencies. The graph embeddings are integrated into a permutation-invariant scoring mechanism enabling a single learned policy to operate across building layouts of diverse topologies and sizes.
AI.result: GPEvac outperforms intelligent baselines across distinct architectural layouts, significantly reducing total threat exposure. It computes global evacuation routes in just 14.73 ms on local CPU hardware, enabling seamless integration with live surveillance systems.
AI.conclusion: GPEvac provides an effective, fast, and generalizable evacuation system for shooting events. The methodologies developed are transferable to other graph-structured decision-making domains including critical infrastructure, intelligent transportation systems, and adaptive sensor networks.

title: Racing in Volume with Flow Ensembles
summary: Streaming 4D reconstruction has been demonstrated only indoors, on dense camera rigs surrounding subjects that move at human pace. Outdoor 4D reconstruction exists but relies either on cameras mounted on the moving vehicle itself, or on limited-coverage arrays observing quasi-static subjects offline. The case that actually matters for spectators is a fast-moving subject, watched from a sparse ring of allocentric cameras, streaming. No method targets this, and no benchmark exists to evaluate one. To this end, we introduce FastFlowGS, a streaming 4D Gaussian Splatting method for reconstructing fast-moving subjects from a small set of fixed external cameras, and Monaco4D, a photorealistic Unreal Engine 5 benchmark for high-speed outdoor reconstruction. FastFlowGS fuses sparse matches, semi-dense tracks, and dense optical flow by lifting each signal to 3D with geometric uncertainty and combining them through a Kalman-style temporal update. Monaco4D provides Formula 1 sequences under varied illumination from trackside, onboard, and drone viewpoints with dense ground truth. On CMU-Panoptic, FastFlowGS exceeds the strongest baseline by 12.6% VMAF at 35% greater efficiency. On Monaco4D, where existing streaming methods degrade severely, it improves dynamic-region PSNR by up to 18.6% with 28.3% lower per-frame optimization time. Dataset and additional details can be found at https://humansensinglab.github.io/monaco4d/.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses streaming 4D reconstruction of fast-moving subjects from sparse external cameras, a previously unsolved problem. The authors propose FastFlowGS, which combines sparse matches, semi-dense tracks, and dense optical flow through a Kalman-style temporal update, and Monaco4D, a photorealistic Unreal Engine 5 benchmark for high-speed outdoor reconstruction.
AI.motivation: Current streaming 4D reconstruction methods are limited to indoor environments with dense camera rigs, while outdoor methods rely on onboard cameras or limited-coverage arrays for quasi-static subjects. The practical case of fast-moving subjects (e.g., Formula 1 cars) observed from sparse trackside cameras lacks both methods and benchmarks for evaluation.
AI.method: FastFlowGS introduces a Kalman-style temporal update framework that fuses three complementary visual signals: (1) sparse feature matches, (2) semi-dense tracks, and (3) dense optical flow. Each signal is lifted to 3D with geometric uncertainty, then combined through a temporal update mechanism to achieve robust streaming 4D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction.
AI.result: On CMU-Panoptic dataset, FastFlowGS exceeds the strongest baseline by 12.6% VMAF (Video Multimethod Assessment Fusion) at 35% greater efficiency. On Monaco4D, where existing streaming methods degrade severely, FastFlowGS improves dynamic-region PSNR by up to 18.6% with 28.3% lower per-frame optimization time.
AI.conclusion: FastFlowGS successfully enables streaming 4D reconstruction of fast-moving subjects from sparse external cameras, outperforming prior methods in both quality and efficiency. Monaco4D provides the first benchmark for evaluating high-speed outdoor reconstruction, filling a critical gap in the field.

title: Non-uniform B-spline optimization method for generating swept surfaces
comment: Updated version of the paper accepted to BDDM 2025
summary: Swept surface construction is widely used in computer-aided design. We propose a novel optimization method using non-uniform B-splines to improve the approximate accuracy of swept surfaces. First, discrete points on the swept shape are computed, and geometric properties such as surface area, discrete curvature, first-order derivatives, and their rotation angles are used to derive a distribution function representing surface irregularity, with weights adjusted from samples. Then, feature points are selected based on the distribution function to determine control points for the approximate non-uniform B-spline surface via inverse calculation, producing an optimized approximation. Finally, the number of feature points is adjusted based on the estimated approximation error. Experiments on 969 randomly generated sweep samples and 1 pipe example show that the proposed algorithm achieves similar accuracy with fewer control points, reducing them by about 15.85% at a specified accuracy of 0.01. Moreover, with ample sampling points, it reduces the average error by approximately 51.35% when the feature point multiple is 10 times the path control points, outperforming comparable methods.

AI.tldr: A novel optimization method using non-uniform B-splines is proposed to improve the approximate accuracy of swept surfaces in computer-aided design. The method uses geometric properties to derive a distribution function for surface irregularity, selects feature points, and determines control points via inverse calculation to produce an optimized approximation.
AI.motivation: Swept surface construction is widely used in CAD, but existing methods often require many control points to achieve desired accuracy. There is a need for an optimization method that can achieve similar or better accuracy while reducing the number of control points needed for surface representation.
AI.method: The proposed method involves: (1) Computing discrete points on the swept shape; (2) Using geometric properties (surface area, discrete curvature, first-order derivatives, and rotation angles) to derive a distribution function representing surface irregularity with weights adjusted from samples; (3) Selecting feature points based on the distribution function to determine control points for approximate non-uniform B-spline surface via inverse calculation; (4) Adjusting the number of feature points based on estimated approximation error.
AI.result: Experiments on 969 randomly generated sweep samples and 1 pipe example show: (1) Similar accuracy with fewer control points, reducing them by about 15.85% at a specified accuracy of 0.01; (2) With ample sampling points, reduces average error by approximately 51.35% when the feature point multiple is 10 times the path control points.
AI.conclusion: The proposed algorithm outperforms comparable methods, achieving significant reduction in control points (15.85%) while maintaining accuracy, and demonstrating even greater error reduction (51.35%) under certain conditions, making it effective for swept surface approximation in CAD applications.

title: Structure Across Voices: Comparing acoustic-event type accumulation and sequence dependence across four vocal repertoires using frozen audio encoders
summary: Vocal repertoires can differ in acoustic-event type accumulation and temporal organization, yet direct comparison is difficult because corpora use different native events and unequal amounts of sequence. We compare sperm whale codas, human speech phones, Bengalese finch syllables, and common marmoset calls using the same frozen-audio-encoder procedure while matching event count and local sequence opportunity. Whale shows the fastest type accumulation; Finch shows the strongest immediate dependence and repeated-subsequence recurrence. Physically interpretable acoustics recover complementary parts of this profile, continuous analyses without clustering support broad Whale acoustic coverage, and source- and position-preserving nulls retain both Finch order effects. Extending predictive context shifts the comparison toward Whale. Thus repertoire differences depend on the acoustic property and temporal scale measured rather than forming a single hierarchy.

AI.tldr: This study compares vocal repertoires across four species (sperm whales, humans, Bengalese finches, and common marmosets) using a unified methodology to examine acoustic event type accumulation and temporal organization, finding that repertoire differences depend on the specific acoustic property and temporal scale measured rather than forming a single hierarchy.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the difficulty in comparing vocal repertoires across different species due to different native events and unequal amounts of sequence data. The authors seek a standardized comparison approach.
AI.method: The study uses a "frozen-audio-encoder" procedure while matching event count and local sequence opportunity across all four species. They employ physically interpretable acoustics, continuous analyses without clustering, and source- and position-preserving null models.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Sperm whale shows fastest type accumulation; (2) Bengalese finch shows strongest immediate dependence and repeated-subsequence recurrence; (3) Physically interpretable acoustics recover complementary parts of the profile; (4) Continuous analyses support broad whale acoustic coverage; (5) Nulls retain both finch order effects; (6) Extending predictive context shifts comparison toward whale.
AI.conclusion: Repertoire differences depend on the acoustic property and temporal scale measured rather than forming a single hierarchy. This challenges the notion of a simple ranking of vocal repertoire complexity across species.

title: AgentGuard: Learning Execution Guardrails from Anomalous Coding-Agent Trajectories
summary:
AI coding agents increasingly rely on execution harnesses to interact with repositories and external tools. However, task success does not guarantee reliable execution. Agents may still modify unrelated files, rewrite tests, issue unsafe commands, or ignore failed validations, motivating behavioral guardrails for reliable execution. We present AgentGuard, an instruction-level guardrail framework that learns conditional execution constraints from anomalous trajectories of coding agents. Rather than relying on manually specified safety rules, AgentGuard automatically extracts recurring execution failure patterns, generalizes them into instruction-level behavioral constraints, and organizes them as a lightweight guardrail skill that dynamically activates only the rules relevant to the current instruction.
  This design enables behavioral guidance while minimizing unnecessary restrictions on normal execution. We evaluate AgentGuard using 642 documented failure traces collected from real coding-agent executions across 382 repository tasks. Guardrails are learned from 461 traces covering 282 tasks and evaluated on a disjoint set of 100 tasks. Using Claude Code with Claude Haiku 4.5 as the underlying coding agent, we compare the baseline agent with the same agent augmented by AgentGuard. Experimental results show that AgentGuard reduces the Abnormal Execution Rate from 69.0% to 26.7% and increases the Successful Task Completion Rate from 21.7% to 35.0%. These results demonstrate that execution guardrails learned from historical failures can substantially improve the reliability of AI coding agents while highlighting the remaining challenge of balancing safety and task completion.

AI.tldr: AgentGuard is an instruction-level guardrail framework that learns behavioral constraints from historical execution failures of AI coding agents, automatically extracting failure patterns and generalizing them into guardrail rules that dynamically activate relevant constraints to improve execution reliability.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents increasingly rely on execution harnesses to interact with repositories and external tools. While task success can be achieved, agents may still exhibit problematic behaviors: modifying unrelated files, rewriting tests, issuing unsafe commands, or ignoring failed validations. These issues motivate the need for behavioral guardrails to ensure reliable execution.
AI.method: AgentGuard learns conditional execution constraints from anomalous trajectories of coding agents. It automatically extracts recurring execution failure patterns from historical failure data, generalizes them into instruction-level behavioral constraints, and organizes them as a lightweight guardrail skill that dynamically activates only rules relevant to the current instruction. This approach avoids relying on manually specified safety rules.
AI.result: Using Claude Code with Claude Haiku 4.5 as the underlying coding agent, AgentGuard was evaluated on 100 disjoint tasks (learned from 461 traces covering 282 tasks). Results show: Abnormal Execution Rate reduced from 69.0% to 26.7%; Successful Task Completion Rate increased from 21.7% to 35.0%.
AI.conclusion: Execution guardrails learned from historical failures can substantially improve the reliability of AI coding agents. The approach demonstrates that automatically deriving behavioral constraints from past failures is effective. However, challenges remain in balancing safety and task completion, indicating room for further improvement in guardrail design.

title: Driver Behavior Estimation at Signalized Intersections Using a Physics-Constrained Decision-Conditioned Autoregressive Transformer
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC 2026)
summary: Red-light violations and harsh braking at signalized intersections are major contributors to traffic accidents. This paper analyzes and predicts human driver decision-making and longitudinal trajectory behavior during traffic light signal transitions. We collected a diverse real-world dataset comprising 449 approach runs under varying speed and distance conditions. Vehicle motion was recorded using RTK-corrected GNSS with centimeter-level accuracy, and driver heart rate and multi-level comfort ratings were monitored. Spatial and temporal calibration ensured precise alignment between vehicle state and signal timing. Statistical analysis identifies required deceleration as the dominant single predictor of the stop-go decision, and heteroscedastic Gaussian modeling of peak deceleration reveals five empirical comfort ranges derived from human stopping behavior. Based on this insight, we propose a two-stage modeling framework. Stage 1 predicts the binary maneuver decision, and Stage 2 generates the longitudinal acceleration trajectory using a decision-conditioned autoregressive Transformer with physics constraints, including target-state conditioning and jerk limits. The proposed architecture outperforms baseline methods and achieves 0.49m/s^2 acceleration MAE and 0.62m distance MAE. It also estimates the future stopping-comfort level of the human driver from a single yellow-onset snapshot. Qualitative results demonstrate realistic human-like braking behavior. The dataset and source code are publicly available.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses red-light violations and harsh braking at signalized intersections by analyzing human driver decision-making and longitudinal trajectory behavior during traffic light signal transitions. The study proposes a two-stage modeling framework that predicts stop-go decisions and generates longitudinal acceleration trajectories using a decision-conditioned autoregressive Transformer with physics constraints.
AI.motivation: Red-light violations and harsh braking at signalized intersections are major contributors to traffic accidents. Understanding and predicting human driver decision-making and longitudinal trajectory behavior during traffic light signal transitions is crucial for improving traffic safety and developing advanced driver assistance systems.
AI.method: The researchers collected a diverse real-world dataset of 449 approach runs under varying speed and distance conditions. Vehicle motion was recorded using RTK-corrected GNSS with centimeter-level accuracy, while driver heart rate and multi-level comfort ratings were monitored. Statistical analysis identified required deceleration as the dominant predictor of stop-go decisions. Heteroscedastic Gaussian modeling of peak deceleration revealed five empirical comfort ranges. A two-stage modeling framework was proposed: Stage 1 predicts binary maneuver decisions, and Stage 2 generates longitudinal acceleration trajectories using a decision-conditioned autoregressive Transformer with physics constraints, including target-state conditioning and jerk limits.
AI.result: The proposed architecture outperforms baseline methods, achieving 0.49 m/s² acceleration MAE and 0.62 m distance MAE. It also estimates the future stopping-comfort level of the human driver from a single yellow-onset snapshot. Qualitative results demonstrate realistic human-like braking behavior.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage modeling framework with decision-conditioned autoregressive Transformer effectively predicts human driver behavior during traffic light signal transitions. The model achieves high accuracy in acceleration and distance prediction while estimating driver comfort levels. The dataset and source code are publicly available, facilitating future research in this domain.

title: Position: AI Is Not Ready for Strategic Conflicts
comment: Published at the Social Sim'26 Workshop at COLM 2026. 4 pages body (22 pages total including appendices)
summary: Open-ended strategic wargames are high-stakes LM-based social simulations: they model adversaries, institutions, escalation, plan brittleness, doctrine, and crisis response. Language models (LMs) are attractive because they can play agents, generate scenario branches, adjudicate ambiguous actions, and summarize lessons, but the same affordances make open-ended roles dangerous: model language determines both what an actor attempts and what becomes simulated reality. This position paper argues that no LM-enabled wargame should inform planning, doctrine, policy, or crisis response without an auditable safety case, and that the proper use of open-ended wargames today is to stress-test decision-influencing LM agents. We identify five failure modes: decision laundering, adjudication opacity, role collapse, escalation-through-adjudication, and failure of strategic imagination. Ordinary benchmarks cannot establish safety for these settings. Wargames can expose failures as stress tests; they are not themselves safety cases for consequential use.

AI.tldr: Position paper arguing that Language Model (LM)-enabled open-ended strategic wargames should not inform actual planning, doctrine, policy, or crisis response without an auditable safety case. The paper identifies five failure modes and proposes that the proper use of such wargames is only as stress-tests for decision-influencing LM agents, not as safety validation.
AI.motivation: Address the inherent dangers of using LMs in high-stakes strategic wargaming contexts where model language determines both actor attempts and simulated reality. The authors recognize that while LMs offer valuable affordances (playing agents, generating scenarios, adjudicating actions, summarizing lessons), these same capabilities create significant risks when applied to consequential decision-making.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis identifying five distinct failure modes through critical examination of LM-enabled wargaming: (1) decision laundering - obfuscating responsibility for decisions, (2) adjudication opacity - lack of transparency in how LMs resolve ambiguous actions, (3) role collapse - LM's inability to maintain distinct actor personas, (4) escalation-through-adjudication - LM-driven escalation logic, and (5) failure of strategic imagination - inability to generate novel strategic thinking.
AI.result: The paper establishes that ordinary benchmarks cannot establish safety for these settings. Wargames can expose failures as stress tests but are not themselves safety cases for consequential use. This creates a fundamental distinction between using wargames for discovery of failure modes versus using them as validation for real-world application.
AI.conclusion: The proper use of open-ended LM-enabled wargames today is limited to stress-testing decision-influencing LM agents. No LM-enabled wargame should inform actual planning, doctrine, policy, or crisis response without developing an auditable safety case. The paper provides a framework for understanding why these tools are unsuitable for consequential decision-making without significant safety infrastructure.

title: Reasoning with Image Generation
comment: Accepted to COLM 2026. Code https://github.com/multimodal-ai-lab/reimagin and website https://hector.gr/reimagin/
summary: Chain-of-thought reasoning has revolutionized natural language processing by enabling large language models (LLMs) to decompose problems into intermediate steps before answering. Yet confining reasoning to the textual domain presents limitations for tasks requiring direct manipulation of visual representations. Recent efforts augment multimodal LLMs with external visual expert tools such as depth estimation or object detection modules, but these remain fundamentally limited by their reliance on narrow, rigid operations that cannot flexibly generate or transform visual content. We propose ReImaGin, which leverages image generation models as a flexible visual reasoning mechanism for multimodal LLMs: unlike fixed-function tools, they accept natural language commands and can perform open-ended visual operations, like removing an occlusion or generating a floorplan from multiple disjoint views of a room. Across six diverse visual reasoning tasks including multi-view spatial reasoning and collision prediction, ReImaGin consistently outperforms both text-only reasoning and specialist vision-tool baselines, with gains of up to 25\%, demonstrating the advantage of flexible, generative visual reasoning.

AI.tldr: ReImaGin enables multimodal LLMs to use image generation models as a flexible visual reasoning mechanism, outperforming text-only reasoning and specialist vision-tool baselines by up to 25% across six visual reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought reasoning is limited to the textual domain and cannot flexibly manipulate visual representations. Existing multimodal approaches rely on narrow, rigid external tools (depth estimation, object detection) that cannot generate or transform visual content.
AI.method: ReImaGin leverages image generation models as a flexible visual reasoning mechanism for multimodal LLMs. Unlike fixed-function tools, these models accept natural language commands and can perform open-ended visual operations like removing occlusions or generating floorplans from multiple disjoint views.
AI.result: ReImaGin consistently outperforms both text-only reasoning and specialist vision-tool baselines across six diverse visual reasoning tasks (including multi-view spatial reasoning and collision prediction), with gains of up to 25%.
AI.conclusion: Flexible, generative visual reasoning through image generation models provides significant advantages over rigid, narrow-function visual tools for multimodal LLM reasoning tasks.

title: Delayed-Light Rendering for Superluminal Objects
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 1 supplemental video; submitted to ACM Transactions on Graphics
summary: We present a real-time rendering method for scenes perceived through signals of finite speed $c$ in a non-relativistic setting: $c$ is a property of the imaging signal, not the causal speed limit, so bodies may move faster than $c$. A superluminal body presents several simultaneous images; pairs are created and annihilated in caustic flashes, and some branches play backward in time. Rather than approximating these effects, we enumerate them as roots of an emission condition posed against recorded state history, exact at every point solved, up to one stated approximation for moving observers. Because a fixed-step simulation records piecewise-linear history, the emission condition restricted to one history segment is a quadratic whose discriminant detects image-pair creation and whose slope classifies each image's playback direction, rate, and brightness. Perception is not tied to a single reference point: a global perceived state is built for an arbitrary finite set of observation events, and the delay landscape is the upper envelope of their backward light cones. A monotonic emission clamp guarantees the picture never regresses to images older than those already shown. Per-vertex solves shear bodies straddling delay gradients, and pre-generated frame-sequence assets are adapted by treating them as $(x,y,t)$ volumes sliced by the solved emission surface, so playback rate, reversal, and intra-body de-phasing arise with no animation-specific code. The exposition and implementations are planar: the emission condition and its per-segment solve are norm conditions, independent of dimension, but the visibility and occlusion questions a 3D renderer must answer are out of scope. The method is deployed in a released real-time strategy game; we describe the optimizations that make it run at interactive rates, and measure the algorithms through independent reference implementations.

AI.tldr: A real-time rendering method for visualizing scenes where imaging signals (e.g., light, sound) propagate at finite speed c, in a non-relativistic setting where objects can move faster than c. The method solves an emission condition against recorded state history to enumerate all simultaneous images, including time-reversed playback, without approximating these effects.
AI.motivation: Standard rendering assumes infinite signal speed (instantaneous light propagation). When signals have finite speed and objects can move faster than that signal (superluminal), multiple simultaneous images appear, with image pairs created/annihilated at caustic flashes and some images playing backward in time. Existing methods approximate these effects; this work seeks exact solutions.
AI.method: The method enumerates images as roots of an emission condition posed against recorded state history. For piecewise-linear history (from fixed-step simulation), the emission condition becomes a quadratic equation per segment. The discriminant detects image-pair creation/annihilation, while slope classifies playback direction, rate, and brightness. A global perceived state is built for multiple observation events using the upper envelope of their backward light cones. A monotonic emission clamp prevents regression to older images. Implementation adapts pre-generated frame sequences as (x,y,t) volumes sliced by the emission surface.
AI.result: The method runs at interactive rates in a released real-time strategy game. The paper provides optimizations enabling real-time performance and validates through independent reference implementations.
AI.conclusion: The planar emission condition and per-segment solve are norm conditions (dimension-independent), making the approach theoretically applicable to 3D. However, 3D visibility and occlusion questions remain out of scope. The method successfully handles superluminal motion, time-reversed playback, and variable playback rates without animation-specific code, demonstrating practical viability in commercial game deployment.

title: Taming Long-form Text-to-Speech
summary: Long-form text-to-speech (TTS) enables multi-turn conversations with consistent prosody and higher quality voice cloning from longer reference audio. Recent open-weights autoregressive TTS models such as Qwen3-TTS and VoxCPM2 attain state-of-the-art word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) on short-form prompts but significantly deteriorate when used with long-form prompts. We propose Localized Attention-Constrained Inference (LACI), an inference-only method to detect TTS errors in near real-time, roll back to the error onset and regenerate with temporary guardrails, adding negligible computational overhead. Using LACI, we improve worst-of-N WER across 10 RNG seeds for Qwen3-TTS-0.6B from 35.2% to 3.4% on prompts longer than 1500 words, even surpassing its short-form reliability of 5.4\% on prompts with fewer than 500 words. To demonstrate the efficacy of LACI on voice cloning reliability, we propose a sliding-window version of the SIM metric that we call wSIM. wSIM exposes several novel failure patterns that are not captured by SIM. LACI improves worst-of-N wSIM from 0.01 to 0.47 on 120 seconds of reference audio while reducing the rate of catastrophic generations with WER above 30% from 26% to below 1%

AI.tldr: LACI (Localized Attention-Constrained Inference) is an inference-only method that detects TTS errors in near real-time, rolls back to error onset, and regenerates with temporary guardrails. It improves worst-of-N WER from 35.2% to 3.4% on prompts >1500 words and wSIM from 0.01 to 0.47, reducing catastrophic generation rate from 26% to below 1%.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive TTS models (Qwen3-TTS, VoxCPM2) achieve state-of-the-art performance on short-form prompts but significantly deteriorate on long-form prompts (>1500 words), with WER degrading to 35.2% and speaker similarity dropping to 0.01.
AI.method: LACI detects TTS errors in near real-time during inference, rolls back to the error onset point, and regenerates with temporary guardrails. The method introduces a new metric wSIM (sliding-window SIM) to capture voice cloning failure patterns that standard SIM misses.
AI.result: Using LACI with Qwen3-TTS-0.6B: (1) WER on prompts >1500 words improved from 35.2% to 3.4%, even surpassing short-form performance (5.4% on <500 words); (2) wSIM on 120-second reference audio improved from 0.01 to 0.47; (3) Catastrophic generations (WER >30%) reduced from 26% to <1%.
AI.conclusion: LACI effectively addresses long-form TTS degradation with negligible computational overhead, making autoregressive TTS models reliable for long-form synthesis and voice cloning applications.

title: What Do Hallucinations Reveal About Multimodal Reasoning? Diagnosing Visual Grounding Failures via Contrastive Decoding Probes
summary: When strong multimodal models are widely available, progress requires new scientific methodologies beyond benchmark scores---using models as instruments for understanding behavior. We address this by asking: can we use large vision-language models (LVLMs) as experimental instruments for studying their own failure dynamics? Focusing on visual hallucination, we introduce SAFE, a training-free decoding framework that contrasts visually-grounded and vision-ablated generation paths to produce a token-level contrastive grounding score that identifies when the model favors linguistic priors over visual evidence. This signal serves dual roles: as a practical proxy for detecting visually-ungrounded tokens, and as the basis for decoding-time penalties. Our analysis yields three empirical observations: visual dependency decays over generation, hallucinations co-occur in temporal clusters, and early intervention reduces clustering without substantially degrading fluency. On MMHalBench, SAFE substantially outperforms all compared baselines; results elsewhere are more mixed. We argue that designing contrastive probes exemplifies a broader mission: using models as instruments for scientific understanding. Code: https://github.com/zhaozhipeng1997/SAFE_public.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SAFE, a training-free decoding framework that uses large vision-language models (LVLMs) as experimental instruments to study their own failure dynamics, specifically visual hallucination. The method contrasts visually-grounded and vision-ablated generation paths to produce token-level contrastive grounding scores that detect when models favor linguistic priors over visual evidence.
AI.motivation: When strong multimodal models are widely available, progress requires new scientific methodologies beyond benchmark scores. The authors aim to use models as instruments for understanding behavior, specifically studying visual hallucination dynamics in LVLMs.
AI.method: SAFE is a training-free decoding framework that contrasts visually-grounded and vision-ablated generation paths to produce a token-level contrastive grounding score. This score identifies when the model favors linguistic priors over visual evidence. The signal serves dual roles: (1) as a practical proxy for detecting visually-ungrounded tokens, and (2) as the basis for decoding-time penalties.
AI.result: Three empirical observations: (1) visual dependency decays over generation, (2) hallucinations co-occur in temporal clusters, and (3) early intervention reduces clustering without substantially degrading fluency. On MMHalBench, SAFE substantially outperforms all compared baselines; results elsewhere are more mixed.
AI.conclusion: Designing contrastive probes exemplifies a broader mission: using models as instruments for scientific understanding. The work demonstrates that LVLMs can be used to study their own failure dynamics, providing a new methodology for understanding multimodal model behavior beyond benchmark scores.

title: Assurance Envelopes for Autonomous Coding Agents: Minimum-Cost Evidence for Software Change
summary: When a coding agent returns to existing software, it inherits evidence from earlier engineering work: tests, type checks, proofs, static analyses, and traces. Reloading all of it is wasteful, but dropping a piece the change depends on can leave a required property unsupported. Given the properties a change must preserve, its obligations, we ask which least-cost subset of the available evidence re-establishes them, and we call such a subset a task-conditioned assurance envelope. Evidence and the rules that combine it form a typed inference graph; an obligation is met when forward chaining from the selected evidence reaches it, and we validate every selection by that closure rather than by trusting the optimizer. The software-derived graphs in our evaluation come from preserved outcomes of prior AI coding-agent runs; we freeze those artifacts and ask which accumulated evidence should be restored for a later task. Small graphs from Rust, IronBlocks, and Pong outcomes show that the minimum envelope depends on the task, that none may exist when current evidence cannot re-establish a required property, that some properties need several pieces of evidence together, and that expanding the requirements adds evidence rather than replacing it. A prespecified synthetic benchmark of 249 instances characterizes computation: a baseline that discards the 'several pieces together' structure necessarily fails to re-derive them; every completed exact cross-check agreed with the CP-SAT optimizer; and median solve time stayed below 20 ms at 500-evidence graphs, except that graphs with many alternative derivations per target timed out at far smaller sizes, so structure, not raw size, drives difficulty. The contribution is a bounded application of established optimization to selecting assurance context for a software change; discovering the obligations and downstream agent benefit remain open.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of selecting the minimum subset of available evidence (tests, type checks, proofs, static analyses, traces) needed to re-establish required properties when a coding agent returns to existing software. The authors formulate this as finding a "task-conditioned assurance envelope" using typed inference graphs, where obligations are met through forward chaining from selected evidence.
AI.motivation: When coding agents return to existing software, they inherit accumulated evidence from prior engineering work. Reloading all evidence is wasteful, but dropping evidence that a change depends on can leave required properties unsupported. The problem is determining which least-cost subset of evidence re-establishes the required properties (obligations) for a given task.
AI.method: The authors model evidence and combining rules as a typed inference graph. An obligation is met when forward chaining from selected evidence reaches it. They use CP-SAT optimization to find the minimum-cost envelope and validate selections by closure rather than trusting the optimizer. Evaluation uses software-derived graphs from prior AI coding-agent runs (Rust, IronBlocks, Pong) and a synthetic benchmark of 249 instances.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) The minimum envelope depends on the task; (2) No envelope may exist when current evidence cannot re-establish a required property; (3) Some properties require several pieces of evidence together (synergistic effects); (4) Expanding requirements adds evidence rather than replacing it; (5) A baseline that discards the "several pieces together" structure necessarily fails; (6) All exact cross-checks agreed with CP-SAT optimizer; (7) Median solve time stayed below 20ms at 500-evidence graphs, except graphs with many alternative derivations per target timed out at smaller sizes—structure, not raw size, drives difficulty.
AI.conclusion: The contribution is a bounded application of established optimization (CP-SAT) to selecting assurance context for software changes. The approach correctly identifies minimum evidence subsets needed to satisfy obligations. Open problems include discovering obligations and measuring downstream agent benefit.

title: HintMiner: Automatic Question Hints Mining From Q&A Web Posts with Language Model via Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Users often need ask questions and seek answers online. The Question - Answering (QA) forums such as Stack Overflow cannot always respond to the questions timely and properly. In this paper, we propose HintMiner, a novel automatic question hints mining tool for users to help them find answers. HintMiner leverages the machine comprehension and sequence generation techniques to automatically generate hints for users' questions. It firstly retrieve many web Q\&A posts and then extract some hints from the posts using MiningNet that is built via a language model. Using the huge amount of online Q\&A posts, we design a self-supervised objective to train the MiningNet that is a neural encoder-decoder model based on the transformer and copying mechanisms. We have evaluated HintMiner on 60,000 Stack Overflow questions. The experiment results show that the proposed approach is effective. For example, HintMiner achieves an average BLEU score of 36.17\% and an average ROUGE-2 score of 36.29\%. Our tool and experimental data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: HintMiner is an automatic question hints mining tool that leverages machine comprehension and sequence generation techniques to help users find answers by retrieving web Q&A posts and extracting hints using MiningNet, a transformer-based neural encoder-decoder model with copying mechanisms trained via self-supervised learning.
AI.motivation: Question-Answering forums like Stack Overflow cannot always respond to user questions timely and properly, creating a need for automated tools to help users find answers or hints for their questions.
AI.method: HintMiner uses a two-stage approach: (1) retrieve relevant web Q&A posts for user questions, then (2) extract hints from these posts using MiningNet. MiningNet is a neural encoder-decoder model built on transformer architecture with copying mechanisms, trained using a self-supervised objective on large amounts of online Q&A data.
AI.result: HintMiner was evaluated on 60,000 Stack Overflow questions, achieving an average BLEU score of 36.17% and an average ROUGE-2 score of 36.29%.
AI.conclusion: The experiment results demonstrate that the proposed approach is effective. The tool and experimental data are publicly available.

title: Calibrate, Then Route: A Measured Study of Learned Request Routing for Disaggregated LLM Serving
summary: Disaggregated LLM serving places compute heavy prefill and memory heavy decode on separate GPU pools. Systems such as DistServe, Splitwise, and Mooncake make this separation fast, but routing still determines which instances handle each request. We study a router that estimates the additional completion time on each instance using exact prompt length, predicted output length, post admission KV cache pressure, and SLO class. We develop the policy in a discrete event simulator and validate it on eight NVIDIA A40 GPUs, each running a vLLM engine, with NIXL transferring KV caches between pools. All workloads run at measured saturation. Across three mixed, bursty arrival traces, the calibrated router achieves the highest mean goodput at 0.864, compared with 0.835 to 0.847 for round robin, least loaded, and a length heuristic. It also shows the lowest variance across traces. It beats round robin and the length heuristic on all three traces and least loaded on two. On the third, it trails by 0.003, within run to run noise. Hardware calibration matters: simulator derived constants cost 4.5 goodput points and roughly 40 percent of the tail latency advantage, reducing the scorer to little more than queue counting. Benefits grow with decode pool size and traffic heterogeneity but disappear in pools with three instances, where queue counts are often enough. Under extreme scarcity, greedy cost minimization concentrates requests on the cheapest scored instance, and blind spreading performs better. With calibrated costs, the learned router matches the goodput of round robin using six GPUs instead of seven.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a router for disaggregated LLM serving that estimates completion time using prompt length, predicted output length, KV cache pressure, and SLO class. Evaluated on 8 NVIDIA A40 GPUs with vLLM and NIXL, the calibrated router achieves 0.864 mean goodput, outperforming round robin, least loaded, and length heuristic methods (0.835-0.847).
AI.motivation: Disaggregated LLM serving separates compute-heavy prefill and memory-heavy decode onto different GPU pools for efficiency. However, routing decisions—which instances handle each request—significantly impact system performance. Existing routing policies are suboptimal, and proper hardware calibration was found to be critical for accurate cost estimation.
AI.method: The researchers developed a router that estimates additional completion time on each instance using exact prompt length, predicted output length, post-admission KV cache pressure, and SLO class. They built the policy in a discrete event simulator and validated it on a real testbed with eight NVIDIA A40 GPUs, each running a vLLM engine, with NIXL transferring KV caches between pools. They tested across three mixed, bursty arrival traces at measured saturation.
AI.result: The calibrated router achieved the highest mean goodput at 0.864, compared with 0.835 to 0.847 for round robin, least loaded, and length heuristic. It showed the lowest variance across traces and beat round robin and length heuristic on all three traces, and least loaded on two (trailing by 0.003 on the third, within noise). Simulator-derived constants without calibration cost 4.5 goodput points and ~40% of tail latency advantage. Benefits increase with decode pool size and traffic heterogeneity but disappear with three instances. Under extreme scarcity, greedy cost minimization outperforms blind spreading. With calibrated costs, the learned router matches round robin's goodput using six GPUs instead of seven.
AI.conclusion: Hardware calibration is essential for accurate routing in disaggregated LLM serving. A well-calibrated router can achieve superior goodput and lower variance than existing methods, with benefits scaling with system complexity. The approach enables significant hardware efficiency gains, reducing GPU requirements while maintaining performance.

title: Decentralized Gossip Learning and Federated Averaging for Histopathology Image Classification
comment: Recently accepted to Neural Computing and Applications
summary: Breast histopathology analysis increasingly relies on distributed learning because direct data pooling across institutions is often restricted by privacy, governance, and communication constraints. This study compares server-based Federated Averaging (FedAvg), fully decentralized gossip learning, and Hybrid Gossip-FedAvg for invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) patch classification. Experiments used 277,524 color image patches with patient-disjoint training, validation, and test partitions and a workload-balanced, Dirichlet-guided allocation across six nodes. Ring, random degree-3, and fully connected gossip topologies were evaluated together with sensitivity analyses for statistical heterogeneity, mixing coefficient, learning rate, model drift, prediction disagreement, calibration, clinically motivated operating points, communication payload, and patient-level IDC burden, together with auxiliary backbone robustness analyses. In the principal alpha=0.3 experiment, Hybrid Gossip-FedAvg achieved a test area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.8811, closely followed by FedAvg at 0.8801 and fully connected gossip at 0.8751. Across three independent patient-level repetitions, FedAvg and Hybrid Gossip-FedAvg obtained the same mean ROC-AUC of 0.9082, with standard deviations of 0.0037 and 0.0043, respectively. Hybrid achieved the highest mean area under the precision-recall curve of 0.8240, whereas FedAvg produced the lowest mean Brier score of 0.1335. Denser gossip graphs improved discrimination but increased theoretical model payload, while ring gossip remained sensitive to learning rate and mixing strength. Overall, FedAvg provided the most consistently reliable server-based baseline, topology-aware gossip offered a viable decentralized alternative, and Hybrid Gossip-FedAvg provided a balanced compromise between peer-to-peer diffusion and periodic global coordination.

AI.tldr: This study compares three distributed learning approaches (FedAvg, gossip learning, and Hybrid Gossip-FedAvg) for invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC) patch classification across six nodes using 277,524 breast histopathology images. FedAvg and Hybrid Gossip-FedAvg both achieved the highest mean ROC-AUC of 0.9082, with Hybrid achieving the best precision-recall curve (0.8240) and FedAvg the lowest Brier score (0.1335).
AI.motivation: Breast histopathology analysis increasingly relies on distributed learning because direct data pooling across institutions is restricted by privacy, governance, and communication constraints. This study aims to compare different distributed learning paradigms to find the most effective approach for IDC patch classification.
AI.method: The study compares server-based Federated Averaging (FedAvg), fully decentralized gossip learning, and Hybrid Gossip-FedAvg for IDC patch classification using 277,524 color image patches. Experiments used patient-disjoint training, validation, and test partitions with workload-balanced Dirichlet-guided allocation across six nodes. Ring, random degree-3, and fully connected gossip topologies were evaluated, along with extensive sensitivity analyses for statistical heterogeneity, mixing coefficient, learning rate, model drift, prediction disagreement, calibration, operating points, communication payload, and patient-level IDC burden.
AI.result: In the principal alpha=0.3 experiment, Hybrid Gossip-FedAvg achieved test ROC-AUC of 0.8811, FedAvg 0.8801, and fully connected gossip 0.8751. Across three independent patient-level repetitions, FedAvg and Hybrid Gossip-FedAvg both achieved mean ROC-AUC of 0.9082 (std: 0.0037 and 0.0043). Hybrid achieved highest mean precision-recall AUC (0.8240), while FedAvg had lowest mean Brier score (0.1335). Denser gossip graphs improved discrimination but increased payload; ring gossip remained sensitive to learning rate and mixing strength.
AI.conclusion: FedAvg provides the most consistently reliable server-based baseline, topology-aware gossip offers a viable decentralized alternative, and Hybrid Gossip-FedAvg provides a balanced compromise between peer-to-peer diffusion and periodic global coordination.

title: Dichoptic Foveation
summary: Interocular differences in visual perception can induce a variety of effects when fused by the brain. For example, prior works have found that carefully crafted binocular differences in local detail can improve contrast. It has also been found that when the frequency content of two stimuli are slightly different, blur suppression leads to a fused percept that is typically dominated by the sharper image. In this paper, we develop a psychophysical framework to measure the perception of natural image stimuli with interocular frequency differences across the visual field. To this end, we study the effect of dichoptic foveation, which we define as the application of blur to one eye and a simultaneous sharpening filter to the other. Stimuli were viewed in a virtual reality (VR) head-mounted display (HMD) and placed at different retinal eccentricities. Study data were scaled to a perceptual just objectionable difference (JOD) scale, and a 4D model was fit to it; our results suggest that interocular frequency differences can be well described by a simple computational model. We applied the model in a realistic VR scenario with free exploration of 360° videos to improve a base foveated rendering system by enhancing high frequency information dichoptically.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates dichoptic foveation - applying blur to one eye while sharpening the other - and its effects on visual perception in VR. The study develops a psychophysical framework to measure how the brain fuses images with interocular frequency differences across the visual field, with applications in improving foveated rendering for VR headsets.
AI.motivation: The research addresses how interocular differences in visual perception affect fused visual experience. Prior work showed that binocular differences in local detail can improve contrast, and that the sharper image dominates when frequency content differs between eyes. This study aims to quantify this phenomenon systematically and apply it to practical VR rendering improvements.
AI.method: The researchers developed a psychophysical framework using natural image stimuli with interocular frequency differences. Experiments were conducted using a VR head-mounted display with stimuli placed at different retinal eccentricities. Data were scaled to a perceptual just objectionable difference (JOD) scale, and a 4D computational model was fit to the results. The model was then applied in a realistic VR scenario with free exploration of 360° videos to enhance a base foveated rendering system.
AI.result: Interocular frequency differences can be well described by a simple computational model. The application of this model to VR scenarios demonstrated improved foveated rendering by dichoptically enhancing high-frequency information.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest that a simple computational model can effectively describe perceptual responses to interocular frequency differences. This enables practical applications in VR, where dichoptic foveation can be used to improve rendering quality while potentially reducing computational requirements through strategic blur/sharpening manipulation between eyes.

title: Audio-Visual Turn-taking Prediction in Cocktail Party Scenarios
comment: Accepted to IEEE SLT 2026. This version includes an appendix about manual verified labels for AVCocktail
summary: Current predictive turn-taking models (PTTMs) achieve strong performance on benchmarks with controlled acoustic conditions and clean audio signals. Their generalisation to conversations with overlapping speech and background interference remains underexplored. In this research, we evaluate audio-visual PTTMs trained with clean data on a challenging cocktail-party testbed derived from the AVCocktail dataset, and analyse their adaptation behaviour to this new domain. Experimental results show consistent performance degradation across audio and visual modalities under noisy conditions, with up to 38% relative drop in weighted F1. Fine-tuning on the new domain improves robustness, but gains vary across modalities and depend on the size of the available pre-training data. These findings provide insights into the different generalisation and adaptation capabilities of the audio and visual modalities, and indicate the need for robust modelling strategies to adapt to the complexities of human interactions in noise. All code and turn labels are made publicly available to facilitate further research.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates audio-visual predictive turn-taking models (PTTMs) trained on clean data when applied to challenging cocktail-party conditions, revealing significant performance degradation (up to 38% relative drop in weighted F1) and investigating fine-tuning as an adaptation strategy.
AI.motivation: Current PTTMs perform well in controlled acoustic conditions but lack evaluation on real-world scenarios with overlapping speech and background noise. This research addresses the gap in understanding model generalization to complex, noisy conversational environments like cocktail parties.
AI.method: The study evaluates audio-visual PTTMs trained on clean data using a challenging cocktail-party testbed derived from the AVCocktail dataset. It analyzes adaptation behavior through fine-tuning experiments, examining how performance varies across modalities and with different amounts of pre-training data.
AI.result: Consistent performance degradation was observed across both audio and visual modalities under noisy conditions, with up to 38% relative drop in weighted F1. Fine-tuning on the new domain improves robustness, but gains vary across modalities and depend on the size of available pre-training data.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight different generalization and adaptation capabilities between audio and visual modalities. There is a clear need for robust modeling strategies to adapt PTTMs to the complexities of human interactions in noisy environments. All code and turn labels are publicly available to support further research.

title: ViD: Vision-Dominant Gender Bias Mitigation for Large Vision-Language Models
summary: Gender bias in large vision-language models (LVLMs) undermines their fairness and reliability, compromising output trustworthiness. Current mitigation methods rely on training-phase adjustments or post-hoc calibration, but face limitations in dynamic visual bias mitigation. These include inability to capture real-time visual-textual incongruence, dependence on predefined gender bias taxonomies, and degraded cross-modal alignment with emergent bias patterns. To address these challenges, we propose ViD, a causally-inspired framework that analyzes attention mechanisms across five distinct patterns, revealing confounding effects from strong language priors. ViD demonstrates that visual-to-language cross-attention effectively suppresses bias while preserving general reasoning capabilities and text generation quality. ViD incorporates dual mechanisms: backdoor adjustment counters strong language priors, while refined token selection in decoding layers optimizes processing. This enhances model robustness and inference efficiency. Our integrated approach significantly mitigates gender bias across multidimensional social attributes in LVLMs, improving visual grounding and output fairness. Cross-benchmark validation shows ViD reduces gender bias by 14.7\% on single-attribute evaluations (FACET) and achieves significant improvements on image captioning tasks (MS COCO), with gender bias score improving from 0.6708 to 0.9978 for LLaVA. Crucially, these improvements require no additional training overhead, making ViD a scalable and practical solution for bias mitigation in LVLMs.

AI.tldr: ViD is a causally-inspired framework for mitigating gender bias in large vision-language models (LVLMs) by analyzing attention mechanisms across five distinct patterns and using dual mechanisms (backdoor adjustment and refined token selection) to suppress bias without training overhead.
AI.motivation: Gender bias in LVLMs undermines fairness and reliability, compromising output trustworthiness. Current mitigation methods (training-phase adjustments or post-hoc calibration) have limitations: inability to capture real-time visual-textual incongruence, dependence on predefined gender bias taxonomies, and degraded cross-modal alignment with emergent bias patterns.
AI.method: ViD analyzes attention mechanisms across five distinct patterns to reveal confounding effects from strong language priors. It incorporates dual mechanisms: (1) backdoor adjustment counters strong language priors, and (2) refined token selection in decoding layers optimizes processing. The approach enhances visual grounding and output fairness while preserving general reasoning capabilities and text generation quality.
AI.result: ViD reduces gender bias by 14.7% on single-attribute evaluations (FACET) and significantly improves image captioning tasks (MS COCO), with gender bias score improving from 0.6708 to 0.9978 for LLaVA. These improvements require no additional training overhead.
AI.conclusion: ViD presents a scalable and practical solution for bias mitigation in LVLMs, effectively suppressing gender bias while preserving model capabilities and inference efficiency.

title: FairLint-DL: An IDE-Native Tool for Fairness Debugging of Deep Learning Software
comment: In the Tools and Datasets track of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026). Artifact awarded Available, Functional and Reusable badges. Tool: https://open-vsx.org/extension/ArchitRathod/fairlint-dl
summary: Existing fairness analysis tools predominantly operate as post-training evaluation frameworks, requiring practitioners to complete the full model development lifecycle before assessing bias. We present FairLint-DL, a Visual Studio Code extension that implements a shift-left approach to fairness testing by enabling pre-training, IDE-native bias detection directly on tabular datasets. FairLint-DL trains a configurable deep neural network as a proxy model and applies information-theoretic Quantitative Individual Discrimination (QID) metrics. Grounded in Shannon and min-entropy, QID quantifies the causal influence of protected attributes on predictions. The system implements a two-phase gradient-guided search algorithm for discovering discriminatory instances, a causal debugging pipeline that localizes bias to specific network layers and neurons via sensitivity analysis, and dual explainability engines using SHAP and LIME for feature-level attribution. Evaluation on three tabular benchmarks (Adult Census Income, German Credit, and Bank Marketing) reveals fairness concerns that vary widely across datasets: on Adult, 96.0% of analyzed instances exhibit QID above the 0.1-bit significance threshold, with a mean QID of 0.619 bits and a disparate impact ratio of 0.581, violating the four-fifths legal rule. FairLint-DL produces these results within 12 seconds on cached models, demonstrating the feasibility of integrating fairness analysis into the developer workflow without significant overhead.

AI.tldr: FairLint-DL is a Visual Studio Code extension that implements a shift-left approach to fairness testing, enabling pre-training, IDE-native bias detection on tabular datasets using information-theoretic Quantitative Individual Discrimination (QID) metrics and dual explainability engines.
AI.motivation: Existing fairness analysis tools operate as post-training evaluation frameworks, requiring practitioners to complete the full model development lifecycle before assessing bias. This creates a need for earlier bias detection in the development workflow.
AI.method: The system uses: (1) a configurable deep neural network as proxy model; (2) information-theoretic QID metrics based on Shannon and min-entropy to quantify causal influence of protected attributes; (3) two-phase gradient-guided search algorithm for discovering discriminatory instances; (4) causal debugging pipeline with sensitivity analysis to localize bias to specific network layers and neurons; (5) dual explainability engines using SHAP and LIME for feature-level attribution.
AI.result: Evaluation on three tabular benchmarks (Adult Census Income, German Credit, and Bank Marketing) shows: on Adult dataset, 96.0% of analyzed instances exhibit QID above 0.1-bit significance threshold, with mean QID of 0.619 bits and disparate impact ratio of 0.581, violating the four-fifths legal rule. Results produced within 12 seconds on cached models.
AI.conclusion: FairLint-DL demonstrates the feasibility of integrating fairness analysis into the developer workflow without significant overhead, enabling bias detection earlier in the ML development lifecycle.

title: POSPAN: Position-Constrained Span Masking for Language Model Pre-training
summary: Span-level masked language modeling (MLM) has shown to be advantageous to pre-trained language models over the original single-token MLM, as entities/phrases and their dependencies are critical to language understanding. Previous works only consider span length with some discrete distributions, while the dependencies among spans are ignored, i.e., assuming that the positions of masked spans are uniformly distributed. In this paper, we present POSPAN, a general framework to allow diverse position-constrained span masking strategies via the combination of span length distribution and position constraint distribution, which unifies all existing span-level masking methods. To verify the effectiveness of POSPAN in pre-training, we evaluate it on the datasets from several NLU benchmarks. Experimental results indicate that the position constraint is capable of enhancing span-level masking broadly, and our best POSPAN setting consistently outperforms its span-length-only counterparts and vanilla MLM. We also conduct theoretical analysis for the position constraint in masked language models to shed light on the reason why POSPAN works well, demonstrating the rationality and necessity of POSPAN.

AI.tldr: POSPAN is a general framework for span-level masked language modeling that combines span length distribution with position constraint distribution. It unifies all existing span-level masking methods and consistently outperforms span-length-only counterparts and vanilla MLM on NLU benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Previous span-level MLM works only consider span length distributions while ignoring position dependencies (assuming uniform distribution of masked spans). The authors argue that entities/phrases and their dependencies are critical to language understanding.
AI.method: POSPAN combines span length distribution with position constraint distribution to create diverse position-constrained span masking strategies, unifying all existing span-level masking methods.
AI.result: Experimental results on NLU benchmarks show that position constraint enhances span-level masking broadly. The best POSPAN setting consistently outperforms span-length-only counterparts and vanilla MLM. Theoretical analysis demonstrates the rationality and necessity of position constraint in masked language models.
AI.conclusion: Position constraint is a valuable addition to span-level masking. The theoretical analysis provides insight into why POSPAN works well, validating its effectiveness and necessity for pre-trained language models.

title: Artificial intelligence and biosecurity: capabilities, threat pathways, and defense-in-depth governance
summary: Artificial intelligence is reshaping biological research across an increasingly connected digital-to-physical workflow. General-purpose large language models can retrieve and integrate scientific information, support experimental planning, and computational analysis; biological foundation models can predict, optimize, and generate proteins, genes, and genome-scale sequences; agentic systems can coordinate multistep research tasks; automated laboratories can partially close the design-build-test-learn cycle. These technologies could greatly benefit medicine, public health, and biotechnology. However, their biosecurity risk depends not only on what the AI can do, but also on who uses it, their expertise and intent, their access to laboratory tools and materials, and the safeguards in place. Current evidence shows that AI uplift exists but primarily affects digital rather than physical tasks. Frontier systems have exceeded expert baselines on in-silico, and screening-evasion benchmarks, whereas controlled wet-laboratory studies find that tacit knowledge and physical execution remain substantial barriers. This review describes the different biological threats from AI tool use, from information gathering and biological design to procurement, synthesis, testing, scale-up, and potential release. We further examine why alignment techniques for general-purpose models transfer poorly to biological ones, and the emerging role of interpretability in auditing whether hazardous capabilities are genuinely removed. We argue for defense-in-depth governance that links capability thresholds to proportionate responsibilities across the biological AI ecosystem, reducing high-consequence risk while preserving beneficial use.

AI.tldr: This review examines how AI technologies (large language models, biological foundation models, agentic systems, automated laboratories) are transforming biological research and the associated biosecurity risks. It argues for defense-in-depth governance that balances beneficial use with risk reduction.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand and address the biosecurity risks posed by AI tools in biological research, as these technologies could potentially enable harm from information gathering through synthesis, testing, scale-up, and release. The authors aim to inform governance approaches.
AI.method: This is a review paper that synthesizes current evidence on AI capabilities in biological tasks, examining empirical studies on "AI uplift" in digital vs physical domains, benchmark performance on in-silico and screening-evasion tasks, and wet-laboratory studies. It also analyzes why alignment techniques fail to transfer and explores interpretability's role in auditing.
AI.result: Key findings: AI uplift exists but primarily affects digital rather than physical tasks. Frontier systems exceed expert baselines on in-silico and screening-evasion benchmarks, but tacit knowledge and physical execution remain substantial barriers in wet-laboratory settings. Alignment techniques transfer poorly to biological models, and interpretability may help audit hazardous capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue for defense-in-depth governance that links AI capability thresholds to proportionate responsibilities across the biological AI ecosystem, aiming to reduce high-consequence risks while preserving beneficial applications in medicine, public health, and biotechnology.

title: A multimodal large language model for evidence-based autism spectrum disorder screening
summary: The clinical management of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) faces a bottleneck in early screening, mainly because trained specialists are scarce and conventional assessment tools are subjective. Here, we introduce ASDchat, a multimodal large language model designed for evidence-based ASD screening, which takes video, audio, and dialogue as input. ASDchat adopts a dual-branch architecture, where the decision branch generates screening probabilities and the evidence branch generates traceable, timestamped behavioral evidence aligned with standardized clinical criteria (ADOS-2). The model was trained and evaluated on a dataset of 1,035 participants from 27 sites in China, which covered typically developing (TD) children, children with ASD, and children with other disorders. For ASD versus TD, ASDchat reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.953 $\pm$ 0.021. On 9 held-out sites that were not used for training, the mean AUC was 0.932. Furthermore, unsupervised clustering of the behavioral dimensions split the ASD cases into six subtypes with different phenotypic profiles, and ASDchat suggests an intervention for each subtype. ASDchat provides a feasible path for large-scale, evidence-based early ASD screening in clinical practice.

AI.tldr: ASDchat is a multimodal large language model for evidence-based autism spectrum disorder (ASD) screening that takes video, audio, and dialogue as input. It uses a dual-branch architecture with a decision branch for screening probabilities and an evidence branch for traceable behavioral evidence aligned with ADOS-2 clinical criteria. Trained on 1,035 participants from 27 sites in China, it achieved AUC of 0.953 for ASD vs TD classification and 0.932 on held-out sites. It can also cluster ASD cases into 6 phenotypic subtypes with intervention recommendations.
AI.motivation: The clinical management of ASD faces a bottleneck in early screening due to scarcity of trained specialists and subjectivity of conventional assessment tools. There is a need for a scalable, objective, and evidence-based screening method.
AI.method: ASDchat uses a dual-branch architecture: (1) decision branch generates screening probabilities, (2) evidence branch generates traceable, timestamped behavioral evidence aligned with ADOS-2 criteria. The model takes video, audio, and dialogue as multimodal input. Training and evaluation was performed on a dataset of 1,035 participants from 27 sites in China, including typically developing children, children with ASD, and children with other disorders.
AI.result: For ASD versus TD classification, ASDchat achieved an AUC of 0.953 ± 0.021. On 9 held-out sites not used for training, the mean AUC was 0.932. Unsupervised clustering of behavioral dimensions identified six ASD subtypes with different phenotypic profiles.
AI.conclusion: ASDchat provides a feasible path for large-scale, evidence-based early ASD screening in clinical practice. It offers both accurate screening and subtype-specific intervention recommendations.

title: HairCS: Reconstructing Strand-Based Hair from Hair Cards
summary: We present an automated pipeline that converts hair-card models into high-quality strand-based hairstyles. Given a collection of textured triangular or quad strips as input, our method produces a strand-based representation that preserves the original hairstyle while enriching it with fine-scale geometric detail and adhering to standard production requirements: strands originate from the scalp, roots are uniformly distributed, and the hair volume is plausibly filled. The resulting assets are directly compatible with strand-based rendering, physics-based simulation, and common grooming modifiers (e.g., clumping, curling, noise) for enhanced realism and artistic control. We validate our approach on a large and diverse set of hairstyles, including short and long hair, curly styles, and complex styles such as buns and ponytails.

AI.tldr: Automated pipeline converts hair-card models to high-quality strand-based hairstyles, preserving style while adding geometric detail and meeting production requirements for rendering, simulation, and grooming.
AI.motivation: Hair-card models lack fine-scale geometric detail and are incompatible with strand-based production pipelines, requiring manual conversion that is time-consuming
AI.method: Automated pipeline converting hair-card models (textured triangular/quad strips) into strand-based representation with geometric detail enhancement
AI.result: Method preserves original hairstyle while adding fine-scale detail, ensures strands originate from scalp with uniform root distribution and plausible volume filling
AI.conclusion: The pipeline produces production-ready strand-based hair assets that are compatible with standard rendering, simulation, and grooming tools, validated across diverse hairstyle types.

title: Self-Distilled Pronunciation and Accent Control for Neural Text-to-Speech
summary: Text-to-speech that reads raw text has no lexicon: a rare word is read as guessed. Remedies train a reading-and-accent channel on recorded speech or edit words one at a time from exemplars. We do neither. The frozen backbone reads a sentence containing a common word it already says correctly, and its own output then serves as the teacher for the same sentence, with that word replaced by a tagged, accented reading; this training pair is the whole idea. On Sarashina2.2-TTS, screened raters at Fleiss' kappa = 0.85 hear the prescribed accent on 0.89 of unseen words against 0.57 for kana, which cannot express one; kana wins no pair; naturalness is not measurably hurt. Moved untuned to autoregressive, diffusion, and encoder-decoder backbones, it transfers reading, 0.25 to 0.47 above no edit on 319 words, and on CosyVoice 2 accent on two words in three, but not on Irodori; the paper locates why.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a self-training method for text-to-speech (TTS) systems to learn correct pronunciation of rare/accented words without explicit lexicon training or manual editing. The approach uses a frozen TTS model as its own teacher—generating a correct reading of a sentence, then using that as supervision for the same sentence with a target word replaced by an accented variant.
AI.motivation: Current TTS systems reading raw text have no lexicon, leading to mispronunciation of rare words. Existing remedies require either training on recorded speech or manual editing of exemplars. This paper seeks a simpler approach that doesn't require either.
AI.method: Self-training approach: A frozen TTS backbone reads a sentence containing a common word it already says correctly. This output serves as the teacher for the same sentence with that word replaced by a tagged, accented reading. This creates a training pair for the model to learn proper pronunciation.
AI.result: On Sarashina2.2-TTS, human raters (Fleiss' kappa = 0.85) heard the prescribed accent on 89% of unseen words vs 57% for kana. Kana wins no pair; naturalness is not measurably hurt. When transferred to autoregressive, diffusion, and encoder-decoder backbones, the method achieved 0.25 to 0.47 improvement above no-edit baseline on 319 words. On CosyVoice 2, accent was achieved on two out of three words, but not on Irodori.
AI.conclusion: The self-training approach effectively teaches TTS systems to pronounce accented/rare words without explicit lexicon training or manual editing. The method transfers across different TTS architectures (autoregressive, diffusion, encoder-decoder), though performance varies across different TTS systems. The paper analyzes why transfer fails on some systems (Irodori).

title: VideoMM: Adaptive Macro-Micro Inference for Efficient Video MLLMs
summary: Scaling Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to long-form video understanding is bottlenecked by the explosion of visual tokens, which saturates context windows and incurs prohibitive costs. Current solutions predominantly rely on auxiliary models for token reduction but face a fundamental dilemma: lightweight encoder-driven approaches often overlook critical semantic information, whereas heavyweight MLLM-driven reduction negates the efficiency gains. {In this work, we identify a more fundamental inefficiency underlying this dilemma: while fine-grained visual details are essential for detailed understanding, they are largely redundant for the preliminary task of selecting semantically relevant regions. } Motivated by this, we introduce \textbf{VideoMM}, which marks a paradigm shift from model-centric downsizing to adaptive perceptual granularity. Specifically, our framework {decouples selection from reasoning} by executing semantic filtering on a cost-effective \textit{Macro Proxy} (derived from downscaled frames), and projecting the selected regions onto high-fidelity \textit{Micro Tokens} for detailed understanding only when necessary. Extensive evaluations show that VideoMM significantly outperforms existing solutions. It achieves a 6.13$\times$ speedup and a 7.4\% accuracy gain over full-context baselines on LongVideoBench, and further accelerates inference by 2.73$\times$ over current leading methods, establishing a highly scalable paradigm for long-video understanding. Our code is available at: https://github.com/adfh917k/VideoMM.

AI.tldr: VideoMM introduces an adaptive perceptual granularity approach for long-form video understanding in multimodal LLMs. It decouples semantic region selection (using a lightweight Macro Proxy from downscaled frames) from detailed reasoning (using high-fidelity Micro Tokens only when necessary), achieving 6.13× speedup and 7.4% accuracy gain over full-context baselines on LongVideoBench.
AI.motivation: Scaling MLLMs to long-form video is bottlenecked by the explosion of visual tokens that saturate context windows and incur high costs. Existing solutions rely on auxiliary models for token reduction but face a dilemma: lightweight encoder approaches lose critical semantic information, while heavyweight MLLM-driven reduction negates efficiency gains.
AI.method: The paper identifies a fundamental inefficiency: while fine-grained visual details are essential for detailed understanding, they are largely redundant for preliminary semantic region selection.
