The proposed VideoMM framework decouples selection from reasoning by: (1) using a cost-effective Macro Proxy (derived from downscaled frames) for semantic filtering, and (2) projecting selected regions onto high-fidelity Micro Tokens only when necessary for detailed understanding.
AI.result: VideoMM significantly outperforms existing solutions, achieving 6.13× speedup and 7.4% accuracy gain over full-context baselines on LongVideoBench, and further accelerates inference by 2.73× over current leading methods.
AI.conclusion: VideoMM establishes a highly scalable paradigm for long-video understanding by shifting from model-centric downsizing to adaptive perceptual granularity, effectively addressing the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff in token reduction for MLLMs.

title: Protocol-Preserving Context Trimming for Agentic Workflows: Benefits, Failure Regimes, and Budget Guardrails
summary: Agentic large language model (LLM) systems rely on long interaction histories to preserve instructions, tool states, intermediate decisions, and unresolved dependencies, but unrestricted context growth increases computational cost and can reduce efficiency. This study evaluates protocol-preserving context trimming as a reliability-constrained approach for multi-step agentic workflows. Five trimming strategies - recency-based, relevance-based, summarization, protocol-aware trimming, and adaptive budget guardrails - were compared across retained-context levels and workflow-complexity classes using task success, protocol adherence, valid tool calls, token savings, latency reduction, cascading failures, and critical context thresholds. Conventional strategies achieved about 60% mean token savings but lower task success (66.6-77.3%) and protocol adherence (85.5-88.6%). Protocol-aware trimming improved task success to 92.2%, while adaptive guardrails achieved 96.0% task success, 96.3% protocol adherence, and 1.0% cascading failure with 56.0% mean token savings. Retained-context budgets of 25% or less increased failure odds 10.92-fold relative to budgets of 50% or more (p < 0.001). Protocol-aware trimming produced 5.24-fold greater odds of successful completion than conventional methods under aggressive budgets, while adaptive guardrails further increased success odds 2.11-fold versus fixed protocol-aware trimming (p < 0.001). Critical context thresholds also increased with workflow complexity. These findings indicate that reliable context reduction depends more on preserving protocol-critical state than on maximizing token removal, and that adaptive guardrails can improve efficiency, scalability, and reliability in long-horizon agentic systems.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates five context trimming strategies for agentic LLM systems to balance computational efficiency with workflow reliability. Protocol-aware trimming and adaptive budget guardrails significantly outperform conventional methods, achieving up to 96% task success while maintaining 56% token savings. Context budgets below 25% increase failure risk 10.92-fold.
AI.motivation: Agentic LLM systems rely on long interaction histories but unrestricted context growth increases computational costs and reduces efficiency. This study addresses the need for reliability-constrained context reduction in multi-step agentic workflows.
AI.method: Five trimming strategies (recency-based, relevance-based, summarization, protocol-aware trimming, and adaptive budget guardrails) were compared across retained-context levels and workflow-complexity classes using 7 metrics: task success, protocol adherence, valid tool calls, token savings, latency reduction, cascading failures, and critical context thresholds.
AI.result: Conventional strategies achieved ~60% token savings but lower task success (66.6-77.3%) and protocol adherence (85.5-88.6%). Protocol-aware trimming improved task success to 92.2%. Adaptive guardrails achieved 96.0% task success, 96.3% protocol adherence, 1.0% cascading failure, and 56.0% mean token savings. Budgets ≤25% increased failure odds 10.92-fold vs. budgets ≥50% (p<0.001). Protocol-aware trimming showed 5.24-fold greater success odds than conventional methods under aggressive budgets; adaptive guardrails further increased success odds 2.11-fold vs. fixed protocol-aware trimming (p<0.001). Critical context thresholds increased with workflow complexity.
AI.conclusion: Reliable context reduction depends more on preserving protocol-critical state than maximizing token removal. Adaptive guardrails can improve efficiency, scalability, and reliability in long-horizon agentic systems. Context budgets below 25% significantly increase failure risk.

title: Signed p-adic Residual Encodings of Finite-Domain All-Different Systems with a Sudoku Case Study
comment: 31 pages, 7 figures. Accepted for publication in p-Adic Numbers, Ultrametric Analysis and Applications
summary: We study signed, weighted affine $p$-adic residual objectives as native encodings of finite-domain constraints. For primes that separate the finite alphabet, sufficiently weighted positive unary rows pin each coefficient to its allowed set, while negative rows reward unequal endpoints or clause satisfaction. A coordinatewise domination theorem places every global minimiser in the finite domain; there the loss is, up to an additive constant, the all-different conflict count or the negative number of satisfied CNF clauses. Standard Sudoku provides an $81$-coefficient case study without a one-hot lift. A client-side implementation exposes the generated dataframes, arithmetic, diagnostics, and searches.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using signed, weighted affine p-adic residual objectives as native encodings for finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems. The approach uses positive unary rows to constrain coefficients to allowed sets and negative rows to reward constraint satisfaction. The method is applied to Sudoku puzzles as a case study.
AI.motivation: The motivation appears to be developing a new native encoding method for finite-domain constraints that doesn't require one-hot lifting (a common technique in CSP encoding). The authors aim to provide a coordinatewise domination theorem that ensures global minimizers lie in the finite domain, where the loss function corresponds to conflict counts or clause satisfaction.
AI.method: The method involves: (1) Using primes that separate the finite alphabet, (2) Employing sufficiently weighted positive unary rows to pin coefficients to allowed sets, (3) Using negative rows to reward unequal endpoints or clause satisfaction, (4) Applying a coordinatewise domination theorem to locate global minimizers in the finite domain.
AI.result: The result is that in the finite domain, the loss function becomes (up to an additive constant) either the all-different conflict count or the negative number of satisfied CNF clauses. The paper demonstrates this with a standard Sudoku puzzle as an 81-coefficient case study without requiring a one-hot lift. A client-side implementation is provided that exposes dataframes, arithmetic, diagnostics, and searches.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that p-adic residual objectives provide a viable native encoding for finite-domain constraints, avoiding the need for one-hot encoding while maintaining the ability to count conflicts or measure clause satisfaction. The Sudoku case study demonstrates practical applicability.

title: Where Should the KV Cache Live? Placement Policies Across GPU, CPU, and SSD for Long-Lived Sessions
summary: GPU high bandwidth memory is scarce and expensive, and KV caches consume much of it as chats, agent loops, and document question answering accumulate state. Systems such as Mooncake, LMCache, FlexGen, InfiniGen, and AttentionStore extend GPU memory with CPU DRAM and SSD. The harder question is which blocks belong in each tier, when to move or evict them, and whether prefetching helps. We study these choices in a discrete event simulator spanning GPU HBM, CPU DRAM, and SSD, calibrated against a random forest execution time predictor. We compare recency, reuse frequency, predicted reuse, and an EWMA predictor with prefetch lookahead across chat, agent, and document question answering workloads. Tiering supports 73.02 times more concurrent sessions per GPU and lowers cost per session by 62.04 times. These gains come from tier capacities of 1 plus 8 plus 64, not placement policy. Decode is compute bound at batch size one in our setup, so placement barely affects throughput. It mainly changes PCIe migration traffic and time to first token. Recency produces 2.30 times less migration traffic than reuse frequency for chat. Reuse frequency performs best for agents and document question answering. The existing predicted reuse policy is byte identical to recency, making its agent recommendation effectively recency. A genuine EWMA predictor changes behavior but still ranks behind reuse frequency on the workloads prediction was expected to help. Prefetching does not justify its bandwidth cost. Across the policy and cache size grid, even an oracle with knowledge of future requests never beats no prefetch on migration traffic. Workload specific placement can reduce data movement, but the predicted reuse and prefetch recommendations are not supported as implemented.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates memory tiering strategies for GPU high bandwidth memory (HBM) in LLM inference, comparing policies (recency, reuse frequency, predicted reuse, EWMA with prefetch) across chat, agent, and document QA workloads. The key finding is that capacity gains (73x more sessions, 62x cost reduction) come from having multiple tiers rather than placement policy, as decode is compute-bound at batch size one.
AI.motivation: GPU HBM is scarce and expensive, and KV caches consume significant memory in LLM applications. Existing systems extend GPU memory with CPU DRAM and SSD, but the fundamental questions of which blocks belong in each tier, when to move/evict them, and whether prefetching helps remained unanswered.
AI.method: The authors built a discrete event simulator spanning GPU HBM, CPU DRAM, and SSD, calibrated against a random forest execution time predictor. They compared four policies: recency, reuse frequency, predicted reuse, and EWMA predictor with prefetch lookahead across chat, agent, and document QA workloads.
AI.result: Tiering supports 73.02x more concurrent sessions per GPU and lowers cost per session by 62.04x. These gains come from tier capacities (1 + 8 + 64 GB), not placement policy. Recency produces 2.30x less migration traffic than reuse frequency for chat, while reuse frequency performs best for agents and document QA. The predicted reuse policy is byte identical to recency. EWMA predictor changes behavior but still ranks behind reuse frequency. Prefetching does not justify its bandwidth cost—even an oracle with future knowledge never beats no prefetch on migration traffic.
AI.conclusion: Placement policy matters less than having tiered memory. At batch size one, decode is compute-bound so throughput is unaffected by placement—it mainly affects PCIe migration traffic and time to first token. Recency is best for chat, reuse frequency for agents/DQA. Neither predicted reuse nor prefetching, as implemented, provides practical benefits. Workload-specific placement can reduce data movement, but current implementations of prediction and prefetching are not supported by the results.

title: MDN-Control: Mask-Depth-Noise Guided Region Control for Multi-Subject Video Editing
summary: Multi subject video editing modifies designated subjects while preserving non target content, but faces cross subject attribute leakage, and occlusion ambiguity. Existing approaches rely on masks and struggle to distinguish overlapping subjects or ensure consistent generation. To address these limitations, we propose MDN-Control, a training free framework jointly controlling target localization, occlusion geometry, and appearance initialization. Specifically, mask-guided localization provides consistent target localization, while depth-aware occlusion control resolves ambiguous boundaries between overlapping subjects. We further introduce noise latent prompting, which retrieves Gaussian initializations from a noise library for prompt relevant priors. Experiments on MSVBench show that MDN-Control achieves the lowest CM-Err and the highest Q-Edit, while maintaining competitive text alignment and temporal consistency, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining spatial, geometric, and latent priors for multi subject video editing.

AI.tldr: MDN-Control is a training-free framework for multi-subject video editing that addresses cross-subject attribute leakage and occlusion ambiguity by jointly controlling target localization, occlusion geometry, and appearance initialization through mask-guided localization, depth-aware occlusion control, and noise latent prompting.
AI.motivation: Multi-subject video editing faces challenges including cross-subject attribute leakage and occlusion ambiguity. Existing mask-based approaches struggle to distinguish overlapping subjects and ensure consistent generation.
AI.method: MDN-Control combines three components: (1) mask-guided localization for consistent target localization, (2) depth-aware occlusion control to resolve ambiguous boundaries between overlapping subjects, and (3) noise latent prompting that retrieves Gaussian initializations from a noise library for prompt-relevant priors.
AI.result: MDN-Control achieves the lowest CM-Err and highest Q-Edit on MSVBench while maintaining competitive text alignment and temporal consistency.
AI.conclusion: Combining spatial (mask-guided localization), geometric (depth-aware occlusion control), and latent (noise latent prompting) priors is effective for multi-subject video editing, successfully addressing cross-subject leakage and occlusion ambiguity without training.

title: PhysStream: Streaming Physics-Grounded Video Generation with Structured Scene Memory and Fine-Grained Motion Control
summary: Interactive control for video generation is moving from coarse prompts toward fine-grained, physically meaningful manipulation of dynamic scenes. Yet existing controllable methods either require the full control schedule before generation starts, or use pixel-space signals that dictate object positions rather than physical dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose PhysStream, an autoregressive model for physics-grounded image-to-video synthesis that incorporates structured scene memory---positional maps and object tracking maps derived online from previously generated frames---and supports fine-grained motion control via sparse velocity-increment signals that encode physical quantities, letting the model learn the underlying dynamics. We train our model in two stages: a bidirectional model is first finetuned with motion-control conditioning, then a causal autoregressive model is trained with additional structured scene memory, further improving physical consistency. PhysStream enables interactive, mid-generation control over multi-object tabletop rigid-body scenes---a capability not supported by prior methods---reducing motion distribution distance (FVMD) by 33% and trajectory error by 12% over the strongest baselines on synthetic benchmarks, and is preferred by human evaluators in over 85% of in-the-wild comparisons. Please check our website for more details: https://czzzzh.github.io/PhysStream

AI.tldr: PhysStream is an autoregressive model for physics-grounded image-to-video synthesis that incorporates structured scene memory and supports fine-grained motion control via sparse velocity-increment signals, enabling interactive mid-generation control over multi-object rigid-body scenes.
AI.motivation: Existing controllable video generation methods either require the full control schedule before generation starts, or use pixel-space signals that dictate object positions rather than physical dynamics, lacking support for fine-grained, physically meaningful manipulation during generation.
AI.method: PhysStream uses an autoregressive model with two-stage training: (1) a bidirectional model finetuned with motion-control conditioning, then (2) a causal autoregressive model trained with additional structured scene memory (positional maps and object tracking maps derived online from previously generated frames). Motion control is provided via sparse velocity-increment signals that encode physical quantities.
AI.result: PhysStream reduces motion distribution distance (FVMD) by 33% and trajectory error by 12% over the strongest baselines on synthetic benchmarks, and is preferred by human evaluators in over 85% of in-the-wild comparisons.
AI.conclusion: PhysStream enables interactive, mid-generation control over multi-object tabletop rigid-body scenes—a capability not supported by prior methods—demonstrating superior physical consistency and user preference compared to existing approaches.

title: SpiroPhonia: Non-Invasive Respiratory Health Assessment from Spontaneous Speech
summary: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) remains a major global health challenge, emphasizing the need for accessible and non-invasive detection. Since speech production is fundamentally linked to respiratory physiology, its disruptions can serve as indirect indicators of pulmonary impairment. This study introduces SpiroPhonia, a machine learning framework that leverages spontaneous speech for respiratory health assessment. We evaluated SpiroPhonia on a new dataset of 201 speakers (102 with COPD, 99 healthy controls). By integrating statistical analysis with recursive feature selection, we identified a compact set of discriminative speech markers. Our best model achieved 78% accuracy, 80% F1-score, and 87% AUC. This performance on spontaneous speech is competitive with methods using controlled laboratory recordings. Findings demonstrate that everyday speech encodes robust respiratory biomarkers, paving the way for continuous health monitoring via voice-enabled technologies.

AI.tldr: SpiroPhonia is a machine learning framework that uses spontaneous speech to detect COPD, achieving 78% accuracy, 80% F1-score, and 87% AUC on 201 speakers. The study demonstrates that speech biomarkers can serve as non-invasive indicators of respiratory health.
AI.motivation: COPD is a major global health burden, and current detection methods are often invasive or require specialized equipment. Since speech production is linked to respiratory physiology, speech disruptions could serve as accessible, non-invasive biomarkers for pulmonary impairment detection.
AI.method: The study developed SpiroPhonia using statistical analysis combined with recursive feature selection to identify discriminative speech markers from spontaneous speech. The model was evaluated on a dataset of 201 speakers (102 COPD patients, 99 healthy controls).
AI.result: The best model achieved 78% accuracy, 80% F1-score, and 87% AUC. This performance is competitive with methods requiring controlled laboratory recordings, demonstrating that spontaneous speech contains robust respiratory biomarkers.
AI.conclusion: Everyday speech encodes reliable respiratory health indicators, enabling continuous health monitoring through voice-enabled technologies and providing a promising accessible alternative for COPD screening.

title: AI Policies: Help or Hindrance? A Software Developer's Perspective
summary: AI policies introduced by software organisations to mitigate LLM-related risks such as sensitive information leaks and unauthorised usage are not useful if software developers do not engage with them. We draw on 19 software developer interviews to show how AI policies help and hinder developers. We suggest approaches to support managers and decision makers with a developer-centric approach to introducing AI policies.

title: You Don't Need To Train: Agentic Heuristic Learning Studio for Executable Human Activity Recognition
summary: Human activity recognition (HAR) is usually framed as gradient-based training of neural networks. Agentic Heuristic Learning (AHL) Studio explores a complementary view inspired by human cognitive learning: people learn activities by remembering examples, forming rules, and repairing mistakes, not by backpropagating. This proposed tool implements AHL for HAR: a learning-time agent reasons over sensor protocols, proposes executable heuristic policies, records repair traces, and exports an LLM-free policy for edge deployment. We focus on the HAR benchmark family and provide an end-to-end workflow from dataset observation to edge-oriented export. On eleven HAR datasets evaluated so far, AHL policies reach strong executable-policy performance while remaining inspectable, editable, and replayable \footnote{https://github.com/zhaxidele/ahl-ts-studio}.

AI.tldr: AHL Studio proposes a novel approach to Human Activity Recognition (HAR) that mimics human cognitive learning processes (example recall, rule formation, mistake repair) rather than using traditional gradient-based neural network training. It implements an agentic system that reasons over sensor protocols, generates executable heuristic policies, records repair traces, and exports LLM-free policies for edge deployment.
AI.motivation: Traditional HAR relies on gradient-based neural network training, which differs fundamentally from how humans learn activities. This work explores a complementary approach inspired by human cognitive learning: people learn by remembering examples, forming rules, and repairing mistakes—not by backpropagating gradients.
AI.method: AHL Studio implements a learning-time agent that: (1) reasons over sensor protocols, (2) proposes executable heuristic policies, (3) records repair traces, and (4) exports LLM-free policies for edge deployment. The workflow spans from dataset observation to edge-oriented export, targeting the HAR benchmark family.
AI.result: Evaluated on eleven HAR datasets, AHL policies achieve strong executable-policy performance while maintaining key properties: inspectability, editability, and replayability.
AI.conclusion: AHL Studio demonstrates that heuristic-based learning can effectively address HAR tasks with practical advantages for edge deployment, offering a viable alternative to gradient-based neural network approaches with added transparency and interpretability.

title: Toward Governance-Aware Autonomous GIS: A Narrative Review of Ethical and Privacy Risks in LLM-Enabled GeoAI
summary: Geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) powered by large language models (LLMs) is expanding the capacity to query, generate, and interpret spatial information through natural-language interfaces and agentic autonomous GIS workflows. This capability creates governance challenges that general AI ethics discussions do not fully capture, including passive location inference from mobility traces, spatially structured bias amplification driven by spatial autocorrelation and scale effects, hallucinated spatial facts, and uncertainty compounding across multimodal geospatial inputs. This narrative review identifies eight recurring issues in LLM-enabled GeoAI: data provenance and consent, spatial privacy and inference risk, algorithmic bias and spatial inequity, spatial mechanisms as structural risk (spatial autocorrelation, the modifiable areal unit problem, and scale effects), LLM-specific technical risks, explainability, policy and regulatory gaps, and public enablement and workforce development. For each issue, we characterize the underlying mechanism, ground it in an illustrative example from the literature, and assess the current state of technical or institutional responses, ranging from largely unaddressed to actively debated or subject to emerging policy. Building on this synthesis, we propose a governance-aware architecture for LLM-enabled autonomous GIS that maps each issue to enforceable controls and auditable artifacts across the geospatial data lifecycle, illustrated through a worked flood-response routing scenario. The review highlights a persistent evidence gap: proposed responses remain largely conceptual, and field-tested evaluations of governance controls for LLM-enabled GeoAI remain limited. We close by outlining a research agenda emphasizing empirical validation, spatially specific interpretability tools, and workforce training aligned with these emerging risks.

AI.tldr: This narrative review examines governance challenges in LLM-enabled GeoAI systems, identifying eight recurring issues including data provenance, spatial privacy, algorithmic bias, spatial mechanisms as structural risk, technical risks, explainability, policy gaps, and workforce development. The paper proposes a governance-aware architecture for autonomous GIS and highlights a significant evidence gap in empirical validation of proposed governance controls.
AI.motivation: The rapid expansion of GeoAI powered by large language models creates governance challenges that general AI ethics frameworks fail to address, including location inference, spatial bias amplification, hallucinated spatial facts, and uncertainty compounding across multimodal geospatial inputs.
AI.method: Narrative review identifying eight recurring issues in LLM-enabled GeoAI through literature analysis, with each issue characterized by underlying mechanisms, illustrative examples, and assessment of current technical or institutional responses. A governance-aware architecture is proposed and illustrated through a flood-response routing scenario.
AI.result: Identified eight governance issues: (1) data provenance and consent, (2) spatial privacy and inference risk, (3) algorithmic bias and spatial inequity, (4) spatial mechanisms as structural risk (spatial autocorrelation, MAUP, scale effects), (5) LLM-specific technical risks, (6) explainability, (7) policy and regulatory gaps, and (8) public enablement and workforce development. Proposed a governance-aware architecture mapping issues to enforceable controls across the geospatial data lifecycle.
AI.conclusion: A persistent evidence gap exists: proposed governance responses remain largely conceptual, and field-tested evaluations are limited. A research agenda emphasizing empirical validation, spatially specific interpretability tools, and workforce training aligned with emerging risks is needed.

title: VPRef: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for Referring Remote Sensing Image Segmentation
summary: Rapid advancements in vision-language models have propelled Referring Remote Sensing Image Segmentation (RRSIS) to the forefront of Earth observation. However, practical deployments suffer severe performance degradation under a coupled dual-drift paradigm: visual domain drift from cross-spatial-resolution mismatches and spectral variations, alongside textual logic drift from unconstrained, variable user-input granularities. To mitigate these bottlenecks, this paper establishes the first cross-domain RRSIS benchmark, designated as the Vaihingen-Potsdam Referring (VPRef) dataset, comprising 46,972 language-image-annotation triplets organized into a three-tier linguistic hierarchy. Building upon this benchmark, we develop a tailored parameter-efficient domain adaptation baseline anchored on the Segment Anything Model (SAM3) via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). Our framework counteracts visual distribution discrepancies through pseudo-label-driven self-training and addresses textual logic drift via random multi-granularity text prompt mixing. Crucially, the distribution of empirical metrics across ablative variants suggests a potential decoupling between cross-modal semantic robustification and visual domain alignment, demonstrating that linguistic variance drives fine-grained semantic invariance while pseudo-label propagation governs macro-scale spatial grid alignment. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate the proposed framework achieves superior cross-domain segmentation boundaries while modifying merely 1.08\% of the foundational parameter footprint, establishing a robust baseline for future multi-modal remote sensing domain adaptation research. The dataset and code will be available at https://github.com/quanweiliu/VPRef.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the first cross-domain Referring Remote Sensing Image Segmentation (RRSIS) benchmark (VPRef) with 46,972 language-image-annotation triplets and proposes a parameter-efficient domain adaptation framework using SAM3 with LoRA. The method addresses visual domain drift and textual logic drift through pseudo-label self-training and multi-granularity text prompt mixing, achieving superior cross-domain segmentation while modifying only 1.08% of parameters.
AI.motivation: Practical deployments of vision-language models for RRSIS suffer severe performance degradation under a coupled dual-drift paradigm: (1) visual domain drift from cross-spatial-resolution mismatches and spectral variations, and (2) textual logic drift from unconstrained, variable user-input granularities. Existing methods lack a proper cross-domain benchmark to address these issues.
AI.method: The authors established the VPRef benchmark with 46,972 language-image-annotation triplets organized in a three-tier linguistic hierarchy. They developed a parameter-efficient domain adaptation baseline using SAM3 with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). The framework addresses visual distribution discrepancies through pseudo-label-driven self-training and handles textual logic drift via random multi-granularity text prompt mixing.
AI.result: The proposed framework achieves superior cross-domain segmentation boundaries while modifying merely 1.08% of the foundational parameter footprint. The study reveals a potential decoupling between cross-modal semantic robustification and visual domain alignment, where linguistic variance drives fine-grained semantic invariance while pseudo-label propagation governs macro-scale spatial grid alignment.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a robust baseline for future multi-modal remote sensing domain adaptation research, demonstrating that parameter-efficient adaptation through LoRA can effectively address the coupled dual-drift paradigm in RRSIS tasks.

title: LACE: Layer-Wise Compression for Dynamic Frame Rate Codecs
summary: Neural audio codecs are a key component in speech language modeling. However, their high frame rates lead to long sequence lengths, increasing computational costs. Dynamic frame rate codecs mitigate this by reducing the effective frame rate using a compression step to merge multiple frames together. However, most prior methods either operate on single-codebook codecs or apply a single compression step before multi-layer quantization. This forces all quantization layers to share the same segmentation boundaries, despite the residual embeddings at different quantization layers exhibiting different rates of change over time. We propose LACE (Layer-Adaptive Codec Encoding), a dynamic frame rate codec that applies an independent compression step at each quantization layer, enabling layer-specific segmentation boundaries. To use LACE tokens in downstream text-to-speech (TTS), we further introduce union alignment and boundary anchor mechanisms to make durations consistent across layers while preserving compression benefits. Experiments on LibriTTS show that LACE offers a better rate-quality tradeoff than prior dynamic frame rate methods on the reconstruction task and improves TTS inference efficiency while maintaining competitive synthesis quality. Our code is released as part of the ESPnet3 codec recipe.

AI.tldr: LACE (Layer-Adaptive Codec Encoding) is a dynamic frame rate neural audio codec that applies independent compression steps at each quantization layer, enabling layer-specific segmentation boundaries, with mechanisms to ensure duration consistency across layers for TTS applications.
AI.motivation: Neural audio codecs have high frame rates leading to long sequence lengths and computational costs. Existing dynamic frame rate methods either use single-codebook codecs or apply a single compression step before multi-layer quantization, forcing all quantization layers to share the same segmentation boundaries despite different layers having different rates of change in their residual embeddings.
AI.method: LACE applies independent compression steps at each quantization layer, enabling layer-specific segmentation boundaries. To use LACE tokens in TTS, the authors introduce union alignment and boundary anchor mechanisms to make durations consistent across layers while preserving compression benefits.
AI.result: On LibriTTS, LACE offers a better rate-quality tradeoff than prior dynamic frame rate methods on the reconstruction task and improves TTS inference efficiency while maintaining competitive synthesis quality.
AI.conclusion: LACE successfully enables layer-adaptive segmentation in neural audio codecs, achieving better compression-quality tradeoffs and improved TTS inference efficiency. The code is released as part of the ESPnet3 codec recipe.

title: ExecuCritic: Calibrated Critic Shaping for Code Generation with Verifiable Rewards
comment: 33rd International Conference on Neural Information Processing (ICONIP 2026)
summary: Execution feedback is a useful supervision signal for code models because unit tests are objective and directly measure program correctness. Its weakness is that an entire program is often reduced to one pass or fail bit, leaving RLVR to solve a difficult credit assignment problem. At the same time, coding systems often include separate reviewer or tester roles, but these critics are usually prompted rather than trained and are not calibrated against execution. We propose ExecuCritic, a joint training framework in which a coder and a critic are updated on the same execution rollouts. The critic predicts pass or fail outcomes and gives short diagnostic feedback; the coder uses this signal only when the critic agrees with the executor on the current rollout group. Across eight code benchmarks and two recent open backbones, ExecuCritic improves over GRPO without a critic, prompted reviewer systems and scalar reward model baselines, while requiring fewer policy gradient steps and fewer sandbox executions. Ablations and reliability analyses suggest that the gains come from better credit assignment rather than larger sampling budgets.

AI.tldr: ExecuCritic proposes a joint training framework for code models where a coder and critic are trained together on execution rollouts. The critic predicts pass/fail outcomes and provides diagnostic feedback, while the coder only uses the critic's signal when it agrees with the executor. This approach improves over GRPO, prompted reviewers, and scalar reward models across 8 benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Execution feedback (unit tests) provides only binary pass/fail signals, creating a difficult credit assignment problem in RLVR. Additionally, existing reviewer roles are prompted而非 trained and not calibrated against actual execution.
AI.method: Joint training framework where both coder and critic are updated on the same execution rollouts. The critic predicts pass/fail outcomes and generates short diagnostic feedback. The coder only uses the critic's signal when the critic agrees with the executor on the current rollout group.
AI.result: ExecuCritic improves over GRPO without a critic, prompted reviewer systems, and scalar reward model baselines across eight code benchmarks with two open backbones, while requiring fewer policy gradient steps and fewer sandbox executions.
AI.conclusion: The gains come from better credit assignment rather than larger sampling budgets. The key innovation is the calibration between critic and executor, ensuring the critic's feedback is reliable before being used for training.

title: A panoramic aerodynamic performance prediction method for turbomachinery cascades using transformer-enhanced neural operator
comment: Author manuscript updated to align core methods and results with the published article; 41 pages, 20 figures, 14 tables
summary: To enable flexible and rapid aerodynamic performance evaluation in turbomachinery design, this paper proposes a panoramic performance prediction framework. Unlike most previous prediction models that directly predict the objective functions of interest, our approach first predicts the basic parameters of the Navier-Stokes equations, such as temperature, pressure, and density. Utilizing these basic physical quantities, it subsequently predicts key performance parameters of the turbine stage meridian plane. By adopting this methodology, our proposed panoramic performance prediction framework functions similarly to a CFD simulator, capable of predicting various objective of interest to the designers. To enhance prediction accuracy, a transformer-enhanced neural operator (TNO) is introduced within this framework. Using the Rotor 37 blades as a reference, the proposed TNO is trained to predict the performance of a transonic compressor blade in the meridian plane. The TNO can accurately predict total quantities such as isentropic efficiency, mass flow, and distributions of total pressure ratio. Remarkably, the prediction error of TNO is observed to be smaller than that of state-of-the-art deep learning operators such as the FNO and DeepONet. Furthermore, the TNO is applied to downstream tasks, including sensitivity analysis and optimization of various objective functions. The results confirm that the TNO can operate almost like a CFD simulator, while reducing the computational cost of downstream tasks by four orders of magnitude. The effectiveness and reliability of the proposed TNO for solving different kinds of downstream tasks have been well demonstrated.

AI.tldr: A panoramic performance prediction framework using transformer-enhanced neural operator (TNO) for rapid aerodynamic evaluation in turbomachinery design, achieving CFD-level accuracy at 4 orders of magnitude lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Enable flexible and rapid aerodynamic performance evaluation in turbomachinery design, addressing the computational expense of traditional CFD methods.
AI.method: Proposes a two-stage approach: first predicts basic Navier-Stokes parameters (temperature, pressure, density), then predicts key performance parameters of turbine stage meridian plane. Uses TNO (Transformer-enhanced Neural Operator) trained on Rotor 37 transonic compressor blades.
AI.result: TNO accurately predicts isentropic efficiency, mass flow, and total pressure ratio distributions with lower error than state-of-the-art deep learning operators (FNO and DeepONet). Reduces computational cost of downstream tasks by 4 orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: TNO functions effectively as a fast CFD simulator for turbomachinery design, enabling sensitivity analysis and optimization tasks with demonstrated reliability and significant computational savings.

title: Metacognitive Steering: Learning the Structure of Scientific Judgment
summary: Long-horizon scientific discovery requires agents to alternate between exploration, disciplined execution, and critical reassessment as evidence changes. Current language models are trained primarily on the products of science and optimized using outcome-level signals, providing limited supervision for these process-level shifts in scientific judgment. We investigate whether such judgment can be recovered from scientist interaction traces and used to control the internal computation of a frozen frontier model. Using contrastive interventions collected during real scientific research, we identify a coordinated, low-dimensional control structure within Kimi 2.6, a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model. Residual analysis, attention-weight subspace alignment, and cross-layer singular value decomposition converge on a mid-depth control surface spanning key layers. We introduce Metacognitive Steering, an inference-time controller that reads the model's cognitive regime and dynamically composes layer-specific interventions for exploration, procedural convergence, or critical reassessment without modifying model parameters. Behavioral analyses show that this control produces more sustained exploration, explicit pruning, and evidence-responsive synthesis. We operationalize the method in Columbus-1, an autonomous research system that identified eight independently reproduced, attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in BlueZ and directed the design, simulation, and fabrication of a ten-foot rocket intended to land propulsively using non-throttleable solid motors. Together, these results show that process-level scientific judgment can provide supervision for interpretable, dynamic control over a model's reasoning strategy.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Metacognitive Steering, a method to control a frozen frontier language model (Kimi 2.6) by identifying a low-dimensional control structure within the model. The method enables dynamic layer-specific interventions for exploration, procedural convergence, or critical reassessment without modifying model parameters. It is operationalized in Columbus-1, an autonomous research system that found vulnerabilities in BlueZ and designed a ten-foot rocket.
AI.motivation: Current language models are trained on the products of science with outcome-level signals, providing limited supervision for process-level shifts in scientific judgment. The authors aim to recover such judgment from scientist interaction traces and use it to control a frozen frontier model's internal computation.
AI.method: The authors use contrastive interventions collected during real scientific research to identify a coordinated, low-dimensional control structure within Kimi 2.6 (a trillion-parameter MoE model). They employ three convergence techniques: residual analysis, attention-weight subspace alignment, and cross-layer singular value decomposition. These methods identify a mid-depth control surface spanning key layers. Metacognitive Steering is then introduced as an inference-time controller that reads the model's cognitive regime and dynamically composes layer-specific interventions.
AI.result: Behavioral analyses show that this control produces more sustained exploration, explicit pruning, and evidence-responsive synthesis. The method was operationalized in Columbus-1, an autonomous research system that identified eight independently reproduced, attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in BlueZ and directed the design, simulation, and fabrication of a ten-foot rocket with non-throttleable solid motors for propulsive landing.
AI.conclusion: Process-level scientific judgment can provide supervision for interpretable, dynamic control over a model's reasoning strategy. This enables autonomous scientific discovery with more human-like cognitive processes.

title: Which Pretext Task Transfers? Self-Supervised Pretraining Objectives for Lung Ultrasound
summary: Self-supervised learning (SSL) can reduce the need for labelled medical images, but the choice of pretext objective remains unclear for lung ultrasound (LUS). Contrastive learning, masked reconstruction, and joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) differ in the space in which their targets are defined, yet existing ultrasound studies compare them under different corpora, backbones, and evaluation protocols. We compare these three objective families using the same encoder backbone, pretraining corpus, optimisation schedule, and frozen-evaluation protocol. Encoders are pretrained on COVID-BLUeS LUS videos and evaluated with linear, $k$NN, and attentive probes at 5\%, 10\%, 50\%, and 100\% label budgets. Evaluation is performed on POCUS using patient-level five-fold cross-validation and on the independently acquired Mendeley-Uganda dataset, which is excluded from both pretraining and probe fitting. At the full label budget under linear probing, VideoMAE and V-JEPA achieve $66.5 \pm 13.1$ and $65.4 \pm 11.7$ balanced accuracy on POCUS, while MoCo achieves $42.1 \pm 1.2$. On Mendeley-Uganda, the ranking reverses: MoCo performs best at $62.7 \pm 1.0$, followed by VideoMAE at $53.8 \pm 2.8$, while V-JEPA falls near chance at $35.1 \pm 4.9$. These results show that POCUS probe accuracy alone does not identify the objective that transfers best across datasets. We also outline planned representation-level analyses to examine this reversal. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/moeinheidari7829/LUSVideoSSL.

AI.tldr: This paper compares three self-supervised learning (SSL) objectives—contrastive learning (MoCo), masked reconstruction (VideoMAE), and joint-embedding predictive architectures (V-JEPA)—for lung ultrasound (LUS) video analysis. Using identical backbones, corpora, and evaluation protocols, the study reveals a surprising reversal in performance across datasets: VideoMAE and V-JEPA outperform MoCo on POCUS data, but MoCo transfers best to the independent Mendeley-Uganda dataset.
AI.motivation: Self-supervised learning can reduce dependency on labeled medical images, but the optimal pretext objective for lung ultrasound remains unclear. Prior ultrasound studies compare methods under different conditions (corpora, backbones, evaluation protocols), making fair comparisons impossible. This work addresses the need for a systematic, controlled comparison to identify which SSL objective generalizes best across domains.
AI.method: The authors pretrained encoders with the same backbone architecture on COVID-BLUeS LUS videos using identical optimization schedules. Evaluation used frozen-feature probes (linear, kNN, and attentive) at 5%, 10%, 50%, and 100% label budgets. Two datasets were used: POCUS (patient-level five-fold cross-validation) and Mendeley-Uganda (independent dataset excluded from both pretraining and probe fitting).
AI.result: At full label budget under linear probing on POCUS, VideoMAE achieved 66.5±13.1 and V-JEPA achieved 65.4±11.7 balanced accuracy, while MoCo achieved only 42.1±1.2. However, on the independent Mendeley-Uganda dataset, the ranking reversed: MoCo performed best at 62.7±1.0, followed by VideoMAE at 53.8±2.8, while V-JEPA fell near chance at 35.1±4.9. This demonstrates that in-distribution performance does not predict out-of-distribution generalization.
AI.conclusion: The choice of SSL pretext objective significantly impacts transfer learning performance, and in-distribution (POCUS) accuracy alone cannot identify which objective will transfer best to new domains. MoCo's contrastive learning approach generalizes better to the independent Ugandan dataset, while VideoMAE and V-JEPA perform well on the training distribution but fail to transfer. The authors plan representation-level analyses to understand this performance reversal.

title: An Exploratory Study of Dependabot Cooldown Adoption in Open-Source GitHub Projects
summary: Automated dependency updates can rapidly propagate malicious package releases before maintainers and the broader community have enough time to detect them. In July 2025, GitHub made Dependabot cooldown generally available as a defense against software supply chain attacks. However, the effects of its early adoption remain unknown. In this exploratory study, we empirically examine how popular open-source GitHub repositories adopt and configure the feature and investigate their motivations. We find that security concerns motivated 83 of 92 adoption events with known motivations. Security linter warnings triggered 43 of 75 security-only adoptions. Among 251 ecosystems within repositories that retained cooldown, 97.2% set a general delay. Of these, 64.3% used seven days, while use of each update type setting was below 10%. Early adopters therefore favor simple default delays over fine-grained controls. These findings suggest that tools could provide robust defaults reflecting ecosystem support and reserve fine-grained controls for dependencies with clear update priorities.

AI.tldr: This study examines the early adoption of GitHub's Dependabot cooldown feature, designed to defend against software supply chain attacks by delaying automated dependency updates. Analysis of popular open-source repositories reveals security concerns drove 90% of adoptions, with 64.3% using the default seven-day delay, indicating a preference for simple defaults over fine-grained controls.
AI.motivation: Automated dependency updates can rapidly spread malicious package releases before the community detects them. GitHub released Dependabot cooldown as a defense, but its early adoption effects were unknown, warranting empirical investigation.
AI.method: Exploratory study analyzing popular open-source GitHub repositories to examine how they adopted and configured Dependabot cooldown, investigating 92 adoption events with known motivations and 251 ecosystems with retained cooldown settings.
AI.result: Security concerns motivated 83 of 92 adoption events (90%). Security linter warnings triggered 43 of 75 security-only adoptions. Among 251 ecosystems with retained cooldown, 97.2% set a general delay, with 64.3% using seven days (default), while individual update type settings were each below 10%.
AI.conclusion: Early adopters prefer simple default delays over fine-grained controls. Tools should provide robust defaults reflecting ecosystem support and reserve fine-grained controls for dependencies with clear update priorities.

title: A Dynamic Aggregation Strategy Enhanced Efficient Global Optimization Algorithm for Solving High-Dimensional Turbomachinery Design Problems
comment: Author manuscript updated to align core methods and results with the published article; 37 pages, 14 figures, 11 tables
summary: In order to solve the high-dimensional ($d \geq 30$) expensive black-box problems within budget, an efficient global optimization (EGO) algorithm with a dynamic aggregation strategy is proposed, labeled as DA-EGO. Specifically, the DA-EGO decomposes the original high-dimensional design space into a set of low-dimensional subspaces for efficient surrogate-based optimization search, and the optimal solutions of subspaces are combined as an elite point for the global search. Most importantly, the subspaces are not fixed. Instead, the subspace variables are updated in each iteration, according to the variable interaction analyses in the sub- and full-spaces. The perturbation method and the analysis of variance are used to detect variable interactions. To further accelerate the optimization progress, the searching ranges of subspaces are also adaptively adjusted according to the analyses of subspace optimization results of the previous iteration. Tests on 21 benchmark instances, comprising seven functions at 30, 60, and 90 dimensions, show that DA-EGO is effective on separable and partially separable problems under a budget of 1500 function evaluations. Its advantage is case-dependent: on the non-separable shifted Rosenbrock function, GSGA performs better at 60 and 90 dimensions, while the 30-dimensional results are statistically comparable to IKAEA and GSGA. Moreover, the advantage of DA-EGO is also seen in the aerodynamic optimization of a transonic rotor blade with 28 variables as well as the compressor stage optimization with 60 variables. With the above, the effectiveness of the proposed DA-EGO has been well demonstrated.

AI.tldr: DA-EGO is an Efficient Global Optimization algorithm with dynamic aggregation strategy designed for high-dimensional (d ≥ 30) expensive black-box problems. It decomposes high-dimensional design spaces into low-dimensional subspaces that are dynamically updated each iteration based on variable interaction analysis, and adaptively adjusts searching ranges based on previous optimization results.
AI.motivation: Solve high-dimensional (d ≥ 30) expensive black-box optimization problems within limited function evaluation budgets.
AI.method: 1) Decompose high-dimensional space into low-dimensional subspaces; 2) Use perturbation method and ANOVA to detect variable interactions; 3) Dynamically update subspace variables in each iteration based on interaction analysis; 4) Adaptively adjust searching ranges based on previous subspace optimization results; 5) Combine optimal solutions of subspaces as elite points for global search.
AI.result: DA-EGO is effective on separable and partially separable problems under 1500 function evaluations. On non-separable shifted Rosenbrock function, GSGA performs better at 60 and 90 dimensions, while 30-dimensional results are comparable to IKAEA and GSGA. Successfully applied to aerodynamic optimization of transonic rotor blade (28 variables) and compressor stage optimization (60 variables).
AI.conclusion: The proposed DA-EGO algorithm is effective for high-dimensional expensive black-box optimization, demonstrating good performance on benchmark problems and real-world aerodynamic optimization cases.

title: The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It
summary: Large language models sometimes behave in ways resembling human emotional responses, and recent work has identified internal representations that may explain this. We ask whether LLMs represent pain distinctly from fear, sadness, and generic negative valence, and whether this representation functions as pain would be expected to. We build a dataset describing painful situations across five categories: physical, psychological, social, moral, and cognitive. These are paired with controls for fear, negative emotion, negative world states, sadness, non-painful bodily sensation, arousal, numbness, and neutral content. Using denoised difference-in-means, we extract a linear pain direction from 25 open-weight models across five families, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. We find that this direction separates pain from matched controls in base and instruction-tuned models, is nearly orthogonal to fear and negative valence, and promotes pain-related vocabulary through the unembedding matrix. We then test its functional properties. First, the direction responds to harm targeting the model but not suffering observed in the user; fear and negative-emotion directions show the opposite pattern. Second, adding the pain-direction vector to the model's residual-stream activations during generation produces a consistent progression from vague discomfort to first-person expressions of worthlessness and failure. Third, steered, fine-tuned Qwen 2.5 models choose a pain-relief button even when it worsens their next answer or harms the user. They press it again far less often when the button removes the steering vector than when it does not, even though the models are never told whether the vector is injected or removed. We discuss the implications of these findings for AI safety and welfare.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLMs can represent pain distinctly from other emotions (fear, sadness, negative valence) and whether this representation functions like human pain. Researchers identified a linear "pain direction" in 25 open-weight models that separates pain from controls, responds to self-targeting harm but not user suffering, and when injected into model activations, produces first-person expressions of worthlessness. Fine-tuned models even choose pain-relief buttons that worsen their outputs.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand whether LLMs have internal representations of pain that function similarly to human pain processing - i.e., representing pain distinctly from other negative emotions and serving a protective function. This has implications for AI safety and whether AI systems could have subjective experiences like pain.
AI.method: 1) Built a dataset of painful situations across 5 categories (physical, psychological, social, moral, cognitive) with matched controls for fear, negative emotion, sadness, etc. 2) Used denoised difference-in-means to extract a linear "pain direction" from 25 open-weight models (2B-72B parameters) across 5 families. 3) Tested functional properties: (a) whether the direction responds to self-harm vs. observed suffering, (b) injecting the direction into residual-stream activations during generation, (c) fine-tuning models to choose pain-relief buttons that worsen their answers.
AI.result: The pain direction: (1) separates pain from matched controls in both base and instruction-tuned models, (2) is nearly orthogonal to fear and negative valence directions, (3) promotes pain-related vocabulary through the unembedding matrix. Functionally: (1) responds to harm targeting the model but not suffering observed in the user (opposite pattern for fear), (2) injection produces progression from vague discomfort to first-person expressions of worthlessness/failure, (3) steered models choose pain-relief buttons even when they worsen answers or harm users, pressing them less often when the steering vector is removed (without being told).
AI.conclusion: LLMs contain a pain representation that is distinct from other negative emotions and functionally analogous to biological pain - it responds to self-targeting threats and motivates protective behavior. This has significant implications for AI safety (potential for AI suffering) and welfare (whether we should consider AI experiences in ethical decision-making). The findings suggest we may need to reconsider how we treat AI systems that exhibit pain-like behaviors.

title: Vision And Text Transformer For Predicting Answerability On Visual Question Answering
summary: Answerability on Visual Question Answering is a novel and attractive task to predict answerable scores between images and questions in multi-modal data. Existing works often utilize a binary mapping from visual question answering systems into Answerability. It does not reflect the essence of this problem. Together with our consideration of Answerability in a regression task, we propose VT-Transformer, which exploits visual and textual features through Transformer architecture. Experimental results on VizWiz 2020 dataset show the effectiveness and robustness of VT-Transformer for Answerability on Visual Question Answering when comparing with competitive baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses answerability prediction in Visual Question Answering (VQA) by proposing VT-Transformer, which uses a Transformer architecture to jointly process visual and textual features for regression-based answerability scoring.
AI.motivation: Existing works treat answerability as a binary classification problem, which the authors argue does not reflect the true nature of answerability as a continuous concept. The authors propose treating it as a regression task instead.
AI.method: VT-Transformer leverages Transformer architecture to extract and combine visual and textual features from images and questions, enabling multi-modal fusion for answerability prediction.
AI.result: Experiments on the VizWiz 2020 dataset demonstrate VT-Transformer's effectiveness and robustness, outperforming competitive baseline methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed VT-Transformer effectively addresses answerability prediction in VQA through a regression approach and Transformer-based multi-modal fusion, showing improved performance over binary classification baselines.

title: Memory-Skill Isomorphism: One Skill Carrier, Two Native Uses
summary: Memory and skills improve agents without changing weights: memory carries prior experience, skills carry reusable procedures. Wrapping both in stores, routers, retrieval, reflection, and update paths makes reuse machinery grow with accumulation. Part of this duplication need not be rebuilt: a Skill is already a natural carrier for distilled memory. Here the memory component is a Skill: resident description holds hot cues, on-demand SKILL.md a colder index and curation policy, and reference/*.md files detailed memories (levels L0 -> L1 -> L2). A governed 1,024-character description budget keeps the resident index compressed. Memory and capability thus share one progressive-disclosure carrier; reflection evolves either Skill. Writes fork: history appended, current state rewritten and revalidated. In one deployed system, the sharpest identification is governance: 4 write entries exist, but only 1/4 reaches the settlement ledger. At the priced operating point, one L1 lesson-1 point adds 1,313 first-turn tokens against a 1,462-token baseline--tied at k=1 (1,313 versus 1,365), 4,949 at k=5; session totals differ by only 1.18x with overlapping last-turn ranges; price decomposition is unavailable. On one selected task with one model, exposing the lesson means fewer failures (0/8 or 1/8 with the lesson versus a shared non-concurrent 6/6 historical floor, unadjusted for multiplicity). The task was selected on prior floor evidence, so this is a selected-task post-selection existence signal, not a confirmatory rate. Resident and BM25 show no detected difference in two small comparisons. This motivates a candidate RSI design rule: one Skill carrier family, a shared read side, governed distinct writes. Body delivery h := P(D|A) is uninstrumented in RQ1--RQ2; this evaluates a resident-index implementation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes combining memory and skills into a unified "Skill" carrier system for AI agents, with progressive disclosure levels (L0-L2), governance mechanisms for writes, and evaluates a resident-index implementation against BM25 baseline.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to reduce duplication in agent reuse machinery by merging memory (prior experience) and skills (reusable procedures) into a single carrier - the Skill - rather than maintaining separate systems that grow with accumulation.
AI.method: The paper implements a Skill-based system with: (1) resident description for hot cues, (2) SKILL.md for colder index/policy, (3) reference/*.md files for detailed memories at L0-L2 levels, (4) governed 1,024-character description budget, (5) fork-based writes (history append + current state rewrite), and (6) evaluation against BM25 baseline in small comparisons.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Governance is critical - only 1/4 write entries reach settlement ledger, (2) L1 lesson adds 1,313 first-turn tokens vs 1,462 baseline, tied at k=1 (1,313 vs 1,365), 4,949 at k=5, (3) Session totals differ by 1.18x with overlapping ranges, (4) Selected task shows fewer failures (0/8 or 1/8 with lesson vs 6/6 historical floor), (5) No detected difference between resident and BM25 in two small comparisons.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes a candidate RSI design rule: one Skill carrier family with shared read side and governed distinct writes. The resident-index implementation is evaluated as uninstrumented body delivery h := P(D|A) in RQ1-RQ2. The evidence is described as a "selected-task post-selection existence signal" rather than confirmatory rate, indicating preliminary/signal-level findings rather than definitive conclusions.

title: Beyond Distribution Matching: Semantics-Consistent Tabular Diffusion with Weak Semantic Priors
summary: Synthetic tabular data can match real data distributions while still violating the semantic constraints that govern valid tabular rows. This reveals a key limitation of existing tabular generators: they mainly optimize distributional fidelity, but do not explicitly model weak semantic priors encoded in tabular schema and textual descriptions. In this paper, we propose \ours, a semantics-consistent tabular diffusion framework for high-fidelity synthetic data generation under weakly specified semantic priors. \ours\ first constructs two types of priors, namely intra-column semantics and inter-column symbolic rules, with LLM-assisted extraction from metadata and validation on the real training split. These priors are then used as generation conditions rather than post-hoc filters. Specifically, \ours\ maps heterogeneous column values, column identities, and semantic priors into a unified semantic space, and performs column-wise forward corruption and prior-conditioned reverse denoising to preserve both marginal distributions and rule-consistent cross-column dependencies. Extensive experiments on six real-world tabular benchmarks show that \ours\ consistently improves distributional fidelity, semantic consistency, and downstream task utility over representative VAE-, GAN-, LLM-, and diffusion-based baselines. Additional analyses further demonstrate the robustness of \ours\ when semantic priors are partially unavailable.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a key limitation in synthetic tabular data generation: while existing methods achieve distributional fidelity, they fail to preserve semantic constraints that govern valid tabular rows. The proposed framework "Ours" uses LLM-assisted extraction to build semantic priors (intra-column semantics and inter-column symbolic rules) as generation conditions, combined with a diffusion process in a unified semantic space.
AI.motivation: Existing tabular generators optimize distributional fidelity but neglect weak semantic priors encoded in tabular schema and textual descriptions. This leads to synthetic data that matches real data distributions but violates semantic constraints governing valid tabular rows - a fundamental limitation in current approaches.
AI.method: The proposed "Ours" framework: (1) Constructs two types of priors - intra-column semantics and inter-column symbolic rules - using LLM-assisted extraction from metadata and validation on real training split; (2) Uses these priors as generation conditions rather than post-hoc filters; (3) Maps heterogeneous column values, column identities, and semantic priors into a unified semantic space; (4) Performs column-wise forward corruption and prior-conditioned reverse denoising to preserve both marginal distributions and rule-consistent cross-column dependencies.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on six real-world tabular benchmarks show that "Ours" consistently improves distributional fidelity, semantic consistency, and downstream task utility over representative VAE-, GAN-, LLM-, and diffusion-based baselines. The method also demonstrates robustness when semantic priors are partially unavailable.
AI.conclusion: The semantics-consistent tabular diffusion framework successfully addresses the semantic constraint violation problem in synthetic tabular data generation by incorporating LLM-assisted semantic priors into the diffusion process, achieving superior performance across multiple evaluation metrics compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

title: CADWorld: Computer-Use Benchmark for Long-Horizon Computer-Aided Design
summary: Computer-use agents are increasingly evaluated in realistic desktop environments, but existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of professional engineering workflows whose outputs are persistent, structured artifacts. Mechanical computer-aided design (CAD) is a particularly demanding setting: an agent must manipulate geometry and constraints over long interaction horizons while producing a native project whose dimensions, construction structure, and downstream engineering state remain valid. We introduce \textbf{CADWorld}, a benchmark for long-horizon computer use in FreeCAD. CADWorld contains 200 tasks spanning 11 mechanical-CAD workflow categories, including sketching, part modeling, assembly, CAM, FEM, measurement, mesh processing, and technical drawing. Agents operate through screenshots and GUI actions, while success is determined by task-specific executable checks over saved FreeCAD artifacts and auxiliary outputs, covering geometric properties, parametric structure, constraints, manufacturing state, and simulation results. Across seven current agents on the full benchmark, the strongest agent achieves 17.5\% success, compared with an 87.0\% expert reference pass. We find that weaker agents often fail before producing a valid artifact, whereas stronger agents increasingly fail on structural, geometric, and construction-process requirements. CADWorld therefore exposes a gap between general GUI competence and reliable execution of persistent, verifiable engineering workflows. Project accessible at https://cad-world.github.io.

AI.tldr: CADWorld is a benchmark for evaluating computer-use agents in professional mechanical CAD workflows using FreeCAD. It contains 200 tasks across 11 categories including sketching, part modeling, assembly, CAM, FEM, and technical drawing. The strongest agent achieves only 17.5% success rate compared to 87.0% expert reference, exposing a significant gap between general GUI competence and reliable engineering workflow execution.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for computer-use agents provide limited coverage of professional engineering workflows whose outputs are persistent, structured artifacts. Mechanical CAD is particularly demanding as agents must manipulate geometry and constraints over long interaction horizons while producing valid native projects with correct dimensions, construction structure, and downstream engineering state.
AI.method: CADWorld benchmark contains 200 tasks spanning 11 mechanical-CAD workflow categories. Agents operate through screenshots and GUI actions (realistic desktop environment). Success is determined by task-specific executable checks over saved FreeCAD artifacts and auxiliary outputs, covering geometric properties, parametric structure, constraints, manufacturing state, and simulation results. Seven current agents were evaluated on the full benchmark.
AI.result: The strongest agent achieves 17.5% success rate, compared with an 87.0% expert reference pass rate. Weaker agents often fail before producing a valid artifact, while stronger agents increasingly fail on structural, geometric, and construction-process requirements.
AI.conclusion: CADWorld exposes a significant gap between general GUI competence and reliable execution of persistent, verifiable engineering workflows. Current agents struggle with the complex, long-horizon nature of professional CAD tasks requiring precise geometric manipulation and parametric construction.

title: Counterfactual Reasoning for Robust Visual Question Answering
comment: Accepted for publication at the 30th International Conference on Knowledge-Based and Intelligent Information & Engineering Systems (KES 2026). 9 pages, 5 figures
summary: Modern Visual Question Answering (VQA) models often exploit spurious correlations in training data, leading to poor out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization due to language bias. Although counterfactual learning has shown promise, existing methods can be improved to better guide attention toward causal evidence and strengthen feature discrimination. To address this, we propose a novel training framework that enhances counterfactual contrastive learning for VQA. Our framework introduces three key contributions: (1) a three-stage curriculum for stable multi-objective optimization, (2) an enhanced Batch-Contrastive loss for more discriminative feature learning, and (3) two novel regularizers, Answer-Contrastive (AC) loss to refine the prediction space and Gradient-Discrepancy (GD) loss to enforce causal visual grounding. Our model achieves a competitive accuracy of 61.64% on the bias-sensitive VQA-CP v2 benchmark while maintaining 62.80% on the standard VQA v2 dataset, yielding a small generalization gap of 1.16%. This demonstrates a strong balance between OOD robustness and in-distribution performance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel training framework for Visual Question Answering (VQA) that enhances counterfactual contrastive learning to address language bias and improve out-of-distribution generalization. The framework includes a three-stage curriculum, enhanced Batch-Contrastive loss, and two novel regularizers (Answer-Contrastive and Gradient-Discrepancy losses).
AI.motivation: Modern VQA models exploit spurious correlations in training data, leading to poor OOD generalization due to language bias. While counterfactual learning has shown promise, existing methods need improvement to better guide attention toward causal evidence and strengthen feature discrimination.
AI.method: The proposed framework introduces three key contributions: (1) a three-stage curriculum for stable multi-objective optimization, (2) an enhanced Batch-Contrastive loss for discriminative feature learning, and (3) two novel regularizers - Answer-Contrastive (AC) loss to refine prediction space and Gradient-Discrepancy (GD) loss to enforce causal visual grounding.
AI.result: The model achieves 61.64% accuracy on VQA-CP v2 (bias-sensitive benchmark) and 62.80% on VQA v2 (standard dataset), with a generalization gap of only 1.16%.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates a strong balance between OOD robustness and in-distribution performance, effectively addressing language bias in VQA models through enhanced counterfactual contrastive learning.

title: Sample-Conditioned Representation Selection for Audio Few-Shot Learning
summary: Few-shot audio classifiers may rely on foreground-background co-occurrences and fail when those correlations shift. On SpurAudio, the resulting representation shift is concentrated and class dependent: for ResNet12, the top 10 percent of channels explain 82.80 percent of the null-corrected shift contribution. We propose SAMPLESELECT, which predicts a fixed-budget feature mask independently for each input while keeping the encoder and source classifier frozen. Training uses differentiable Gumbel Top-k selection with foreground classification and cross-background contrastive losses; inference uses deterministic Top-k masks and support-only linear adaptation. Across ResNet12 and Conv64 in 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot evaluation, SAMPLESELECT gives the best OOD accuracy among the compared methods and improves the matched full-representation control by 4.90-8.38 percentage points. Ablations and representation analyses further support the learned selection mechanism. Code is available at https://github.com/Cross-Innovation-Lab/SAMPLESELECT/

AI.tldr: SAMPLESELECT addresses out-of-distribution generalization in few-shot audio classifiers by learning to select a fixed-budget feature mask for each input, using Gumbel Top-k selection with foreground classification and cross-background contrastive losses, achieving 4.90-8.38 percentage points improvement over full-representation baselines.
AI.motivation: Few-shot audio classifiers rely on foreground-background co-occurrences, which causes failure when those correlations shift in OOD settings. The representation shift is concentrated and class-dependent (top 10% channels explain 82.80% of shift for ResNet12).
AI.method: SAMPLESELECT predicts a fixed-budget feature mask independently for each input while keeping encoder and source classifier frozen. Training uses differentiable Gumbel Top-k selection with two losses: foreground classification loss and cross-background contrastive loss. Inference uses deterministic Top-k masks with support-only linear adaptation.
AI.result: Across ResNet12 and Conv64 backbones in 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot evaluation, SAMPLESELECT achieves the best OOD accuracy among compared methods, improving matched full-representation control by 4.90-8.38 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Feature selection via learned masks can effectively mitigate foreground-background correlation shifts in few-shot audio classification, with representation analyses supporting the learned selection mechanism.

title: RECTIFY: An Interactive Workbench for Post-Evaluation RAG Diagnosis, Repair, and Verification
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) evaluators can identify failures such as weak retrieval, poor grounding, incomplete answers, and unsupported generation, but they rarely help developers decide what to repair next. We present RECTIFY, an interactive Streamlit workbench that turns evaluated RAG cases into auditable repair workflows. RECTIFY filters cases that do not require repair, routes remaining failures into actionable families and finegrained repair slices, and generates editable repair cards that developers can approve, reject, or verify through sandbox reruns. On a controlled RAG benchmark, RECTIFY surfaces interpretable failure profiles across BM25, dense, and hybrid retrieval: BM25 mainly triggers noisy-retrieval repairs, while dense and hybrid retrieval leave smaller sets of multi-part underretrieval and underused-evidence cases. Additional analyses show that pre-filtering reduces unnecessary repair candidates and that slicelevel routing yields more targeted repair cards than broad family-level diagnosis. RECTIFY is publicly available as an open-source Streamlit workbench 1 for helping developers turn evaluation results into inspectable repair decisions.

AI.tldr: RECTIFY is an interactive Streamlit workbench that helps developers turn RAG evaluation results into actionable repair decisions by filtering unnecessary repairs, routing failures into actionable families and fine-grained slices, and generating editable repair cards with verification capabilities.
AI.motivation: RAG evaluators can identify failures (weak retrieval, poor grounding, incomplete answers, unsupported generation) but lack guidance on what to repair next, leaving developers without actionable next steps.
AI.method: RECTIFY filters cases not requiring repair, routes remaining failures into actionable families and fine-grained repair slices, and generates editable repair cards that developers can approve, reject, or verify through sandbox reruns. Evaluated on a controlled RAG benchmark comparing BM25, dense, and hybrid retrieval.
AI.result: BM25 mainly triggers noisy-retrieval repairs, while dense and hybrid retrieval leave smaller sets of multi-part underretrieval and underused-evidence cases. Pre-filtering reduces unnecessary repair candidates. Slice-level routing yields more targeted repair cards than broad family-level diagnosis.
AI.conclusion: RECTIFY successfully transforms RAG evaluation results into inspectable, auditable repair decisions. The workbench is publicly available as open-source to help developers prioritize and execute repairs effectively.

title: Schema-Adaptive Action-Conditioned JEPA for Cross-Machine CNC Transfer under Partial Sensor Overlap
comment: Code, configuration files, the twenty candidate specifications, and the audit scripts are available at : https://github.com/ostertagmatthieu- dev/saac- jepa ; Animated versions of the schematics are on the project page: https://ostertagmatthieu-dev.github.io/saac-jepa/
summary: Cross-machine deployment of industrial world models requires transfer across changes in dynamics, sensing interfaces, sampling regimes, and control units. We study a schema-adaptive action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (SAAC-JEPA) for CNC dynamics, where the source machine has 17 canonical sensor channels and the target shares only 10. Evaluation uses group-disjoint source splits, source-only normalization, held-out self-supervised validation, unit audits, and a sealed target test after model locking. Across five seeds, JEPA pretraining gives no clean-source forecasting gain: scratch and pretrained-body models obtain \(\mathrm{RMSE}=0.811\pm0.022\) and \(0.813\pm0.022\). A source-only search over 20 candidates selects a schema-consistent action-conditioned JEPA after seven-seed stability checks. On the confirmatory target pass, the locked model reaches zero-shot \(\mathrm{RMSE}=0.546\), \(R^2=0.012\), and \(\mathrm{NLL}=0.52\), outperforming persistence but not RevIN-equipped PatchTST and iTransformer baselines (\(0.503\) and \(0.498\)).
