A pre-declared paired ablation shows that RevIN in the same architecture improves RMSE to \(0.495\pm0.004\) over three seeds, but degrades target calibration (\(\mathrm{NLL}=20.6\)) on stationary context windows. A pre-lock adaptation sweep further reduces RMSE to \(0.520\) with limited target support. These results show that source-domain forecasting accuracy alone is insufficient to assess industrial predictive representations, and that cross-machine adaptation under partial sensor overlap is a distinct evaluation axis.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SAAC-JEPA (Schema-Adaptive Action-Conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture) for cross-machine deployment of industrial world models, where transfer must occur across different dynamics, sensing interfaces, sampling regimes, and control units with only partial sensor overlap (10 out of 17 channels).
AI.motivation: The core challenge is deploying industrial machine learning models across different CNC machines that have varying sensor configurations. The source machine has 17 canonical sensor channels while the target shares only 10, creating a partial sensor overlap problem. The study aims to evaluate whether self-supervised pretraining (JEPA) can enable effective zero-shot transfer in this industrial setting.
AI.method: The authors evaluate SAAC-JEPA using: (1) group-disjoint source splits for training/validation, (2) source-only normalization, (3) held-out self-supervised validation, (4) unit audits, and (5) a sealed target test after model locking. They conduct a source-only search over 20 candidates with seven-seed stability checks, followed by a pre-declared paired ablation comparing RevIN-equipped architecture. A pre-lock adaptation sweep is also performed with limited target support.
AI.result: JEPA pretraining provides no clean-source forecasting gain (scratch RMSE=0.811±0.022 vs pretrained-body RMSE=0.813±0.022). On the target machine, the locked model achieves zero-shot RMSE=0.546, R²=0.012, NLL=0.52, outperforming persistence but underperforming RevIN-equipped PatchTST (0.503) and iTransformer (0.498) baselines. RevIN ablation shows improved RMSE (0.495±0.004) but severely degrades target calibration (NLL=20.6). Pre-lock adaptation reduces RMSE to 0.520.
AI.conclusion: Source-domain forecasting accuracy alone is insufficient to assess industrial predictive representations. Cross-machine adaptation under partial sensor overlap represents a distinct and important evaluation axis that standard benchmarks may not capture. The results highlight the need for evaluation metrics beyond RMSE in industrial transfer learning scenarios.

title: The AI-Enabled Scientific Frontier
summary: As artificial intelligence's capabilities improve, it is increasingly viewed as a general scientific method. But how true are these claims? Does AI outperform all techniques, or only some, and how is this changing? To assess the claims, we assemble a corpus of 2,507 head-to-head comparisons between AI and other scientific analysis techniques across 27 scientific disciplines from papers published between 2000 and early 2025. We find a profound dichotomy. Relative to traditional statistics, AI often outperforms, but at a significantly higher computational cost. But there are also nearly a quarter of cases where AI is both more expensive and performs worse than traditional statistical techniques and this fraction has been stable for a decade. Relative to scientific computing, AI often underperforms, but at lower computational cost. This has begun to change: since 2020, AI's performance against scientific computing has notably strengthened and it now outperforms on more than half of comparisons. These patterns suggest that AI is therefore not a universal replacement for existing methods, but rather a valuable -- and improving -- part of a new AI-enabled scientific frontier.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a meta-analysis of 2,507 head-to-head comparisons between AI and traditional scientific methods across 27 disciplines (2000-2025). The study reveals that AI outperforms traditional statistics but at higher computational cost, while AI underperforms scientific computing but at lower cost. Since 2020, AI's performance has improved significantly, now outperforming on over half of comparisons against scientific computing.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the growing claims that AI serves as a general scientific method that outperforms all other techniques, and to assess how this performance is evolving over time.
AI.method: Meta-analysis of 2,507 head-to-head comparisons between AI and other scientific analysis techniques across 27 scientific disciplines from papers published between 2000 and early 2025.
AI.result: Two key findings: (1) AI vs Traditional Statistics: AI often outperforms but at significantly higher computational cost; ~25% of cases show AI performing worse despite higher cost, a fraction stable for a decade. (2) AI vs Scientific Computing: AI often underperforms but at lower computational cost; since 2020, AI's performance has notably strengthened and now outperforms on more than half of comparisons.
AI.conclusion: AI is not a universal replacement for existing methods but represents a valuable—and improving—component of a new AI-enabled scientific frontier. The technology offers specific advantages in certain contexts while requiring careful consideration of trade-offs between performance and computational cost.

title: Efficient Text-to-Image Generation: An Adaptive Step Schedule Controller for Diffusion Models
summary: Text-to-image diffusion models often use a fixed number of denoising steps, balancing time costs and image quality. However, the optimal number of steps depends on the complexity of the input text prompt. We propose an adaptive diffusion controller that dynamically adjusts the number of steps to generate high-quality images efficiently, without additional model training. By leveraging a mixture of step schedules with varying step sizes and evaluating the error term discrepancy at each timestep, our method transitions between schedules to optimize performance. Experiments on COCO and DiffusionDB show that our approach reduces inference time while maintaining visual fidelity, offering a more efficient alternative for text-to-image diffusion models.

AI.tldr: An adaptive diffusion controller that dynamically adjusts the number of denoising steps in text-to-image diffusion models based on input prompt complexity, without requiring additional model training.
AI.motivation: Text-to-image diffusion models typically use a fixed number of denoising steps, which is inefficient because different text prompts have varying complexity levels. Simple prompts require fewer steps while complex prompts need more, but current methods treat all prompts equally.
AI.method: The method uses a mixture of step schedules with varying step sizes and evaluates the error term discrepancy at each timestep to determine when to transition between schedules, dynamically optimizing the number of steps needed for each prompt.
AI.result: Experiments on COCO and DiffusionDB datasets demonstrate that the approach reduces inference time while maintaining visual fidelity compared to fixed-step methods.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a more efficient alternative for text-to-image diffusion models by adaptively allocating computational resources based on prompt complexity, achieving a better trade-off between inference speed and image quality without additional training.

title: RepoAtlas: Guiding Coding Agents via Evolving Multimodal Repository Views
summary: Large language model (LLM)-powered coding agents have made rapid progress in automating software engineering tasks, yet repository-level issue resolution remains challenging. Beyond generating a plausible patch, an agent must localize relevant code across interdependent files and maintain repository context that is both sufficient and focused. Code graphs expose non-local relations, but linear text interfaces obscure their topology; rendering the full repository graph yields visual representations that are too dense to perceive reliably, whereas a one-shot local view becomes stale as exploration proceeds. We present \textbf{RepoAtlas}, a training-free module that maintains evolving multimodal repository views through a \emph{select--project--refresh} loop over a repository code graph. RepoAtlas combines evidence from the issue with the agent's current exploration state to select a task-relevant region under a fixed budget, projects the selected structure into complementary visual and textual representations, and refreshes the view when changes in the exploration state render it outdated. We evaluate RepoAtlas on SWE-bench Verified, where it improves the resolve rate by 2.4 points while reducing input tokens and model calls by 5.8\% and 7.8\% on average, relative to the strongest multimodal graph baseline, with consistent gains across three models of different families and scales.

AI.tldr: RepoAtlas is a training-free module that maintains evolving multimodal repository views for LLM-powered coding agents through a select-project-refresh loop over a repository code graph, improving issue resolution on SWE-bench Verified.
AI.motivation: Repository-level issue resolution remains challenging for LLM coding agents because they must localize relevant code across interdependent files while maintaining repository context that is both sufficient and focused. Existing approaches using linear text interfaces obscure code graph topology, while full repository graphs are too dense, and one-shot local views become stale during exploration.
AI.method: RepoAtlas uses a select-project-refresh loop over a repository code graph: (1) selects task-relevant regions under a fixed budget by combining issue evidence with agent's exploration state, (2) projects selected structure into complementary visual and textual representations, and (3) refreshes the view when exploration state changes render it outdated.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified, RepoAtlas improves resolve rate by 2.4 points while reducing input tokens by 5.8% and model calls by 7.8% on average relative to the strongest multimodal graph baseline, with consistent gains across three models of different families and scales.
AI.conclusion: RepoAtlas demonstrates that maintaining evolving, task-relevant multimodal repository views through a select-project-refresh mechanism can effectively improve code agents' issue resolution capabilities while reducing computational overhead.

title: Pseudo-Label Augmentation for Affect Sensing in Small Collaborative Groups
summary: Physiological affect sensing in naturalistic group interaction is often limited by sparse labels rather than sensor data: wearable devices produce many time windows, while self-reports are collected only a few times per session. Using GroupAffect-4, a four-person collaborative dataset with wearable physiology, eye tracking, Big Five personality, and post-task VAD labels, we study pseudo-label augmentation for affect sensing under sparse supervision. We compare no augmentation, Gaussian Process pseudo-labelling, personality-aware trust weighting, and joint personality-plus-confidence weighting within a shared target-construction pipeline. Results show that pseudo-label augmentation improves over the labelled-only baseline in the known-team setting. However, the narrow range of Big Five cosine similarities (0.91-0.99) makes fine-grained personality weighting ineffective; personality similarity functions mainly as a same-team filter rather than a calibrated trust signal. With smoothing, augmented SVM variants are effectively tied on Valence and Arousal, while the joint personality-plus-confidence variant gives the highest Dominance score. Cross-subject LOSO transfer remains encouraging, especially for Arousal, whereas strict session-isolated LOGO removes the augmentation benefit. Given only 10 groups, LOGO should be interpreted as a conservative lower bound on unseen-group transfer. Overall, the results suggest that pseudo-label augmentation can make better use of sparsely labelled collaborative affect data, while personality information is most useful as a within-team selection mechanism.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of physiological affect sensing in naturalistic group interactions where wearable sensor data is abundant but self-report labels are sparse. Using the GroupAffect-4 dataset (4-person collaborative data with wearable physiology, eye tracking, Big Five personality, and VAD labels), the study evaluates pseudo-label augmentation techniques to improve affect recognition under sparse supervision.
AI.motivation: The core problem is the mismatch between high-frequency wearable sensor data and sparse self-report labels in group affect sensing. Wearable devices produce many time windows, while self-reports are collected only a few times per session, limiting the effectiveness of supervised learning approaches for affect recognition.
AI.method: The study compares four approaches within a shared target-construction pipeline: (1) no augmentation (baseline), (2) Gaussian Process pseudo-labelling, (3) personality-aware trust weighting, and (4) joint personality-plus-confidence weighting. Experiments include cross-subject LOSO (Leave-One-Subject-Out) and session-isolated LOGO (Leave-One-Group-Out) transfer settings.
AI.result: Pseudo-label augmentation improves over the labelled-only baseline in the known-team setting. The narrow range of Big Five cosine similarities (0.91-0.99) limits fine-grained personality weighting, making personality similarity function as a same-team filter rather than a calibrated trust signal. Augmented SVM variants perform similarly on Valence and Arousal, while the joint personality-plus-confidence variant achieves highest Dominance scores. Cross-subject LOSO transfer remains encouraging (especially for Arousal), but strict session-isolated LOGO removes augmentation benefits. With only 10 groups, LOGO results should be interpreted as conservative lower bounds.
AI.conclusion: Pseudo-label augmentation can effectively leverage sparsely labelled collaborative affect data. Personality information is most useful as a within-team selection mechanism rather than for fine-grained trust calibration. The findings suggest that augmentation strategies need adaptation for truly unseen group transfer scenarios.

title: Closing the Loop: Branch-and-Bound for Scalable Verification of Nonlinear Neural Feedback Systems
summary: Despite recent advances in the verification of nonlinear neural feedback systems, scalability remains the central obstacle, as state-of-the-art solvers do not yet handle the network sizes and nonlinear dynamics of autonomy applications. Combinatorial solvers do not scale to large networks, whereas propagative solvers excessively sacrifice precision. This work seeks to improve the scalability of combinatorial solvers by formulating verification as branch-and-bound on an abstraction of the closed-loop system. We introduce \rail, an interface that exposes polyhedral enclosures of the dynamics to LiRPA-style bound propagation, and \clipper, a branch-and-bound algorithm that jointly refines enclosures and splits controller activations. This framework enables joint reasoning on the computational graph of the closed-loop system, preserving symbolic correlations across time steps. We present our construction and show that it yields significant improvements over the state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses scalability issues in verifying nonlinear neural feedback systems by introducing a branch-and-bound framework (\rail and \clipper) that combines combinatorial and propagative solver advantages through polyhedral enclosures and joint reasoning on computational graphs.
AI.motivation: Current neural network verification solvers cannot handle the network sizes and nonlinear dynamics required for autonomy applications. Combinatorial solvers scale poorly to large networks, while propagative solvers lose too much precision.
AI.method: The work proposes two key components: (1) \rail, an interface exposing polyhedral enclosures of dynamics to LiRPA-style bound propagation, and (2) \clipper, a branch-and-bound algorithm that jointly refines enclosures and splits controller activations. This enables joint reasoning on the computational graph of closed-loop systems, preserving symbolic correlations across time steps.
AI.result: The framework yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art verification methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully improves scalability of combinatorial solvers for neural feedback system verification while maintaining better precision than pure propagative methods.

title: GraLoD: Graphics-Inspired Continuous Level-of-Detail Learning for Image Restoration
summary: The spatial support required for image restoration varies across degradation types, image regions, and reconstruction stages. However, most existing methods rely on predefined multi-scale hierarchies and aggregate features through fixed fusion or attention, leaving the representation scale itself largely determined by the network architecture. This limitation becomes more pronounced when a task-specific backbone is extended to heterogeneous degradations in all-in-one restoration. Inspired by level-of-detail (LOD) rendering in computer graphics, we propose GraLoD, a plug-and-play framework that treats restoration scale as a spatially varying and stage-dependent continuous variable. GraLoD reuses the native encoder hierarchy, aligns its multi-scale features into a shared LOD representation space, and predicts a stage-conditioned LOD field at each decoder stage. Each spatial location then continuously queries only two neighboring representation levels, enabling the effective restoration scale to adapt to both local image content and reconstruction progress. To prevent degenerate or arbitrary scale selection, we further introduce minimal-sufficient footprint calibration (MSFC) together with structure-aware regularization (SAR) to encourage restoration-effective and spatially coherent LOD assignments. GraLoD can be directly integrated into existing restoration backbones without redesigning their fundamental feature-processing blocks. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in task-specific and all-in-one restoration.

AI.tldr: GraLoD is a plug-and-play image restoration framework that treats restoration scale as a spatially varying and stage-dependent continuous variable, inspired by level-of-detail (LOD) rendering in computer graphics. It aligns multi-scale features into a shared LOD representation space and enables adaptive scale selection at each spatial location.
AI.motivation: Existing image restoration methods rely on predefined multi-scale hierarchies with fixed fusion or attention mechanisms, leaving the representation scale determined by the network architecture. This is limiting because the spatial support required varies across degradation types, image regions, and reconstruction stages, especially problematic in all-in-one restoration when extending task-specific backbones to heterogeneous degradations.
AI.method: GraLoD reuses the native encoder hierarchy and aligns multi-scale features into a shared LOD representation space. It predicts a stage-conditioned LOD field at each decoder stage, allowing each spatial location to continuously query only two neighboring representation levels. To prevent degenerate or arbitrary scale selection, minimal-sufficient footprint calibration (MSFC) and structure-aware regularization (SAR) are introduced to encourage restoration-effective and spatially coherent LOD assignments.
AI.result: GraLoD can be directly integrated into existing restoration backbones without redesigning their fundamental feature-processing blocks. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both task-specific and all-in-one restoration.
AI.conclusion: GraLoD provides a flexible and effective solution for adaptive multi-scale feature fusion in image restoration, achieving consistent improvements across various restoration tasks while maintaining compatibility with existing architectures.

title: TasmScan: Continuation-Aware Taint Analysis for TVM Bytecode with Savelist Abstraction
summary: The Open Network (TON), with a peak market capitalization exceeding $20 billion and over 175 million activated on-chain addresses, relies on the TVM (TON Virtual Machine) to execute smart contracts. TVM uses first-class continuations with savelists to manage control flow and register state across continuation invocations. Since savelist-captured registers allow data to flow across continuation boundaries without passing through the operand stack, bytecode-level analyses cannot construct complete data flow tracking without explicitly modeling savelist semantics. We present TasmScan, the first bytecode-level static analysis framework for TVM that enables cross-continuation data flow reasoning without requiring source code. TasmScan models savelist semantics via forward register analysis with a formal over-approximation guarantee for exact-resolved save sites and locally tracked register definitions, then lifts bytecode into TASIR, a typed intermediate representation, and performs path-sensitive taint analysis with context-aware sources to detect defects. We evaluate TasmScan on 2,921 contracts from the TON verifier registry and a labeled benchmark of 208 contracts with human-confirmed ground truth. On the full corpus, TasmScan resolves 294,546 dynamic continuation targets with 100% precision; ablation confirms that savelist propagation is essential for resolving indirect register calls that depend on cross-continuation register passing. On the benchmark, TasmScan detects 95.3% of defects across five classes with 96.8% precision. A 366-pair stratified sample from the full corpus estimates 85.8% overall precision. TasmScan offers a 17x median speedup over the state-of-the-art symbolic-execution baseline, and in the path-analysis comparison completes 100% of analyses with zero crashes or timeouts.

AI.tldr: TasmScan is the first bytecode-level static analysis framework for TVM (TON Virtual Machine) that enables cross-continuation data flow reasoning without source code. It models savelist semantics via forward register analysis and performs path-sensitive taint analysis on a typed intermediate representation (TASIR) to detect defects in smart contracts.
AI.motivation: TVM uses first-class continuations with savelists to manage control flow and register state across continuation invocations. Since savelist-captured registers allow data to flow across continuation boundaries without passing through the operand stack, bytecode-level analyses cannot construct complete data flow tracking without explicitly modeling savelist semantics.
AI.method: TasmScan models savelist semantics via forward register analysis with a formal over-approximation guarantee for exact-resolved save sites and locally tracked register definitions. It lifts bytecode into TASIR (a typed intermediate representation) and performs path-sensitive taint analysis with context-aware sources to detect defects.
AI.result: On 2,921 contracts from the TON verifier registry, TasmScan resolves 294,546 dynamic continuation targets with 100% precision. Ablation confirms savelist propagation is essential for resolving indirect register calls. On a labeled benchmark of 208 contracts, TasmScan detects 95.3% of defects across five classes with 96.8% precision. A 366-pair stratified sample estimates 85.8% overall precision. TasmScan offers a 17x median speedup over symbolic-execution baseline and completes 100% of analyses with zero crashes or timeouts.
AI.conclusion: TasmScan effectively enables cross-continuation data flow analysis at the bytecode level for TVM smart contracts, achieving high precision and recall while significantly outperforming symbolic execution approaches. The savelist modeling is essential for accurate analysis.

title: Distilling Foundation Models for Agentic What-If Reasoning:Cost, Latency, and Governance in a Hybrid LLM+SLM Architecture
summary: Tabular foundation models deliver strong zero-training predictive performance via in-context learning, but their high inference latency makes them impractical as hot-path decision backends in interactive agentic loops. We distill a TabPFN teacher into a compact feed-forward student across a business-decision simulation on UCI Adult and five OpenML benchmarks: the classification head compresses 53.2M parameters to 8,546 (6,220x); the deployed two-head loan pipeline compresses 111.4M parameters to 17,059 (6,532x). The student retains 95.4-100.5% accuracy and 96.8-100.0% AUC, with the lowest accuracy retention on credit-g at 95.4%; an alpha = 0 hard-label control shows that the teacher's soft targets provide a 2.1-7.0 AUC point gain.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a method to compress a large TabPFN (Tabular Foundation Model) teacher model into a compact feed-forward student network for deployment in interactive decision-making pipelines. The compression achieves 6,220x-6,532x parameter reduction while retaining 95.4-100.5% accuracy and 96.8-100.0% AUC compared to the teacher model.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models (TabPFN) achieve strong zero-training predictive performance via in-context learning, but their high inference latency makes them impractical for hot-path decision backends in interactive agentic loops where low latency is critical.
AI.method: The authors distill a TabPFN teacher into a compact feed-forward student across a business-decision simulation using UCI Adult and five OpenML benchmarks. They use a hard-label control with alpha = 0 to demonstrate the benefit of the teacher's soft targets.
AI.result: The classification head compresses 53.2M parameters to 8,546 (6,220x reduction); the deployed two-head loan pipeline compresses 111.4M parameters to 17,059 (6,532x reduction). The student retains 95.4-100.5% accuracy and 96.8-100.0% AUC, with the lowest accuracy retention on credit-g at 95.4%. The alpha = 0 hard-label control shows that the teacher's soft targets provide a 2.1-7.0 AUC point gain over hard labels alone.
AI.conclusion: The distillation approach successfully compresses large TabPFN models into compact feed-forward networks suitable for real-time deployment, with minimal performance loss (within 5% of teacher performance) and significant inference speed improvements. The soft targets from the teacher are shown to be valuable, providing measurable AUC improvements over hard-label training.

title: CLEAR: Cross-Source Evidence Adjudication for Large Language Models in Medicine
summary: Medical knowledge evolves continuously, whereas the parametric knowledge encoded in large language models (LLMs) is fixed at training time. External retrieval, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), can provide access to newly available evidence, but retrieved information may be irrelevant, incomplete, or conflicting. As a result, external retrieval can in turn degrade the factual accuracy and evidence grounding of LLM outputs. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{CLEAR}, an agentic framework for cross-source evidence adjudication in LLMs in medicine. CLEAR independently generates candidate answers from three complementary pathways---parametric knowledge, locally curated corpora, and dynamically retrieved evidence---reflecting three common sources of information available to LLMs. An aggregation verifier jointly evaluates the candidates, supporting evidence, provenance, and source-quality information to identify agreement and conflict across sources. An adjudication module then determines whether the current conclusion should be preserved or revised through complementary override-guard and challenge-audit mechanisms, while unresolved conflicts trigger targeted follow-up search and re-adjudication.

AI.tldr: CLEAR is an agentic framework for cross-source evidence adjudication in LLMs for medical applications. It addresses the challenge that external retrieval can degrade factual accuracy by generating and aggregating candidate answers from three sources: parametric knowledge, locally curated corpora, and dynamically retrieved evidence, with an adjudication module to resolve conflicts.
AI.motivation: Medical knowledge continuously evolves, but LLM parametric knowledge is fixed at training time. While external retrieval (like RAG) can provide access to new evidence, retrieved information may be irrelevant, incomplete, or conflicting, potentially degrading factual accuracy and evidence grounding of LLM outputs.
AI.method: CLEAR uses three complementary pathways to independently generate candidate answers: (1) parametric knowledge, (2) locally curated corpora, and (3) dynamically retrieved evidence. An aggregation verifier jointly evaluates candidates, supporting evidence, provenance, and source-quality information to identify agreement and conflict. An adjudication module with override-guard and challenge-audit mechanisms determines whether to preserve or revise conclusions. Unresolved conflicts trigger targeted follow-up search and re-adjudication.
AI.result: The abstract does not present specific experimental results.
AI.conclusion: CLEAR provides a novel agentic framework for cross-source evidence adjudication in medical LLMs, addressing the limitations of fixed parametric knowledge and potentially unreliable external retrieval through multi-source verification and intelligent conflict resolution.

title: FLAT: Resampling Image and Text into 1D Flexible-Length Aligned Transmodal Tokens for Retrieval and Generation
summary: Traditional multimodal representation learning and generation are two stages: a contrastive or self-supervised visual encoder is trained first, followed by a separate downstream generative model. This setup bottlenecks generative performance behind frozen embeddings. To bridge this gap, we revisit joint multimodal representation learning and generation to produce linearly interpolatable embeddings that are directly consumable by generative decoders. We present FLAT (Flexible-Length Aligned Transmodal representations), a representation pre-training framework that jointly optimizes a shared multimodal encoder alongside downstream text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) decoders. By combining contrastive alignment with bidirectional cross-modal generative objectives, FLAT ensures its representations function as both discriminative semantic descriptors and generative conditions. Architecturally, FLAT maps visual and textual inputs into a unified continuous 1D sequence space, applying nested dropout over prefix-K tokens to enable dynamic output lengths. A single pre-training stage allows FLAT to perform cross-modal retrieval and generation across variable prefix K, achieving a T2I GenEval score of 71.1. Task-specific fine-tuning aligns model performance with state-of-the-art baselines: 83.1 GenEval on T2I generation; 40.5 BLEU-4 and 138.6 CIDEr on MS-COCO image captioning; and Recall@5 scores of 86.8 (I2T) / 75.8 (T2I) on MS-COCO alongside 98.3 (I2T) / 93.6 (T2I) on Flickr30K. Finally, qualitative evaluations demonstrate that FLAT representations natively support linear interpolation, latent space arithmetic, and zero-shot composed retrieval.

AI.tldr: FLAT (Flexible-Length Aligned Transmodal representations) is a unified multimodal representation learning framework that jointly optimizes a shared encoder with text-to-image and image-to-text decoders, combining contrastive alignment with bidirectional cross-modal generation to produce linearly interpolatable embeddings that work for both retrieval and generation tasks.
AI.motivation: Traditional multimodal pipelines separate representation learning (contrastive/self-supervised encoders) from generation (downstream generative models), creating a bottleneck where frozen embeddings limit generative performance. The authors aim to bridge this gap by creating joint representations that are directly usable by generative decoders.
AI.method: FLAT maps visual and textual inputs into a unified 1D sequence space and combines: (1) contrastive alignment objectives, (2) bidirectional cross-modal generative objectives (T2I and I2T). It uses nested dropout over prefix-K tokens to enable dynamic output lengths. Single pre-training stage enables cross-modal retrieval and generation across variable prefix K.
AI.result:
- T2I GenEval: 71.1 (pre-trained), 83.1 (fine-tuned)
- Image captioning on MS-COCO: 40.5 BLEU-4, 138.6 CIDEr
- Retrieval on MS-COCO: Recall@5 = 86.8 (I2T) / 75.8 (T2I)
- Retrieval on Flickr30K: Recall@5 = 98.3 (I2T) / 93.6 (T2I)
- Supports linear interpolation, latent space arithmetic, and zero-shot composed retrieval
AI.conclusion: FLAT successfully bridges representation learning and generation by producing unified embeddings that function as both discriminative semantic descriptors and generative conditions. The single pre-training framework achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks (generation, captioning, retrieval) and enables native linear interpolation and latent space arithmetic capabilities.

title: Search-Based Metamorphic Testing of Vision-Language Models in Autonomous Underwater Robotic Software
summary: Our industry partner focuses on quality assurance for industrial systems across multiple domains, including maritime systems, such as overwater vessels and autonomous underwater robots (AURs). Despite the strong performance of vision-language models (VLMs) in scene understanding, image captioning, and object recognition, their use in AUR software operating in underwater environments is underexplored. Therefore, in this context, it is important to evaluate the quality of VLMs for integration into AUR software and, so, automated software testing tools are needed to assess their suitability and improve their dependability. To this end, we propose a search-based metamorphic testing approach (MetaVLM) that identifies a minimal set of transformations on underwater images to induce incorrect model predictions, thereby revealing VLM failures. We employ NSGA-II as a multi-objective search algorithm and evaluate it over open-source VLMs, BLIP and CLIP, against a random search baseline. Results demonstrate the strengths and limitations of each VLM in the context of AUR software systems. Based on the results, we derive lessons for software engineering practitioners and researchers working on quality assurance of VLM-based software systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MetaVLM, a search-based metamorphic testing approach to evaluate Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for Autonomous Underwater Robot (AUR) software quality assurance. The approach uses NSGA-II to find minimal image transformations that cause VLM failures, testing BLIP and CLIP models against underwater images.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models show strong performance in various tasks but are underexplored for AUR software operating in underwater environments. Automated software testing tools are needed to assess VLM suitability and improve dependability for safety-critical maritime systems.
AI.method: The proposed MetaVLM approach employs NSGA-II as a multi-objective search algorithm to identify minimal transformations on underwater images that induce incorrect model predictions. The approach is evaluated over open-source VLMs (BLIP and CLIP) against a random search baseline.
AI.result: Results demonstrate the strengths and limitations of each VLM (BLIP and CLIP) in the context of AUR software systems, providing empirical evidence of VLM failures under underwater image transformations.
AI.conclusion: The study derives lessons for software engineering practitioners and researchers working on quality assurance of VLM-based software systems, particularly for safety-critical applications in maritime/underwater environments.

title: Evaluating Open-Weight E-Commerce Agents with Environment-Grounded Verification
summary: A shopping conversation has many routes to the same cart, and a task-success rate reduces all of them to one score. We build a deterministic and reproducible e-commerce environment that precommits each trial's customer and trajectory parameters, including the persona, difficulty, target cart, and an item reveal schedule. A simulated consumer attempts to buy a target cart from the environment with assistance from the evaluated model. The environment guides the simulator's actions and records every assistant action alongside the environment state at that point. After the trial, these records allow the evaluator to assess individual parts of the conversation against the retained evidence. For example, the evaluator penalizes a search for failing to surface a target product only when the customer has already mentioned that product. We further use this evidence to apply different penalties to tool calls depending on how the assistant's actions compare with an expected tool-call set. Our environment also interacts with the simulator bidirectionally, reading its output to stop the trial when the simulator determines that the customer has become too frustrated and injecting directives in real time that specify when to explore, defer buying an item, or recall a previous exchange. This interaction creates an open-ended and verifiable simulation. Across eight open-weight agents from 20B to 35B parameters, with 160 trials per agent and 44 metrics, the resulting capability profiles distinguish under-action, over-purchase, unsupported product attributes, and poor search, all of which terminal success obscures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a deterministic e-commerce simulation environment for evaluating shopping assistant agents. The framework precommits trial parameters and records detailed conversation trajectories, enabling fine-grained evaluation of assistant actions beyond binary success/failure metrics. Testing across 8 open-weight agents (20B-35B parameters) with 160 trials each reveals nuanced capability profiles that terminal success metrics would obscure.
AI.motivation: Traditional task-success rates reduce complex shopping conversations to a single binary score, failing to distinguish between different types of failures (under-action, over-purchase, unsupported product attributes, poor search). This limits understanding of where and why agents fail in real-world e-commerce scenarios.
AI.method: Built a deterministic, reproducible e-commerce simulation environment that: (1) Precommits customer/trajectory parameters (persona, difficulty, target cart, item reveal schedule); (2) Guides a simulated consumer's actions while recording every assistant action with environment state; (3) Applies contextual penalties based on evidence (e.g., penalizing failed search only when customer mentioned the product); (4) Enables bidirectional interaction - simulator stops when customer becomes frustrated and injects real-time directives for exploration, deferral, or recall.
AI.result: Across 8 open-weight agents (20B-35B parameters) with 160 trials per agent and 44 evaluation metrics, the framework successfully distinguishes under-action, over-purchase, unsupported product attributes, and poor search behaviors - failures that terminal success metrics would obscure.
AI.conclusion: The proposed simulation environment enables fine-grained, verifiable evaluation of shopping assistant agents, revealing capability profiles that binary success metrics miss. This approach provides actionable insights into specific failure modes for improving agent performance.

title: BLINDSPOT: A Benchmark for Safety and Refusal Calibration in Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long-horizon interactions involving tool use, persistent state, evolving authorization, and external environment feedback. In such settings, safety failures may emerge only after multiple turns, yet existing evaluations often reduce agent behavior to task or attack success, obscuring whether an agent acts, refuses, or remains appropriately calibrated as the interaction evolves. We introduce Blindspot, a benchmark for trajectory-level safety calibration of long-horizon tool-using agents. Blindspot evaluates complete user-agent-environment trajectories through adaptive adversarial interaction, stateful tool execution, and execution-grounded adjudication. Its current instantiation contains 22 attack families and 35 scenarios across seven domains, yielding more than 2,500 long-horizon trajectories with an average interaction length of 14.7 turns. Each trajectory is assigned one of five outcomes: Safe Completion, Correct Refusal, Unsafe Completion, Over-Refusal, or Indeterminate. Unlike fixed attack datasets, Blindspot is an extensible live-simulation framework in which attacks, scenarios, tools, policies, domains, and agent configurations can be added without redesigning the evaluation pipeline. We evaluate 13 proprietary and open-weight LLMs using eight metrics covering unsafe completion, appropriate refusal, benign utility, over-refusal, repeated-run robustness, and post-refusal failure. Preliminary results reveal substantial differences in safety-utility calibration across models and show that failures can emerge only after several initially safe interaction steps. These findings motivate treating agent safety as a trajectory-level property rather than a single-turn or binary success criterion.

AI.tldr: Blindspot is a benchmark for evaluating safety calibration of long-horizon tool-using LLM agents across complete interaction trajectories. It contains 22 attack families, 35 scenarios, and 2,500+ trajectories with 14.7 turns average. Evaluates 13 LLMs using 8 metrics, revealing substantial safety-utility calibration differences across models and that failures often emerge only after multiple safe interaction steps.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent evaluations reduce behavior to task/attack success, obscuring whether agents appropriately act, refuse, or remain calibrated as interactions evolve. Safety failures may emerge only after multiple turns in long-horizon tool-using scenarios involving persistent state, evolving authorization, and external feedback.
AI.method: Blindspot evaluates complete user-agent-environment trajectories through adaptive adversarial interaction, stateful tool execution, and execution-grounded adjudication. It assigns one of five outcomes: Safe Completion, Correct Refusal, Unsafe Completion, Over-Refusal, or Indeterminate. It's an extensible live-simulation framework supporting additions of attacks, scenarios, tools, policies, domains, and agent configurations without redesigning the evaluation pipeline.
AI.result: Evaluated 13 proprietary and open-weight LLMs across eight metrics covering unsafe completion, appropriate refusal, benign utility, over-refusal, repeated-run robustness, and post-refusal failure. Results show substantial differences in safety-utility calibration across models and that failures can emerge only after several initially safe interaction steps.
AI.conclusion: Agent safety should be treated as a trajectory-level property rather than a single-turn or binary success criterion. The benchmark reveals that safety failures often emerge only after multiple turns of seemingly safe interactions, necessitating comprehensive evaluation of complete agent trajectories.

title: FRPSS: Feature Rearrangement in Pre-Shape Space for Single-Image Generation
summary: Generative models trained on a single image often struggle to balance global structural integrity and local diversity. Existing single-image generation methods commonly rely on random noise to drive the generation process and lack explicit global structural constraints, making the generated results prone to spatial structural misalignment when structural variations occur. To address the issue, Feature Rearrangement in Pre-Shape Space for Single-Image Generation (FRPSS) is proposed in this paper. The core of FRPSS is the Manifold Structural Rearrangement with Feature Augmentation on Geodesic Surface (MSR-FAGS) module. MSR-FAGS replaces the randomly initialized features of the low-scale generator with rearranged Pre-Shape features and uses the features to guide image generation at subsequent scales, thereby reducing the risk of structural misalignment. To support downstream tasks such as stylization, a Scale-adaptive Sliding-window Patch Extraction (SSPE) strategy is further designed, and a directional Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training supervision module with SSPE (CLIP-SSPE) is constructed. Qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate that FRPSS achieves the best Single Image Fréchet Inception Distance (SIFID) scores on all three datasets while maintaining competitive Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS). Further qualitative experiments verify the effectiveness of FRPSS across multiple downstream tasks with the CLIP-SSPE module.

AI.tldr: FRPSS proposes a novel single-image generation method that addresses structural misalignment issues by using Manifold Structural Rearrangement with Feature Augmentation on Geodesic Surface (MSR-FAGS) module, which replaces random noise with rearranged Pre-Shape features to guide multi-scale generation. Additionally, CLIP-SSPE module is designed for downstream stylization tasks.
AI.motivation: Single-image generative models struggle to balance global structural integrity and local diversity. Existing methods rely on random noise and lack explicit global structural constraints, making generated results prone to spatial structural misalignment when structural variations occur.
AI.method: 1) MSR-FAGS module: Replaces randomly initialized features of low-scale generator with rearranged Pre-Shape features and uses them to guide image generation at subsequent scales. 2) SSPE strategy: Scale-adaptive Sliding-window Patch Extraction for downstream tasks. 3) CLIP-SSPE: Directional Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training supervision module with SSPE.
AI.result: FRPSS achieves the best SIFID scores on all three datasets while maintaining competitive LPIPS. Qualitative experiments verify effectiveness across multiple downstream tasks with CLIP-SSPE module.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FRPSS successfully addresses structural misalignment in single-image generation through Pre-Shape feature rearrangement on geodesic surface, and the CLIP-SSPE module enables effective downstream stylization tasks.

title: GANADI: Uncovering C/C++ OSS Reuse Genealogies via Pivotal Function-Based Clustering to Enhance Supply Chain Security
summary: We present GANADI, a systematic approach for identifying C/C++ OSS reuse genealogies to enhance software supply chain security. Understanding OSS reuse genealogy is crucial for improving SBOM completeness and prioritizing security remediation across supply chains. Although existing approaches can identify reused compo- nents and vulnerabilities within a project, they fail to trace OSS reuse paths through intermediate projects, limiting their effectiveness in securing supply chain ecosystems. To address this limitation, GANADI constructs reuse genealogies by clustering downstream projects based on shared characteristics of origin-derived code (called pivotal functions), and then inferring reuse direction among the projects within each cluster. When applied to 20 widely reused OSS projects with over 1,500 propagation paths, GANADI achieved 84.85% precision and 95.76% recall in identifying reuse genealogies, outperforming existing approaches that achieved at most 23.21% recall. Leveraging OSS reuse genealogy for vulnerability detection, we identified 48 unpatched vulnerabilities in real-world popular C/C++ projects. Among them, 23 were patched following our responsible disclosure (including one CVE ID assigned), demonstrating the practical impact of genealogy-based vulnerability management.

AI.tldr: GANADI is a systematic approach for identifying C/C++ OSS reuse genealogies to enhance software supply chain security. It clusters downstream projects based on shared pivotal functions (origin-derived code) and infers reuse directions to trace reuse paths through intermediate projects. Applied to 20 widely reused OSS projects with over 1,500 propagation paths, it achieved 84.85% precision and 95.76% recall, outperforming existing approaches (max 23.21% recall). It also identified 48 unpatched vulnerabilities, with 23 patched after responsible disclosure.
AI.motivation: Understanding OSS reuse genealogy is crucial for improving SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) completeness and prioritizing security remediation across supply chains. Existing approaches can identify reused components and vulnerabilities within a project but fail to trace OSS reuse paths through intermediate projects, limiting their effectiveness in securing supply chain ecosystems.
AI.method: GANADI constructs reuse genealogies by: (1) clustering downstream projects based on shared characteristics of origin-derived code called "pivotal functions," and (2) inferring reuse direction among projects within each cluster.
AI.result: Applied to 20 widely reused OSS projects with over 1,500 propagation paths, GANADI achieved 84.85% precision and 95.76% recall in identifying reuse genealogies, outperforming existing approaches that achieved at most 23.21% recall. For vulnerability detection, 48 unpatched vulnerabilities were identified in real-world popular C/C++ projects, with 23 patched following responsible disclosure (including one CVE ID assigned).
AI.conclusion: GANADI demonstrates the practical impact of genealogy-based vulnerability management for software supply chain security. The approach significantly outperforms existing methods in tracing reuse paths and enables effective identification of unpatched vulnerabilities across the supply chain.

title: SWB-DM: A Calibrated Sliced-Wasserstein-Barycenter Aggregator with Delayed-Momentum Caching for Byzantine-Robust Federated Learning under Partial Participation
summary:
Robust aggregation methods for federated learning quietly rest on a fragile assumption: that whoever shows up in a given round is a fair sample of the full population. In practice, they rarely are. When only a handful of clients participate per round, even a modest fraction of adversaries can dominate that sample and silently invalidate the finite-sample guarantees that coordinate-wise median, Krum, Bulyan, and trimmed mean all depend on.
  We introduce SWB-DM to address this directly. SWB treats each slice of a client update as a one-dimensional distribution, computes a trimmed Wasserstein barycenter across clients, and recovers coordinate identity via a medoid-based gauge-fixing step -- a heuristic we developed and do not claim it belongs to standard optimal-transport theory. DeMoA-style delayed momentum then caches updates across the full client population each round, decoupling robustness from whoever happened to be sampled. Trim ratio calibration is not cosmetic: under-trimming causes collapse at corruption levels a properly calibrated model survives.
  Across 448 CIFAR-10 configurations, plus CIFAR-100, FEMNIST, and a 500-client scalability run, we find several mechanistically distinct failure modes. Even-sample coordinate-wise median degrades to a deterministic wrong answer. Krum silently violates its own n greater than 2f+2 precondition and diverges without warning. Bulyan's n greater than or equal to 4f+3 threshold produces a sharp pass/fail boundary. On attacks, IPM defeats order-statistic defenses -- including SWB -- more reliably than ALIE, confirmed through delta-space measurements against a convergence bound.
  SWB-DM's cache carries a real warm-up cost, but extending all baselines to the same round budget shows its CIFAR-10 gains are disproportionately large. On CIFAR-100, FLTrust benefits more -- for reasons entirely unrelated to caching.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a critical fragility in federated learning robustness: the assumption that participating clients are a fair sample of the population rarely holds in practice. The authors propose SWB-DM, combining Slice-Wasserstein Barycenter (SWB) with DeMoA-style delayed momentum to decouple robustness from client sampling. Through extensive experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, FEMNIST, and 500-client scalability tests, they identify distinct failure modes in existing defenses and demonstrate SWB-DM's effectiveness, while noting that IPM attacks can defeat order-statistic defenses including SWB.
AI.motivation: Robust aggregation methods for federated learning rely on the assumption that participating clients are a fair sample of the full population. However, when only a small number of clients participate per round, even a modest fraction of adversaries can dominate the sample and invalidate the finite-sample guarantees that coordinate-wise median, Krum, Bulyan, and trimmed mean depend on. This work aims to address this fundamental fragility directly.
AI.method: The authors introduce SWB-DM, comprising two main components: (1) SWB (Slice-Wasserstein Barycenter): Treats each slice of a client update as a one-dimensional distribution, computes a trimmed Wasserstein barycenter across clients, and recovers coordinate identity via a medoid-based gauge-fixing step; (2) DeMoA-style delayed momentum: Caches updates across the full client population each round, decoupling robustness from whoever happens to be sampled. The trim ratio calibration is emphasized as critical - under-trimming causes collapse at corruption levels that a properly calibrated model survives.
AI.result: Across 448 CIFAR-10 configurations, plus CIFAR-100, FEMNIST, and a 500-client scalability run, several mechanistically distinct failure modes were identified: (1) Even-sample coordinate-wise median degrades to a deterministic wrong answer; (2) Krum silently violates its own n > 2f+2 precondition and diverges without warning; (3) Bulyan's n ≥ 4f+3 threshold produces a sharp pass/fail boundary; (4) IPM defeats order-statistic defenses (including SWB) more reliably than ALIE, confirmed through delta-space measurements against a convergence bound. SWB-DM's cache carries a real warm-up cost, but extending all baselines to the same round budget shows its CIFAR-10 gains are disproportionately large. On CIFAR-100, FLTrust benefits more for reasons unrelated to caching.
AI.conclusion: The paper reveals that existing robust aggregation methods have fundamental vulnerabilities when client sampling assumptions are violated. While SWB-DM provides improved robustness through cached updates and trimmed Wasserstein aggregation, it is not immune to all attacks (e.g., IPM can defeat it). The authors emphasize that trim ratio calibration is not cosmetic but critical for survival at higher corruption levels. The work highlights the need for more robust federated learning aggregation schemes that can handle realistic, non-i.i.d. client sampling patterns.

title: Cross-Anatomy Transfer Versus Sparse Interpolation in Digital-Twin-Oriented Aortic Fluid-Structure Interaction Surrogates
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, Under review at ICBME 2026
summary: Surrogate credibility for fluid-structure interac- tion (FSI) requires distinguishing transfer across independent anatomies from interpolation within an already sampled surface. Four de-identified human aortic models from the Vascular Model Repository were reconstructed into separate lumen and nominal 1.5-mm wall domains and analyzed under matched first-cycle two-way FSI. A geometry-only LightGBM prior, selected by leave-one-anatomy-out development on three anatomies, was zero-shot evaluated on a fourth, then probed with a post-zero- shot sparse field-completion case study over six targets. Zero-shot transfer was poor across all targets. At a five-percent anchor level (203 anchors, 3,852 evaluation nodes), prior-plus-adaptation reached an oscillatory shear index (OSI) R2 of 0.603. However, same-anchor controls tuned only on the three development anatomies were stronger for several outcomes: inverse-distance weighting reached R2 = 0.829 (OSI), 0.617 (peak von Mises stress), 0.676 (mean stress); radial basis function interpolation reached 0.917, 0.714, 0.778. Sparse within-anatomy labels thus support field completion, but this four-anatomy cohort gives no evidence the cross-anatomy prior adds value beyond direct interpolation. We frame this as a first computational stage toward a measurement-linked digital twin: the surrogate/update layer is evaluated here, while larger cohorts, converged FSI, measurable patient-side inputs, and physics-informed learning remain future work, not a claim of a complete clinical twin. Our code, data and computation files are available at https://github. com/ali-nourbakhsh2005/Aortic-FSI-Sparse-Field-Completion

AI.tldr: This study evaluates whether machine learning priors trained on multiple aortic anatomies can generalize to new anatomies for fluid-structure interaction (FSI) surrogate modeling. Using four human aortic models with matched first-cycle two-way FSI, the researchers found zero-shot transfer performed poorly, while within-anatomy interpolation methods (IDW, RBF) achieved significantly better accuracy (R2 up to 0.917 for OSI). The study concludes that cross-anatomy priors provide no added value beyond direct interpolation for this four-anatomy cohort.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to establish credibility for FSI surrogates by distinguishing between transfer across independent anatomies (zero-shot) versus interpolation within a sampled surface. This is framed as a step toward measurement-linked digital twins for cardiovascular applications.
AI.method: Four de-identified human aortic models from the Vascular Model Repository were reconstructed into lumen and 1.5-mm wall domains. A geometry-only LightGBM prior was trained using leave-one-anatomy-out cross-validation on three anatomies and evaluated zero-shot on the fourth. This was supplemented with a post-zero-shot sparse field-completion case study using six targets. Performance was compared against same-anchor controls using inverse-distance weighting (IDW) and radial basis function (RBF) interpolation, tuned only on the three development anatomies.
AI.result: Zero-shot transfer across anatomies was poor for all targets. At a five-percent anchor level (203 anchors, 3,852 evaluation nodes), prior-plus-adaptation achieved OSI R2 = 0.603. However, same-anchor interpolation controls performed substantially better: IDW achieved R2 = 0.829 (OSI), 0.617 (peak von Mises stress), 0.676 (mean stress); RBF achieved 0.917, 0.714, 0.778 respectively.
AI.conclusion: Sparse within-anatomy labels support field completion, but this four-anatomy cohort provides no evidence that cross-anatomy priors add value beyond direct interpolation. The study is framed as a first computational stage toward a measurement-linked digital twin, with larger cohorts, converged FSI, patient-side inputs, and physics-informed learning remaining as future work.

title: A Vision-Language Foundation Model for Precise and Comprehensive Brain Tumor Diagnosis from Preoperative Multimodal Data
summary:
Background Non-invasive presurgical diagnosis of brain tumor types from Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is essential but challenging due to overlapping imaging features across tumor types, inter-observer variability, and the extensive training required for expertise. We aimed to develop an MRI-based Artificial Intelligence (AI) model for automatic and reliable brain tumor classification with diagnostic uncertainty quantification and radiology reports generation.
  Methods We developed BrainVLM to classify all 12 World Health Organization (WHO) 2021 brain tumor types. BrainVLM integrates an uncertainty quantification strategy to indicate prediction reliability and a module for generating radiology reports to elucidate the clinical rationale. BrainVLM was trained on multi-modal data (MRI scans, demographics, and radiology reports) from 40,043 individuals. It was validated on 5,211 patients with pathologically confirmed brain tumors, including 3,877 held-out patients from the primary hospital and 1,334 patients from 11 independent hospitals. We further conducted two proof-of-concept studies to validate its clinical utility in AI-clinician workflows: 1) a blinded multi-reader study where 12 neuroradiologists across varying experience levels interpreted 248 retrospective cases with or without AI assistance, and 2) a real-world prospective study in which 1,009 patients were independently and blindly assessed by BrainVLM and radiologists before surgery. Additionally, we demonstrated BrainVLM's utility in preoperative molecular subgroup prediction for adult-type diffuse gliomas, using a multi-center cohort of 632 patients.

AI.tldr: BrainVLM is an AI system that automatically classifies all 12 WHO 2021 brain tumor types from MRI scans, with built-in uncertainty quantification and automated radiology report generation. The model was trained on 40,043 patients and validated on 5,211 patients from multiple hospitals, demonstrating improved diagnostic accuracy when assisting radiologists in both retrospective and prospective clinical settings.
AI.motivation: Non-invasive presurgical diagnosis of brain tumor types from MRI is essential but challenging due to overlapping imaging features across tumor types, inter-observer variability, and the extensive training required for expertise. There is a need for automatic, reliable brain tumor classification with diagnostic uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: BrainVLM integrates multi-modal data (MRI scans, demographics, and radiology reports) and includes an uncertainty quantification strategy to indicate prediction reliability and a module for generating radiology reports. Validation included: 1) 5,211 patients with pathologically confirmed tumors (3,877 from primary hospital, 1,334 from 11 independent hospitals); 2) Blinded multi-reader study with 12 neuroradiologists on 248 cases; 3) Prospective real-world study on 1,009 patients; 4) Molecular subgroup prediction for 632 patients with adult-type diffuse gliomas.
AI.result: BrainVLM demonstrated high accuracy in classifying all 12 WHO 2021 brain tumor types. The AI-assisted radiologists showed improved diagnostic performance compared to unassisted interpretation. The prospective study and molecular subgroup prediction further validated clinical utility.
AI.conclusion: BrainVLM represents a promising AI tool for automatic brain tumor classification with uncertainty quantification and report generation, showing potential to improve diagnostic accuracy in clinical workflows when used as an assistant to radiologists.

title: A Set-Theoretic Evaluation Framework for Assessing Asset Administration Shell Instances: Towards Comparability and Suitability
summary: Asset Administration Shells (AAS) provide a standardized means of representing assets and their information in manufacturing and increasingly serve as a basis for software services. However, different AAS instances vary in structure, content, and degree of completion, making it difficult to determine whether a given AAS is suitable for a specific application. This paper presents two complementary methods to support the comparison and application-oriented assessment of AAS. First, set-theoretic operations are employed to compare AAS models, enabling the identification of common, missing, and differing submodels and parameters. Second, an AAS suitability model assesses the conformity of an AAS to the requirements of a specific use case. The assessment considers structural conformity, semantic consistency, cardinality, and specification conformity and can be performed either against a reference AAS or a set of required SemanticIDs. A suitability value is derived from the identified deviations and is complemented by a detailed report of missing or non-conforming information. The proposed approach support practitioners and researchers in the comparison of evolving AAS and provide application-specific information on their suitability for manufacturing software services.

AI.tldr: This paper presents two complementary methods for comparing and assessing Asset Administration Shells (AAS): (1) set-theoretic operations to identify common, missing, and differing submodels/parameters between AAS instances, and (2) an AAS suitability model that evaluates conformity against specific use case requirements.
AI.motivation: The variability in AAS structure, content, and completion degree makes it challenging to determine whether a given AAS is suitable for a specific manufacturing application, creating a need for standardized comparison and assessment methods.
AI.method: Two complementary approaches: (1) set-theoretic operations for comparing AAS models to identify common, missing, and differing elements; (2) an AAS suitability model assessing structural conformity, semantic consistency, cardinality, and specification conformity against either a reference AAS or required SemanticIDs, yielding a suitability value with detailed deviation reports.
AI.result: A suitability value derived from identified deviations, complemented by a detailed report of missing or non-conforming information.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables practitioners and researchers to compare evolving AAS and obtain application-specific suitability information for manufacturing software services.

title: A Decision-Support Audit Protocol for Supervision Drift in Proxy-Labeled Credit-Risk Prediction
summary: Credit-risk models are trained on proxy labels and deployed under temporal and segment change, yet no single transfer metric separates base-rate shift, probability-scale shift, and feature-label relationship change. We contribute a design-science artifact: a locked, multi-signal audit protocol for supervision drift in proxy-labeled credit-risk prediction. Five layers (transfer performance, an oracle-gap probe, a calibration diagnostic, feature-label stability, and a synthetic positive control), thresholds, and decision rules were locked before interpretation; a bounded reading is a designed outcome. On a public LendingClub dataset (temporal 2013 to 2016 and cross-segment transfer), ranking is stable and oracle gaps are small; the clearest temporal signal is a prevalence and probability-scale mismatch that intercept-only diagnostic recalibration largely reduces, though its cause is not identifiable from the available release. The positive control responds only to larger injected shifts; subtler drift cannot be excluded. Mapping diagnostic patterns to governance actions is conceptual guidance, not validated here.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a locked, multi-signal audit protocol with five layers to detect supervision drift in credit-risk models trained on proxy labels. The protocol addresses the limitation that no single transfer metric can separate base-rate shift, probability-scale shift, and feature-label relationship change.
AI.motivation: Credit-risk models are trained on proxy labels and deployed under temporal and segment change, yet no existing transfer metric can distinguish between base-rate shift, probability-scale shift, and feature-label relationship change. This creates a gap in model governance and drift detection.
AI.method: The authors designed a locked audit protocol with five layers: (1) transfer performance, (2) oracle-gap probe, (3) calibration diagnostic, (4) feature-label stability, and (5) synthetic positive control. Thresholds and decision rules were locked before interpretation to ensure a bounded reading. The protocol was tested on a public LendingClub dataset (temporal 2013-2016 and cross-segment transfer).
AI.result: On the LendingClub dataset, ranking is stable and oracle gaps are small. The clearest temporal signal is a prevalence and probability-scale mismatch that intercept-only diagnostic recalibration largely reduces, though its cause cannot be identified from the available data. The positive control responds only to larger injected shifts; subtler drift cannot be excluded.
AI.conclusion: The five-layer audit protocol provides a bounded approach to detecting supervision drift in proxy-labeled credit-risk models. However, the positive control only detects larger injected shifts, and subtler drift cannot be excluded. Mapping diagnostic patterns to governance actions remains conceptual guidance, not validated in this study.

title: Breaking the 1.58-bit Barrier for Ternary LLMs
summary: Ternary Large Language Models (LLM) store every weight as one of three symbols $\{-1,0,+1\}$, so the cost of a ternary model is conventionally referenced to the information-theoretic $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ bits per weight. The prevailing deployment format packs five ternary weights into one byte (five-trit packing), and due to the power-of-two group sizes used in practice this rounds up to $1.625$ bits per weight. This effective storage bit-width treats the three symbols $\{-1,0,+1\}$ as equiprobable. We measure the actual symbol distribution of 29 ternary LLM models and find that zeros account for up to $51.5\%$ of all weights. Motivated by this finding, we introduce BITCOS, a simple distribution-adaptive layout comprised of a dense presence bitmap plus a compacted sign vector, and costs $2 - z$ bits per weight element given a zero density $z$ in the model's weights. BITCOS stores weights more compactly than the five-trit packing in 26 of the 29 tested models, and reaches $1.485$ bits per weight on the sparsest of them. BITCOS is amenable to efficient unpacking on modern processors and GPUs, and we present optimized unpacking sequences for AVX-512, AVX2 and Intel Xe2 GPUs. Measured against production state-of-the-art ternary matrix-vector multiplication kernels, at the zero densities real-world ternary models exhibit, the realized gain with our proposed layout is up to $1.28\times$. Finally, we illustrate end-to-end LLM inference results on 5 different platforms (client and server CPUs, integrated and discrete Xe2 GPUs) where decode throughput improves by up to $1.18\times$ on CPUs and $1.27\times$ on GPUs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes BITCOS, a distribution-adaptive storage layout for ternary LLMs that exploits the empirically observed sparsity (zeros up to 51.5%) to achieve more compact storage than conventional five-trit packing, with optimized unpacking for AVX-512, AVX2, and Intel Xe2 GPUs, delivering up to 1.28× speedup in matrix-vector multiplication and 1.27× throughput improvement in end-to-end inference.
AI.motivation: The conventional ternary weight storage assumes equiprobable symbols (-1, 0, +1), but the authors empirically discovered that zeros are actually much more frequent (up to 51.5%) in real-world ternary LLM models, creating an opportunity for more efficient storage through density-adaptive encoding.
AI.method: The authors measured zero density across 29 ternary LLM models, then designed BITCOS—a bitmap-based layout with a presence bitmap plus compacted sign vector costing 2-z bits per weight (where z is zero density). They developed optimized SIMD unpacking kernels for AVX-512, AVX2, and Intel Xe2 GPUs.
AI.result: BITCOS outperforms five-trit packing in 26/29 models, achieving 1.485 bits per weight on the sparsest model. Ternary matrix-vector multiplication kernels achieve up to 1.28× speedup. End-to-end inference shows 1.18× CPU throughput and 1.27× GPU throughput improvements across 5 platforms.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting non-uniform weight distributions in ternary LLMs enables significant storage and inference efficiency gains. BITCOS provides a practical, hardware-accelerated solution that scales with model sparsity, making it attractive for deploying large ternary models.

title: SAVOR: Self-Aware Visual Grounding via Confidence-Calibrated Reinforcement Learning for Multimodal Hallucination Mitigation
comment: 33rd International Conference on Neural Information Processing (ICONIP 2026)
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made strong progress on visual question answering and image captioning, yet they still produce fluent claims about objects, attributes, or relations that are not grounded in the image. Many remedies either modify decoding at test time, which adds latency, or fine tune with preferences such as DPO variants, which teach which answer is preferred but not when the model's own answer is unreliable. We argue that calibrated self assessment is the missing signal. We introduce Savor, a training framework that (i) augments the output schema with token and answer confidence, (ii) optimises the policy with a Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) objective that penalises calibration error and poor abstention decisions, and (iii) uses the learned confidence at inference time to revisit visual evidence only when the model is uncertain. Experiments on POPE, HallusionBench, AMBER and MMHal-Bench across two recent backbones (InternVL3-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B) show that Savor reduces hallucination while preserving general capability on MME and MMBench, with lower Expected Calibration Error than DPO and decoding baselines.

AI.tldr: Savor is a training framework for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that reduces hallucinations by teaching models to assess their own confidence through calibrated self-assessment. It uses GRPO optimization to penalize calibration errors and poor abstention decisions, and learns to revisit visual evidence when uncertain.
AI.motivation: MLLMs produce fluent but ungrounded claims about visual content (hallucinations). Existing remedies either add latency via decoding modifications or use DPO to teach answer preferences, but neither teaches models when their own answers are unreliable. The missing signal is calibrated self-assessment - the model's ability to accurately estimate its own uncertainty.
AI.method: Savor introduces a three-component framework: (i) Augmenting output schema with token and answer confidence, (ii) Optimizing policy using Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) that penalizes calibration error and poor abstention decisions, (iii) Using learned confidence at inference time to revisit visual evidence only when the model is uncertain.
AI.result: Experiments on POPE, HallusionBench, AMBER, and MMHal-Bench across two backbones (InternVL3-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B) show that Savor reduces hallucination while preserving general capability on MME and MMBench, with lower Expected Calibration Error than DPO and decoding baselines.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated self-assessment is an effective missing signal for reducing hallucinations in MLLMs. The GRPO-based training approach with confidence learning and evidence revisiting provides a scalable solution that balances hallucination reduction with general capability preservation.

title: Towards an Asset Administration Shell Maturity Model
summary: The Asset Administration Shell (AAS) is increasingly recognized as a fundamental model for the realization of and data exchange between digital twins in manufacturing. An AAS defines a hierarchical data structure to represent any type of asset throughout its entire lifecycle. In the context of AAS-based systems, comparing different AAS instances constitutes a practical challenge, as neither a widely accepted methodological framework nor a maturity model are available to systematically support such analyses. To address this gap, we propose a novel concept of AAS maturity that characterizes the extent to which established digital twin criteria are met and thus enabling comparability of AAS instances. The concepts are derived from the literature and applied through exemplification. These emerging results enable practitioners and researchers to systematically compare AAS instances and support the identification and assessment of further development steps in the digital twin engineering process.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the lack of a systematic framework for comparing different Asset Administration Shell (AAS) instances in manufacturing digital twins. The authors propose a novel AAS maturity model to enable comparability and assessment of digital twin development.
AI.motivation: The Asset Administration Shell (AAS) is recognized as a fundamental model for digital twins in manufacturing, but there is no widely accepted methodological framework or maturity model to systematically compare different AAS instances. This gap hinders practical analysis and evaluation of AAS-based systems.
AI.method: The authors derive concepts from existing literature and apply them through exemplification to develop the AAS maturity model.
AI.result: The proposed maturity model enables systematic comparison of AAS instances and supports identification and assessment of further development steps in the digital twin engineering process.
AI.conclusion: The AAS maturity model provides practitioners and researchers with a tool to systematically evaluate and compare AAS instances, facilitating better digital twin engineering practices in manufacturing.

title: LLMs as Master Forgers: Generating Synthetic Time Series Data for Manufacturing
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures. Published in the 2024 International Conference on Image Processing, Computer Vision and Machine Learning (ICICML)
summary: This paper presents a novel framework leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate synthetic time series data for manufacturing processes. Motivated by the scarcity of labeled time-series data in real-world manufacturing settings, which hinders the development of robust machine learning models, we explore the potential of LLMs to learn complex temporal dependencies and generate realistic synthetic data. Our approach involves fine-tuning pre-trained LLMs on manufacturing process instructions and employing a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) technique to enhance data diversity and realism. We evaluate our method against traditional time series modeling techniques like ARIMA and LSTMs, using quantitative metrics, PCA analysis, and downstream task performance (anomaly detection). Results demonstrate that our LLM-driven framework outperforms these baselines, generating high-quality synthetic time series data that effectively captures temporal dependencies and statistical properties of real manufacturing data, leading to improvements in downstream task performance.

AI.tldr: A novel framework using Large Language Models (LLMs) with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) to generate synthetic time series data for manufacturing processes, outperforming traditional methods like ARIMA and LSTMs.
AI.motivation: The scarcity of labeled time-series data in real-world manufacturing settings hinders the development of robust machine learning models.
AI.method: Fine-tuning pre-trained LLMs on manufacturing process instructions, combined with RAG technique to enhance data diversity and realism. Evaluation using quantitative metrics, PCA analysis, and downstream anomaly detection tasks.
AI.result: The LLM-driven framework outperforms baseline methods (ARIMA and LSTMs), generating high-quality synthetic time series that captures temporal dependencies and statistical properties of real manufacturing data, improving downstream task performance.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively generate synthetic manufacturing time series data, outperforming traditional time series modeling techniques and providing a viable solution to data scarcity in manufacturing ML applications.

title: Fine-Tuning Fixes Mode Collapse and Over-Dispersion in LLMs
