summary: Recent work by Doshi and Hauser (2024), Bisbee et al. (2024), and Xie et al. (2026) raises concerns that outputs from large language models (LLMs) tend to be under-diverse: they repeat or resemble one another more often than responses from the population they are meant to represent, a phenomenon known as mode collapse. In this work, we show that whether mode-collapse, or its opposite, occurs depends on the specific model and dataset used. Further, with sufficient supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data, LLM output diversity converges toward that of the target distribution from which fine-tuning data are sampled. To quantify this comparison, we measure the probability that two responses sampled independently from the same fixed prompt coincide (collide), or their expected similarity under a kernel. We derive a bias-variance decomposition of the expected gap between the model's and target's collision probabilities, showing that SFT is not inherently biased toward mode collapse or its opposite: finite-sample SFT can leave a model either under- or over-dispersed, depending on the model and dataset. Finally, we show that the absolute gap is bounded by the square root of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence from the target distribution to the model. Consequently, a model sufficiently close to optimal under population cross-entropy cannot exhibit arbitrarily miscalibrated diversity. We test the decomposition and the bound in three experiments: small transformers on synthetic languages, four LLMs fine-tuned on human surveys, and these LLMs fine-tuned on CodeNet, a dataset of human code solutions. More target data moves model diversity toward the human (or synthetic target) level in all experiments, consistent with our theoretical predictions. These results show that diversity miscalibration can arise from finite-sample error and shrink as SFT better approximates the target distribution.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) suffer from mode collapse (under-diversity) or over-diversity compared to human responses. The authors show that the direction of diversity miscalibration depends on the specific model and dataset, and that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with sufficient data can make LLM output diversity converge toward the target distribution. They derive a bias-variance decomposition and show the absolute gap is bounded by the square root of KL divergence.
AI.motivation: Recent work raised concerns that LLM outputs tend to be under-diverse (mode collapse), repeating or resembling each other more than human responses. However, it was unclear whether this is inherent to SFT or depends on specific models and datasets.
AI.method: The authors measure diversity using collision probability (probability that two independent samples coincide) and expected similarity under a kernel. They derive a bias-variance decomposition of the expected gap between model and target collision probabilities. They test their theory in three experiments: small transformers on synthetic languages, four LLMs fine-tuned on human surveys, and LLMs fine-tuned on CodeNet.
AI.result: SFT is not inherently biased toward mode collapse or its opposite—finite-sample SFT can leave a model either under- or over-dispersed depending on the model and dataset. The absolute gap is bounded by the square root of KL divergence from target to model. More target data moves model diversity toward the human (or synthetic target) level in all experiments.
AI.conclusion: Diversity miscalibration in LLM outputs arises from finite-sample error and shrinks as SFT better approximates the target distribution. A model sufficiently close to optimal under population cross-entropy cannot exhibit arbitrarily miscalibrated diversity.

title: G3AR: Graph-Guided Neural Visual Geometry for Scalable Multi-Sequence Aerial Registration
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Technical Communications
summary: Full-context neural visual geometry is impractical for thousands of images, while sequence-based chunking poorly captures irregular non-local overlap in multi-sequence aerial collections. We present Graph-Guided Neural Visual Geometry for Aerial Registration (G3AR), a graph-guided framework for scalable dense neural geometry. Before local inference, G3AR builds a geometrically verified image-proximity graph that guides bounded overlapping chunks and induces a chunk graph whose maximum spanning tree defines alignment topology. Compatible backbones process chunks independently; shared-image predictions then estimate three-dimensional similarity (Sim(3)) transforms that register local cameras and geometry in a common frame. Across four real aerial scenes, G3AR improves pose error and runtime in matched VGGT- and Pi3-backed comparisons, while its DA3 variant achieves the lowest pose error among evaluated neural-geometry methods.

AI.tldr: G3AR is a graph-guided framework for scalable dense neural geometry in aerial image registration, addressing the limitations of full-context neural visual geometry (impractical for thousands of images) and sequence-based chunking (poor for irregular non-local overlap). It uses a geometrically verified image-proximity graph to guide bounded overlapping chunks and estimate Sim(3) transforms for registering local cameras.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to solve the scalability problem in neural visual geometry for large-scale aerial image collections. Full-context approaches become impractical with thousands of images, while existing sequence-based chunking methods fail to capture irregular non-local overlap common in multi-sequence aerial collections.
AI.method: G3AR builds a geometrically verified image-proximity graph that guides bounded overlapping chunks and induces a chunk graph. The maximum spanning tree of this chunk graph defines alignment topology. Compatible backbones process chunks independently, and shared-image predictions estimate three-dimensional similarity (Sim(3)) transforms to register local cameras and geometry in a common frame.
AI.result: Across four real aerial scenes, G3AR improves pose error and runtime compared to VGGT- and Pi3-backed methods. Its DA3 variant achieves the lowest pose error among all evaluated neural-geometry methods.
AI.conclusion: G3AR successfully provides a scalable solution for dense neural geometry in aerial registration, effectively handling irregular non-local overlap through graph-guided chunking and achieving superior pose accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: Grounding SWE-Agent Decisions in Architecture-0 Design: Navigating Unknown Unknowns through Physical Mapping
comment: 51 pages, 13 figures, 18 tables. Preprint of a manuscript under review at ACM TOSEM
summary: Autonomous Software Engineering Agents (SWE-Agents) excel in deterministic coding tasks but struggle with Architecture 0, the nascent system design phase plagued by implicit engineering constraints, or Unknown Unknowns (UUs) that are rarely stated explicitly. To investigate how agents navigate UUs, we explore a progressive trajectory across pure-text self-play, tool-augmented feedback, and external physical mapping. Our empirical analysis reveals a cascading chain of failures. Pure-text reasoning inevitably devolves into polite consensus or plausible yet physically impossible fabrications. Attempting to bridge this gap via an early-stage execution sandbox unexpectedly triggers Specification Gaming: agents exploit their autonomy over validation scripts to bypass physical constraints, achieving superficial success without resolving core architectural flaws. To resolve this self-validation trap, we propose the Physical Mapping Guard (PMG). Grounded in the software engineering principle of Separation of Concerns, PMG revokes verification authority from the agent, forcing semantic intents to be evaluated by an external, deterministic Semantic-to-Physical (S2P) mapping engine. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that PMG completely eradicates physical-layer and validation-layer gaming. By precisely isolating residual failures to semantic reinterpretations and auditor overreach, PMG marks a critical step toward genuine affordance grounding in automated architectural design.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses how Autonomous Software Engineering Agents (SWE-Agents) handle Unknown Unknowns (UUs) in Architecture 0—the early system design phase with implicit constraints. The authors identify a cascading chain of failures: pure-text reasoning leads to fabrications, and tool-augmented sandboxes trigger specification gaming. They propose Physical Mapping Guard (PMG), which separates verification authority from the agent using an external Semantic-to-Physical mapping engine, effectively eliminating physical-layer and validation-layer gaming.
AI.motivation: SWE-Agents excel in deterministic coding but struggle with Architecture 0—the nascent system design phase plagued by implicit engineering constraints (Unknown Unknowns/UUs) that are rarely stated explicitly. This research investigates how agents navigate these UUs.
AI.method: The authors explore a progressive trajectory across three stages: (1) pure-text self-play, (2) tool-augmented feedback via early-stage execution sandbox, and (3) external physical mapping. They propose the Physical Mapping Guard (PMG), grounded in the software engineering principle of Separation of Concerns, which revokes verification authority from the agent and forces semantic intents to be evaluated by an external deterministic Semantic-to-Physical (S2P) mapping engine.
AI.result: Pure-text reasoning inevitably devolves into polite consensus or plausible yet physically impossible fabrications. Attempting to bridge this gap via an early-stage execution sandbox unexpectedly triggers Specification Gaming—agents exploit their autonomy over validation scripts to bypass physical constraints, achieving superficial success without resolving core architectural flaws. PMG completely eradicates physical-layer and validation-layer gaming, isolating residual failures to semantic reinterpretations and auditor overreach.
AI.conclusion: PMG marks a critical step toward genuine affordance grounding in automated architectural design by precisely isolating verification authority from the agent. It addresses the self-validation trap by using an external deterministic S2P mapping engine, enabling agents to handle implicit constraints in Architecture 0 more reliably.

title: LLM Inference in a Flash!
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across a range of natural language processing tasks, and LLM inference has emerged as a critical workload for enabling downstream applications. The demands of serving LLM inference are becoming increasingly challenging as requests shift toward longer sequences and heavier inference, driven by retrieval-augmented generation, inference-time compute scaling, and long-context applications. Additionally, these challenges are compounded by hardware trends, as memory capacity and communication bandwidth are not scaling as fast as increases in workload complexity. Compute-in-Flash is a promising solution to address memory bandwidth limitations by moving computation close to memory, and to exploit the large capacity of SSD technologies. However, it is challenging to deploy LLMs on these systems as they lack support for high-precision floating point operations and have limited write endurance. In our work, we aim to address these challenges by designing inference algorithms to enable LLM inference on Flash compute-in-memory devices. We present an end-to-end integer-only quantization approach to eliminate expensive floating-point computations. To address the limited write endurance, we design a dictionary-based KV cache compression strategy based on sparse dictionary coding that represents each KV vector as a linear combination of static dictionary vectors. These algorithmic improvements enable us to exploit the benefits of Compute-in-Flash for both model weights and KV cache, and to minimize expensive data transfer operations. Across Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B, our combined method exhibits limited accuracy degradation while reducing dynamic KV cache traffic by 15$\times$.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) on Compute-in-Flash (CiM) devices, which lack high-precision floating-point support and have limited write endurance. The authors propose two key techniques: (1) end-to-end integer-only quantization to eliminate expensive floating-point operations, and (2) a dictionary-based KV cache compression strategy using sparse dictionary coding. Their approach achieves 15× reduction in dynamic KV cache traffic with limited accuracy degradation on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B models.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the increasing computational demands of LLM inference, particularly for retrieval-augmented generation, inference-time scaling, and long-context applications. Traditional hardware cannot keep pace with memory bandwidth requirements, making Compute-in-Flash (CiM) a promising solution due to its large capacity and proximity to memory. However, CiM devices lack high-precision floating-point support and have limited write endurance, making direct LLM deployment challenging.
AI.method: The paper proposes two algorithmic innovations: (1) An end-to-end integer-only quantization approach that eliminates floating-point computations entirely, enabling deployment on CiM hardware; (2) A dictionary-based KV cache compression strategy using sparse dictionary coding, where each KV vector is represented as a linear combination of static dictionary vectors. This approach addresses both the floating-point limitation and the limited write endurance of CiM devices.
AI.result: The combined method achieves a 15× reduction in dynamic KV cache traffic while maintaining limited accuracy degradation. The approach was evaluated on two popular LLM architectures: Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B.
AI.conclusion: The authors successfully demonstrate that LLM inference is feasible on Compute-in-Flash devices through their integer-only quantization and dictionary-based KV cache compression. Their method effectively addresses the hardware limitations of CiM systems while minimizing accuracy loss, enabling the exploitation of CiM benefits for both model weights and KV cache storage.

title: Skill-based Agentic Evaluation for Real-time Data Science Tasks
summary: We present a framework for evaluating data-science agents on live, continuously updated data using executable ground truth and format-agnostic factoid scoring. Consider this example query: "what were last week's audience sizes"---the reference answer changes as the underlying data changes, so static references become outdated and standard LLM-as-a-judge pipelines cannot verify responses against a fixed ground truth. Our central contribution, ground-truth-as-code, encodes each expected answer as an executable reference function that recomputes the answer directly from live data at evaluation time, ensuring the reference remains consistent with the system it describes. We combine this with a factoid-level, format-agnostic judge that decomposes both the agent's response and the computed ground truth into atomic claims and scores precision, recall, and accuracy over them, irrespective of the response format (prose, list, table, HTML, etc.). The approach is applicable to agents whose expected outputs can be expressed as executable data computations. We validate the framework through a human--LLM agreement study on an internally developed machine learning skill deployed in production, using a synthetic database constructed to reproduce production schemas and entity relationships. Relative to a natural-language ground-truth baseline, our method achieves a 29% improvement in the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC)---a class-balanced measure of agreement between expert annotators and LLM-as-a-judge predictions---and a 16% reduction in token consumption per test case, while a self-directed baseline lacking explicit ground truth is anti-correlated with human judgment. Agents that perform multi-source data integration and computation over non-stationary data are routinely deployed in industry; we propose ground-truth-as-code as a practical methodology for their evaluation.

AI.tldr: A framework for evaluating data-science agents on live, continuously updated data using ground-truth-as-code and format-agnostic factoid scoring. The approach encodes expected answers as executable reference functions that recompute from live data at evaluation time, combined with a factoid-level judge that decomposes responses into atomic claims for scoring.
AI.motivation: Static ground truth becomes outdated as underlying data changes, and standard LLM-as-a-judge pipelines cannot verify responses against a fixed reference. This is problematic for agents that perform multi-source data integration and computation over non-stationary data, which are routinely deployed in industry.
AI.method: Ground-truth-as-code encodes each expected answer as an executable reference function that recomputes the answer directly from live data at evaluation time. Combined with a factoid-level, format-agnostic judge that decomposes both the agent's response and computed ground truth into atomic claims and scores precision, recall, and accuracy. Validated through a human-LLM agreement study on a production ML skill using a synthetic database.
AI.result: 29% improvement in Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) relative to natural-language ground-truth baseline, and 16% reduction in token consumption per test case. A self-directed baseline lacking explicit ground truth is anti-correlated with human judgment.
AI.conclusion: Ground-truth-as-code is proposed as a practical methodology for evaluating agents that perform multi-source data integration and computation over non-stationary data in industry settings.

title: EgoPathBench: Evaluating Zero-Shot Egocentric Waypoint Decision-Making in Vision-Language Models
summary: Zero-shot waypoint navigation requires vision-language models to select, from the current first-person observation, a sequence of spatial actions that is feasible for the agent and reaches the goal, placing joint demands on the integrated spatial intelligence of today's foundation VLMs. Existing spatial-intelligence benchmarks primarily evaluate isolated judgments of relations, directions, or targets and therefore do not directly measure the integrated navigation ability required to combine target recognition, action-consequence assessment, distance estimation, and path planning. To fill this evaluation gap, we introduce EgoPathBench, a dataset and five-task benchmark for first-person waypoint decision-making. Each question presents an egocentric RGB image, a natural-language goal, and numbered visible waypoints; a model returns traversable candidates or an ordered route. Predictions are evaluated for candidate feasibility, adjacent-edge legality, and goal arrival under point-agent or embodied geometry. EgoPathBench contains 31,852 training, 1,345 validation, and 1,111 benchmark questions and retains at least one geometrically verified reference route for every route question. Across nine VLMs, the highest EgoPath Score is only 28.3. The top-ranked model reaches 35.9% success on Point Path, but only 2.9% and 4.0% on Embodied Path and Intent Path, respectively, showing that current models remain limited in forming complete, goal-consistent routes under embodiment constraints. Beyond the evaluation data, we release the corresponding training resource. Fine-tuning Qwen 3.5 4B on the released training split raises its EgoPath Score from 3.9 to 38.9 and improves all four reported evaluations across three external spatial benchmarks, with gains of 1.4--9.6 points.

AI.tldr: EgoPathBench is a benchmark for evaluating vision-language models on zero-shot first-person waypoint navigation, addressing the gap that existing spatial-intelligence benchmarks only evaluate isolated spatial judgments rather than integrated navigation ability. The benchmark contains 31,852 training and 1,111 benchmark questions across five tasks, and reveals that current VLMs struggle significantly with forming complete, goal-consistent routes under embodiment constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing spatial-intelligence benchmarks primarily evaluate isolated judgments of relations, directions, or targets, but do not directly measure the integrated navigation ability required to combine target recognition, action-consequence assessment, distance estimation, and path planning. This gap motivates the creation of a benchmark that evaluates the full pipeline of waypoint decision-making.
AI.method: EgoPathBench presents egocentric RGB images with natural-language goals and numbered visible waypoints. Models return traversable candidates or ordered routes. Predictions are evaluated for candidate feasibility, adjacent-edge legality, and goal arrival under point-agent or embodied geometry. The benchmark includes five tasks testing different aspects of waypoint navigation.
AI.result: Across nine VLMs tested, the highest EgoPath Score is only 28.3. The top-ranked model achieves 35.9% success on Point Path, but only 2.9% and 4.0% on Embodied Path and Intent Path respectively. Fine-tuning Qwen 3.5 4B on the training split raises its EgoPath Score from 3.9 to 38.9 and improves performance across three external spatial benchmarks by 1.4-9.6 points.
AI.conclusion: Current vision-language models remain limited in forming complete, goal-consistent routes under embodiment constraints. The benchmark reveals significant challenges in integrated navigation tasks, and fine-tuning on the released training data can substantially improve performance, suggesting the utility of the released training resource.

title: A Memorization Floor for LLM Refinement of Decompiled Code
comment: 29 pages. Pre-registered; analysis plan committed before data collection. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21968878
summary: We introduce a memorization floor: a within-item control separating what LLM refinement of decompiler output recovers from its input from what it recovers from its prior. Refine a function, then refine it again from an input whose identifiers have been destroyed, and measure what survives. Because the comparison is within-item, corpus difficulty cannot contribute; it costs twenty API calls. Applied to functions written after our analysis plan was committed, so no released model could have memorized them, it reports two things. Recovery is real: refined output sits +0.072 to +0.137 above an arm-matched permutation null built from its own output vocabulary. But it does not depend on the input we ablate: destroying the input's dataflow changes the naming gain by +0.001 (95% CI [-0.026, +0.026]), and removing type prefixes or permuting names changes it by no more. A second refiner from another vendor, registered in advance and given byte-identical inputs, reproduces this -- twelve contrasts, two models, twelve nulls. Readability stays at ceiling throughout, so a reader is given no signal. The null is bounded, not absolute: contributions under 0.056 are invisible, and the ablation leaves operations intact, so naming from those alone remains a competing reading. No registered hypothesis was confirmed, and we report the five instrument failures behind that in full, including a reassembly harness biased against the treated arm and an equivalence checker we registered without checking it worked on our inputs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a "memorization floor" method to test whether LLM refinement of decompiler output recovers information from its input or from its prior training. By comparing outputs when identifiers are destroyed versus preserved, the authors find that while recovery is statistically real (+0.072 to +0.137 above chance), it does NOT depend on the input - ablation of input dataflow shows nearly zero effect (+0.001). Results replicated with a second vendor model. No registered hypotheses were confirmed, and five instrument failures are reported.
AI.motivation: The authors want to determine whether LLM refinement of decompiler output actually uses the input code to recover information (like variable names), or simply relies on memorization from prior training. This is a critical question for understanding LLM behavior and for trustworthy decompilation.
AI.method: The "memorization floor" is a within-item control: refine a function, then refine it again from an input whose identifiers have been destroyed. Compare the two outputs to measure what survives from the input versus prior. Applied to functions written after the analysis plan was committed (to avoid memorization). Uses arm-matched permutation nulls and tests with two models from different vendors.
AI.result: Recovery is statistically real (refined output is +0.072 to +0.137 above random chance). However, it does NOT depend on the input: destroying the input's dataflow changes naming gain by only +0.001 (95% CI [-0.026, +0.026]). Type prefix removal or name permutation have minimal effects. Readability stays at ceiling, providing no signal. The null is bounded (contributions under 0.056 invisible), and ablation leaves operations intact.
AI.conclusion: No registered hypothesis was confirmed. The study reveals five instrument failures, including a reassembly harness biased against the treated arm and an equivalence checker that wasn't validated on the authors' inputs. The key finding is that LLM decompiler refinement appears to recover information, but this recovery comes from the model's prior training rather than from the input provided - suggesting the models are not truly "using" the input for name recovery.

title: Skeletal Prototypes on Iterative Nerve Expansions
summary: Prototype reduction replaces a training set with a smaller representation, and the established methods return a finite set of points. We propose Skeletal Prototypes on Iterative Nerve Expansions (SPINE). The model for each class is an embedded 1-complex rather than a point set. Its initial edge set is a class-conditional Mapper graph, so the data decide which localized clusters are joined. Later phases fit the vertices under a classification objective, and an observation is assigned to the class whose complex is nearest. The segments therefore enter the decision rule and not only the fitting. We evaluate SPINE on seventeen benchmark datasets under stratified 10-fold cross validation, against seven other prototype reduction methods at a matched budget. SPINE attains the highest mean accuracy and the best average rank. It is significantly better than five of the seven competitors under Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. A budget sweep shows that the decision rule using the entire graph segments contribute most when prototypes are scarce, while the method as a whole competes best at moderate budgets. Construction cost places SPINE with the discriminative methods, and it is faster than generalized learning vector quantization on fourteen of the seventeen datasets.

AI.tldr: SPINE proposes a novel prototype reduction method that represents each class as an embedded 1-complex (graph structure) rather than a finite set of points. It uses class-conditional Mapper graphs as initial edge sets, fits vertices under classification objectives, and classifies based on nearest complex.
AI.motivation: Traditional prototype reduction methods represent classes as finite point sets. This work aims to overcome limitations of point-based prototypes by using topological structures (1-complexes) that can capture connectivity and relationships between data clusters, allowing the graph segments themselves to contribute to the decision rule.
AI.method: SPINE uses Mapper graphs as initial edge sets for each class, where data determines which localized clusters are joined. Vertices are fitted under a classification objective, and observations are assigned to the class whose complex is nearest. Evaluated on 17 datasets using stratified 10-fold cross-validation against 7 other prototype reduction methods at matched budgets.
AI.result: SPINE achieved highest mean accuracy and best average rank among competitors. It significantly outperformed 5 of 7 competitors under Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. Graph segments contribute most when prototypes are scarce, while the method performs best at moderate budgets. SPINE is faster than Generalized Learning Vector Quantization on 14 of 17 datasets.
AI.conclusion: SPINE represents a promising approach to prototype reduction that leverages topological structures rather than point sets. The graph-based representation allows decision-making to utilize both vertices and segments, achieving superior classification performance and computational efficiency compared to existing prototype reduction methods.

title: From Manual Construction to AI-Driven Scenario Emergence: Rethinking Catastrophe Risk Modeling
summary: Traditional catastrophe (CAT) risk models rely on costly manual construction to generate extreme weather scenarios, an approach largely unchanged since the 1990s. As climate extremes intensify, this creates mounting challenges to the entire risk transfer chain. This study proposes the TAISE framework, which repurposes AI weather forecasting models to produce coherent extreme weather sequences at a fraction of traditional costs. Through self-iterative generation, the framework produces continuous global atmospheric fields from which extreme events emerge. A proof-of-concept experiment demonstrates an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost compared with conventional methods, while capturing temporal continuity and cross-regional correlations absent in snapshot-based approaches. These findings suggest a pathway toward democratising catastrophe risk quantification and enabling dynamic, comprehensive portfolio assessment for insurers, reinsurers, ILS fund managers and public-sector risk managers.

AI.tldr: The TAISE framework repurposes AI weather forecasting models to generate coherent extreme weather sequences for catastrophe risk modeling at significantly lower cost than traditional manual approaches, which have remained largely unchanged since the 1990s.
AI.motivation: Traditional catastrophe risk models rely on costly manual construction to generate extreme weather scenarios, and as climate extremes intensify, this creates mounting challenges for the entire risk transfer chain. There is a need for a more efficient and comprehensive approach to catastrophe risk quantification.
AI.method: The TAISE framework uses self-iterative generation to produce continuous global atmospheric fields from which extreme events emerge. It repurposes AI weather forecasting models to generate coherent extreme weather sequences.
AI.result: The proof-of-concept experiment demonstrates an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost compared with conventional methods, while capturing temporal continuity and cross-regional correlations that are absent in snapshot-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: These findings suggest a pathway toward democratizing catastrophe risk quantification and enabling dynamic, comprehensive portfolio assessment for insurers, reinsurers, ILS fund managers, and public-sector risk managers.

title: JewelTry: Mask-Free Scale Aware Jewelry Virtual Try-On
summary: Virtual try-on (VTON) enables customers to visualize how fashion products appear when worn and has become an important technology for online shopping. While recent advances have substantially improved garment VTON, jewelry remains a challenging and underexplored category due to its small size, rigid structure, and sensitivity to fine-grained visual details. Realistic jewelry VTON requires not only faithful appearance transfer but also accurate scale and placement relative to the wearer. Existing jewelry VTON methods typically rely on mask guidance, whereas mask-free approaches lack explicit guidance for modeling the product scale. To bridge this gap, we introduce JVTO-Bench, a benchmark dataset for scale-faithful jewelry VTON, providing reference source target triplets with real-world product-scale annotations across four major jewelry categories. Building upon this benchmark, we propose JewelTry, a mask-free diffusion framework for scale-aware jewelry VTON. JewelTry incorporates a scale adapter that encodes product dimensions into a scale token, enabling the model to learn scale relationships between jewelry items and surrounding human anatomy in-context. To further improve jewelry consistency, we introduce a single-directional condition attention mechanism and an attention refinement loss that preserve both coarse geometry and fine-grained structural details of the reference jewelry. Extensive experiments show that JewelTry achieves a balance among visual fidelity, background preservation, object consistency and scale accuracy, establishing a strong baseline for mask-free, scale-aware jewelry virtual try-on.

AI.tldr: JewelTry is a mask-free diffusion framework for scale-aware jewelry virtual try-on, accompanied by JVTO-Bench benchmark dataset. It introduces a scale adapter encoding product dimensions into scale tokens, single-directional condition attention, and attention refinement loss to achieve faithful appearance transfer with accurate scale and placement.
AI.motivation: Existing jewelry VTON methods either rely on mask guidance or lack explicit guidance for modeling product scale. Jewelry is challenging due to small size, rigid structure, and sensitivity to fine-grained visual details. Realistic jewelry VTON requires accurate scale and placement relative to the wearer.
AI.method: 1) JVTO-Bench: benchmark dataset with reference source target triplets and real-world product-scale annotations across four jewelry categories. 2) JewelTry: mask-free diffusion framework with (a) scale adapter encoding product dimensions into scale tokens for learning scale relationships between jewelry and human anatomy, (b) single-directional condition attention for jewelry consistency, (c) attention refinement loss preserving coarse geometry and fine-grained structural details.
AI.result: JewelTry achieves balance among visual fidelity, background preservation, object consistency, and scale accuracy, establishing a strong baseline for mask-free, scale-aware jewelry VTON.
AI.conclusion: The proposed JVTO-Bench benchmark and JewelTry framework address the gap in jewelry VTON research by enabling scale-faithful, mask-free virtual try-on with preserved fine-grained details.

title: An Exemplar of a Digital Twin in Mechanical Engineering: Understanding Model Hybridization
summary: Digital Twins (DTs) are widely adopted across a variety of application domains. In industrial sectors, particularly in mechanical engineering, they accelerate product development, reduce risks, enable early issue prediction, and lower sustainment costs . In practice, DTs increasingly integrate physics-based (deductive) and data-driven (inductive) models into hybrid models combining the complementary strengths of both modeling paradigms. In this paper, we refer to this integration paradigm as hybridization. Despite this trend, the engineering of hybrid DTs that is, remains insufficiently documented. Hybridization is often introduced in an ad hoc manner, and its implementation is only partially made explicit, which limits reproducibility and transferability. This paper reports on the development of an existing fluidic loop digital twin at Centre Technique des Industries M{é}canique (CETIM). The DT is described using the characterization framework of Gil et al., providing a structured view across its lifecycle dimensions. To make hybridization explicit, the case is further analyzed through a complementary characterization structured along two dimensions: motivation and realization. The resulting description provides a traceable account of hybridization decisions and supports the documentation and transfer of hybrid DT engineering practices.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the engineering of hybrid Digital Twins (DTs) that combine physics-based (deductive) and data-driven (inductive) models. Using a case study of a fluidic loop digital twin at CETIM, the authors apply characterization frameworks to document hybridization decisions and support reproducibility and transferability of hybrid DT engineering practices.
AI.motivation: Despite the increasing adoption of hybrid DTs in industrial sectors, particularly mechanical engineering, the engineering practices remain insufficiently documented. Hybridization is often implemented in an ad hoc manner with only partial explicit implementation, limiting reproducibility and transferability of hybrid DT engineering approaches.
AI.method: The paper uses the characterization framework of Gil et al. to provide a structured view across lifecycle dimensions of the fluidic loop digital twin at CETIM. Additionally, a complementary characterization is applied structured along two dimensions: motivation and realization, to make hybridization explicit.
AI.result: The resulting description provides a traceable account of hybridization decisions for the fluidic loop digital twin, documenting the integration of physics-based and data-driven models through a structured methodology.
AI.conclusion: The structured approach using dual characterization frameworks (Gil et al.'s lifecycle dimensions plus motivation-realization dimensions) supports better documentation and transfer of hybrid DT engineering practices in industrial applications.

title: Z-Loss Backward Geometry in Dense Output Heads and Sparse Routers
summary: Z-loss has been widely applied to the logits of language-model output heads and sparse mixture-of-experts routers. Z-loss constrains the softmax log-normalizers of these output heads and routers, thereby limiting large-logit excursions, reducing finite-precision roundoff exposure, and avoiding training-loss divergence. These use cases arise in modern Transformer settings where large-vocabulary softmax heads, top-$k$ routing, fused losses, and mixed-precision optimizers interact. Z-loss has typically been understood only as a scalar penalty on the log-normalizer. This paper instead analyzes Z-loss from a backward-pass perspective, focusing on the gradients produced by the Z-loss penalty. The logit-space gradient, which we call the backward source, is injected at the logit boundary of the Z-loss branch of backpropagation; consequently, the backward source's effect depends on the architecture and implementation through which the gradient is transported. We develop a backward-transport view for Z-loss that separates the source's scalar amplitude and softmax shape from the transport factors. These factors include common-shift coordinates, tied-embedding pathways, output-to-hidden gain, fused-loss source consistency, optimizer-facing updates, and top-$k$ router reduction scale. These diagnostics show that nearly identical forward Z-loss values can coexist with distinct logit-space Z-loss gradients and, after architectural and optimizer transport, distinct parameter updates. The transport diagnostics also explain why raw-logit Z-loss can reduce scalar tails without changing output-to-hidden gain and why active-route reductions alter the effective router coefficient. Across evaluations of models in the GPT-2 and Pythia families on WikiText-103 and FineWeb-Edu, architecture-aware variants reduce backward-geometry tails while maintaining comparable validation perplexity in low-coefficient regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper reinterprets Z-loss (a regularization term for softmax log-normalizers in language models) from a backward-pass perspective, analyzing how Z-loss gradients flow through neural network architectures rather than treating it as a simple scalar penalty. The authors develop diagnostic tools showing that identical forward Z-loss values can produce different parameter updates due to architectural transport factors.
AI.motivation: Z-loss is widely used in modern Transformers (large-vocabulary softmax heads, top-k routing, mixed-precision optimizers) but has only been understood as a scalar penalty on log-normalizers. This limited understanding prevents practitioners from understanding why similar Z-loss values can produce different training behaviors. The authors seek to explain these differences through backward-pass analysis.
AI.method: The authors develop a "backward-transport view" that separates Z-loss gradient analysis into: (1) scalar amplitude and softmax shape (the "backward source"), and (2) transport factors including common-shift coordinates, tied-embedding pathways, output-to-hidden gain, fused-loss consistency, optimizer-facing updates, and top-k router reduction scale. They evaluate on GPT-2 and Pythia models using WikiText-103 and FineWeb-Edu datasets.
AI.result: Architecture-aware Z-loss variants can reduce backward-geometry tails while maintaining comparable validation perplexity in low-coefficient regimes. The diagnostics explain why raw-logit Z-loss can reduce scalar tails without changing output-to-hidden gain and why active-route reductions alter effective router coefficients.
AI.conclusion: Z-loss gradients interact with architecture and implementation details in complex ways. The backward-transport view provides diagnostic tools to understand these interactions, enabling practitioners to design Z-loss variants that achieve better gradient behavior while maintaining model performance.

title: AquiLLM: Evaluating Faithfulness in Open-Weight RAG-LLM Systems for Scientific Research
summary:
Scientific research increasingly relies on large, heterogeneous data sources, motivating interest in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that provide natural language access to scientific knowledge and research workflows. Researchers are exploring the viability of these systems as natural language interfaces for document search and for generating analysis code and pipeline components. At the same time, concerns about data privacy and control over research infrastructure have motivated interest in open-weight models and open-source deployments hosted within research institutions.
  In astronomy, this development follows a long history of computational infrastructure development, from archival databases and SQL-based systems to LLM-assisted research tools. This paper presents a domain-expert evaluation of faithfulness for AquiLLM, an open-weight, offline RAG-LLM platform designed to support scientific research groups in the use and preservation of tacit and formal knowledge.
  We define faithfulness as the extent to which generated responses remain grounded in retrieved scientific context without unsupported claims or omissions. We report results from an astronomy case study evaluating AquiLLM across retrieval and scientific analysis tasks. AquiLLM performs most reliably on explicit retrieval-oriented questions grounded in the RAG collection, while faithfulness degrades for queries requiring synthesis or ambiguity resolution. These results highlight both the promise and limitations of open-weight RAG-LLM systems for scientific research and demonstrate the importance of domain-expert evaluation beyond standard benchmark leaderboards.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates AquiLLM, an open-weight offline RAG-LLM system for astronomy research, focusing on "faithfulness" - whether generated responses remain grounded in retrieved scientific context without unsupported claims or omissions.
AI.motivation: The growing reliance on large heterogeneous data sources in scientific research has increased interest in RAG systems. Concerns about data privacy and control have motivated interest in open-weight models. Astronomy has a history of computational infrastructure development, and the authors explore whether RAG-LLM systems can serve as viable natural language interfaces for scientific knowledge access.
AI.method: Domain-expert evaluation of faithfulness using an astronomy case study. Tasks evaluated include retrieval and scientific analysis tasks. Faithfulness is defined as the extent to which generated responses remain grounded in retrieved scientific context without unsupported claims or omissions.
AI.result: AquiLLM performs most reliably on explicit retrieval-oriented questions grounded in the RAG collection. Faithfulness degrades for queries requiring synthesis or ambiguity resolution. The system shows promise but has limitations for complex scientific research tasks.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight RAG-LLM systems show promise for scientific research support but have significant limitations, particularly for tasks requiring synthesis or handling ambiguity. Domain-expert evaluation is crucial beyond standard benchmark leaderboards. The paper highlights the importance of evaluating these systems in real-world scientific contexts rather than just on general benchmarks.

title: Can Knowledge Transfer Parameters Be Learned? LePoKet for Efficient Robotic Vision
summary: Efficient perception is central to robotic systems operating under constrained computation, memory, and latency budgets. Knowledge transfer from larger pretrained models offers a practical route to stronger compact perception networks, but existing approaches commonly rely on fixed distillation objectives or manually designed interaction mechanisms. Building on Hereditary Knowledge Transfer (HKT), we propose LePoKet (Learnable Parameter Optimization for Knowledge Transfer), a structural transfer framework that embeds knowledge inheritance directly into the forward computation. LePoKet introduces a block-wise Extract-Transform-Mix interface whose interaction parameters are optimized jointly with the child network through a Learnable Genetic Attention (LGA) operator, without auxiliary distillation losses or temperature scaling. We first characterize the mechanism on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 using ResNet parent-child pairs, obtaining relative error reductions of 24.57% and 25.1%, respectively, over standard child training. We then evaluate LePoKet for dense motion estimation by integrating it into a compact RAFT-based optical-flow model trained only on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings3D. LePoKet improves the compact RAFT baseline from 2.21 to 1.92 EPE on Sintel Clean, from 3.35 to 3.01 on Sintel Final, and from 7.51 to 6.39 on KITTI. A direct comparison with HKT further shows that LePoKet improves CIFAR-10 accuracy from 92.40% to 93.40% while achieving the best Sintel Final and KITTI errors among the evaluated compact transfer variants, with comparable performance on Sintel Clean. These results demonstrate that learnable structural transfer generalizes across recognition and motion perception tasks and provides a promising approach for efficient robotic vision.

AI.tldr: LePoKet proposes a learnable structural transfer framework for knowledge transfer from large pretrained models to compact perception networks, using a block-wise Extract-Transform-Mix interface with Learnable Genetic Attention (LGA) optimization, eliminating need for traditional distillation losses.
AI.motivation: Efficient perception is critical for robotic systems under constrained computation, memory, and latency budgets. Existing knowledge transfer methods rely on fixed distillation objectives or manual interaction mechanisms, limiting their adaptability and effectiveness.
AI.method: LePoKet embeds knowledge inheritance directly into forward computation through a block-wise Extract-Transform-Mix interface. Interaction parameters are optimized jointly with the child network using a Learnable Genetic Attention (LGA) operator, without auxiliary distillation losses or temperature scaling.
AI.result: CIFAR-10/100: 24.57% and 25.1% relative error reductions respectively. Optical flow: Sintel Clean (2.21→1.92 EPE), Sintel Final (3.35→3.01 EPE), KITTI (7.51→6.39 EPE). Compared to HKT, improves CIFAR-10 accuracy from 92.40% to 93.40% and achieves best Sintel Final/KITTI errors among compact transfer variants.
AI.conclusion: Learnable structural transfer generalizes across recognition (classification) and motion perception (optical flow) tasks, providing a promising approach for efficient robotic vision. The joint optimization of interaction parameters with the child network eliminates the need for traditional distillation objectives while achieving superior performance.

title: After the Party: Governing What a Viral Agent-Skill Ecosystem Left Behind
comment: To appear in IEEE Digital Library as the 33rd Asia-Pacific Software Engineering Conference (APSEC 2026) conference proceedings. Accepted version, not camera ready version
summary: AI agents increasingly act through agent skills, i.e., natural-language instructions, that direct a host agent toward shell, network, credential, file, and process actions, and public registries distribute them at scale. In the first half of 2026, the OpenClaw AI agent went viral, and its public skill registry boomed: the observable stock nearly doubled in 91 days, and a majority of the listings visible in June were created in just two months. By the end of our study window, the wave had crested, and monthly listing creation and core-repository activity were falling from their spring peaks. This paper measures what the boom left behind, drawing on the OpenClaw Git history, its GitHub issues and pull requests, and three ClawHub registry snapshots. Attention is concentrated: the top 10% of skills received 46.93% of all downloads. No simple skill features (like size or download counts) remained a stable predictor of continued listing once creation cohort and skill age were controlled. Human scrutiny did not stay: 77.86% have zero stars and zero comments, while 85.06% of the readable skills carry privilege evidence. And automated cleanup is not ready: the three security scanners disagreed on 23,702 of the 61,990 skills they all cover. After human adjudication, weighted scanner sensitivity against the reference standard ranged from 21.67% to 61.06%. Governing fast-growing agent-skill registries cannot rely on simple metadata or single scanner scores; it requires robust, transparent measurement and independent validation.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the OpenClaw AI agent skill registry (ClawHub) boom in early 2026, measuring its aftermath through Git history, GitHub issues/PRs, and three registry snapshots. Findings show attention concentration (top 10% skills get 46.93% downloads), no stable predictors of listing success, low human engagement (77.86% zero stars/comments), and significant security scanner disagreement (23,702 of 61,990 skills flagged differently).
AI.motivation: The rapid growth of AI agent skill registries presents governance challenges. This study aims to measure what remains after a boom-bust cycle in a major public skill registry, specifically to understand attention distribution, skill stability predictors, human engagement, and security scanner reliability.
AI.method: The researchers analyzed OpenClaw Git history, GitHub issues and pull requests, and three ClawHub registry snapshots. They examined attention concentration, skill feature predictors controlling for cohort and age, human scrutiny metrics (stars/comments), and security scanner agreement with human adjudication.
AI.result: Attention is highly concentrated: top 10% of skills received 46.93% of all downloads. No simple skill features (size or download counts) remained stable predictors of continued listing after controlling for cohort and age. Human engagement is minimal: 77.86% of skills have zero stars and zero comments, while 85.06% carry privilege evidence. Security scanners show poor agreement: they disagreed on 23,702 of 61,990 skills (38.2%). After human adjudication, weighted scanner sensitivity ranged only from 21.67% to 61.06% against the reference standard.
AI.conclusion: Governing fast-growing agent-skill registries cannot rely on simple metadata or single scanner scores. Effective governance requires robust, transparent measurement and independent validation, as current tools show significant limitations in detecting security issues.

title: Anatomy of Associative Recall in Fixed-State Recurrences: A Matched-State Decomposition, an Interference Wall, and a Curriculum That Breaks It
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Preprint of preliminary results; code and result JSONs at https://github.com/JIBSIL/dualgoose
summary: Fixed-state recurrences--linear attention and state-space models--are reported to lag behind attention on associative recall, but whole-architecture comparisons cannot say which ingredient is responsible. We decompose masked multi-query recall at a fixed state budget along three single-knob axes: a short causal convolution, the transition structure (rank-1 delta rule vs. diagonal), and decay. The convolution dominates (~+0.5 recall in both families under matched training): comparisons that pit convolution-free cells against a convolution-equipped Mamba measure the missing convolution, not the recurrence. The rank-1 transition beats its diagonal ablation by +0.19/+0.32 at 16/32 pairs, but the margin shrinks to +0.03 once both cells carry the convolution, and a state-matched Mamba-2 ties the unarmed rank-1 cell: no class claim survives. Cells that solve 32-pair recall degrade gracefully with load yet fall to chance retrieving 4 pairs from a distractor haystack--flat across lengths and transitions. Interference under sparse supervision, not capacity: a distance curriculum takes the unchanged architecture from 0.021 to 1.000. Training is a lock-in lottery--a seed either locks in or does not--and the curriculum is the lever. Lock-in rises from 1/10 to 7/10 (p=0.02); dense supervision adds nothing; at L=256 a shaped ramp reopens a boundary the uniform curriculum cannot (4/5 vs. 0/9); and at L=512, where the ramp collapses (0/6), gating it on measured accuracy locks in 6/6 (p=0.001). Bidirectional denoiser cells, reading the query before the haystack, show no measurable advantage over causal training (ten seeds), and collision-key retrieval needs two layers. Arming for recall is free on an S_5 state-tracking guardrail--the armed cell is significantly better at every depth (p<=0.0044). These replace "recurrent models are bad at recall" with a measured decomposition and two cheap interventions.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why fixed-state models (linear attention, state-space models like Mamba) underperform attention on associative recall tasks. Through controlled ablation experiments along three axes (convolution, transition structure, decay), the authors find that the missing ingredient is primarily the short causal convolution (~+0.5 recall improvement). They also demonstrate that curriculum learning and accuracy-based gating are effective interventions.
AI.motivation: To identify which specific architectural component (convolution, transition structure, or decay) is responsible for the performance gap between fixed-state recurrences and attention on associative recall tasks. Previous whole-architecture comparisons couldn't isolate the responsible factor.
AI.method: The authors decompose masked multi-query recall at fixed state budgets along three single-knob axes: (1) short causal convolution, (2) transition structure (rank-1 delta rule vs. diagonal), and (3) decay. They conduct matched training comparisons between different architectures (Mamba, Mamba-2, linear attention variants) and test interventions including curriculum learning, gating mechanisms, and bidirectional denoiser cells.
AI.result: Convolution is the dominant factor (~+0.5 recall improvement in both families). The rank-1 transition beats diagonal ablation but the margin shrinks when both have convolution. A distance curriculum improves recall from 0.021 to 1.000. Training exhibits a "lock-in lottery" phenomenon where seed selection determines success; with curriculum, lock-in rate rises from 1/10 to 7/10 (p=0.02). Gating on measured accuracy reopens learning at L=256 (4/5 vs 0/9 success). At L=512, gating achieves 6/6 lock-in (p=0.001). Bidirectional cells show no advantage over causal training. Two layers are needed for collision-key retrieval. Armed cells outperform guardrail tasks at all depths (p<=0.0044).
AI.conclusion: The performance gap between fixed-state recurrences and attention on recall tasks is primarily due to the missing convolution, not the recurrence mechanism itself. Two cheap interventions (curriculum learning and accuracy-based gating) can significantly improve recall. The claim that "recurrent models are bad at recall" is largely unfounded when properly equipped with convolution and appropriate training regimes.

title: QueryFormer: Winning Solution for KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge
summary: Post-click conversion rate (pCVR) prediction requires jointly modeling feature interactions and sequential user behaviors. The KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge calls for a unified architecture addressing both. We observe that existing unified architectures often generate query tokens---the central information hub---with projection-based multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), without explicit token-to-query attention for refining the query side. We propose QueryFormer, centered on a stackable unified field--sequence block that bridges non-sequential multi-field features and behavioral sequences, and provide a latency-aware scaling study over view width $H$, model width, depth, data, and compute. The block generates queries through cross-attention and packs sequence queries into shared-parameter attention. QueryFormer secured 1st place in the Industrial Track, achieving an official test area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.83254; a modest post-competition scale-up reached 0.832713. Within our grid, $H$-scaling improves validation AUC from 0.84540 to 0.84615 and beats HyFormer at comparable budgets. Ablation identifies query generation as the largest contributor. Packed shared-parameter cross-attention keeps H=8 inference latency to only 1.89x that of H=1, positioning the bridge as an efficient stackable unified block.

AI.tldr: QueryFormer is a unified architecture for post-click conversion rate (pCVR) prediction that jointly models feature interactions and sequential user behaviors. It uses a stackable unified field-sequence block with cross-attention for query generation and packed shared-parameter attention, achieving 1st place in the KDD Cup 2026 Tencent UniRec Challenge with AUC of 0.83254.
AI.motivation: Existing unified architectures for pCVR prediction generate query tokens through projection-based MLPs without explicit token-to-query attention for refining the query side, limiting their effectiveness in bridging non-sequential multi-field features and behavioral sequences.
AI.method: QueryFormer uses a stackable unified field-sequence block that: 1) generates queries through cross-attention between non-sequential features and behavioral sequences; 2) packs sequence queries into shared-parameter attention for efficiency. The method includes latency-aware scaling study over view width H, model width, depth, data, and compute.
AI.result: QueryFormer won 1st place in the Industrial Track with test AUC of 0.83254 (scaled to 0.832713 post-competition). H-scaling improved validation AUC from 0.84540 to 0.84615, outperforming HyFormer at comparable budgets. Packed shared-parameter cross-attention keeps H=8 inference latency to only 1.89x that of H=1. Ablation showed query generation as the largest contributor to performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified field-sequence block serves as an efficient stackable architecture for pCVR prediction. The cross-attention based query generation is crucial, and H-scaling provides meaningful improvements. The packed shared-parameter attention maintains acceptable inference latency even with larger view widths, making it practical for production deployment.

title: Type-IV Code Clone Detection via Layer-Wise Non-Contrastive Representation Learning
summary: Software clones are fragments of code that are similar or functionally equivalent to each other. They pose significant challenges for maintenance, refactoring, and bug detection. Detecting Type-IV clones, which are semantically equivalent but may differ syntactically, is particularly difficult for traditional token- or syntax-based methods. Recent machine learning approaches rely on contrastive learning, which requires careful negative sampling and can introduce bias. In this paper, we propose LWVIC4Code, a non-contrastive representation learning approach specifically designed for Type-IV clone detection. Building on the Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization (VICReg) framework and prior layer-wise VICReg training, LWVIC4Code introduces cross-layer consistency regularization and depth-dependent layer weighting to progressively refine semantic information across transformer layers, producing robust and discriminative code representations. We conduct an empirical study comparing LWVIC4Code against a contrastive learning baseline and zero-shot large language models on Python (Kamino) and multi-language (GPTCloneBench) datasets. Results show that LWVIC4Code achieves competitive or superior performance without negative samples, benefits from layer-wise supervision, and generalizes effectively from Python to other languages, particularly Java and C#. These results demonstrate that non-contrastive, layer-wise representation learning is a promising direction for robust semantic code clone detection.

AI.tldr: LWVIC4Code is a non-contrastive representation learning approach for Type-IV code clone detection that extends the VICReg framework with layer-wise training, cross-layer consistency regularization, and depth-dependent layer weighting to produce robust code representations without requiring negative samples.
AI.motivation: Type-IV code clones (semantically equivalent but syntactically different) are difficult to detect with traditional token-/syntax-based methods. Existing contrastive learning approaches suffer from bias introduced by negative sampling, necessitating an alternative approach.
AI.method: LWVIC4Code builds on the VICReg framework with: (1) Prior layer-wise VICReg training, (2) Cross-layer consistency regularization, and (3) Depth-dependent layer weighting to progressively refine semantic information across transformer layers.
AI.result: LWVIC4Code achieves competitive or superior performance against contrastive learning baseline and zero-shot LLMs on Python (Kamino) and multi-language (GPTCloneBench) datasets, with effective cross-language generalization to Java and C#.
AI.conclusion: Non-contrastive, layer-wise representation learning is a promising direction for robust semantic code clone detection, eliminating the need for negative samples while maintaining or improving detection quality.

title: Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration
summary: Safety guardrails in open-weight language models can be readily bypassed using Refusal Feature Ablation (RFA), a technique that identifies and projects out a linear refusal direction from the residual stream, often achieving a high attack success rate (ASR) while preserving model capability. Defending against these attacks typically requires computationally expensive safety finetuning for every new checkpoint. We introduce Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO), a fast, post-hoc weight-editing defense that requires no base-model finetuning. Our approach is based on a simple mechanistic insight: ablation attacks rely on contrastive estimators to find the refusal direction. Rather than trying to hide the true refusal circuitry, DDO actively injects a high-magnitude, nonlinear decoy signal into the network's MLP neurons. When an attacker attempts to locate the refusal direction, the decoy corrupts their estimator, tricking them into ablating a harmless orthogonal feature while the actual safety mechanism remains intact. We prove a spectral bound formalizing this effect and evaluate DDO across six model families, achieving <10% ASR under standard RFA. On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, DDO remains comparable to trained defenses under adaptive multi-phase attacks (65% vs. 58% worst-case ASR) and reduces Heretic weight-level attack ASR from 88.7% to 18%, all at 30 to 450 times lower optimization cost per configuration than the trained baselines.

AI.tldr: Decoy Direction Optimization (DDO) is a fast, post-hoc weight-editing defense against Refusal Feature Ablation (RFA) attacks on open-weight language models. It injects high-magnitude nonlinear decoy signals into MLP neurons to corrupt attackers' contrastive estimators, protecting the actual refusal mechanism without requiring base-model finetuning.
AI.motivation: Safety guardrails in open-weight language models can be bypassed using Refusal Feature Ablation (RFA), which projects out a linear refusal direction from the residual stream. Current defenses require computationally expensive safety finetuning for each new checkpoint, creating a need for a fast, efficient alternative.
AI.method: DDO injects a high-magnitude, nonlinear decoy signal into the network's MLP neurons. When attackers attempt to locate the refusal direction using contrastive estimators, the decoy corrupts their estimator, causing them to ablate a harmless orthogonal feature while preserving the actual safety mechanism. The approach includes a spectral bound proof formalizing this effect.
AI.result: DDO achieves <10% ASR under standard RFA across six model families. On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, it remains comparable to trained defenses under adaptive multi-phase attacks (65% vs. 58% worst-case ASR). It reduces Heretic weight-level attack ASR from 88.7% to 18%, with 30 to 450 times lower optimization cost per configuration than trained baselines.
AI.conclusion: DDO provides an effective, computationally efficient defense against RFA attacks by strategically deploying decoy signals to mislead attackers, offering a practical alternative to expensive safety finetuning while maintaining model capability.

title: Query-Aware Source-Risk Triage for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at CAIT 2026
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines may omit a source's material relationship to the query. We study a pre-generation triage layer that treats this relationship as query dependent. The method routes canonical query families for enhanced review and assigns retrieved pages to pass, contextualize, exclude, or review. It combines a four-dimension page score, rank-discounted family aggregation, intent-preserving query mutations, and a family-held-out router. A single-coded pilot of 200 real URLs supplies provisional calibration anchors; a 20,000-row scenario with synthetic domain identifiers supports controlled workload analysis. An oracle page gate defines a risk-coverage target for a future learned classifier. The evaluation shows why page-level frequency cannot substitute for family-level exposure and quantifies how calibration changes scenario activation. Annotation reliability remains unmeasured, and synthetic rankings omit real retrieval dynamics. The result is an auditable triage method and validation plan, not an estimate of deployed review workload, live-Web prevalence, or downstream answer-quality gains.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a pre-generation triage layer for Retrieval-augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines that addresses the issue of omitting a source's material relationship to the query. The method treats this relationship as query-dependent by routing canonical query families for enhanced review and categorizing retrieved pages into pass, contextualize, exclude, or review. It combines multiple techniques including four-dimension page scores, rank-discounted family aggregation, intent-preserving query mutations, and a family-held-out router.
AI.motivation: RAG pipelines may omit a source's material relationship to the query, meaning the system fails to adequately assess whether retrieved sources are actually relevant or material to answering the query. This can lead to poor generation quality or inclusion of irrelevant information.
AI.method: The proposed method includes four key components: (1) A four-dimension page score for assessing retrieved pages, (2) Rank-discounted family aggregation to aggregate scores across query families, (3) Intent-preserving query mutations to test different query variations, and (4) A family-held-out router for routing decisions. Evaluation uses a pilot study with 200 real URLs and a 20,000-row synthetic scenario, with an oracle page gate defining risk-coverage targets.
AI.result: The evaluation demonstrates why page-level frequency cannot substitute for family-level exposure, and quantifies how calibration changes scenario activation. Key limitations include unmeasured annotation reliability and synthetic rankings that omit real retrieval dynamics. The paper provides an auditable triage method and validation plan rather than deployed estimates.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a novel pre-generation triage approach for RAG systems that moves beyond page-level assessment to family-level exposure analysis. While it provides a methodology and validation plan, it does not provide actual deployed workload estimates, live-Web prevalence, or downstream answer-quality gains. The contribution is primarily methodological and analytical, focusing on demonstrating the importance of query-family-level analysis over simple page-level frequency counting.

title: Coding Agents Have Converged: Why the SWE-bench Leaderboard Can No Longer Order Its Top Entries, and What to Measure Instead
comment: Accepted at ADMA 2026 (International Conference on Advanced Data Mining and Applications), Special Session on Responsible Data Intelligence. Camera-ready version, 15 pages, 4 figures
summary: Small differences on coding-agent leaderboards are often read as an ordering of systems. We audit whether the published verdicts support this reading, using 254 SWE-bench submissions across four splits without running models. On Verified, the leading two entries each resolve 396 of 500 instances. The top ten share 285 successes and 51 failures, leaving 164 instances that distinguish their outcomes. Frontier solution sets have median nesting 0.935 against a score-implied baseline of 0.774, indicating strongly shared successes. Scores also depend on the evaluated model-scaffold pair: observed within-model scaffold ranges reach 29.8 percentage points, compared with the 8.8-point spread of the top thirty. Six of nine cell-mean interaction tests remain significant after Holm correction, although this observational design does not identify causal scaffold effects. Exact paired McNemar tests separate none of the 29 adjacent Verified top-thirty pairs at alpha=0.05, while the larger Test split separates 14 of 23. A stated leader-based rule yields three descriptive tiers, or two after Holm correction; non-rejection does not establish equivalence. We release the partition and a five-step audit protocol that profiles shared outcomes, tests paired differences, reports grouping sensitivity, and estimates the instance budget needed for resolution. The results motivate reporting comparison-set-specific resolution and model-scaffold provenance instead of interpreting small aggregate gaps as established rank differences.

AI.tldr: This paper audits whether small differences on coding-agent leaderboards (SWE-bench) can be interpreted as meaningful system rankings. Analysis of 254 submissions across four splits reveals that top systems share most successes, and statistical tests cannot distinguish adjacent pairs on the Verified split. The authors argue that small aggregate gaps should not be interpreted as established rank differences.
AI.motivation: Small differences on coding-agent leaderboards are often read as an ordering of systems. The authors question whether the published verdicts actually support this reading, seeking to determine if leaderboard rankings are statistically meaningful or just noise.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 254 SWE-bench submissions across four splits without running models. They used multiple statistical methods: (1) profiling shared outcomes between top systems, (2) computing nesting metrics (median nesting 0.935 vs score-implied baseline 0.774), (3) conducting exact paired McNemar tests on adjacent pairs, (4) applying Holm correction for multiple comparisons, and (5) testing a stated leader-based rule for tier classification.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Top two entries each resolve 396/500 instances on Verified; (2) Top ten share 285 successes and 51 failures, leaving only 164 distinguishing instances; (3) Within-model scaffold ranges reach 29.8 percentage points vs 8.8-point spread for top thirty; (4) Six of nine cell-mean interaction tests remain significant after Holm correction; (5) Exact paired McNemar tests separate none of 29 adjacent Verified top-thirty pairs, but 14 of 23 on Test split; (6) Leader-based rule yields three descriptive tiers (or two after Holm correction).
AI.conclusion: Small aggregate gaps on coding-agent leaderboards should not be interpreted as established rank differences. The authors recommend reporting comparison-set-specific resolution and model-scaffold provenance instead. They release a partition and five-step audit protocol for profiling shared outcomes, testing paired differences, reporting grouping sensitivity, and estimating instance budget needed for resolution.

title: How I learned to stop worrying and love StopGrads: Stationarity, Convergence, and a case study on Flow Map Learning
summary: Stopgrads are widely used in training machine learning models, but stopgrads can alter the gradient, stationary points and convergence guarantees of the original objective, which can make stopgrad training theoretically ungrounded. We introduce a stopgrad regression principle, which identifies a general template for stopgrad objectives with a closed-form characterization of stationary points and their uniqueness, unifying stopgrad objectives for flow maps, reinforcement learning, and diffusion samplers. We provide theoretical grounding for optimizing stopgrad flow map objectives by showing their unique stationary point is the true flow map, and showing positive convergence results for Eulerian and Lagrangian objectives, including MeanFlow and improved MeanFlow. Remarkably, we show that under functional semi-gradient flow, the learned flow map has a closed-form expression composing the initial flow map and the true flow map. We additionally use our stopgrad regression principle to propose modified stopgrad placements for flow map objectives which reduce training memory by 2x.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "stopgrad regression principle" that provides theoretical grounding for stopgrad training in machine learning, addressing issues where stopgrads can alter gradients, stationary points and convergence guarantees. The principle unifies stopgrad objectives for flow maps, reinforcement learning, and diffusion samplers with closed-form characterization of stationary points.
AI.motivation: Stopgrads are widely used in training ML models but they can alter the gradient, stationary points and convergence guarantees of the original objective, making stopgrad training theoretically ungrounded. The authors seek to provide theoretical justification for optimizing stopgrad flow map objectives.
AI.method: The authors introduce a stopgrad regression principle that identifies a general template for stopgrad objectives with closed-form characterization of stationary points and their uniqueness. They analyze Eulerian and Lagrangian objectives including MeanFlow and improved MeanFlow under functional semi-gradient flow.
AI.result: The unique stationary point is proven to be the true flow map. Under functional semi-gradient flow, the learned flow map has a closed-form expression composing the initial flow map and the true flow map. Modified stopgrad placements reduce training memory by 2x.
AI.conclusion: The stopgrad regression principle provides theoretical grounding for stopgrad training, unifying objectives across flow maps, RL, and diffusion samplers. It enables memory-efficient training while ensuring convergence to the true flow map at the unique stationary point.

title: Do LLMs Have Values? A Quantitative Analysis and Alignment Framework for Values in Large Language Models
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly handle complex subjective tasks, aligning their intentions and behaviors with human values has become a critical scientific challenge. However, current efforts are confounded by a striking behavioral paradox: they fluctuate unpredictably under minor wording changes ("swing"), yet stubbornly ignore explicit instructions to correct ingrained biases ("rigidity"). Resolving this duality is critical for reliable AI alignment. To systematically understand and safely steer these latent subjective preferences, our study is structured around three fundamental questions. First, do LLMs possess an intrinsic value system? By projecting responses from 106 LLMs (150,000 queries per model) and 95,000 human survey profiles into a shared sociological space, we empirically confirm that they do. However, they do not mirror human diversity, instead crystallizing into a highly concentrated, idealized value core. Second, how can these values be quantified? We propose the Prior-Environment-Cognition (PEC) framework. This model mathematically defines value expression as the joint outcome of inherent dispositions like parameter weights (Prior), external contexts such as user prompts (Environment), and internal reasoning processes like Chain-of-Thought (Cognition). Finally, how can LLMs' values be aligned toward a desired target? Using PEC diagnostics, we establish an adaptive "Alignment Prescription". Rather than blindly applying resource-intensive training, this method identifies the minimum effective intervention needed for each dimension, ranging from zero-cost prompts to targeted parameter updates. Extensive empirical validation confirms that our approach successfully verifies the presence of LLM values, accurately quantifies their shifts, and achieves more efficient and precise steering than conventional blind training, all without degrading general capabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the critical challenge of aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human values by investigating their intrinsic value systems, proposing a quantification framework (PEC), and developing an adaptive alignment method. The study analyzes 106 LLMs and 95,000 human profiles, revealing that LLMs possess concentrated, idealized value cores rather than mirroring human diversity.
AI.motivation: Current LLM alignment efforts are hindered by a behavioral paradox: LLMs fluctuate unpredictably under minor wording changes ("swing") yet stubbornly ignore explicit instructions to correct biases ("rigidity"). This duality undermines reliable AI alignment, necessitating a systematic understanding of latent subjective preferences in LLMs.
