ICE v2 shows a quality-cost trade-off rather than superior efficiency, with severe multi-session and temporal failures accompanied by conservative abstention.

title: PriorPose: Reference-Guided Joint Deformation and Alignment for Category-Level Object Pose Estimation
summary: Category-level object pose estimation seeks to recover a similarity transform $(R,t,s)$ for unseen instances without instance-specific CAD models. Most competitive methods are correspondence-based: prior-free variants regress canonical (NOCS) coordinates directly from local observations and implicitly memorize the canonical frame in the weights, which ties the parameters to category-typical orientations and hurts generalization under distribution shift; prior-based variants introduce a category prior but typically follow a serial deform-then-align pipeline, where underconstrained canonical completion can corrupt correspondences and induce error cascades in pose. We propose PriorPose, a reference-guided correspondence framework that keeps the category prior explicit and solves canonicalization and alignment jointly in a shared feature space. A reference-guided seeded transformer embeds the partial observation and the category prior as token sets and fuses them via geometry-aware seeds, from which the network jointly predicts a per-point NOCS field for visible points and a canonical deformation of the prior that reconstructs a full canonical instance, while a deep pose head regresses $(R,t,s)$ from the induced correspondences. A two-part shape consistency objective, with canonical-space and camera-space consistency losses, couples correspondence, deformation, and pose, reducing reliance on memorized canonical orientations and avoiding deform-then-align error cascades. Experiments on standard and larger-category benchmarks demonstrate that PriorPose sets new state-of-the-art results on most evaluated metrics, especially under strict pose thresholds, while remaining competitive on relaxed pose and IoU metrics and showing improved robustness under shape variation and domain shift.

AI.tldr: PriorPose is a reference-guided correspondence framework for category-level object pose estimation that jointly solves canonicalization and alignment in a shared feature space, avoiding the error cascades of prior deform-then-align methods and the generalization issues of prior-free methods that memorize canonical orientations.
AI.motivation: Existing correspondence-based methods have two key limitations: (1) prior-free variants regress NOCS coordinates directly and implicitly memorize the canonical frame in network weights, tying parameters to category-typical orientations and hurting generalization under distribution shift; (2) prior-based variants follow a serial deform-then-align pipeline where underconstrained canonical completion can corrupt correspondences and induce error cascades in pose estimation.
AI.method: PriorPose uses a reference-guided seeded transformer that embeds partial observation and category prior as token sets, fusing them via geometry-aware seeds. The network jointly predicts: (1) per-point NOCS field for visible points, and (2) canonical deformation of the prior that reconstructs a full canonical instance. A deep pose head regresses (R,t,s) from induced correspondences. A two-part shape consistency objective (canonical-space and camera-space consistency losses) couples correspondence, deformation, and pose.
AI.result: PriorPose sets new state-of-the-art results on most evaluated metrics, especially under strict pose thresholds, while remaining competitive on relaxed pose and IoU metrics. It shows improved robustness under shape variation and domain shift.
AI.conclusion: PriorPose effectively addresses the limitations of both prior-free and prior-based pose estimation methods through joint optimization of canonicalization and alignment. The explicit category prior and geometry-aware fusion mechanism reduce reliance on memorized canonical orientations and avoid deform-then-align error cascades, leading to superior generalization and robustness.

title: Generative models for simulation based filtering: Formulations and Empirical Comparisons
summary: This letter presents a unified formulation and a controlled numerical comparison of generative-model approaches to the nonlinear filtering problem. Under this formulation the analysis step is realized by a transport of the forecast distribution to the posterior, the approaches differing only in how that transport is selected and learned. We derive three new filters, based on stochastic interpolants, their deterministic flow-matching limit, and Schrödinger bridges realized through forward--backward SDEs. We develop a two-stage tuning procedure that separates the training of the generative model from its online refinement. The resulting methods are compared against the optimal transport filter (OTF), the Knothe--Rosenblatt filter (KRF), the sequential importance resampling (SIR) particle filter and the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF), in terms of accuracy, computational time, and sensitivity to ensemble size and state dimension. The results indicate that every generative filter resolves multimodal posteriors that the EnKF and SIR do not, that no single generative framework dominates, the preferred method being set by the available online budget and ensemble size, and that the filters differ in the regularity of the particle trajectories they produce.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified framework for generative-model-based approaches to nonlinear filtering, deriving three new filters (stochastic interpolants, flow-matching, Schrödinger bridges) and comparing them against existing methods (OTF, KRF, SIR, EnKF).
AI.motivation: The motivation is to provide a systematic comparison of generative-model approaches to nonlinear filtering, which differ primarily in how they transport the forecast distribution to the posterior. The authors seek to understand the trade-offs between different methods in terms of accuracy, computational time, and sensitivity to ensemble size and state dimension.
AI.method: The authors develop a unified formulation where the analysis step is realized by transporting the forecast distribution to the posterior. They derive three new filters based on: (1) stochastic interpolants, (2) deterministic flow-matching limit, and (3) Schrödinger bridges via forward-backward SDEs. A two-stage tuning procedure is used that separates model training from online refinement. The methods are compared through controlled numerical experiments.
AI.result: The results show that: (1) all generative filters can resolve multimodal posteriors that EnKF and SIR cannot; (2) no single generative framework dominates—the preferred method depends on available online budget and ensemble size; (3) the filters differ in the regularity of particle trajectories they produce.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion indicates that generative-model-based filters offer significant advantages for handling multimodal posteriors in nonlinear filtering, but the choice of method should be guided by specific computational constraints and ensemble size requirements. Each approach has distinct strengths suited to different operational scenarios.

title: Beyond Episodic AI: Cognitive Field Networks for Biologically Inspired Persistent Cognition
summary: Cognitive Field Theory (CFT) proposes that cognition arises from memory-dressed collective dynamics that generate a persistent macroscopic cognitive field. Here we develop a Cognitive Field Network (CFN), a recurrent Transformer in which the organized hidden field re-enters subsequent inference through \[ Φ_{n+1}=F_θ(X_{n+1},Φ_n). \] Rather than prescribing an explicit memory operation, the CFN allows new information to act on an already history-dependent collective state. We find that learning organizes persistent, content-dependent recurrent dynamics whose timescale increases systematically with the trained recurrent horizon. Semantic continuation propagates the recurrent state far beyond this horizon without replay of the target answer. Without content-specific support, the field exhibits finite passive relaxation, whereas periodic re-exposure to relevant input repeatedly renews the surviving state and drives it toward an approximately stationary nonzero regime. Unrelated-input and recurrence-off controls do not reproduce this behavior, while near-paraphrased re-exposure produces weaker renewal, demonstrating representation-sensitive persistence. These results distinguish three dynamical processes: collective memory dressing forms and sustains a history-dependent cognitive field, structured input reorganizes this field, and cross-cycle re-entry makes the resulting state causally available to subsequent inference. The CFN therefore provides a controlled computational platform for studying persistent, history-dependent cognitive dynamics without a separately prescribed memory system.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Cognitive Field Network (CFN), a recurrent Transformer architecture implementing Cognitive Field Theory (CFT), where the hidden field re-enters subsequent inference through recurrence (Φ_{n+1}=F_θ(X_{n+1},Φ_n)). The CFN learns persistent, content-dependent recurrent dynamics without explicitly prescribed memory, demonstrating that collective memory dressing forms a history-dependent cognitive field that can persist beyond training horizons through semantic continuation.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a fundamental question in cognitive science and machine learning: how can persistent, history-dependent cognitive dynamics emerge without explicitly prescribed memory systems? Traditional models require separate memory mechanisms, but Cognitive Field Theory (CFT) proposes that cognition arises from memory-dressed collective dynamics generating a persistent macroscopic cognitive field. The motivation is to develop a controlled computational platform to study these persistent cognitive dynamics.
AI.method: The authors developed a Cognitive Field Network (CFN), a recurrent Transformer architecture where the organized hidden field re-enters subsequent inference through the equation Φ_{n+1}=F_θ(X_{n+1},Φ_n). This allows new information to act on a history-dependent collective state. They trained the network and analyzed: (1) timescale of recurrent dynamics vs. trained recurrent horizon, (2) semantic continuation beyond the horizon, (3) field relaxation without input, (4) renewal with re-exposure to relevant input, and (5) controls with unrelated inputs and recurrence-off conditions.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Learning organizes persistent, content-dependent recurrent dynamics with timescales increasing systematically with trained recurrent horizon; (2) Semantic continuation propagates the recurrent state far beyond the trained horizon without replay of target answers; (3) Without content-specific support, the field exhibits finite passive relaxation; (4) Periodic re-exposure to relevant input repeatedly renews the surviving state, driving it toward an approximately stationary nonzero regime; (5) Unrelated-input and recurrence-off controls do not reproduce this behavior; (6) Near-paraphrased re-exposure produces weaker renewal, demonstrating representation-sensitive persistence.
AI.conclusion: The CFN provides a controlled computational platform for studying persistent, history-dependent cognitive dynamics without a separately prescribed memory system. Three dynamical processes are distinguished: (1) collective memory dressing forms and sustains a history-dependent cognitive field, (2) structured input reorganizes this field, and (3) cross-cycle re-entry makes the resulting state causally available to subsequent inference. This work bridges cognitive science theory with modern deep learning architectures, offering a novel approach to understanding memory, persistence, and recurrent cognitive processing.

title: De-GAN - Dynamic Parameter Tuned GAN for 3D Medical Image Segmentation: A Step Towards Generalisation
summary: Brain tumor segmentation remains difficult because enhancing tumor (ET) has low contrast and overlaps surrounding tissue, while scanner and site variation causes domain shift. We propose DE-GAN, a contrast-enhancing conditional GAN that combines input-adaptive dynamic convolutions, style-aware feature mixing, and coordinate encoding to synthesize slice-adaptive FLAIR images. A label-guided, class-conditional target separates tumor-core (TC) and ET intensities while preserving anatomy. The generated FLAIR is concatenated with the original MR modalities and used to train a 3D U-Net. Across BraTS 2015, 2018, and 2019, DE-GAN improves segmentation over the baseline and static EnhGAN replacement on most reported TC/ET metrics, with the largest gains from retaining both original and enhanced FLAIR. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/zkhansuri-ui/DE-GAN.

AI.tldr: DE-GAN is a contrast-enhancing conditional GAN that synthesizes slice-adaptive FLAIR images to improve brain tumor segmentation. It uses input-adaptive dynamic convolutions, style-aware feature mixing, and coordinate encoding, combined with a label-guided class-conditional target to separate tumor-core and enhancing tumor intensities. The generated FLAIR is concatenated with original MR modalities to train a 3D U-Net.
AI.motivation: Brain tumor segmentation is challenging due to: (1) Enhancing tumor (ET) has low contrast and overlaps with surrounding tissue, making it difficult to distinguish; (2) Scanner and site variation causes domain shift, affecting model generalization across different imaging设备和centers.
AI.method: DE-GAN combines three key components: (1) Input-adaptive dynamic convolutions for slice-adaptive feature extraction; (2) Style-aware feature mixing to handle domain shift; (3) Coordinate encoding for spatial awareness. A label-guided, class-conditional target separates tumor-core (TC) and ET intensities while preserving anatomy. The generated FLAIR is concatenated with original MR modalities and used to train a 3D U-Net for segmentation.
AI.result: Across BraTS 2015, 2018, and 2019 datasets, DE-GAN improves segmentation over baseline and static EnhGAN replacement on most reported TC/ET metrics. The largest gains come from retaining both original and enhanced FLAIR, demonstrating the benefit of combining synthesized and original imaging data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DE-GAN effectively addresses brain tumor segmentation challenges through contrast-enhanced FLAIR synthesis. By leveraging input-adaptive mechanisms and preserving original modalities, the method achieves improved segmentation performance across multiple BraTS datasets, with particular improvements in tumor-core and enhancing tumor detection.

title: Channel-Informed Neural Network for Physical Layer Key Generation
summary: Physical-layer key generation (PKG) enables wireless devices to establish shared keys from reciprocal channel observations without directly exchanging the key. This capability is attractive for edge networks, where distributed and resource-constrained devices may require lightweight key establishment with limited access to centralized infrastructure. We introduce a channel-informed neural network for PKG that derives binary key features directly from received IQ measurements while explicitly grounding the learned representation in the underlying multipath channel. The proposed multi-task recurrent neural network jointly learns reciprocity-preserving binary features and an auxiliary channel estimate using a training objective that combines deep metric learning with channel-informed supervision. Structured channel sounding enables channel estimation from over-the-air measurements, while Sionna-RT ray tracing is used to augment training with additional propagation conditions. We evaluate the framework using indoor and outdoor software-defined-radio measurements collected on the POWDER radio testbed. Across all evaluated scenarios, the proposed model produces lower bit disagreement for reciprocal Alice-Bob observations than for Eve-related observations. Ray-traced data augmentation substantially improves key diversity, increasing the unique-key rate to 0.94, 0.99, and 0.99 across the indoor and two outdoor scenarios, respectively. Successfully reconciled channel-informed keys pass the selected NIST randomness tests prior to SHA-3 privacy amplification. The results demonstrate the potential of channel-informed representation learning for decentralized wireless key establishment while highlighting an important tradeoff between key diversity and reconciliation reliability.

AI.tldr: A channel-informed neural network for physical-layer key generation (PKG) that learns binary key features from IQ measurements while leveraging multipath channel information. The framework uses Sionna-RT ray tracing for data augmentation and is evaluated on the POWDER radio testbed.
AI.motivation: Edge networks require lightweight key establishment for resource-constrained devices with limited access to centralized infrastructure. PKG enables wireless devices to establish shared keys from reciprocal channel observations without directly exchanging the key.
AI.method: Multi-task recurrent neural network that jointly learns reciprocity-preserving binary features and auxiliary channel estimates using a training objective combining deep metric learning with channel-informed supervision. Uses structured channel sounding and Sionna-RT ray tracing for data augmentation.
AI.result: The model produces lower bit disagreement for reciprocal Alice-Bob observations than for Eve-related observations. Ray-traced data augmentation increases unique-key rate to 0.94, 0.99, and 0.99 across indoor and two outdoor scenarios. Successfully reconciled keys pass NIST randomness tests prior to SHA-3 privacy amplification.
AI.conclusion: Channel-informed representation learning shows potential for decentralized wireless key establishment, with an important tradeoff identified between key diversity and reconciliation reliability.

title: Turn-level Multiscale Density Ratio Estimation for LLM Agents
summary: With the rapid development of Large language model (LLM), agent systems enhanced by LLMs show huge potential in being able to deal with complex tasks, especially involving multi-step thinking or interaction with tools. For applying LLM techniques with a well-designed agent paradigm, post-training of LLM in multiple agent scenarios is necessary to achieve better performance. Among the variable post-training techniques, alignment methods such as PPO, DPO, DIL, and GRPO become popular because many papers show a significant positive impact on the model's performance by punishing negative samples while keeping acceptable training complexity. However, most alignment methods address simple single-turn tasks, and there remains room for improvement for complex multi-turn tasks. We propose Turn-level Multiscale Density Ratio Estimation (tlm-DRE), which assigns different weights on corresponding turns and proposes asymmetric token-level training based on the positive-negative space gaps across multiple turns of tasks. The results of the experiment on a wide range of agent benchmarks show that the proposed method performs competitively compared to traditional alignment methods. The proposed training method enables LLMs to perform robustly in multi-turn reasoning tasks with both in-domain and out-of-domain conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes tlm-DRE (Turn-level Multiscale Density Ratio Estimation), a novel alignment method for improving LLM agents in complex multi-turn tasks. Unlike traditional alignment methods (PPO, DPO, DIL, GRPO) that target single-turn tasks, tlm-DRE assigns turn-level weights and uses asymmetric token-level training based on positive-negative space gaps across multiple turns.
AI.motivation: The rapid development of LLMs has enabled agent systems to handle complex tasks involving multi-step thinking and tool interaction. However, existing alignment methods (PPO, DPO, DIL, GRPO) primarily address simple single-turn tasks, leaving a gap for complex multi-turn scenarios. Post-training in multiple agent scenarios is necessary to achieve better performance in these complex tasks.
AI.method: The proposed tlm-DRE method introduces two key innovations: (1) Turn-level weight assignment - assigning different weights to corresponding turns in multi-turn tasks, and (2) Asymmetric token-level training - training based on positive-negative space gaps across multiple turns of tasks. This approach enables the model to learn from the differences between positive and negative samples at both turn and token levels.
AI.result: Experimental results on a wide range of agent benchmarks show that tlm-DRE performs competitively compared to traditional alignment methods. The method enables LLMs to perform robustly in multi-turn reasoning tasks under both in-domain and out-of-domain conditions.
AI.conclusion: tlm-DRE successfully extends alignment techniques to complex multi-turn agent tasks. By incorporating turn-level weighting and asymmetric token-level training, the method achieves robust performance across different domains, addressing the limitation of traditional alignment methods that focus on single-turn tasks.

title: HLC-GS: Risk-Map-Guided Height-Layer Consistency Gaussian Splatting for DSM Reconstruction from Optical Satellite Imagery
summary: A Digital Surface Model (DSM) is a fundamental geospatial data product for representing the elevation of the Earth's surface. Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has shown considerable potential for DSM reconstruction from multi-view optical satellite imagery due to its explicit scene representation and efficient optimization. However, in 3DGS-based DSM generation, alpha-weighted aggregation of Gaussian altitudes may blend splats from different height layers at the same rendered pixel or DSM sampling location, producing non-physical intermediate elevations and height-layer mixing errors. To address this problem, we propose HLC-GS, a risk-map-guided height-layer consistency Gaussian Splatting method for DSM reconstruction from optical satellite imagery. HLC-GS consists of a risk map module, a dominant-layer reliability correction module, and a secondary-layer suppression module. The risk map localizes high-risk pixels with abnormal height dispersion and unreliable dominant-layer responses, while the latter two modules regularize unreliable dominant-layer responses and suppress weakly supported far secondary-layer responses. Extensive experiments are conducted on the DFC2019 and IARPA2016 datasets. Compared with six state-of-the-art DSM reconstruction methods, HLC-GS achieves better overall accuracy. Compared with the latest and precision-enhanced EOGS, HLC-GS reduces the average MAE from 1.46 m to 1.18 m and the average RMSE from 2.78 m to 2.58 m over the evaluated scenes, while improving PAG$_{2.5}$ from 86.09\% to 88.61\%. Overall, these results demonstrate that explicitly modeling per-pixel height-layer consistency alleviates height-layer mixing and improves the geometric quality of 3DGS-based DSM reconstruction from optical satellite imagery.

AI.tldr: HLC-GS is a novel 3D Gaussian Splatting method for Digital Surface Model (DSM) reconstruction from multi-view optical satellite imagery that addresses height-layer mixing errors through risk-map-guided height-layer consistency modeling.
AI.motivation: Current 3DGS-based DSM reconstruction suffers from alpha-weighted aggregation that blends splats from different height layers at the same pixel, producing non-physical intermediate elevations and height-layer mixing errors. This limits the geometric quality of DSM products derived from satellite imagery.
AI.method: HLC-GS employs three key modules: (1) A risk map module that localizes high-risk pixels with abnormal height dispersion and unreliable dominant-layer responses; (2) A dominant-layer reliability correction module that regularizes unreliable dominant-layer responses; (3) A secondary-layer suppression module that suppresses weakly supported far secondary-layer responses. The method is evaluated on DFC2019 and IARPA2016 datasets against six state-of-the-art methods.
AI.result: HLC-GS outperforms all comparison methods. Compared with the latest EOGS method, HLC-GS reduces average MAE from 1.46 m to 1.18 m (19.2% improvement) and average RMSE from 2.78 m to 2.58 m (7.2% improvement), while improving PAG₂.₅ from 86.09% to 88.61%.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling per-pixel height-layer consistency in 3D Gaussian Splatting effectively alleviates height-layer mixing and significantly improves the geometric quality of DSM reconstruction from optical satellite imagery, demonstrating the value of addressing this previously overlooked source of error.

title: Multi-Label Proportion Learning for Sea-Ice Type Prediction
summary: Sea-ice type prediction is important for climate monitoring, maritime navigation, and decision-making in polar regions. The main source of label data for this task is the ice chart, produced manually by ice analysts who interpret satellite imagery to delineate ice zones into polygons. Although ice charts are valuable, their production is labor-intensive and expensive, motivating recent efforts to automate the process using deep learning. However, deep learning models require patch-level (or pixel-level) label data for training, while ice charts provide only polygon-level annotations. As a workaround, supervised approaches often create approximate patch-level labels from polygon-level ice chart labels by assigning each sample the dominant ice type of its parent polygon. This approach enables supervised training but creates an ill-posed learning problem with intrinsically approximate solution. In this paper, we redefine sea-ice type prediction as a weakly supervised multi-label proportion learning problem to be able to directly use the polygon-level ice chart labels and avoid unnecessary label approximation for improved prediction accuracy. To address this problem, we propose a two-module framework where first Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) is used for water--ice classification, and then a multi-label proportion learning (MLPL) is introduced for ice-type composition prediction. We further extend this framework with a multimodal model that integrates SAR imagery with AMSR2 brightness temperatures and ERA5 reanalysis data through modality-guided auxiliary regularization. Evaluated on the AI4Arctic dataset, the SAR-only model reduces MAE by 14.5\% and more than doubles mean ice-class F1 over the best supervised baseline. The multimodal model further reduces MAE by 21.5\% and raises mean F1 by 41.2\% over the SAR-only model, and by 52.7\% over the supervised multimodal baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses sea-ice type prediction by reframing it as a weakly supervised multi-label proportion learning problem, avoiding the need for approximate patch-level labels derived from polygon-level ice charts. The proposed two-module framework uses MIL for water-ice classification followed by MLPL for ice-type composition prediction, with a multimodal extension integrating SAR, AMSR2, and ERA5 data.
AI.motivation: Ice charts are manually produced and labor-intensive, motivating automation with deep learning. However, supervised approaches require patch-level labels, while ice charts only provide polygon-level annotations. Current workarounds create approximate labels, leading to an ill-posed learning problem.
AI.method: Two-module framework: (1) Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) for water-ice classification, (2) Multi-label proportion learning (MLPL) for ice-type composition prediction. Extended with multimodal model integrating SAR imagery, AMSR2 brightness temperatures, and ERA5 reanalysis data through modality-guided auxiliary regularization.
AI.result: SAR-only model reduces MAE by 14.5% and more than doubles mean ice-class F1 over best supervised baseline. Multimodal model further reduces MAE by 21.5% and raises mean F1 by 41.2% over SAR-only model, and by 52.7% over supervised multimodal baseline.
AI.conclusion: The weakly supervised multi-label proportion learning approach effectively leverages polygon-level ice chart labels directly, eliminating the need for label approximation. The multimodal integration significantly improves prediction accuracy, demonstrating the value of combining SAR, AMSR2, and ERA5 data for sea-ice type prediction.

title: Coverage-Aware Virtual IMU Augmentation for Low-Resource Human Activity Recognition
summary: IMU-based human activity recognition (HAR) enables continuous, privacy-friendly monitoring of daily activities using wearable sensors. However, building reliable HAR models that generalize across diverse users and real-world conditions requires large amounts of labeled IMU data, which are expensive and difficult to collect. Existing approaches mainly rely on augmentation or synthesis to expand available data, but indiscriminately adding virtual samples may provide little new coverage and introduce unreliable supervision. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel coverage-aware virtual IMU augmentation framework that decides where to supplement real data, how to generate and select virtual candidates, and how strongly to weight them during training. Specifically, we select diversity and scarcity anchors in a learned sensor embedding space, convert anchor dynamics into prompts, and generate virtual IMU candidates for each anchor. We then rank candidates by a selection cost combining anchor proximity and label consistency, and incorporate the selected candidates into HAR training with reliability-based weights. Experiments on public HAR benchmarks show that our method consistently improves recognition performance over competitive baselines, and ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the proposed framework design.

AI.tldr: A coverage-aware virtual IMU augmentation framework for human activity recognition that addresses data scarcity by intelligently selecting, generating, and weighting virtual IMU samples in a learned embedding space.
AI.motivation: IMU-based HAR requires large labeled datasets for reliable generalization across diverse users and real-world conditions, but collecting such data is expensive and difficult. Existing augmentation/synthesis methods indiscriminately add virtual samples that may provide little new coverage and introduce unreliable supervision.
AI.method: The framework has three key components: (1) Select diversity and scarcity anchors in a learned sensor embedding space; (2) Convert anchor dynamics into prompts and generate virtual IMU candidates for each anchor; (3) Rank candidates by a selection cost combining anchor proximity and label consistency, then incorporate selected candidates into training with reliability-based weights.
AI.result: Experiments on public HAR benchmarks show consistent improvement over competitive baselines, and ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the proposed framework design.
AI.conclusion: The coverage-aware approach effectively addresses data scarcity in IMU-based HAR by intelligently selecting where to augment, generating appropriate virtual samples, and weighting them based on reliability. This provides a principled way to expand training data while maintaining quality.

title: FSANet: Frequency-Spatial Aware Network for Image Segmentation
summary: Image segmentation remains challenging due to occlusions, poor lighting, and irregular structures. Although transformer-based methods achieve high accuracy, they rely heavily on long-range spatial features, leading to high computational costs and neglecting prior knowledge or noise patterns, resulting in missing details and unclear boundaries. To address these issues, we propose Frequency Spatial Aware Network (FSANet), which integrates prior knowledge with a dual-domain solver to sequentially adapt to diverse segmentation tasks. Specifically, we design three key modules: (1) Structure Prior Module, which recovers overlooked details; (2) Dual-Domain Awareness Module, which captures salient features while disentangling noise; and (3) Edge Estimation Module, which enhances edge awareness for more precise segmentation. In addition, the limited availability of comprehensive segmentation datasets covering various real-world scenarios hinders the performance of existing methods. To address this, we introduce SceneX, a novel open-source dataset featuring 10 challenging non-ideal scenarios, establishing a new benchmark for evaluating and improving the robustness and real-world applicability of the segmentation models. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of FSANet.

AI.tldr: FSANet is a novel image segmentation network that addresses limitations of transformer-based methods by integrating prior knowledge with a dual-domain solver. It uses three key modules (Structure Prior, Dual-Domain Awareness, and Edge Estimation) to handle occlusions, poor lighting, and irregular structures. The paper also introduces SceneX, a dataset with 10 challenging non-ideal scenarios for benchmarking.
AI.motivation: Image segmentation faces challenges from occlusions, poor lighting, and irregular structures. While transformer-based methods achieve high accuracy, they suffer from high computational costs, neglect prior knowledge/noise patterns, and produce missing details and unclear boundaries.
AI.method: FSANet integrates prior knowledge with a dual-domain solver through three modules: (1) Structure Prior Module recovers overlooked details; (2) Dual-Domain Awareness Module captures salient features while disentangling noise; (3) Edge Estimation Module enhances edge awareness for precise segmentation. The paper also introduces SceneX dataset with 10 challenging non-ideal scenarios.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of FSANet.
AI.conclusion: FSANet successfully addresses the limitations of existing transformer-based segmentation methods by incorporating prior knowledge and dual-domain processing, achieving improved performance on challenging scenarios through the proposed modules and new benchmark dataset.

title: Federated stochastic bilevel optimization with fully first-order gradients
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the Thirty-Fourth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 2025). The official version is available at https://doi.org/10.24963/ijcai.2025/784
summary: Federated stochastic bilevel optimization has been actively studied in recent years due to its widespread applications in machine learning. However, most existing federated stochastic bilevel optimization algorithms require the computation of second-order Hessian and Jacobian matrices, which leads to longer running times in practice. To address these challenges, we propose a novel federated stochastic variance-reduced bilevel gradient descent algorithm that relies solely on first-order oracles. Specifically, our approach does not require the computation of second-order Hessian and Jacobian matrices, significantly reducing running time. Furthermore, we introduce a novel learning rate mechanism, i.e., a constant single-timescale learning rate, to coordinate the update of different variables. We also present a new strategy to establish the convergence rate of our algorithm. Finally, the extensive experimental results confirm the efficacy of our proposed algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel federated stochastic variance-reduced bilevel gradient descent algorithm that uses only first-order oracles, avoiding computationally expensive second-order Hessian and Jacobian matrices. It introduces a constant single-timescale learning rate mechanism and a new convergence analysis strategy.
AI.motivation: Existing federated stochastic bilevel optimization algorithms require computation of second-order Hessian and Jacobian matrices, which leads to longer running times in practice. The authors aim to address this computational efficiency challenge.
AI.method: The proposed algorithm uses first-order oracles only (no second-order Hessian/Jacobian computations), and employs a constant single-timescale learning rate mechanism to coordinate variable updates. A new strategy for establishing convergence rate is also introduced.
AI.result: The algorithm significantly reduces running time compared to existing methods while maintaining effectiveness. Extensive experimental results confirm the algorithm's efficacy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed federated stochastic variance-reduced bilevel gradient descent algorithm achieves computational efficiency through first-order oracles while maintaining convergence performance, offering a practical solution for federated bilevel optimization problems.

title: Integrating the Analytic Hierarchy Process with Large Language Models for Transparent Multi-Criteria Decision-Making
summary: LLMs are increasingly employed in a wide range of decision-making tasks. However, the opacity of their internal reasoning makes it difficult to validate or interpret their outputs, and the need for interpretability becomes especially critical in high-stakes settings. This study examines the decision-making capabilities of LLMs through the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP), a classical and widely used multicriteria decision-making framework. We construct a new annotated benchmark based on AHP and propose the first end-to-end approach that enables LLMs to perform the complete AHP workflow. Experiments in real-world decision problems in the legal and higher-education ranking domains show that our method significantly improves alignment with expert judgments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an end-to-end method for Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform decision-making using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) framework, along with a new annotated benchmark. The approach addresses the interpretability challenges of LLM-based decision-making in high-stakes domains.
AI.motivation: The opacity of LLM internal reasoning makes it difficult to validate or interpret outputs, which is critical in high-stakes decision-making settings. The authors aim to improve the interpretability and alignment of LLM decisions with expert judgments.
AI.method: The study constructs a new annotated benchmark based on AHP (a classical multicriteria decision-making framework) and proposes the first end-to-end approach enabling LLMs to perform the complete AHP workflow. Experiments are conducted in legal and higher-education ranking domains.
AI.result: The method significantly improves alignment with expert judgments in real-world decision problems across legal and higher-education ranking domains.
AI.conclusion: The proposed AHP-based approach provides a promising framework for interpretable LLM decision-making, with demonstrated effectiveness in real-world high-stakes applications.

title: IMVS: Interactive Medical Volume Segmentation with Test-Time Adaptation - A New Method for Annotating Radiology Datasets
summary: Annotating large radiology datasets is bottlenecked by the manual effort of delineating structures slice-by-slice in 3D volumes. Interactive methods reduce this effort but stay interaction-inefficient: slice-wise methods (including many foundation models) ignore inter-slice continuity, while 3D and video-based methods propagate a prompt with a \emph{fixed} propagator that never adapts to the target volume, so it drifts on low-contrast or pathological structures and must be re-prompted. We present IMVS, a human-in-the-loop annotation framework that composes three components into a closed loop rather than a new segmentation primitive: a lightweight 2D Slice Mask Adapter (SMA) fine-tuned online from user scribbles, a frozen Volume Mask Tracker (VMT) that propagates corrected masks across adjacent slices, and a soft teacher--student alignment that limits forgetting. The SMA is backbone-agnostic (UNet++, DeepLabV3, TransUNet). Across 8 public CT/MRI datasets, IMVS matches strong interactive baselines in quality while sharply cutting annotation effort: $14.4\times$ faster than a proficient copy-based manual workflow ($22.3\times$ over naive manual), $4.6\times$ over slice-wise and $1.9\times$ over 3D interactive methods. MedSAM2 and ScribblePrompt stay competitive or stronger on well-delineated organs; IMVS's advantage is largest on challenging targets and on interaction efficiency. Source code and Demo Video: https://github.com/AbhilakshSinghReen/imvs.

AI.tldr: IMVS is a human-in-the-loop annotation framework for 3D medical imaging that combines a lightweight 2D Slice Mask Adapter (fine-tuned from user scribbles), a frozen Volume Mask Tracker (for mask propagation), and soft teacher-student alignment to prevent forgetting. It achieves 14.4× faster annotation than manual workflows while matching quality of strong baselines.
AI.motivation: Manual annotation of large 3D radiology datasets is extremely time-consuming, requiring slice-by-slice delineation. Existing interactive methods are inefficient: slice-wise methods ignore inter-slice continuity, while 3D/video-based methods use fixed propagators that cannot adapt to target volumes and drift on low-contrast or pathological structures, requiring frequent re-prompting.
AI.method: IMVS employs a closed-loop human-in-the-loop framework with three components: (1) A lightweight 2D Slice Mask Adapter (SMA) that is fine-tuned online from user scribbles, (2) A frozen Volume Mask Tracker (VMT) that propagates corrected masks across adjacent slices, and (3) A soft teacher-student alignment mechanism to prevent forgetting. The SMA is backbone-agnostic, supporting UNet++, DeepLabV3, and TransUNet.
AI.result: Across 8 public CT/MRI datasets, IMVS matches strong interactive baselines in segmentation quality while significantly reducing annotation effort: 14.4× faster than proficient copy-based manual workflow (22.3× over naive manual), 4.6× faster than slice-wise methods, and 1.9× faster than 3D interactive methods. MedSAM2 and ScribblePrompt remain competitive on well-delineated organs, but IMVS shows its largest advantage on challenging targets and in interaction efficiency.
AI.conclusion: IMVS represents a significant advancement in interactive medical image annotation by combining adaptive learning (SMA) with stable propagation (VMT) and continuity preservation (teacher-student alignment). Its backbone-agnostic design and particular strength on challenging targets (low-contrast, pathological structures) make it a practical tool for accelerating radiology dataset annotation. The open-source implementation enables further research and adoption.

title: Autonomous Droplet Navigation via Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
comment: 43 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables including supplementary material. The source code is available via GitHub at https://github.com/rajneeshanand/DropletRunner. An archived version of all supplementary movies has also been uploaded to Google Drive: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1ewK2dxWxfzjd4kk6Df4cqKE3-3xCbOgf?usp=sharing
summary: Precise manipulation of liquid droplets underpins lab-on-a-chip platforms for diagnostics, chemical synthesis, and biological assays. Yet autonomous droplet transport through confined geometries of varying complexity remains an open challenge. Droplets exhibit contact-angle hysteresis, deformability, and capillary pinning, which make their response to actuation nonlinear and history dependent, that classical controllers and pre-programmed trajectories cannot cope in multi-turn environments. Here we demonstrate autonomous navigation of a liquid droplet through geometries of increasing complexity on a gravity driven (Labyrinth) platform using model-based reinforcement learning. A thin silicone oil film reduces contact-line pinning while two-axis tilt supplies the gravitational driving force, and an overhead camera tracks the droplet in real time. An offline-trained policy discovers effective tilt strategies from limited physical interaction data, without simulation or analytical droplet models. The system operates under partial observability, as oil-film thickness, instantaneous contact angle, and droplet deformation state remain hidden from the controller. Despite these challenges, the learned policy achieves reliable navigation across straight, right-angle, and curved-arc paths, including outside-corner geometries. We further demonstrate that a policy trained on a simpler geometry transfers to complex ones, succeeding zero-shot on right-angle and staircase paths and reaching full success on a curved arc with a fifth of the training data. The findings suggest promising avenues for enabling droplet based microfluidic systems to serve as intelligent chemical laboratories.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed a reinforcement learning-based system that autonomously navigates liquid droplets through complex geometries on a lab-on-a-chip platform, using two-axis tilt actuation and real-time visual tracking, achieving successful transfer learning between geometries of varying complexity.
AI.motivation: Autonomous droplet transport in confined geometries remains challenging due to contact-angle hysteresis, deformability, and capillary pinning, which create nonlinear and history-dependent responses that classical controllers cannot handle in multi-turn environments.
AI.method: A gravity-driven (Labyrinth) platform with two-axis tilt for gravitational driving force, thin silicone oil film to reduce contact-line pinning, overhead camera for real-time tracking, and offline-trained model-based reinforcement learning policy without simulation or analytical models. Operates under partial observability (oil thickness, contact angle, deformation state hidden).
AI.result: Learned policy achieves reliable navigation across straight, right-angle, curved-arc paths, and outside-corner geometries. Policy transfer from simpler to complex geometries succeeds zero-shot on right-angle and staircase paths, and reaches full success on curved arc with only 20% of training data.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates promising potential for enabling droplet-based microfluidic systems to serve as intelligent chemical laboratories, with effective transfer learning capabilities reducing data requirements for complex geometries.

title: Layers, Sinks, and Scaling: Adaptive Evidence Selection for Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can answer knowledge-intensive visual questions by combining visual evidence from images with facts retrieved from external sources. However, MLLMs may overlook relevant evidence in both modalities, attending weakly to the textual sentences or visual regions needed for the correct answer. Recent efforts address this by highlighting retrieved text and marking visual regions before generation, but apply a fixed, one-shot policy that cannot adapt to three sources of variation: whether highlighting is necessary, how much evidence different examples require, and when different textual evidence becomes relevant as the answer unfolds. We introduce Adaptive Relevance-guided Evidence Allocation (AREA), a training-free inference-time method that formulates evidence highlighting as adaptive allocation. AREA generates a single probe token to read visual and textual relevance from fixed backbone layers, then makes three decisions: i) whether to intervene (controlled by natural attention coverage and visual sink contamination), ii) how much evidence to expose (determined by relevance entropy), and iii) when to refresh text during generation (triggered by causal context-attention peaks). Across four KB-VQA and seven standard multimodal benchmarks with nine frozen MLLM checkpoints, establishes the best performance among training-free highlighting methods.

title: Unifying Semantic Priors and High-Frequency Traces: Enhancing V-JEPA with Mixture-of-Experts for Robust Synthetic Image Forensics
summary: The unchecked proliferation of manipulated images on social media platforms has increased the spread of misinformation, posing a severe threat to public trust and information integrity. Modern deepfake detectors typically rely on Vision Transformers (ViTs) to capture the low-level inconsistencies that characterize fully synthetic or locally tampered images. However, the global understanding of such foundation models is not enough to discriminate alone between real and fake multimedia content, especially in challenging scenarios where images are compressed or transmitted through social media. In this paper we pioneer the application of Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models to deepfake detection, taking advantage of the generalized representation of visual reality that such World Models have exhibited. We hypothesize, and empirically demonstrate, that the intrinsic world understanding of JEPA models can be used as a strong prior for a deepfake detector. To fully exploit JEPA capabilities, we propose MoE-JEPA, a dual-stream architecture for deepfake detection. By enhancing a V-JEPA 2 backbone with a Residual Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism, along with a noise stream branch, our model dynamically internalizes forensic knowledge. Furthermore, a Gated Attention Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) module is employed to ensure precise spatial semantic understanding. Evaluated on the SID-Set benchmark, comprising 300K AI-generated, tampered and authentic images, MoE-JEPA establishes a new state-of-the-art with an accuracy of 95.54%, successfully outperforming vastly larger models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MoE-JEPA, a dual-stream deepfake detection model that leverages Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) combined with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) and Gated Attention MIL to achieve 95.54% accuracy on the SID-Set benchmark, outperforming larger models.
AI.motivation: Current Vision Transformer-based deepfake detectors fail to capture global understanding needed to distinguish real from fake content, especially in challenging scenarios involving image compression or social media transmission. The authors hypothesize that JEPA models' world understanding can serve as a strong prior for deepfake detection.
AI.method: The proposed MoE-JEPA uses a dual-stream architecture: (1) V-JEPA 2 backbone enhanced with Residual Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism and a noise stream branch for dynamic forensic knowledge internalization; (2) Gated Attention Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) module for precise spatial semantic understanding.
AI.result: On the SID-Set benchmark (300K AI-generated, tampered, and authentic images), MoE-JEPA achieves 95.54% accuracy, establishing a new state-of-the-art and outperforming vastly larger models.
AI.conclusion: JEPA-based models with world understanding capabilities can effectively serve as priors for deepfake detection, and the MoE-JEPA architecture successfully combines JEPA representations with expert mechanisms to achieve superior detection performance.

title: Certified Uncertainty Propagation in One-Shot Federated Bayesian Models via Posterior Event Transport
summary: Probabilistic certification of Bayesian neural networks lower-bounds the posterior probability that a model satisfies a verifier-defined safety property. In one-shot federated Bayesian learning, however, the deployed model is obtained by aggregating parameters drawn from client-specific posterior distributions, so local certificates do not directly guarantee safety of the aggregated model. This paper develops a deployment-consistent certification framework by propagating local posterior events through the deployment aggregation rule, with an exact geometric characterization for Federated Averaging (FedAvg). Each client constructs disjoint hyper-rectangular regions in parameter space and computes their probability masses. The server forms Cartesian products of these regions, maps them through the deployment rule, and retains a product event only when its aggregation image is verified to satisfy the safety property. Under independent client posteriors, each product-event probability factorizes into local masses, and summing verified disjoint events yields a lower bound on safety probability of the deployed model. For FedAvg with nonnegative aggregation coefficients, the image of a Cartesian product of axis-aligned hyper-rectangles is exactly a weighted hyper-rectangle, introducing no set over-approximation. We distinguish the proposed transported-event certificate from direct certification under posterior distributions induced by FedAvg and Product-of-Gaussians aggregation. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST under label-Dirichlet heterogeneity show that the transported FedAvg certificate ranges from 22.51% to 46.89%, while direct global certificates range from 72.05% to 91.39%. Results show that predictive accuracy and certifiable safety do not necessarily follow the same trend, and that global posterior constructions can exhibit distinct certification behavior across architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a deployment-consistent certification framework for federated Bayesian neural networks that propagates local posterior events through the FedAvg aggregation rule to lower-bound the safety probability of the deployed model. The approach uses hyper-rectangular regions in parameter space, where the image of Cartesian products under FedAvg with nonnegative coefficients is exactly a weighted hyper-rectangle with no over-approximation.
AI.motivation: In one-shot federated Bayesian learning, local safety certificates from clients do not directly guarantee safety of the aggregated model because the deployed model is obtained by aggregating parameters from client-specific posterior distributions. This gap between local certification and global deployment safety needs to be addressed.
AI.method: The framework has clients construct disjoint hyper-rectangular regions in parameter space and compute their probability masses. The server forms Cartesian products of these regions, maps them through the deployment rule (FedAvg), and retains product events only when their aggregation image satisfies the safety property. Under independent client posteriors, each product-event probability factorizes into local masses, and summing verified disjoint events yields a lower bound on safety probability. For FedAvg with nonnegative aggregation coefficients, the image of a Cartesian product of axis-aligned hyper-rectangles is exactly a weighted hyper-rectangle.
AI.result: Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST under label-Dirichlet heterogeneity show that transported FedAvg certificates range from 22.51% to 46.89%, while direct global certificates range from 72.05% to 91.39%. The results reveal that predictive accuracy and certifiable safety do not necessarily follow the same trend, and global posterior constructions can exhibit distinct certification behavior across architectures.
AI.conclusion: The transported-event certificate provides a deployment-consistent lower bound on safety probability but yields lower bounds than direct certification under posterior distributions induced by FedAvg and Product-of-Gaussians aggregation. The discrepancy highlights the importance of considering the actual deployment process in safety certification for federated learning.

title: Can We Do Interpretable NLI with Graphs Based on Atomic Propositions?
summary: While Large Language Model (LLM)-based Natural Language Inference (NLI) systems achieve high accuracy, their decision-making processes lack auditable structures. This paper explores whether NLI can be performed using only interpretable, graph-based representations of evidence. We introduce a fully graph-based pipeline where the classifier never directly processes the input text. Instead, sentences are decomposed into atomic propositions, converted into ConceptNet triples via constrained decoding, and represented as three graphs per pair: premise, hypothesis, and a retrieved ConceptNet subgraph. These graphs are then fed into a fine-tuned 0.8-billion-parameter language model. On the SNLI dataset, our pipeline achieves 89.7% accuracy, just 1.9 points below an identically trained text-based model. On ANLI, it matches the published performance of RoBERTa-large on rounds R2 and R3 (50% accuracy) but trails by 16 points on R1, resulting in an overall gap of 9 to 14 points compared to its text counterpart. We term this gap the price of interpretability and demonstrate that it stems from representational limitations rather than data constraints. Ablation studies further reveal that graphs and text are complementary: combining both modalities achieves 92.1% accuracy on SNLI.

AI.tldr: This paper explores whether Natural Language Inference (NLI) can be performed using only interpretable, graph-based representations instead of raw text. The proposed pipeline decomposes sentences into atomic propositions, converts them to ConceptNet triples, and represents them as three graphs (premise, hypothesis, and retrieved ConceptNet subgraph) fed into a fine-tuned 0.8B parameter language model. The approach achieves 89.7% on SNLI (1.9 points below text-based) and reveals a "price of interpretability" gap of 9-14 points on ANLI, but combining both modalities achieves 92.1% accuracy.
AI.motivation: While LLM-based NLI systems achieve high accuracy, their decision-making processes lack auditable and interpretable structures. This paper aims to perform NLI using only interpretable, graph-based representations of evidence to make the classification process more transparent and auditable.
AI.method: A fully graph-based pipeline where the classifier never directly processes input text. Sentences are decomposed into atomic propositions, converted into ConceptNet triples via constrained decoding, and represented as three graphs per pair: premise, hypothesis, and a retrieved ConceptNet subgraph. These graphs are fed into a fine-tuned 0.8-billion-parameter language model.
AI.result: On SNLI dataset, the pipeline achieves 89.7% accuracy, just 1.9 points below an identically trained text-based model. On ANLI, it matches RoBERTa-large on rounds R2 and R3 (50% accuracy) but trails by 16 points on R1, resulting in an overall gap of 9 to 14 points compared to its text counterpart. Ablation studies show that combining both modalities (graphs + text) achieves 92.1% accuracy on SNLI.
AI.conclusion: The performance gap between graph-based and text-based models is termed the "price of interpretability" and stems from representational limitations rather than data constraints. Graphs and text are complementary modalities—combining both improves performance beyond either alone, suggesting future work should explore hybrid approaches for balancing interpretability and accuracy.

title: PSMP-CLIP: Patch-Prompt SAM and Multi-Semantic Prompting for CLIP-Based Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection
summary: Zero-shot anomaly detection aims to localize anomalies without target-domain samples. Existing CLIP-based methods suffer from coarse anomaly maps and limited semantic prompts. We propose PSMP-CLIP, integrating patch-prompt SAM2 segmentation (PPSS) and multi-semantic guided prompt regularization (MSGPR). PPSS samples prompts directly from intermediate patch features, avoiding threshold drift and guiding SAM2 to produce precise masks. MSGPR uses multiple learnable prompts constrained by semantic anchors to preserve generalization. Experiments on 14 datasets show highly competitive performance, achieving the best pixel-level AUROC on MVTec AD, BTAD, DTD-Synthetic, CVC-ClinicDB, TN3K, Endo, and Kvasir.

AI.tldr: PSMP-CLIP is a zero-shot anomaly detection method that combines patch-prompt SAM2 segmentation (PPSS) and multi-semantic guided prompt regularization (MSGPR) to overcome limitations of existing CLIP-based methods, which suffer from coarse anomaly maps and limited semantic prompts.
AI.motivation: Existing CLIP-based zero-shot anomaly detection methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) coarse anomaly maps that lack precision, and (2) limited semantic prompts that restrict generalization capability. This work aims to address both issues simultaneously.
AI.method: The proposed PSMP-CLIP integrates two novel components: (1) PPSS (Patch-Prompt SAM2 Segmentation) - samples prompts directly from intermediate patch features to avoid threshold drift and guide SAM2 to produce precise masks; (2) MSGPR (Multi-Semantic Guided Prompt Regularization) - uses multiple learnable prompts constrained by semantic anchors to preserve generalization ability.
AI.result: Experiments conducted on 14 datasets demonstrate highly competitive performance. The method achieves the best pixel-level AUROC on MVTec AD, BTAD, DTD-Synthetic, CVC-ClinicDB, TN3K, Endo, and Kvasir datasets.
AI.conclusion: PSMP-CLIP effectively addresses the limitations of existing CLIP-based zero-shot anomaly detection methods by introducing patch-prompt sampling and multi-semantic prompt regularization, achieving state-of-the-art or highly competitive results across multiple benchmark datasets.

title: Bounded Adjustment with Reliability-Guided Embedding for Imbalanced Learning with Noisy Labels
summary: Class-balanced learning and label noise create a coupled failure mode: frequency correction prevents majority classes from dominating the decision rule, but can amplify incorrectly labeled minority examples. We introduce BARGE (Bounded Adjustment with Reliability-Guided Embeddings), a single-stage objective combining a bounded, prior-adjusted density-power score with reliability-guided angular geometry. Its classification score is strictly proper in the adjusted probability space and recovers balanced Bayes ordering under clean supervision and the true class prior. Under label contamination, its finite range bounds classification-risk perturbation at a fixed predictor, while its logit gradient redescends when the model confidently contradicts the supplied label. The adjusted target probability also weights class-equal feature compactness, and a one-sided separation term discourages aligned class directions. BARGE requires neither a noise rate nor a transition matrix, uses one network, and leaves inference unchanged. We evaluate it on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under long-tail and step imbalance, clean labels, and 20% and 40% random incorrect-label replacement. Across 12 clean settings, BARGE ranks second overall and attains the lowest error in four. Under corruption, it achieves the lowest mean balanced error in all six dataset-corruption settings, reducing the six-setting average from 72.32% for the strongest competitor to 70.00%. It also obtains the highest macro-F1 and macro-AUPRC in every corrupted-label setting. Ablations show that class-equal angular compactness improves on the bounded score alone. These results support bounded predictive influence and reliability-guided geometry as complementary mechanisms for imbalanced learning with uncertain labels.

AI.tldr: BARGE addresses the coupled failure mode where class-balanced learning amplifies label noise in minority classes. It combines a bounded, prior-adjusted density-power score with reliability-guided angular geometry in a single-stage objective that works without noise rate estimation or transition matrices.
AI.motivation: Class-balanced learning prevents majority classes from dominating but inadvertently amplifies incorrectly labeled minority examples. This creates a coupled failure mode where frequency correction and label noise interact negatively. Existing methods typically require noise rate estimation, transition matrices, or multiple networks, adding complexity and potential failure points.
AI.method: BARGE introduces a single-stage objective combining: (1) bounded prior-adjusted density-power score that is strictly proper in adjusted probability space, recovering balanced Bayes ordering under clean supervision; (2) reliability-guided angular geometry where adjusted target probability weights class-equal feature compactness; (3) one-sided separation term discouraging aligned class directions. The method bounds classification-risk perturbation under label contamination and uses logit gradient redescent when model confidently contradicts supplied labels.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under long-tail/step imbalance with clean and corrupted labels (20%, 40%): (1) Across 12 clean settings, BARGE ranks second overall with lowest error in 4; (2) Under corruption, achieves lowest mean balanced error in all 6 settings (72.32% → 70.00% reduction); (3) Highest macro-F1 and macro-AUPRC in every corrupted-label setting; (4) Ablations confirm class-equal angular compactness improves over bounded score alone.
AI.conclusion: Bounded predictive influence and reliability-guided geometry are complementary mechanisms for imbalanced learning with uncertain labels. The method successfully handles the coupled failure mode without requiring noise rate estimation, transition matrices, or multiple networks, while maintaining unchanged inference.

title: Execution Flexibility in Automated Planning: A Comparative Evaluation of Deordering and Reordering Strategies
summary: This study covers foundational concepts for enhancing plan-execution flexibility, including partial-order planning, the producer-consumer-threat formalism, and a range of deordering and reordering strategies. Creating a partial-order plan from a sequential one by removing unnecessary ordering constraints is a practical way to improve execution flexibility, and several methods have been proposed for this task. This study analyzes their capabilities across ordering, action handling, parameter handling, plan structure, concurrency, and complexity, and evaluates them against each other on a shared benchmark. The central finding is that block deordering-based approaches, which restructure causal dependencies through block-level grouping and subplan substitution, substantially outperform MaxSAT-based approaches despite the latter's theoretical guarantees of minimum reordering. The reason is structural: minimum reordering optimizes within the causal structure already present in the plan, whereas block deordering-based methods change that structure, exposing orderings that would otherwise appear necessary. A further distinction is practical: block deordering-based methods are anytime algorithms that always return a valid result, while MaxSAT-based methods fail entirely on a substantial portion of plans and offer no partial solution when they do. Block substitution further extends the parallel execution by formalizing non-concurrency constraints, though its impact is limited to domains with resource-based interactions. On efficiency, block deordering-based approaches achieve the highest flex gain per unit of computation time, while MaxSAT-based encodings incur large computational overhead.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes methods for enhancing plan-execution flexibility by converting sequential plans into partial-order plans through deordering strategies. It compares block deordering-based approaches against MaxSAT-based methods across multiple dimensions, finding that block deordering substantially outperforms MaxSAT-based approaches despite theoretical guarantees of the latter, due to structural changes in causal dependencies and practical advantages as anytime algorithms.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to improve plan-execution flexibility in planning systems. Sequential plans have unnecessary ordering constraints that, when removed, can increase parallelism and execution flexibility. The study addresses the lack of comprehensive analysis and comparison of existing deordering methods.
AI.method: The paper analyzes capabilities of various deordering and reordering methods across six dimensions: ordering, action handling, parameter handling, plan structure, concurrency, and complexity. Methods are evaluated against each other on a shared benchmark. Two main approaches are compared: block deordering-based methods (which restructure causal dependencies through block-level grouping and subplan substitution) and MaxSAT-based approaches (which optimize for minimum reordering within existing causal structure).
AI.result: Block deordering-based approaches substantially outperform MaxSAT-based approaches. The key reasons are: (1) Structural: minimum reordering optimizes within existing causal structure, while block deordering changes the structure itself, exposing orderings that would otherwise appear necessary; (2) Practical: block deordering is anytime (always returns valid result) while MaxSAT fails on a substantial portion of plans. Block substitution further extends parallel execution by formalizing non-concurrency constraints, though its impact is limited to domains with resource-based interactions. Block deordering achieves the highest flex gain per unit of computation time, while MaxSAT incurs large computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Block deordering-based methods are superior to MaxSAT-based methods for enhancing plan-execution flexibility. The structural modification of causal dependencies is more effective than optimizing within existing structure. The anytime property of block deordering provides practical reliability over MaxSAT's brittleness. These findings guide practitioners in selecting appropriate deordering strategies for planning systems.

title: TEDi: Temporal Memory-Enhanced and Denoising Transformer for Surgical Instrument Segmentation
summary: Query-based segmentation methods have shown promising potential for surgical instrument segmentation and recognition, which is essential for scene understanding and downstream tasks in computer assisted surgery. However, most existing approaches predominantly rely on per-frame predictions and overlook cross-frame temporal priors as well as temporal-consistency constraints. This limitation often leads to unstable query representations and suboptimal category recognition. In this paper, we propose TEDi, a Temporal memory-Enhanced and Denoising transformer for surgical instrument segmentation that addresses these is sues through Memory Search Enhancement and Temporal Consistency Denoising. The former introduces a query-level memory bank and a memory search enhancement encoder to retrieve discriminative representations from historical frames, enriching current-frame features. The latter constructs a temporally consistent reference as a cross-frame semantic anchor to suppress temporally unstable predictions and promote semantic coherence across frames. Extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets, EndoVis 2017 and EndoVis 2018, demonstrate that TEDi consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, highlighting its potential to further advance computer-assisted surgery. Our code is available at github.com/argon-xixi/TEDi.

AI.tldr: TEDi is a transformer-based method for surgical instrument segmentation that addresses temporal consistency issues in query-based methods by introducing memory search enhancement and temporal consistency denoising modules.
AI.motivation: Query-based segmentation methods for surgical instrument segmentation predominantly rely on per-frame predictions and overlook cross-frame temporal priors and temporal-consistency constraints, leading to unstable query representations and suboptimal category recognition.
AI.method: TEDi proposes two key components: (1) Memory Search Enhancement - introduces a query-level memory bank and memory search enhancement encoder to retrieve discriminative representations from historical frames, enriching current-frame features; (2) Temporal Consistency Denoising - constructs a temporally consistent reference as a cross-frame semantic anchor to suppress temporally unstable predictions and promote semantic coherence across frames.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on EndoVis 2017 and EndoVis 2018 benchmark datasets demonstrate that TEDi consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: TEDi successfully addresses temporal limitations in query-based surgical instrument segmentation and has potential to further advance computer-assisted surgery.

title: Attention Mean Fields Predict Average Representation Dynamics and Reveal Context-Specific Computation
summary:
A language model's representation geometry is not predetermined; it evolves as the model runs. A faithful account of that geometry must capture that dynamic process, and so cannot be based solely on model-independent statistics such as co-occurrence. Here we introduce a mean-field analysis of attention. The average attention from one token to another defines a kernel that carries representations layer to layer and can be iterated through the network to model how the geometry is transformed. We condition this average two ways. Conditioned on a whole corpus, the kernel predicts the average-case evolution of representation geometry. Conditioned instead on a single context, it predicts the expected geometry for that context. A head's departure from that prediction, its \emph{mean-field deviation}, isolates the context-specific computation that the mean field misses.
  Under the corpus-conditional reading, the kernel yields an open-loop model: from the input embeddings and the frozen weights alone, we can iterate the kernel and the model's own MLPs over token representations, never consulting a measured deviation at any layer. The resulting prediction is highly accurate.
  In early training the model and its corpus mean field are indistinguishable. Replace every attention head with its mean field, and the substitution leaves the loss on real text unchanged. Around the onset of induction, the two diverge, and the gap widens as representations become contextualized.
  Under the context-conditional reading, deviation from the mean field is a task-agnostic measure of context-specific computation. The residual decomposes additively into unusual attention routing and contextualization of the transported values. Across controlled induction and few-shot settings, greater deviation tracks greater reliance on in-context information.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a mean-field analysis of attention in language models, where the average attention kernel carries representations layer by layer. The analysis has two variants: corpus-conditional (predicting average-case geometry from input embeddings and weights alone) and context-conditional (measuring context-specific computation via deviation from the mean field). The model and its mean field are indistinguishable in early training but diverge around induction onset, with deviation tracking in-context learning reliance.
AI.motivation: Current understanding of language model representation geometry relies on model-independent statistics like co-occurrence, but this fails to capture the dynamic evolution of geometry as the model processes tokens. The authors seek a faithful account that captures how geometry transforms layer by layer through the network.
AI.method: The mean-field analysis uses average attention from one token to another as a kernel that carries representations layer to layer. This kernel can be iterated through the network. Two conditioning approaches: (1) Corpus-conditional - predicts average-case evolution from input embeddings and frozen weights without consulting measured deviations; (2) Context-conditional - predicts expected geometry for a specific context and measures deviation (mean-field deviation) to capture context-specific computation.
AI.result: Under corpus-conditional reading, the open-loop model (iterating kernel and MLPs from input alone) yields highly accurate predictions. In early training, the model and corpus mean field are indistinguishable - replacing attention heads with mean fields leaves loss unchanged. Around induction onset, they diverge and the gap widens as representations become contextualized. Under context-conditional reading, mean-field deviation is a task-agnostic measure of context-specific computation that decomposes into unusual attention routing and contextualization of transported values. Greater deviation tracks greater reliance on in-context information across induction and few-shot settings.
AI.conclusion: The mean-field analysis provides a principled framework for understanding how representation geometry evolves through transformer layers. The deviation from mean-field predictions serves as a useful measure of context-specific computation, with applications in understanding in-context learning and model internals.

title: CoAdapt: An LLM-based Framework for Adaptive Collaborative Perception in IIoT Robotic Swarms
summary: Industrial IoT environments increasingly deploy autonomous mobile robots for tasks such as material handling, product assembly, or infrastructure inspection. In such deployments, collaborative perception enables robots to share LiDAR observations and collectively construct a richer model of their environment than an individual agent could produce alone. However, industrial environments are dynamic spaces where robot positions shift continuously, network bandwidth fluctuates, and the marginal contribution of robots to perception quality varies at runtime. Existing collaborative perception approaches are designed for static participation assumptions and cannot adapt to these dynamics without sacrificing either detection precision or communication efficiency. This paper presents CoAdapt, an adaptive collaborative perception framework for IIoT robotic swarms in which a Large Language Model (LLM) serves as a runtime fusion controller, jointly deciding which robots participate in the fusion process and which fusion algorithm to apply based on the current spatial configuration and network state. The LLM reasons over structured natural language descriptions of the scene derived from raw LiDAR point clouds, requiring no taskspecific training and generalizing to unseen swarm topologies. Evaluated on the OPV2V benchmark across 25 scenarios, our approach achieves a 38% reduction in communication cost while maintaining detection precision comparable to static baseline approaches.

AI.tldr: CoAdapt is an adaptive collaborative perception framework for Industrial IoT robotic swarms that uses a Large Language Model (LLM) as a runtime fusion controller. It dynamically decides which robots participate in fusion and which fusion algorithm to use based on spatial configuration and network state, eliminating the need for task-specific training.
AI.motivation: Industrial IoT environments deploy autonomous mobile robots for tasks like material handling and infrastructure inspection. Existing collaborative perception approaches assume static participation and cannot adapt to dynamic robot positions, fluctuating network bandwidth, and varying marginal contributions of robots to perception quality. This creates a trade-off between detection precision and communication efficiency.
AI.method: CoAdapt uses an LLM as a runtime fusion controller that reasons over structured natural language descriptions of the scene derived from raw LiDAR point clouds. The LLM jointly decides: (1) which robots participate in the fusion process, and (2) which fusion algorithm to apply, based on current spatial configuration and network state. This approach requires no task-specific training and generalizes to unseen swarm topologies.
