In the evaluated transformers, concentrating updates in the most plastic layers increases catastrophic forgetting, while this tier-dependent effect disappears in the evaluated Mamba-style SSMs.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates layer importance in Transformers versus State-Space Models (SSMs), decomposing it into Necessity (how much a model depends on a layer's output) and Plasticity (where a model absorbs new information during fine-tuning). The key finding is that these two metrics anti-align in Transformers but overlap in SSMs, with significant implications for downstream adaptation behavior.
AI.motivation: The central question is how analytical knowledge built for Transformers transfers to SSMs, given that both are dominant sequence model families. Layer importance is crucial for compression, selective fine-tuning, and interpretability, making it a natural lens for comparison.
AI.method: The authors decompose layer importance into two distinct notions: (1) Necessity—measured by loss increase from bypassing a layer, capturing how much the pretrained model depends on that layer's contribution; and (2) Plasticity—measured by the magnitude of task-specific weight updates during fine-tuning, capturing where new information is absorbed. They evaluated residual Transformers up to 14B parameters and Mamba-style SSMs.
AI.result: The two model families exhibit fundamentally different behavior: In every evaluated Transformer (up to 14B parameters), Necessity and Plasticity anti-align across depth—layers that are most necessary tend to be least plastic, and vice versa. In contrast, in Mamba-style SSMs, Necessity and Plasticity point to overlapping regions. Furthermore, the sign of this alignment predicts downstream adaptation behavior: in Transformers, concentrating updates in the most plastic layers increases catastrophic forgetting, while this tier-dependent effect disappears in SSMs.
AI.conclusion: Transformers and SSMs behave fundamentally differently in terms of layer importance patterns. This finding suggests that fine-tuning strategies optimized for Transformers may not transfer to SSMs, and that the architectural differences between these families lead to distinct learning dynamics. The anti-alignment in Transformers explains why certain fine-tuning strategies cause catastrophic forgetting, while the overlapping pattern in SSMs explains the absence of such tier-dependent effects.

title: Sparse MLLM Anchors, Dense Adaptation: Breaking the Self-Referential Loop in Wild Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Wild test-time adaptation (WTTA) updates a source model online under small test batches, concurrent distribution shifts, and time-varying class imbalance. Most WTTA methods derive their adaptation signals, including predictive uncertainty, sample reliability, and local feature geometry, from the model being adapted. When the source model is unreliable under shift, these signals can reinforce its own errors, forming a self-referential loop. We introduce MASA (Multimodal-LLM-Anchored Semantic Adaptation), which complements model-internal evidence with structured semantic descriptions from a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM). To limit inference cost, MASA queries the MLLM only for a small set of diverse, reliability-ranked anchors. The resulting descriptions capture the object family and nuisance factors such as style, viewpoint, and occlusion. MASA encodes these descriptions, propagates them to neighboring test samples, and stores the resulting visual-semantic information in an online prototype memory. Descriptor-aware retrieval from this memory provides an auxiliary target for lightweight adaptation of normalization-affine parameters. We evaluate MASA on the WTTA ImageNet-C benchmark under limited-batch, mixed-domain, and imbalanced-label-shift settings with ResNet and ViT backbones.

AI.tldr: MASA addresses Wild Test-Time Adaptation (WTTA) by using a frozen multimodal LLM to provide semantic descriptions for anchor samples, which are then propagated to neighboring test samples and stored in an online prototype memory for lightweight normalization-affine adaptation.
AI.motivation: Current WTTA methods derive adaptation signals from the model itself, which can reinforce errors when the source model is unreliable under distribution shift, creating a self-referential loop. This paper aims to complement model-internal evidence with external semantic knowledge.
AI.method: MASA queries a frozen multimodal LLM for a small set of diverse, reliability-ranked anchor samples to obtain semantic descriptions capturing object family and nuisance factors. These descriptions are encoded, propagated to neighboring test samples, and stored in an online prototype memory. Descriptor-aware retrieval provides auxiliary targets for adapting normalization-affine parameters.
AI.result: MASA was evaluated on the WTTA ImageNet-C benchmark under limited-batch, mixed-domain, and imbalanced-label-shift settings with ResNet and ViT backbones.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MASA method successfully addresses the self-reinforcement problem in WTTA by leveraging multimodal LLM-generated semantic descriptions, providing a novel approach to handle distribution shifts with unreliable source models.

title: GRACE: Geometry- and Ray-Aware Camera-Efficient Multi-View Pedestrian Tracking
summary: Reducing the number of cameras reduces the deployment cost but removes views that correct BEV responses stretched away from true pedestrian positions by projection and short score drops that can split tracks} in Bird's-Eye View (BEV) tracking. We introduce GRACE, a camera-efficient multi-view tracker with three components. Volumetric-Guided Fusion combines homography-based BEV features with features lifted through 3D space. Ray Conditioning exposes each camera's viewing direction to the fusion network. Its tracking component, BEV Track Recovery (BTR), uses low-confidence detections only to continue existing tracks. The same detections cannot start new tracks. With two WildTrack cameras, GRACE improves MOTA from 83.54 for TrackTacular, our baseline, to 91.07.

AI.tldr: GRACE is a camera-efficient multi-view tracker for Bird's-Eye View (BEV) tracking that reduces camera deployment costs while maintaining high accuracy through three novel components: Volumetric-Guided Fusion, Ray Conditioning, and BEV Track Recovery.
AI.motivation: Reducing camera numbers lowers deployment costs but removes critical views needed to correct BEV responses and maintain track continuity. The goal is to achieve similar tracking performance with fewer cameras.
AI.method: Three-component approach: (1) Volumetric-Guided Fusion combines homography-based BEV features with 3D space-lifted features; (2) Ray Conditioning exposes each camera's viewing direction to the fusion network; (3) BEV Track Recovery uses low-confidence detections exclusively to continue existing tracks, preventing them from starting new tracks.
AI.result: Using only 2 WildTrack cameras, GRACE improves MOTA from 83.54 (TrackTacular baseline) to 91.07, a significant improvement in multi-object tracking accuracy.
AI.conclusion: GRACE successfully achieves camera-efficient multi-view tracking with substantial accuracy gains, demonstrating that the proposed fusion and tracking mechanisms effectively compensate for reduced camera views.

title: On the Importance of Gating: Memorization vs. In-Context Learning in State Space Models
summary: State Space Models (SSMs) have emerged as a compelling alternative to Transformers, enabling sequence modeling with constant memory and linear compute. Although SSMs exhibit reasonable performance and favorable computational characteristics, they continue to lag behind Transformers on tasks that require in-context learning and precise retrieval, slowing their adoption for large-scale language modeling. In this work, we demonstrate that both the success and failure of SSMs in these domains can be explained by studying the role of the gating mechanism, a prevalent component in modern recurrent networks. Specifically, we show through theory and experiments that this gating mechanism causes SSMs to first learn an in-weights "memorization" solution, while delaying, or even preventing, convergence to a correct in-context learning solution. Importantly, this happens even in cases where there are no fundamental limitations due to the architecture or its memory capacity. On the other hand, we find that gating is often beneficial for improving generalization to long sequence lengths. Our results illuminate the crucial role of the gating mechanism in shaping both the training dynamics and generalization of SSMs, and provide a basis for understanding and improving linear-time models.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why State Space Models (SSMs) underperform Transformers on in-context learning and retrieval tasks, identifying the gating mechanism as the culprit that causes SSMs to prioritize memorization over proper in-context learning, though gating can benefit long-sequence generalization.
AI.motivation: SSMs have emerged as efficient alternatives to Transformers with linear compute and constant memory, but they lag behind on tasks requiring in-context learning and precise retrieval, hindering their adoption for large-scale language modeling. The authors seek to understand why.
AI.method: The authors use both theoretical analysis and experiments to study the role of the gating mechanism in modern recurrent networks, examining how it affects training dynamics and generalization in SSMs.
AI.result: The gating mechanism causes SSMs to first learn an in-weights "memorization" solution while delaying or preventing convergence to correct in-context learning solutions, even when there are no fundamental architectural limitations. However, gating is often beneficial for generalization to long sequence lengths.
AI.conclusion: The gating mechanism plays a crucial role in shaping both training dynamics and generalization of SSMs. This finding provides a basis for understanding and improving linear-time models for large-scale language modeling.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Hierarchical Intention Anticipation in Human Behavior
summary: Assistive autonomous systems must anticipate human goals before an observed behavior is complete. This article formulates anticipation as goal inference from a partially observed multimodal episode together with structured prediction of the remaining behavior, rather than exact motor forecasting. A compact Hierarchical Planning Decoder (HPD) is attached to a frozen neuro-symbolic recognition encoder and predicts, at four ontological levels, the next actions, the remaining activities and low-level intentions, and the episode high-level intention(HLI). The decoder is trained with soft neuro-symbolic regularization combining transition-coherence and hierarchical continuity losses, and is decoded with hard reachability masks that enforce ontological validity at inference. On a compositional four-level benchmark of 15,002 multimodal episodes built over NTU RGB+D 120 features, three headline properties are observed together. The advantage over the strongest sequential baseline grows with the anticipation horizon, from +1.7 points at step 1 to +7.3 points at step 3 (top-5). Under compositional generalization, where one parent association per multi-parent low level intention is held out, this advantage widens to +4.9 points at step 1. At the episode level, 96.8% of anticipated trajectories satisfy the joint logic constraints, above the 88.1% strongest-baseline value and the 73.9% ground-truth floor; soft logic terms alone account for a 59.8 to 71.1% relative reduction of HLI-reachability violations, and the hard masks then eliminate them entirely. Neural generation supplies predictive ranking, symbolic constraints supply onto logical validity, and their combination yields coherent hierarchical anticipation while exposing remaining challenges in compositional goal generalization and unordered set prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Hierarchical Planning Decoder (HPD) for anticipating human goals in assistive autonomous systems. The method combines neural prediction with symbolic constraints to infer goals from partially observed multimodal episodes, predicting at four ontological levels (next actions, remaining activities, low-level intentions, and high-level episode intention).
AI.motivation: Assistive autonomous systems need to anticipate human goals before observed behavior is complete. The key insight is to formulate anticipation as goal inference from partially observed multimodal episodes with structured prediction of remaining behavior, rather than exact motor forecasting.
AI.method: A compact Hierarchical Planning Decoder (HPD) is attached to a frozen neuro-symbolic recognition encoder. It predicts at four ontological levels: next actions, remaining activities, low-level intentions, and episode high-level intention (HLI). Training uses soft neuro-symbolic regularization combining transition-coherence and hierarchical continuity losses. Inference uses hard reachability masks that enforce ontological validity. The benchmark is a compositional four-level dataset with 15,002 multimodal episodes built over NTU RGB+D 120 features.
AI.result: The method shows advantages over the strongest sequential baseline that grow with anticipation horizon: +1.7 points at step 1 to +7.3 points at step 3 (top-5). Under compositional generalization (holding out one parent association per multi-parent low-level intention), the advantage widens to +4.9 points at step 1. At the episode level, 96.8% of anticipated trajectories satisfy joint logic constraints, above the 88.1% baseline and 73.9% ground-truth floor. Soft logic terms alone account for 59.8-71.1% relative reduction of HLI-reachability violations, and hard masks eliminate them entirely.
AI.conclusion: The combination of neural generation (predictive ranking) and symbolic constraints (logical validity) yields coherent hierarchical anticipation. Remaining challenges include compositional goal generalization and unordered set prediction.

title: NeuroTS-Net: Multi-Class Semantic Segmentation of Pediatric Brain Tumors in Multi-Modal MRI
comment: Accepted at the 2026 International Conference on Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) - BraTS Cluster of Challenges: Pediatric Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS-PEDs)
summary: Pediatric brain tumors are a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in children, and their small, rare, and often low-contrast subregions make accurate manual delineation challenging. Reliable automated segmentation is therefore needed to support diagnosis, treatment planning, and response assessment. Accordingly, we introduce NeuroTS-Net, a three-dimensional encoder-decoder convolutional neural network architecture for multi-class semantic segmentation that incorporates a dual-scale raw-detail stream, adaptive low-resolution context selection, and detail-preserving multipath downsampling. These components preserve fine intensity and boundary information while efficiently modeling broader tumor context. NeuroTS-Net was trained on the BraTS 2026 pediatric dataset without external data or pretrained weights and evaluated against nnU-Net and MedNeXt under the same experimental protocol. NeuroTS-Net outperformed the baseline methods, achieving whole-tumor and tumor-core Dice scores of 0.938 and 0.937 on the internal validation set and 0.927 and 0.926 on the official challenge validation set. The code is open-sourced at: https://github.com/maenstru56/NeuroTS.

AI.tldr: NeuroTS-Net is a 3D encoder-decoder CNN for pediatric brain tumor segmentation that incorporates dual-scale raw-detail stream, adaptive low-resolution context selection, and detail-preserving multipath downsampling. It achieved Dice scores of 0.938 (whole-tumor) and 0.937 (tumor-core) on internal validation, and 0.927/0.926 on challenge validation, outperforming nnU-Net and MedNeXt.
AI.motivation: Pediatric brain tumors are leading causes of cancer-related mortality in children. Their small, rare, and often low-contrast subregions make accurate manual delineation challenging, creating a need for reliable automated segmentation to support diagnosis, treatment planning, and response assessment.
AI.method: NeuroTS-Net is a three-dimensional encoder-decoder convolutional neural network featuring: (1) dual-scale raw-detail stream to preserve fine intensity and boundary information, (2) adaptive low-resolution context selection for efficient broader tumor context modeling, and (3) detail-preserving multipath downsampling. The model was trained on the BraTS 2026 pediatric dataset without external data or pretrained weights and evaluated against nnU-Net and MedNeXt under identical experimental protocols.
AI.result: NeuroTS-Net outperformed baseline methods. On internal validation set: whole-tumor Dice = 0.938, tumor-core Dice = 0.937. On official challenge validation set: whole-tumor Dice = 0.927, tumor-core Dice = 0.926.
AI.conclusion: NeuroTS-Net successfully addresses the challenges of pediatric brain tumor segmentation through its specialized architecture components that preserve fine details while modeling broader tumor context. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance without requiring external data or pretrained weights, demonstrating its effectiveness for clinical pediatric brain tumor analysis.

title: AsyncCouple-Flow: Asynchronous Cross-Modal Coupling and Flow Matching for Spatio-Temporal Forecasting
comment: Accepted at the International Conference on Neural Information Processing (ICONIP 2026)
summary: Multi-modal spatio-temporal forecasting (MM-STF) supports weather nowcasting, traffic prediction, and earth-system modeling by combining heterogeneous sources such as physical fields, satellite imagery, and in-situ sensors. Three obstacles persist: (i) modalities have different spatio-temporal sampling rates, forcing lossy interpolation onto a unified grid; (ii) modalities are frequently missing at deployment due to sensor outages or revisit gaps, while most methods train with full availability; and (iii) autoregressive decoders accumulate errors over long horizons, amplified by multi-modal conditioning. We propose AsyncCouple-Flow to address these issues jointly. A Modality-Aware Token Sparsification (MATS) module performs scale-aware tokenization and uses a shared importance scorer to select top-k tokens per timestep, producing equal-length sequences. An Asynchronous Cross-Modal Coupling Graph (ACCG) replaces fixed cross-attention with a learnable graph whose edges encode time offsets, semantic similarity, and modality-specific physical priors, enabling fusion under arbitrary asynchrony and missingness. A Flow-Matching Forecasting Head models multi-step prediction as a conditional ODE, trained with stochastic modality dropout and integrated jointly to avoid autoregressive drift. Experiments on ERA5+GOES+ISD weather forecasting and PEMS-BAY traffic prediction with multi-source side information show that AsyncCouple-Flow outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and remains robust with up to two missing modalities. The code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: AsyncCouple-Flow is a novel framework for multi-modal spatio-temporal forecasting that addresses three key challenges: heterogeneous sampling rates, missing modalities at deployment, and error accumulation in autoregressive decoding. It uses a Modality-Aware Token Sparsification module, an Asynchronous Cross-Modal Coupling Graph, and a Flow-Matching Forecasting Head to achieve robust performance on weather and traffic prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Multi-modal spatio-temporal forecasting (MM-STF) is important for weather nowcasting, traffic prediction, and earth-system modeling. However, three persistent obstacles limit its effectiveness: (1) modalities have different spatio-temporal sampling rates requiring lossy interpolation; (2) modalities are frequently missing at deployment due to sensor outages or revisit gaps, while most methods train with full availability; (3) autoregressive decoders accumulate errors over long horizons, amplified by multi-modal conditioning.
AI.method: The proposed AsyncCouple-Flow consists of three key components: (1) Modality-Aware Token Sparsification (MATS) - performs scale-aware tokenization and uses a shared importance scorer to select top-k tokens per timestep, producing equal-length sequences; (2) Asynchronous Cross-Modal Coupling Graph (ACCG) - replaces fixed cross-attention with a learnable graph whose edges encode time offsets, semantic similarity, and modality-specific physical priors, enabling fusion under arbitrary asynchrony and missingness; (3) Flow-Matching Forecasting Head - models multi-step prediction as a conditional ODE, trained with stochastic modality dropout and integrated jointly to avoid autoregressive drift.
AI.result: Experiments on ERA5+GOES+ISD weather forecasting and PEMS-BAY traffic prediction with multi-source side information show that AsyncCouple-Flow outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and remains robust with up to two missing modalities.
AI.conclusion: AsyncCouple-Flow successfully addresses the three key challenges in multi-modal spatio-temporal forecasting through its novel architecture combining token sparsification, asynchronous graph-based fusion, and flow-matching based prediction. The method demonstrates superior performance and robustness, particularly in scenarios with missing modalities.

title: Accelerated Decoding of Centroid Positional Encoding for Instance Segmentation
comment: Presented at 2026 Joint International Conference on AI, Big Data and Blockchain. Granada, Spain
summary: Beyond model inference, the decoding stage, which converts raw network outputs into task-level representations, constitutes a significant portion of the execution cost. Despite its practical impact, prediction decoding has received comparatively little attention and is often implemented using generic CPU routines or inefficient GPU kernels, limiting the benefits of advances in model efficiency. In this work, we investigate the decoding overhead associated with a recent sinusoidal centroid encoding for Instance Segmentation, in which each pixel regresses a positional embedding of its instance centroid. This approach allows flexible segmentation without predefined proposals, but extracting instance masks from dense embeddings incurs a high computational cost. We present an optimized CUDA-based implementation of the decoding algorithm tailored to this encoding, explicitly addressing challenges related to parallelization, synchronization, and memory access on modern GPUs. Our solution significantly reduces decoding overhead and improves End-to-End inference latency, outperforming both CPU-based approaches and naive GPU implementations. The results demonstrate that efficient decoding is essential to fully exploit the advantages of advanced output representations and highlight the importance of jointly designing encoding schemes and their decoding algorithms for real-time computer vision systems.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the often-overlooked computational overhead in the decoding stage of neural network inference, specifically for sinusoidal centroid encoding used in instance segmentation. The authors present an optimized CUDA implementation that significantly reduces decoding overhead and improves end-to-end inference latency compared to CPU-based and naive GPU approaches.
AI.motivation: While model efficiency has received significant attention, the decoding stage—which converts raw network outputs into task-level representations—has been comparatively neglected and is often implemented using inefficient routines. This creates a bottleneck that limits the benefits of advances in model efficiency, particularly for instance segmentation methods that use positional embedding encodings.
AI.method: The authors developed an optimized CUDA-based implementation of the decoding algorithm specifically tailored for sinusoidal centroid encoding in instance segmentation. This approach addresses key GPU challenges including parallelization, synchronization, and memory access patterns on modern GPUs.
AI.result: The optimized CUDA implementation significantly reduces decoding overhead and improves end-to-end inference latency, outperforming both CPU-based approaches and naive GPU implementations.
AI.conclusion: Efficient decoding is essential to fully exploit the advantages of advanced output representations. The work highlights the importance of jointly designing encoding schemes and their decoding algorithms for real-time computer vision systems.

title: Recovering Physical Parameters from Fragmented Observations via Exact Distributed Spline Merging
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Under review at ICLR 2027
summary: Scientific measurements are frequently distributed across locations, time periods, and institutions. Combining such fragments into a continuous, differentiable field enables recovering governing physical parameters from its derivatives. This paper makes two contributions toward that goal. First, the established additive structure of fixed-basis ridge-regression statistics is applied to tensor-product spline fields: each data holder computes a local Gram matrix and moment vector, and the merged solution is mathematically identical to centralized fitting, with no raw data shared and no iterative synchronization. This property is specific to the fixed-feature squared-error setting; the present derivation does not establish an analogous guarantee for general jointly trained multilayer networks. Second, a complete pipeline connects distributed observations to physical parameter inference through field reconstruction, derivative extraction, and linear regression. The diffusion coefficient is recovered to 0.11% error and wave speed to 0.12% error; in both cases, distributed merging introduces zero degradation relative to centralized fitting. Application to 41 years of NOAA sea-surface temperature data confirms the result on real spatiotemporal observations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a privacy-preserving distributed method for combining fragmented scientific measurements into continuous differentiable fields, enabling recovery of physical parameters. The approach uses fixed-basis ridge-regression with tensor-product splines, where each data holder computes local Gram matrices and moment vectors that can be merged without sharing raw data. The method achieves 0.11% error for diffusion coefficient and 0.12% error for wave speed recovery, with validation on 41 years of NOAA sea-surface temperature data.
AI.motivation: Scientific measurements are frequently distributed across locations, time periods, and institutions. Combining these fragments into a continuous, differentiable field enables recovering governing physical parameters from its derivatives. However, data sharing is often restricted due to privacy or logistical constraints.
AI.method: The authors apply the additive structure of fixed-basis ridge-regression statistics to tensor-product spline fields. Each data holder computes a local Gram matrix and moment vector locally, which are then merged to produce a solution mathematically identical to centralized fitting. This approach requires no raw data sharing and no iterative synchronization. The complete pipeline connects distributed observations to physical parameter inference through field reconstruction, derivative extraction, and linear regression.
AI.result: The diffusion coefficient is recovered to 0.11% error and wave speed to 0.12% error. In both cases, distributed merging introduces zero degradation relative to centralized fitting. Application to 41 years of NOAA sea-surface temperature data confirms the result on real spatiotemporal observations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed distributed method preserves accuracy while maintaining data privacy. The property is specific to fixed-feature squared-error settings and does not extend to general multilayer networks. This enables privacy-preserving scientific inference across distributed datasets.

title: Interactive Memory Learning for Long-Term Conversations
summary: Recent advancements in large language models have significantly enhanced the capabilities of agents in modeling long-term conversations. Despite these successes, existing approaches typically adopt a static heuristic paradigm, where information is passively archived without adaptive memory valuation. Consequently, these methods fail to self-evolve or align their memory management with evolving user needs. To address this, we propose ICML (InteraCtive Memory Learning), a multi-agent framework that transforms the memory mechanism from a passive archive into a learnable, interactive memory policy. Specifically, we first employ a session synthesis pipeline to generate expert data, facilitating rapid test-time adaptation in unseen scenarios. Building on this, ICML utilizes an online reinforcement learning mechanism where a Planner agent selectively encodes high-value information and a Trigger agent dynamically retrieves it to optimize response quality, whereby the two agents co-evolve through continuous interaction feedback. Crucially, both agents are synchronized through a delayed reward mechanism that propagates future feedback back to earlier storage decisions, ensuring memory policies are precisely aligned with user expectations. Experimental results demonstrate that ICML significantly outperforms strong baselines, exhibiting the unique capability to continuously improve response quality as interactions accumulate.

AI.tldr: ICML (InteraCtive Memory Learning) is a multi-agent framework that transforms static, passive memory mechanisms in conversational AI agents into learnable, adaptive memory policies through online reinforcement learning, featuring a Planner agent for selective encoding and a Trigger agent for dynamic retrieval, synchronized via delayed reward mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to memory in long-term conversation modeling use static heuristic paradigms where information is passively archived without adaptive memory valuation. These methods fail to self-evolve or align with evolving user needs, limiting the system's ability to improve response quality over time.
AI.method: ICML employs: (1) a session synthesis pipeline to generate expert data for rapid test-time adaptation in unseen scenarios; (2) an online reinforcement learning mechanism with two co-evolving agents - a Planner agent that selectively encodes high-value information and a Trigger agent that dynamically retrieves it; (3) a delayed reward mechanism that propagates future feedback back to earlier storage decisions to align memory policies with user expectations.
AI.result: ICML significantly outperforms strong baselines and demonstrates the unique capability to continuously improve response quality as interactions accumulate.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ICML framework successfully transforms memory from a passive archive into a learnable, interactive policy. By using multi-agent RL with delayed reward synchronization, the system can self-evolve and adapt to user needs over time, showing continuous improvement with accumulated interactions.

title: Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility
summary: Upgrading embedding models typically requires expensive database re-indexing, as new query embeddings are incompatible with existing database embeddings. While Backward Compatible Training (BCT) mitigates this by enforcing compatibility during training, existing approaches often require updating the backbone model. This is impractical because of significant training cost, the risk of performance regression, and limited access to proprietary model weights. We introduce Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter (MKP-Adapter), the first adapter-only BCT approach for Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that requires no backbone updates. We identified that the primary challenge in adapter-only BCT is preserving the knowledge of the new embeddings while enforcing backward compatibility. Hence, we propose a multi-level preservation loss that maintains the geometric structure of the embedding spaces throughout BCT. Furthermore, a focal re-weighting strategy is integrated to prioritize learning from challenging samples. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves strong backward compatibility across diverse multi-modal benchmarks (image, text, visual document, and video retrieval tasks) and model types. Notably, MKP-Adapter is trained solely on pre-extracted embeddings and requires only negligible additional latency relative to the original backbone forward pass, highlighting its efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MKP-Adapter, the first adapter-only Backward Compatible Training (BCT) method for Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that enables embedding model upgrades without database re-indexing or backbone model updates. It uses a multi-level preservation loss to maintain embedding space geometry and a focal re-weighting strategy for challenging samples.
AI.motivation: Upgrading embedding models typically requires expensive database re-indexing due to incompatibility between new and existing embeddings. While BCT mitigates this, existing approaches require updating the backbone model, which is impractical due to high training costs, performance regression risks, and limited access to proprietary weights.
AI.method: The proposed MKP-Adapter is an adapter-only BCT approach requiring no backbone updates. It uses: (1) a multi-level preservation loss to maintain the geometric structure of embedding spaces throughout BCT, and (2) a focal re-weighting strategy to prioritize learning from challenging samples. Training is done solely on pre-extracted embeddings.
AI.result: The method achieves strong backward compatibility across diverse multi-modal benchmarks including image, text, visual document, and video retrieval tasks, with different model types. It requires only negligible additional latency relative to the original backbone forward pass.
AI.conclusion: MKP-Adapter successfully enables embedding model upgrades without database re-indexing or backbone updates, providing an efficient and practical solution for backward compatible training in multi-modal large language models.

title: A Weighted Kernel Method for Approximation that Adapts to Learned Multivariable Structure
summary: Approximating the input-output behavior of a multivariable black-box function from limited data is challenging when blind to the importance of its inputs and their interactions. We introduce total sensitivity kernels (TSKs), a method based on families of weighted ANOVA kernels that learn and adapt to this multivariable structure. TSKs parameterize the weights on each multivariable component of the target function by factors for each input. We propose learning these factors directly from function evaluations by selecting the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) in which the target function has minimum norm. Under suitable conditions, we show that this norm-minimization problem admits a unique solution, and we establish consistency of a finite-data formulation based on minimum-norm interpolation. The learned TSK factors characterize the participation of individual inputs across interactions and main effects, providing a kernel-dependent notion of input sensitivity related to total Sobol indices. Numerical experiments demonstrate that adapting the kernel to learned multivariable structure can substantially improve approximation accuracy over a standard product kernel.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Total Sensitivity Kernels (TSKs), a method using weighted ANOVA kernels to approximate multivariable black-box functions by learning input importance factors directly from data through RKHS norm minimization.
AI.motivation: Approximating multivariable black-box functions is challenging when the importance of inputs and their interactions is unknown. Existing methods lack a way to adapt kernel structure to capture the multivariable function's inherent complexity.
AI.method: TSKs parameterize weights on multivariable components using factors for each input. The method learns these factors by selecting the RKHS in which the target function has minimum norm. A finite-data formulation based on minimum-norm interpolation is used, with conditions established for unique solution and consistency.
AI.result: The learned TSK factors characterize input participation in interactions and main effects, providing a kernel-dependent notion of input sensitivity related to total Sobol indices. Numerical experiments show that adapting the kernel to learned structure substantially improves approximation accuracy over standard product kernels.
AI.conclusion: TSKs provide a principled approach to learning multivariable structure from limited data, with theoretical guarantees and demonstrated practical improvements in approximation accuracy.

title: Scaling-Score Conformal Prediction for Multi-Target Regression
summary: Multi-target regression requires a model to simultaneously predict several related outputs. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free, finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees, but extending these to joint multi-dimensional regions in a model-agnostic, sample-efficient manner remains challenging: max-aggregation ignores scale differences, copula-based methods are only asymptotically valid, rectangular methods typically split the calibration set, and quantile or density-based methods require training a specialised model beyond a plain point predictor. We propose the scaling-score conformal method, which is model-agnostic (requires only component-wise absolute residuals), uses a single calibration set, and yields four nested output types: an outer rectangle (SCO) with valid joint coverage, the exact set R $α$ , a staircase (SC 2 ) over approximation of R $α$ , and an inner rectangle (SCI). A single hyperparameter $γ$ $\in$ (0, 1) controls the base-rectangle quantile level independently of $α$. We prove downward-closedness and a rectangular sandwich bound and derive a closed-form outer rectangle. Experiments on 29 realworld datasets confirm valid joint coverage; SC 2 with $γ$ = 1-$α$ consistently achieves competitive volume relative to baselines, with the advantage growing with output dimension d.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the scaling-score conformal method for multi-target regression, which provides distribution-free, finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees extended to joint multi-dimensional regions. The method is model-agnostic, uses a single calibration set, and yields four nested output types (SCO, R_α, SC2, SCI) controlled by a single hyperparameter γ.
AI.motivation: Conformal prediction provides marginal coverage guarantees but extending these to joint multi-dimensional regions faces challenges: max-aggregation ignores scale differences, copula-based methods are only asymptotically valid, rectangular methods typically split the calibration set, and quantile/density methods require specialized models beyond plain point predictors.
AI.method: The scaling-score conformal method requires only component-wise absolute residuals, uses a single calibration set, and produces four nested output types: (1) SCO outer rectangle with valid joint coverage, (2) exact set R_α, (3) SC_2 staircase over-approximation of R_α, and (4) inner rectangle SCI. A single hyperparameter γ ∈ (0, 1) controls the base-rectangle quantile level independently of α.
AI.result: Experiments on 29 real-world datasets confirm valid joint coverage. SC_2 with γ = 1−α consistently achieves competitive volume relative to baselines, with the advantage growing with output dimension d.
AI.conclusion: The scaling-score conformal method provides a model-agnostic solution for multi-target regression with valid joint coverage and efficient volume, particularly advantageous for high-dimensional outputs.

title: VOR-Bench: A Human Perception-Driven Benchmark for Video Object Removal
summary: Despite its crucial role in video object removal (VOR), existing evaluation paradigms face two critical limitations: questionable references and a misalignment between tradi- tional metrics and human preference. To address these challenges, we introduce VOR- Bench, which advances VOR evaluation through three integrated components. First, we present the VOR Dataset (VORD), the first benchmark dataset providing both paired edited videos and graffiti masks. Its unique strength lies in a diverse data spectrum, which encompasses model-generated, tool-rendered, and camera-captured data, ensuring robust assessment across real-world scenarios. Second, we develop rMPAF, a realistic Motion- capable Paired-video Acquisition Framework. By combining the strengths of image- based object removal and fine-tuned video generation models, rMPAF automatically generates realistic, motion-coherent paired videos. Finally, we propose three evaluation dimensions and introduce VOR-MDSM, the first perception-driven VLM-based scoring model specifically designed for mask-guided VOR. It bridges the gap between arithmetic metrics and human perception by covering the essential visual attributes and matching nuanced human judgment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VOR-Bench yields evaluation results that align closely with human perception, achieving a remarkable cor- relation (\r{ho} > 0.9) with subjective assessments. We will release VOR-Bench along with its documentation to ensure full reproducibility.

AI.tldr: VOR-Bench is a comprehensive evaluation framework for video object removal (VOR) that addresses two critical limitations in existing evaluation paradigms: questionable references and misalignment between traditional metrics and human preference. It consists of three components: VOR Dataset (VORD) - the first benchmark with paired edited videos and graffiti masks covering model-generated, tool-rendered, and camera-captured data; rMPAF - a framework for generating realistic, motion-coherent paired videos; and VOR-MDSM - a perception-driven VLM-based scoring model with three evaluation dimensions.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation paradigms for video object removal (VOR) face two critical limitations: (1) questionable references and (2) misalignment between traditional metrics and human preference. These limitations hinder proper assessment of VOR methods in real-world scenarios.
AI.method: The paper proposes VOR-Bench with three integrated components: (1) VOR Dataset (VORD) - a diverse benchmark dataset providing paired edited videos and graffiti masks across model-generated, tool-rendered, and camera-captured data; (2) rMPAF - Realistic Motion-capable Paired-video Acquisition Framework combining image-based object removal and fine-tuned video generation models to automatically generate realistic, motion-coherent paired videos; (3) VOR-MDSM - a perception-driven VLM-based scoring model with three evaluation dimensions designed specifically for mask-guided VOR, covering essential visual attributes to bridge the gap between arithmetic metrics and human perception.
AI.result: VOR-Bench yields evaluation results that align closely with human perception, achieving a remarkable correlation (ρ > 0.9) with subjective assessments. The diverse data spectrum ensures robust assessment across real-world scenarios.
AI.conclusion: VOR-Bench represents a significant advancement in VOR evaluation by providing the first benchmark with realistic paired videos and a perception-driven scoring model. The high correlation (>0.9) with human subjective assessments demonstrates its effectiveness in bridging the gap between automated metrics and human judgment. The release of VOR-Bench with documentation ensures full reproducibility for the research community.

title: Divergence Timing and Cumulative Disagreement under KV-Cache Eviction
summary: KV-cache eviction perturbs the conditional token distributions governing autoregressive generation. We investigate how first-divergence timing and subsequent token mismatch determine cumulative disagreement. We derive an exact decomposition under a specified stepwise maximal coupling: the expected mismatch fraction equals a first-mismatch contribution plus post-divergence exposure multiplied by its mismatch rate. An explicit construction over unrestricted autoregressive kernel pairs realizes the sharp interval of risks compatible with a finite divergence-aligned observation window. Residual-branch conditional Monte Carlo provides unbiased joint estimates of occurrence, occupation, and window/tail contributions, with per-replicate variance dominance for total token loss. Complete trajectories from Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that SnapKV at 50% retention enters divergence later and less often than SnapKV-512 or recent-token retention with the same 50% prompt-cache budget, while post-divergence total variation (TV) remains high. In an exploratory analysis of 288 documents, post-divergence exposure accounts for 85-90% of four aggregate mismatch gaps. On 288 independent documents at 90% retention, prespecified comparisons show higher branch-aligned TV in the late than in the early window in both models.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how KV-cache eviction in autoregressive language models affects token generation accuracy. The authors develop a mathematical framework using stepwise maximal coupling to quantify how first-divergence timing and subsequent token mismatch lead to cumulative disagreement. They propose a Monte Carlo method for unbiased estimation and validate findings on Llama and Qwen models across 288 documents.
AI.motivation: KV-cache eviction perturbs the conditional token distributions in autoregressive generation, potentially causing token mismatch and reducing output quality. Understanding the dynamics of how divergence timing and token mismatch accumulate is crucial for optimizing memory-efficient inference methods.
AI.method: The authors derive an exact decomposition under stepwise maximal coupling, where expected mismatch fraction equals first-mismatch contribution plus post-divergence exposure multiplied by its mismatch rate. They construct this over unrestricted autoregressive kernel pairs and use residual-branch conditional Monte Carlo for unbiased joint estimates. Empirical validation uses SnapKV, SnapKV-512, and recent-token retention on Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct across 288 documents.
AI.result: SnapKV at 50% retention enters divergence later and less often than SnapKV-512 or recent-token retention with the same 50% prompt-cache budget. Post-divergence total variation remains high. Post-divergence exposure accounts for 85-90% of four aggregate mismatch gaps. At 90% retention, branch-aligned TV is higher in late vs early windows in both models.
AI.conclusion: Post-divergence exposure is the dominant contributor to token mismatch in KV-cache eviction. SnapKV shows better divergence timing than alternatives, but post-divergence TV remains problematic. This suggests that methods reducing post-divergence divergence or its impact are needed for improved quality-efficient inference.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning-Based Genetic Biomarkers Dataset for Multiple-Stage Hepatocellular Carcinoma Prediction
comment: 6 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables, published at the 18th International Conference Series on Developments in eSystems Engineering
summary: Liver cancer is a complex disease responsible for a high number of deaths across the globe each year, making automated solutions for liver cancer classification urgent. The most common form of liver cancer is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), accounting for over 90% of liver cancer cases. There is a distinct lack of publicly available HCC datasets utilizing genomic data, which is necessary for training artificial intelligence (AI) models for automated HCC classification. This study proposes constructing a multi-stage HCC dataset using XGBoost and Semi-Supervised learning on three separate datasets of genomic biomarkers, utilizing their existing labels in the Semi-Supervised learning process to label the proposed dataset. The proposed dataset consists of 770 patient samples in total, categorized into five classes that represent normal tissue alongside different stages of HCC. Each sample in the dataset consists of 11,150 different gene expression levels. The XGBoost model demonstrated a final classification accuracy of 96.5% during the Semi-Supervised learning process.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the lack of publicly available genomic datasets for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) classification by constructing a multi-stage dataset using XGBoost and Semi-Supervised learning. The resulting dataset contains 770 patient samples across 5 classes with 11,150 gene expression features, achieving 96.5% classification accuracy.
AI.motivation: Liver cancer, particularly hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), is a leading cause of global mortality. The critical gap is the scarcity of publicly available HCC datasets utilizing genomic data, which is essential for training AI models for automated classification. This limitation hinders the development of AI-driven diagnostic tools.
AI.method: The study proposes a multi-stage approach: (1) Combine three separate genomic biomarker datasets, (2) Apply XGBoost for initial classification, (3) Use Semi-Supervised learning to leverage existing labels for labeling the proposed dataset. The final dataset comprises 770 patient samples with 11,150 gene expression features, categorized into 5 classes representing normal tissue and different HCC stages.
AI.result: The XGBoost model achieved a classification accuracy of 96.5% during the Semi-Supervised learning process, demonstrating high effectiveness in distinguishing between normal tissue and various HCC stages.
AI.conclusion: The study successfully created a valuable resource for HCC research by developing a multi-stage genomic dataset. The high accuracy (96.5%) validates the potential of XGBoost combined with Semi-Supervised learning for HCC classification, potentially advancing AI-driven diagnostic solutions for liver cancer.

title: Temporally Consistent Graph Extraction and Matching for Longitudinal Angiographic Images
summary: Recent advances in angiographic imaging have enabled longitudinal visualization of the microvasculature. Image processing pipelines based on vessel graphs are able to resolve subtle temporal changes at the level of individual blood vessels. However, current strategies for graph extraction, refinement, and matching are highly sensitive, with even minuscule differences in the underlying segmentation map resulting in substantially different vessel graphs. These artifacts severely inhibit the ability to accurately match sequential vessel graphs of the same subject over time. To address this problem, we propose a strategy that matches graphs before jointly refining them. Specifically, we perform an early matching after basic graph extraction before removing spurious bulges and merging junctions in both graphs using joint information. In experiments with complex retinal vessel graphs, we demonstrate that this strategy results in a higher matched area without graph fragmentation compared to separate or no refinement, respectively.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of matching sequential vessel graphs from angiographic imaging over time. The authors propose performing graph matching before joint refinement, rather than after, to handle the sensitivity of vessel graph extraction pipelines where small segmentation differences cause substantially different vessel graphs.
AI.motivation: Current vessel graph extraction, refinement, and matching strategies are highly sensitive - even minuscule differences in segmentation maps result in substantially different vessel graphs. This severely inhibits accurate matching of sequential vessel graphs of the same subject over time, which is important for longitudinal microvasculature visualization.
AI.method: The proposed strategy performs early matching after basic graph extraction, before removing spurious bulges and merging junctions. Both graphs are then refined jointly using the matched information, rather than separately or after matching.
AI.result: Experiments with complex retinal vessel graphs demonstrate that this strategy results in a higher matched area without graph fragmentation compared to separate or no refinement approaches.
AI.conclusion: Matching graphs before joint refinement is more effective than separate refinement or no refinement for longitudinal vessel graph analysis. This approach improves the ability to track individual blood vessel changes over time in angiographic imaging.

title: Stable by Construction: Variational Latent Markov Operators for Long-Horizon PDE Prediction
summary: Neural PDE solvers provide efficient surrogates for time-dependent physical systems, but autoregressive prediction over long horizons remains challenging because local errors can induce distribution shift and accumulate under recursive deployment. We develop a variational approach to this problem by introducing latent Markov dynamics in which physical states are represented by latent distributions and evolved through probabilistic transitions. The framework is formulated directly on function spaces and specialized to functional Gaussian models, where structured latent perturbations induce a spectral geometry and variational transition alignment regularizes the learned dynamics. We further analyze how these mechanisms affect autoregressive error propagation, providing a theoretical connection between variational training and long-horizon prediction. We instantiate the framework as the Variational Autoencoding Markov Operator (VAMO), which combines spatially resolved latent fields, structured Gaussian perturbations, and a neural-operator transition. Empirically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of VAMO on several fluid-dynamics benchmarks with prediction horizons extending substantially beyond those represented during training, where it consistently reduces error accumulation and improves rollout stability over several deterministic and noise-injection baselines. Overall, these results highlight variational modeling as a complementary approach to robust long-horizon neural PDE dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VAMO, a variational framework for long-horizon neural PDE solvers that uses latent Markov dynamics with functional Gaussian models to reduce error accumulation in autoregressive predictions. The method achieves improved rollout stability on fluid dynamics benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Neural PDE solvers struggle with autoregressive prediction over long horizons because local errors accumulate and cause distribution shift under recursive deployment. This limits their practical applicability for real-world physical systems requiring long-term predictions.
AI.method: The framework introduces latent Markov dynamics where physical states are represented as latent distributions and evolved through probabilistic transitions. It is formulated on function spaces and specialized to functional Gaussian models with structured latent perturbations that induce spectral geometry. Variational transition alignment is used to regularize learned dynamics. The instantiation, VAMO, combines spatially resolved latent fields, structured Gaussian perturbations, and a neural-operator transition.
AI.result: VAMO consistently reduces error accumulation and improves rollout stability over several deterministic and noise-injection baselines on fluid-dynamics benchmarks, with prediction horizons extending substantially beyond training.
AI.conclusion: Variational modeling provides a complementary approach to robust long-horizon neural PDE dynamics, offering a principled way to handle uncertainty and error propagation in physical system predictions.

title: Symbolic Separation: Grounding Deep Agents in Knowledge Graphs for Trustworthy Operational Data Analytics
summary: Generative AI promises natural language access to the massive numerical telemetry of data centers and Industry 4.0 installations, yet text-to-query and tool-using agents stay unreliable: even frontier models answer little more than half of real-world database questions, and far fewer of the multi-step, operational ones, because the LLM must compose how heterogeneous sources relate and hallucinates the relations, not just the fields. We propose symbolic separation: a deep agent reasons freely but may act on data only through an ontology-constrained Virtual Knowledge Graph with deterministic pre-execution validation. Unlike a tool API's interface contract, this domain-semantic contract turns a complex question into one validated graph traversal instead of LLM-inferred joins. Instantiated as the Neurosymbolic Deep Analyst and evaluated on 49.9 TB of superconputer telemetry against a rigid workflow and a non-symbolic ablation, it raises end-to-end task success from 43% to 86%, prevents silent data-integrity errors that no syntactic check catches, and cuts token cost by 2.4x, letting a smaller on-premise model outperform a larger one.

AI.tldr: A neurosymbolic approach called "Symbolic Separation" that constrains LLM agents to interact with data only through an ontology-validated Virtual Knowledge Graph, achieving 86% task success (vs 43% baseline) on 49.9 TB supercomputer telemetry while reducing token costs by 2.4x.
AI.motivation: Generative AI for natural language querying of data center and Industry 4.0 telemetry remains unreliable - even frontier models answer only ~50% of real-world database questions, particularly failing at multi-step operational queries because LLMs hallucinate relationships between heterogeneous data sources rather than accurately inferring them.
AI.method: The paper proposes "symbolic separation": a deep agent that reasons freely but acts on data only through an ontology-constrained Virtual Knowledge Graph with deterministic pre-execution validation. This transforms complex questions into validated graph traversals instead of LLM-inferred joins. The system is instantiated as the "Neurosymbolic Deep Analyst" and evaluated against a rigid workflow and non-symbolic ablation.
AI.result: Raises end-to-end task success from 43% to 86%, prevents silent data-integrity errors that no syntactic check catches, and cuts token cost by 2.4x, enabling a smaller on-premise model to outperform a larger one.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic separation through ontology-constrained Virtual Knowledge Graphs is an effective approach for reliable natural language access to complex industrial telemetry data, combining the reasoning flexibility of LLMs with the correctness guarantees of symbolic systems.

title: PiPS: Post-Hoc Prototypical Explanations for Interpretable Semantic Segmentation
summary: With the increasing deployment of deep neural networks in critical systems, such as medical diagnostics and autonomous vehicles, ensuring their interpretability is crucial to building trust in decision-making systems. In the field of explainable artificial intelligence, prototype-based reasoning has gained particular popularity, as it mimics human cognitive processes by explaining model decisions based on visual similarity under the looks like this paradigm. While this paradigm has been thoroughly investigated in the context of global image classification, the interpretability of dense predictions, particularly semantic segmentation, remains largely unexplored despite its immense importance in tasks requiring precise object localization. Existing prototype-based interpretable segmentation models rely on ante-hoc architectures, which entails significant limitations because they require costly training from scratch and modifications to the network structure, ultimately leading to a noticeable drop in predictive performance compared to standard black-box models. To address this issue, we propose PiPS (Post-hoc interpretable Prototypical Segmentation), the first fully post-hoc solution for generating prototypical explanations for semantic segmentation models. Our method enables the extraction of intuitive, spatially localized explanations from any pre-trained network without modification or fine-tuning, thereby preserving 100% of the model's original predictive performance. This approach opens a new avenue for the safe and cost-effective deployment of transparent systems in advanced computer vision tasks. Codebase available at https://github.com/gmum/PIPS.

AI.tldr: PiPS is the first fully post-hoc method for generating prototypical explanations for semantic segmentation models, enabling extraction of intuitive, spatially localized explanations from any pre-trained network without modification or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing prototype-based interpretable segmentation models require ante-hoc architectures with significant limitations: costly training from scratch, network structure modifications, and noticeable drop in predictive performance compared to black-box models. This work addresses the need for interpretability in dense predictions like semantic segmentation, which is crucial for critical systems like medical diagnostics and autonomous vehicles.
AI.method: PiPS (Post-hoc interpretable Prototypical Segmentation) extracts intuitive, spatially localized explanations from any pre-trained semantic segmentation network without any modification or fine-tuning, preserving 100% of the model's original predictive performance.
AI.result: The method enables generating prototypical explanations for semantic segmentation while preserving full original predictive performance. It is the first fully post-hoc solution for this task, allowing cost-effective deployment of transparent systems in advanced computer vision tasks.
AI.conclusion: PiPS opens a new avenue for safe and cost-effective deployment of transparent systems in advanced computer vision tasks by providing interpretability without sacrificing model performance or requiring retraining.

title: GrowMTP: Can RL Grow Its Own Draft Head?
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training drives the frontier capabilities of large language models, with its wall-clock dominated by autoregressive rollout generation. Speculative decoding is an established remedy for this bottleneck, but existing draft heads must be pretrained or warmed up before RL, introducing substantial training cost outside the RL run to be accelerated. We observe that RL training itself provides both conditions required for online draft-head training: its rollout distribution is far narrower than that of pretraining, and its verification step continuously produces supervision signals aligned with this distribution. Building on these observations, we propose GrowMTP, which uses this supervision to train a draft head from scratch entirely within the RL loop, with all head updates detached from the policy backbone. On Qwen3-4B (no draft head), MiMo-7B-SFT (weak head), and Qwen3.5-4B-Base (strong head), GrowMTP achieves rollout speedups of 2.13x, 1.93x, and 1.36x, and end-to-end speedups of 1.60x, 1.41x, and 1.20x, respectively. GrowMTP therefore serves existing RL training frameworks as a modular component, particularly offering a from-scratch acceleration path for models without pretrained draft heads.

AI.tldr: GrowMTP trains draft heads from scratch entirely within the RL loop to accelerate autoregressive rollout generation, achieving 1.60x-2.13x speedups across different model architectures without requiring pretrained draft heads.
AI.motivation: RL post-training for large language models is bottlenecked by autoregressive rollout generation. Existing speculative decoding methods require pretrained or warmed-up draft heads, introducing substantial training costs outside the RL run. This creates a need for a from-scratch acceleration path for models without pretrained draft heads.
AI.method: GrowMTP leverages RL training's unique properties: narrow rollout distribution and continuous verification-based supervision signals. It trains a draft head from scratch entirely within the RL loop with all head updates detached from the policy backbone, using the supervision produced by the RL verification step.
AI.result: On Qwen3-4B (no draft head), MiMo-7B-SFT (weak head), and Qwen3.5-4B-Base (strong head), GrowMTP achieves rollout speedups of 2.13x, 1.93x, and 1.36x, and end-to-end speedups of 1.60x, 1.41x, and 1.20x, respectively.
AI.conclusion: GrowMTP serves as a modular component for existing RL training frameworks, providing a cost-effective from-scratch acceleration path particularly for models without pretrained draft heads. It eliminates the need for external draft head pre-training while maintaining significant speedups.

title: Shared-Prefix KV Reuse Across Standard LoRA Adapters: Quality and Serving Tradeoffs
summary: A common small-model deployment runs one shared backbone with several LoRA specialists that answer over the same context. Serving them naively re-prefills that shared context once per specialist. We study a narrow, practical question: for already-trained standard LoRA adapters -- not adapters retrained for cache compatibility -- how much task quality is preserved if the backbone's prefill KV cache is computed once and reused across specialists, and what does that buy in serving cost? On a Qwen3-1.7B backbone with two adapters (extractive QA on HotpotQA, arithmetic reasoning on GSM8K), we sweep the boundary at which the specialist takes over from the reused base cache and measure paired quality differences and serving cost. Full-prefix reuse had the lowest prefill cost and a small quality difference on held-out GSM8K (Delta = -4.6 EM at a 160-token budget; -3.0 at 320 tokens; -0.8 under a second training seed -- all favoring native, only the first excluding zero, and the magnitude not consistent). Partial recomputation provided no demonstrated advantage. Neither quality equivalence nor a general boundary-selection rule is established. We also report a closed-form ridge KV translator that did not beat direct reuse, and specialist-dependence contrasts whose intervals all include zero. The measured serving benefit is warm-cache time-to-first-token, which grows with context (~16x at 8K); two-branch peak memory was only 12% lower and, on inspection, the prefix was never physically shared across branches -- this implementation reuses KV values but copies their storage, so shared-cache memory savings are not achieved.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates reusing the prefill KV cache across multiple LoRA adapters (specialists) deployed on a shared backbone model. Experiments on Qwen3-1.7B with two adapters (extractive QA and arithmetic reasoning) show that full-prefix reuse reduces prefill cost but causes small quality degradation (-4.6 to -0.8 EM on GSM8K). Partial recomputation and ridge KV translation provided no advantage. The implementation reuses KV values but copies storage, achieving no memory savings, though warm-cache TTFT improves with context (~16x at 8K).
AI.motivation: Deploying multiple LoRA specialists on a shared backbone typically requires re-prefilling the shared context for each specialist, which is computationally expensive. This work explores cache reuse to reduce serving costs without retraining adapters for cache compatibility, addressing a practical deployment question.
AI.method: Using a Qwen3-1.7B backbone with two standard LoRA adapters (HotpotQA for extractive QA, GSM8K for arithmetic reasoning), the authors sweep the boundary where the specialist takes over from the reused base cache and measure quality differences (EM scores) and serving costs. They test full-prefix reuse, partial recomputation, and a closed-form ridge KV translator, comparing against native (non-reuse) serving.
AI.result: Full-prefix reuse achieved the lowest prefill cost but showed small quality degradation on GSM8K (Delta = -4.6 EM at 160-token budget; -3.0 at 320 tokens; -0.8 with a second training seed). Partial recomputation showed no advantage. The ridge KV translator did not outperform direct reuse. Specialist-dependence confidence intervals all include zero. Warm-cache TTFT improves with context (~16x at 8K), but two-branch peak memory only reduced by 12%. The implementation copies KV storage rather than physically sharing it, so memory savings are not realized.
AI.conclusion: The study finds that while full-prefix reuse reduces prefill computation, it comes with small quality costs that vary across tasks and token budgets. No quality equivalence or general boundary-selection rule is established. Partial recomputation and KV translation offer no demonstrated benefit. The serving benefit is limited to warm-cache TTFT improvement, and physical cache sharing is not achieved in this implementation, limiting memory savings. The approach remains practical for latency-sensitive scenarios where small quality trade-offs are acceptable.

title: NeuroSymbEAD: A Large Scale Neuro-Symbolic Caption Dataset for Omni-Directional Embodied Autonomous Driving
summary: This paper introduces NeuroSymbEAD, a large-scale neuro-symbolic caption dataset featuring an ego-centric knowledge graph (KG) of static and dynamic objects annotated with classes, categories, heading directions, orientations, and distances from the ego-vehicle. These annotations are used on the KITTI-360 dataset to generate multilevel textual captions representing a lightweight version of an ego-centric scene map. Outdoor scene-map reconstruction, visual recognition, and object grounding establish baselines for driving common sense and traffic/scene understanding. For these purposes, natural language-based grounded captioning of objects and their complex relationships is a widely adopted contextual representation for indoor scene tasks. Neuro-symbolic representations have proven effective in handling structured information for various computer vision and language applications. Our data annotation pipeline allows the generation of varied map segments, populating simulated or real objects within the bounding boxes predicted by any 3D object detection network, and building hierarchical text captions. We benchmark our neuro-symbolic and ontological caption generation using pre-trained grounding and learned auto-regressive captioning networks. By converting 3D driving scenes into structured ego-centric language, NeuroSymbEAD provides a benchmark for vision-language and foundation models for traffic-scene explanation, 3D reasoning, and interpretable autonomous-driving perception.

AI.tldr: NeuroSymbEAD is a large-scale neuro-symbolic caption dataset for autonomous driving that combines ego-centric knowledge graphs with multi-level textual captions, built on the KITTI-360 dataset. It provides annotations for static and dynamic objects including classes, categories, heading directions, orientations, and distances from the ego-vehicle, enabling benchmarks for scene understanding, visual recognition, and object grounding.
AI.motivation: Outdoor scene-map reconstruction and visual recognition lack effective contextual representations for driving common sense and traffic/scene understanding. While natural language-based grounded captioning is common for indoor scenes, similar approaches for outdoor/ego-centric driving scenes are limited. The need for structured neuro-symbolic representations that can handle complex object relationships in driving environments drives this research.
AI.method: The method involves creating an annotation pipeline that: (1) generates ego-centric knowledge graphs with static and dynamic object annotations (classes, categories, heading directions, orientations, distances); (2) builds multi-level textual captions representing ego-centric scene maps; (3) enables generation of varied map segments with simulated or real objects within 3D detection bounding boxes; (4) creates hierarchical text captions; (5) benchmarks using pre-trained grounding and learned auto-regressive captioning networks.
AI.result: The paper establishes baselines for driving common sense and traffic/scene understanding through: outdoor scene-map reconstruction, visual recognition, and object grounding. It provides benchmarks using pre-trained grounding networks and learned auto-regressive captioning networks for neuro-symbolic and ontological caption generation.
AI.conclusion: NeuroSymbEAD provides a benchmark for vision-language and foundation models for traffic-scene explanation, 3D reasoning, and interpretable autonomous-driving perception by converting 3D driving scenes into structured ego-centric language. The dataset enables research in neuro-symbolic representations for outdoor ego-centric scenes, addressing the gap between indoor scene captioning and outdoor driving scene understanding.

title: Right Direction, Wrong Step: Geometric Analysis of Finite-Step Failure in Looped Transformers
summary: Looped Transformers offer a parameter-efficient route to test-time scaling by reusing shared layers for iterative latent reasoning. However, additional iterations can reduce support for a reference answer, leaving unclear whether an update's direction is locally unhelpful or its full displacement moves too far. We study this distinction by analysing reference utility, which measures this support, along the model's own update direction, varying the fraction of the proposed displacement supplied to the readout. This reveals finite-step failures in which a locally improving direction produces a harmful full update. A pathwise curvature decomposition characterises how initial progress is lost, while a local quadratic model predicts full-step gains and useful step scales. Bounds based on accumulated curvature variation characterise the approximation error of these predictions. Experiments across two model families reveal this separation on mathematical and commonsense tasks. A fixed quarter step produces positive gains in reference utility for 72.2--83.2% of selected failures across four settings. These findings identify a mismatch between update direction and step scale as a mechanism of lost progress, explaining how some harmful updates retain useful computation.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates why iterative latent reasoning in Looped Transformers can lose progress despite using locally improving update directions. By analyzing reference utility along the model's update direction and varying displacement fractions, the authors identify a mismatch between update direction and step scale as the root cause of failed updates. A local quadratic model and pathwise curvature decomposition can predict and bound these failures.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers can reuse shared layers for iterative reasoning at test time, but additional iterations sometimes reduce support for a reference answer. The authors aim to understand whether this failure comes from a locally unhelpful direction or from moving too far in a helpful direction.
AI.method: The authors analyze reference utility along the model's update direction, varying the fraction of proposed displacement supplied to the readout. They use pathwise curvature decomposition to characterize lost progress and a local quadratic model to predict full-step gains. Bounds based on accumulated curvature variation characterize approximation errors.
AI.result: Experiments on two model families across mathematical and commonsense tasks reveal that finite-step failures occur when locally improving directions produce harmful full updates. A fixed quarter step produces positive gains in reference utility for 72.2-83.2% of selected failures across four settings.
AI.conclusion: The mismatch between update direction and step scale is a key mechanism of lost progress in Looped Transformers. This explains why some harmful updates retain useful computation - the direction is correct but the step size is too large.

title: FirmCORe: A Benchmark for Structured Reasoning about Inter-Firm Collaboration Opportunities
summary: Comprehensive structured data on inter-firm relationships is often scarce or inaccessible because many relationships are privately negotiated, selectively disclosed, and fragmented across proprietary databases. This scarcity hinders the discovery of collaboration opportunities, particularly for startups and small and medium-sized enterprises. Firm profiles are readily available, but collaboration potential cannot be inferred from business similarity alone, since similar firms may be competitors, whereas dissimilar firms may offer complementary products, technologies, channels, capabilities, or capital. We present FirmCORe (Inter-Firm Collaboration Opportunity Reasoning), a human-annotated benchmark for pairwise reasoning over weakly structured firm profiles, comprising 2,805 labeled firm pairs. Given two firm profiles, a model must determine whether the available evidence supports a collaboration opportunity and, for positive pairs, jointly predict its strength, primary collaboration type, and role direction. FirmCORe also provides parallel Chinese- and English-language evaluation sets containing identical instances and gold labels, enabling controlled analysis of input-language sensitivity. Experiments with representative locally deployed and hosted large language models (LLMs) show that the strongest model achieves a macro-F1 score of 74.51 for opportunity detection but only 61.57% exact match across all four output fields. Language effects vary across models, and high cross-language agreement can mask errors shared across languages. These results indicate that current LLMs are substantially more reliable at detecting broad collaboration opportunities than at identifying their specific types and role directions.

AI.tldr: FirmCORe is a benchmark dataset for evaluating AI models' ability to determine whether two firms have collaboration potential based on their profiles. It contains 2,805 labeled firm pairs and includes both English and Chinese versions for cross-language analysis. The strongest tested model achieved 74.51% macro-F1 for detecting collaboration opportunities but only 61.57% exact match when predicting all four output fields (opportunity, strength, type, and direction).
AI.motivation: Inter-firm collaboration data is scarce because relationships are privately negotiated and fragmented across databases. This limits startups and SMEs from discovering collaboration opportunities. Current firm profiles alone cannot reveal collaboration potential since similar firms may be competitors while dissimilar firms may complement each other.
AI.method: Created FirmCORe, a human-annotated benchmark with 2,805 labeled firm pairs. Given two firm profiles, models must determine if evidence supports collaboration, and for positive pairs, predict collaboration strength, primary type, and role direction. Includes parallel Chinese and English evaluation sets for controlled language analysis. Tested representative locally deployed and hosted LLMs.
AI.result: Strongest model achieved 74.51 macro-F1 for opportunity detection but only 61.57% exact match across all four output fields. Language effects vary across models, and high cross-language agreement can mask errors shared across languages.
