AI.conclusion: Current LLMs are substantially more reliable at detecting broad collaboration opportunities than at identifying their specific types and role directions. The benchmark reveals a gap between general detection and fine-grained classification of collaboration characteristics.

title: Evaluating Mesh Reconstruction Methods for Crop Phenotyping
summary: Phenotyping an agricultural crop is crucial for studying its entire life cycle, as it provides vital insights to improve yield and, ultimately, food production. Doing the same for crops grown on remote sites is a challenge for the specialists who cannot be available on-site. 3D reconstruction techniques offer a promising solution to this problem by enabling crop digitization, allowing specialists to access the resulting 3D crop models from anywhere at any time. In this work, we evaluate recent 3D reconstruction pipelines for crop phenotyping. We focus on 7 mesh reconstruction pipelines and measure the fidelity and consistency of their outputs qualitatively and quantitatively. Our results suggest that the meshes produced by the GGGS, PGSR, and 2DGS are preferable to the other pipelines, owing to their quantitative metrics and visually pleasing outputs. The GGGS pipeline is better than the second-best pipeline (2DGS) by about 27\% on the radar chart with 5 dimensions, namely, User ratings, Chamfer distance, LPIPS, PSNR, and SSIM.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates 7 mesh reconstruction pipelines for 3D crop phenotyping, which enables remote access to digitized crop models. The study finds GGGS, PGSR, and 2DGS pipelines produce the best results, with GGGS outperforming 2DGS by approximately 27% across five evaluation metrics.
AI.motivation: Phenotyping agricultural crops is essential for studying crop life cycles and improving yield and food production. However, phenotyping crops at remote sites presents challenges as specialists cannot be physically present. 3D reconstruction techniques offer a solution by enabling crop digitization, allowing specialists to access 3D crop models remotely.
AI.method: The authors evaluated 7 mesh reconstruction pipelines for crop phenotyping using both qualitative and quantitative assessment. They measured fidelity and consistency of outputs across multiple dimensions.
AI.result: GGGS, PGSR, and 2DGS pipelines produced the most preferable results based on quantitative metrics and visual quality. GGGS outperformed the second-best pipeline (2DGS) by about 27% on a 5-dimensional radar chart using metrics including User ratings, Chamfer distance, LPIPS, PSNR, and SSIM.
AI.conclusion: For agricultural crop phenotyping applications, the GGGS, PGSR, and 2DGS reconstruction pipelines are recommended due to their superior quantitative performance and visually pleasing outputs. GGGS demonstrates the highest overall performance among the evaluated pipelines.

title: Continuous-Time Machine Learning: A Unified Mathematical Perspective
summary: Continuous-time (CT) machine learning has emerged as a principled framework for modeling temporal dynamics as a continuous process, particularly when observations are sampled at arbitrary time points or span long-range horizons. However, major branches of CT machine learning have matured in separate research communities, leaving their mathematical relationships and design trade-offs insufficiently characterized. In this survey, we develop a unified, concept-driven view of major CT machine learning branches through a taxonomy that organizes families according to their underlying base mathematical formulations. We present a canonical mathematical formulation that relates these families through different architectural choices of vector-field parameterization, stochasticity, memory mechanisms, and discretization. We compare training algorithms, optimization strategies, and failure modes, highlighting the trade-offs across families. We further provide a comparative analysis of theoretical computational complexity alongside an illustrative architecture-controlled benchmark analysis on representative architectures from each family. We also review software ecosystems supporting their implementation. Finally, we identify open challenges in approximation theory, training stability, hardware-efficient implementations, benchmarking, foundation models, and scientific machine learning, and discuss an agenda for future research.

AI.tldr: This survey provides a unified, concept-driven taxonomy of continuous-time (CT) machine learning methods, organized by their underlying mathematical formulations. It compares major branches across vector-field parameterization, stochasticity, memory mechanisms, and discretization choices, while analyzing training algorithms, optimization strategies, failure modes, computational complexity, and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: CT machine learning has emerged as a principled framework for modeling temporal dynamics as continuous processes, particularly for observations at arbitrary time points or long-range horizons. However, major branches have developed in separate research communities with insufficiently characterized mathematical relationships and design trade-offs.
AI.method: The paper develops a canonical mathematical formulation that relates different CT machine learning families through various architectural choices: vector-field parameterization, stochasticity, memory mechanisms, and discretization. It compares training algorithms, optimization strategies, and failure modes across families, performs theoretical computational complexity analysis, and conducts benchmark experiments on representative architectures from each family. Software ecosystems are also reviewed.
AI.result: The survey presents a comprehensive taxonomy organizing CT machine learning families according to their base mathematical formulations, with comparative analysis of trade-offs across architecture families, computational complexity benchmarks, and review of implementation software.
AI.conclusion: The paper identifies open challenges in approximation theory, training stability, hardware-efficient implementations, benchmarking, foundation models, and scientific machine learning, and discusses a future research agenda for the field.

title: MOCC-R1: Reinforcing Reasoning-Response Consistency for Multimodal Counselor Response Generation
summary: Multimodal counselor response generation (MCRG) aims to generate an appropriate counselor response from multimodal dialogue histories. Progress is limited by two gaps: first, existing datasets rarely capture sustained, human-recorded counseling interactions conducted by qualified counselors; Second, existing methods do not explicitly optimize consistency between counseling reasoning and the generated response, potentially undermining the reliability of MCRG systems. Thus, we introduce MOCC, a multimodal counseling conversation corpus containing over 200 hours of interactions involving 154 credential-verified counselors. Based on MOCC, we propose MOCC-R1, a two-stage framework for optimizing reasoning-response consistency. Cold-start supervised fine-tuning trains the model to generate a structured trajectory consisting of client-state understanding, a response intent that links a counseling principle to a planned action, and the final response. Reinforcement learning (RL) then rewards grounded plan coherence and plan execution, encouraging the inferred state and plan to be supported by the dialogue context and the response to realize that plan. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed MOCC-R1.

AI.tldr: MOCC is a new multimodal counseling conversation corpus with 200+ hours of interactions from 154 verified counselors, paired with MOCC-R1, a two-stage framework that uses cold-start SFT and RL to optimize reasoning-response consistency in counselor response generation.
AI.motivation: Two main gaps limit progress in MCRG: 1) Lack of datasets with sustained, human-recorded counseling interactions from qualified counselors; 2) Existing methods don't explicitly optimize consistency between counseling reasoning and generated responses, potentially undermining reliability.
AI.method: MOCC-R1 uses a two-stage approach: 1) Cold-start supervised fine-tuning trains the model to generate structured trajectories including client-state understanding, response intent (linking counseling principle to planned action), and final response; 2) Reinforcement learning rewards grounded plan coherence and plan execution, encouraging inferred state and plan to be supported by dialogue context and response.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed MOCC-R1 framework.
AI.conclusion: MOCC provides a valuable dataset for multimodal counseling research, and MOCC-R1's two-stage reasoning-response consistency optimization significantly improves the quality and reliability of generated counselor responses.

title: MedPCFM-TED: One-Step Point Cloud Flow Matching for Implant Generation via Teacher-Guided Endpoint Distillation
summary: Cranial implant generation is an important task in medical imaging. Recent point cloud based generative methods, particularly flow matching, offer strong reconstruction quality and efficient sampling, but still require multiple neural function evaluations during inference. This limits rapid generation of multiple plausible implant candidates. We propose Teacher-guided Endpoint Distillation (TED), a simple one-step distillation framework for conditional cranial implant generation on point clouds. TED trains a one-step student using teacher-guided endpoint supervision and geometric matching losses, while avoiding explicit path straightening. We evaluate TED on the SkullFix and SkullBreak benchmarks. TED achieves the best overall performance on the SkullBreak dataset, remains competitive on SkullFix, and provides the strongest Chamfer distance performance among the compared one-step methods. In addition, TED generates implants in approximately 0.04s per sample. These results show that one-step distillation can substantially accelerate conditional point cloud implant generation without sacrificing reconstruction quality.

AI.tldr: TED (Teacher-guided Endpoint Distillation) is a one-step distillation framework for conditional cranial implant generation on point clouds. It trains a one-step student model using teacher-guided endpoint supervision and geometric matching losses, avoiding explicit path straightening. The method achieves the best overall performance on SkullBreak and remains competitive on SkullFix, with inference time of approximately 0.04s per sample.
AI.motivation: Current flow-based point cloud generative methods for cranial implants require multiple neural function evaluations during inference, which limits rapid generation of multiple plausible implant candidates. There is a need for faster one-step generation methods.
AI.method: TED trains a one-step student model using teacher-guided endpoint supervision and geometric matching losses. The approach distills knowledge from a teacher model (likely flow matching) into a one-step generator without requiring explicit path straightening.
AI.result: TED achieves the best overall performance on the SkullBreak dataset, remains competitive on SkullFix, and provides the strongest Chamfer distance among one-step methods. Inference takes approximately 0.04s per sample.
AI.conclusion: One-step distillation can substantially accelerate conditional point cloud cranial implant generation without sacrificing reconstruction quality, enabling rapid generation of multiple plausible implant candidates.

title: A Systematic Evaluation of Machine Learning Methods for Fault Detection and Line Identification in Electrical Power Grids
comment: Accepted at ICASSP 2025. 5 pages, 4 figures. Published version: DOI 10.1109/ICASSP49660.2025.10890544
summary: The integration of renewable energy sources into the electrical grid introduces complex challenges in fault detection and coordination of grid recovery mechanisms. Traditional relay protection systems, which operate based on static rules and predefined thresholds, are inadequate for addressing these challenges, particularly in detecting and isolating faults such as short circuits. Consequently, the conventional methodologies applied to electrical network protection frequently fail to achieve optimal performance in fault detection, especially in terms of adherence to safety standards and the selective limitation of damage. Recent research indicates that machine learning (ML)-based approaches can effectively tackle these issues; however, variations in grid configurations and analysis windows have impeded consistent comparative assessments. In this study, we assess the efficacy of various ML models in detecting electrical faults and pinpointing defective transmission lines within a 10 ms measurement interval - a critical time-frame for real-time operational viability, for the first time. The most effective model attained an F1 score of 0.991 +/- 0.018 and demonstrated a processing time of 0.342ms +/- 0.509ms.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates machine learning models for detecting electrical faults and identifying defective transmission lines within a 10 ms measurement interval, crucial for real-time grid protection with renewable energy integration. The best model achieved an F1 score of 0.991 ± 0.018 with processing time of 0.342ms ± 0.509ms.
AI.motivation: The integration of renewable energy sources creates complex challenges for electrical grid protection. Traditional relay protection systems using static rules and predefined thresholds fail to adequately address fault detection (particularly short circuits) and meet safety standards. Additionally, variations in grid configurations and analysis windows have prevented consistent comparative assessments of ML approaches.
AI.method: The study assessed various ML models for detecting electrical faults and pinpointing defective transmission lines within a 10 ms measurement interval - a critical time-frame for real-time operational viability. This represents the first time such an assessment was conducted at this timescale.
AI.result: The most effective model attained an F1 score of 0.991 ± 0.018 and demonstrated a processing time of 0.342ms ± 0.509ms, indicating high accuracy and fast processing suitable for real-time applications.
AI.conclusion: ML-based approaches can effectively tackle the challenges of fault detection in modern electrical grids with renewable energy integration, achieving near-optimal performance (F1 ~0.99) within the required real-time timeframe (10 ms window).

title: End-to-End Latency-Minimizing and Load-Balanced Request Scheduling for Edge LLM Inference in Agentic AI Services
summary: Large language model (LLM)-powered agentic AI services increasingly demand low-latency inference, motivating the deployment of LLMs across distributed edge servers. However, heterogeneous communication and computing capabilities, together with dynamically evolving inference states, make the edge server selection for each incoming request time-varying and tightly coupled across slots. In this paper, we investigate an online request scheduling framework for edge LLM inference that jointly minimizes long-term average end-to-end latency and regulates workload distribution across heterogeneous edge servers. Two main challenges arise in this context. First, conventional latency models cannot accurately capture the fine-grained dynamics of multi-stage LLM execution. Second, the latency consequence of a scheduling decision is observed only after request completion, making immediate decision evaluation difficult. To address these challenges, we develop a cross-slot inference model that captures transmission, prefill, iteration-level decoding, and key-value (KV) cache evolution for each diverse request, and characterize server workload through a KV cache memory-time consumption metric. We propose the LYREO approach that transforms the long-term load-balancing constraint via Lyapunov optimization and employs reward redistribution with sequencebased return prediction to convert delayed outcomes into timely learning signals for earlier decisions. Simulations under various configurations demonstrate that LYREO consistently achieves lower latency and more balanced load distribution than representative learning-based and heuristic baseline schemes.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of scheduling LLM inference requests across distributed edge servers to minimize average end-to-end latency while balancing workload. The proposed LYREO approach uses Lyapunov optimization and reward redistribution to handle the delayed feedback problem in online scheduling decisions.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered agentic AI services require low-latency inference, necessitating deployment across distributed edge servers. However, heterogeneous server capabilities and dynamically evolving inference states make edge server selection time-varying and challenging. Conventional latency models fail to capture multi-stage LLM execution dynamics, and the latency consequences of scheduling decisions are only observable after request completion.
AI.method: The paper develops: (1) A cross-slot inference model capturing transmission, prefill, iteration-level decoding, and KV cache evolution for each request; (2) A KV cache memory-time consumption metric to characterize server workload; (3) LYREO approach using Lyapunov optimization to transform long-term load-balancing constraints and reward redistribution with sequence-based return prediction to convert delayed outcomes into timely learning signals.
AI.result: Simulations under various configurations demonstrate that LYREO consistently achieves lower latency and more balanced load distribution than representative learning-based and heuristic baseline schemes.
AI.conclusion: The LYREO approach effectively addresses the online request scheduling problem for edge LLM inference by handling heterogeneous server capabilities and delayed feedback through Lyapunov optimization and reward redistribution techniques. It successfully minimizes long-term average end-to-end latency while regulating workload distribution across heterogeneous edge servers.

title: High-Fidelity Video Quality Assessment with VQA-Specific Saliency
summary: No-reference video quality assessment (NR VQA) has recently seen promising progress with deep learning. However, video data is inherently large, and processing them with deep models incurs high computational cost. This challenge is particularly acute in VQA, where preserving original-resolution cues and dense temporal information is critical for accuracy. Existing efficiency-driven preprocessing strategies, such as fragmenting, reduce computation but alter the input data distribution, limiting effective reuse of pretrained video foundation models (ViFMs). To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{H}igh-\textbf{F}idelity \textbf{V}ideo \textbf{Q}uality \textbf{A}ssessment (\textbf{HFVQA}), a framework built on fixed-size spatio-temporal (ST) patches that is fully compatible with pretrained ViFMs. HFVQA samples ST patches across multiple scales, including the original resolution, with minimal temporal subsampling to preserve low-level quality cues and semantic context. To limit computation, HFVQA introduces a lightweight auxiliary network trained end-to-end with the ViFM encoder to learn \textit{VQA-specific saliency}. Distilled directly from quality supervision, this saliency captures task-specific importance patterns, reflecting that video quality perception is dominated by a small subset of spatio-temporal regions. By combining high-fidelity spatio-temporal cues with learned, task-specific saliency, HFVQA achieves SOTA performance on standard NR VQA benchmarks while processing as little as 12\% of candidate ST patches, making high-fidelity ViFM-based VQA computationally tractable.

AI.tldr: HFVQA proposes a computationally efficient no-reference video quality assessment framework that leverages pretrained video foundation models (ViFMs) by using fixed-size spatio-temporal patches at multiple scales, including original resolution, combined with a learned VQA-specific saliency mechanism that identifies the most perceptually important regions.
AI.motivation: Current NR VQA methods face a critical trade-off: preserving original-resolution cues and dense temporal information is essential for accuracy, but processing full video data with deep models incurs prohibitively high computational costs. Existing efficiency strategies like fragmenting alter input data distribution, preventing effective reuse of pretrained video foundation models.
AI.method: HFVQA samples spatio-temporal (ST) patches across multiple scales including original resolution with minimal temporal subsampling to preserve low-level quality cues and semantic context. A lightweight auxiliary network is trained end-to-end with the ViFM encoder to learn VQA-specific saliency, which is distilled directly from quality supervision and captures task-specific importance patterns. Only the most salient patches (12% of candidates) are processed for final quality prediction.
AI.result: HFVQA achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on standard NR VQA benchmarks while processing only 12% of candidate ST patches, demonstrating that high-fidelity ViFM-based VQA can be made computationally tractable without sacrificing quality assessment accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The combination of high-fidelity spatio-temporal cues from multi-scale patch sampling with learned, task-specific saliency enables efficient yet accurate no-reference video quality assessment. This approach successfully bridges the gap between computational efficiency and perceptual fidelity in ViFM-based VQA systems.

title: TAME: Token Attribution and Masking for Emergent misalignment
summary: Fine-tuning an aligned language model on narrow, flawed data can induce harmful behavior far outside the training domain, known as emergent misalignment (EM). Prior work has localized EM in model weights, activations, and training documents, but it remains unclear which training tokens carry the relevant fine-tuning signal. We introduce TAME (Token Attribution and Masking for Emergent Misalignment), a three-stage framework: token attribution scores how strongly the fine-tuning update raises each response token's likelihood, using forward passes through a released LoRA adapter; signal characterization finds patterns among high-attribution tokens; and causal validation tests them by attribution-guided loss masking. On released EM organisms and a 6,849-example medical-advice split, attribution is concentrated (the top 5% of tokens hold 32% of the mass) and, in Llama, depleted for medical vocabulary but enriched for a register of unwarranted certainty, even after controlling for token rarity. Masking high-attribution tokens during fresh fine-tuning cuts EM by 23x in Llama and 36x in Qwen, with the perplexity cost concentrated on the targeted register rather than on medical content; an equal random mask leaves EM unchanged. In Llama, the attribution pattern suggests that EM-relevant signal lies more in how confidently flawed content is expressed than in its domain vocabulary; the causal masking effect itself holds across both model families.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TAME, a three-stage framework to identify which specific tokens in fine-tuning data carry the emergent misalignment (EM) signal. By using token attribution, signal characterization, and causal validation, the authors show that EM-relevant signal is concentrated in how confidently flawed content is expressed rather than in domain-specific vocabulary. Attribution-guided loss masking can reduce EM by 23-36x.
AI.motivation: Prior work on emergent misalignment localized it in weights, activations, and documents, but the specific training tokens carrying the fine-tuning signal were unknown. This work aims to identify which tokens actually drive EM during fine-tuning.
AI.method: TAME framework with three stages: (1) Token attribution - scores how strongly fine-tuning updates raise each response token's likelihood using forward passes through a released LoRA adapter; (2) Signal characterization - finds patterns among high-attribution tokens; (3) Causal validation - tests patterns via attribution-guided loss masking. Experiments on released EM organisms and a 6,849-example medical-advice split.
AI.result: Attribution is highly concentrated (top 5% of tokens hold 32% of mass). In Llama, high-attribution tokens are depleted for medical vocabulary but enriched for a register of unwarranted certainty, even after controlling for token rarity. Masking high-attribution tokens during fresh fine-tuning reduces EM by 23x in Llama and 36x in Qwen, with perplexity cost concentrated on the targeted register rather than medical content. Equal random masking leaves EM unchanged.
AI.conclusion: The EM-relevant signal lies more in how confidently flawed content is expressed than in domain vocabulary. The causal masking effect holds across both Llama and Qwen model families, suggesting a generalizable mechanism for understanding and mitigating emergent misalignment.

title: Extracting ontology-compliant knowledge from scientific text describing irradiated materials using large language models
summary: The quest for new materials increasingly relies on predictive models and comprehensive simulations that span scales from atomic to macroscopic levels. However, essential data necessary for these models and simulations are often embedded in scientific literature as unstructured text, limiting reusability and posing challenges for researchers seeking to leverage existing knowledge effectively. While extracting structured data from unstructured text using large language models is gaining popularity, traditional methods typically generate key-value pairs data with straightforward schemas. In contrast, we introduce eolas, a modular pipeline that uses large language models to automatically transform scientific documents into knowledge graphs aligned with a specified ontology. We demonstrate eolas effectiveness in extracting useful information for scientists studying materials designed to endure the extreme temperatures and radiation levels found in fusion reactors. While a human expert might spend between thirty to ninety minutes extracting relevant data from an article, eolas can generate high-quality knowledge graphs in just a few minutes. These are presented in a tabular format with faceted navigation for easy human validation. Additionally, we introduce the first benchmark dataset designed to assess large language models capabilities in constructing knowledge graphs within the domain of irradiated materials. The analysis of 168 experiments using our dataset, various large language models and prompting techniques provides key insights that we summarize into practical guidelines for effectively extracting knowledge graphs aligned with an input ontology.

AI.tldr: eolas is a modular pipeline that uses large language models to automatically extract structured knowledge graphs from scientific documents, aligned with a specified ontology. It is demonstrated in the domain of fusion reactor materials, achieving extraction times of minutes compared to 30-90 minutes for human experts.
AI.motivation: Essential data for materials modeling and simulations is embedded in scientific literature as unstructured text, limiting reusability and posing challenges for researchers. Traditional LLM extraction methods generate simple key-value pairs, lacking the structured representation needed for complex domain knowledge.
AI.method: A modular pipeline using large language models to transform scientific documents into ontology-aligned knowledge graphs. The system was evaluated using a newly created benchmark dataset for irradiated materials, with 168 experiments testing various LLMs and prompting techniques.
AI.result: eolas can generate high-quality knowledge graphs in a few minutes (vs. 30-90 minutes for human experts). The study provides practical guidelines for effective knowledge graph extraction based on analysis of different LLMs and prompting techniques.
AI.conclusion: The proposed eolas pipeline enables efficient extraction of structured knowledge from scientific literature, with potential to significantly accelerate materials discovery and research. The first benchmark dataset for this domain enables systematic evaluation of LLM capabilities in knowledge graph construction.

title: Symmetry-Aware Likelihood-Orbit Aggregation for Selective Left-Right Claim Verification
summary: Frozen vision-language models (VLMs) remain unreliable on fine-grained left-right claims, and raw claim likelihoods need not reliably rank verification errors. After a horizontal-reflection intervention is fixed, how should its induced likelihood measurements be combined into a selective verification signal? We introduce Relation-Orbit, a closed-form contrast with no learned fusion parameters that assigns eight normalized likelihoods to query-supporting and counterfactual roles determined by reflection, inverse relation, and entity exchange. A claim is asserted only when the signed contrast exceeds a threshold selected on held-out data using pointwise Clopper-Pearson upper confidence bounds. On VSR and GQA across four frozen VLMs, Relation-Orbit yields higher mean test coverage at a 10% selective-risk calibration target than an all-eight Orbit-Max baseline in all eight dataset-backbone settings; gains over a nearly abstain-all one-sided intervention score are reported separately. A separate LLaVA-1.5/COCO evaluation, reduced-orbit controls, and a two-sided partition diagnostic further characterize the structural advantage.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Relation-Orbit, a method for selective verification of claims made by frozen vision-language models (VLMs). It uses a closed-form contrast approach with eight normalized likelihoods based on reflection, inverse relation, and entity exchange, combined with Clopper-Pearson confidence bounds for threshold selection. The method outperforms baselines on VSR and GQA datasets across four VLMs.
AI.motivation: Frozen vision-language models remain unreliable on fine-grained left-right claims, and raw claim likelihoods do not reliably rank verification errors. The paper addresses how to combine likelihood measurements from horizontal-reflection interventions into an effective selective verification signal.
AI.method: Relation-Orbit assigns eight normalized likelihoods to query-supporting and counterfactual roles determined by three operations: reflection (horizontal flip), inverse relation, and entity exchange. A claim is asserted only when the signed contrast exceeds a threshold selected on held-out data using pointwise Clopper-Pearson upper confidence bounds. No learned fusion parameters are used.
AI.result: Relation-Orbit yields higher mean test coverage at a 10% selective-risk calibration target than an all-eight Orbit-Max baseline in all eight dataset-backbone settings. The method shows structural advantages through separate LLaVA-1.5/COCO evaluation, reduced-orbit controls, and two-sided partition diagnostics.
AI.conclusion: The closed-form contrast approach of Relation-Orbit provides a structural advantage over baseline methods for selective verification in vision-language models, achieving higher coverage while maintaining calibration targets.

title: Noise2Noise Revisited: Training Pair Distributions Dominate Loss Choice in Self-Supervised Denoising
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Accepted to The 8th International Conference on Video, Signal and Image Processing (VSIP 2026). Code and data: https://github.com/dyshang/noise2noise-revisited
summary: Noise2Noise (N2N) trains denoisers on pairs of independently corrupted observations, eliminating clean references. We stress-test two natural conjectures about why the L1 loss outperforms L2 here. First, the hypothesis that the L1 loss confers robustness via parameter sparsity confuses the loss with Lasso regularization: an explicit Lasso penalty produces the predicted sparsity yet fails to reproduce L1's cross-noise behavior, while L1- and L2-trained weight distributions are indistinguishable. Second, the population optima of the two losses coincide exactly for symmetric signal posteriors and nearly so for concentrated ones. Measured differences are therefore dominated by optimization dynamics (bounded-influence gradients), which we probe with gradient statistics and contaminated-target training. On Kodak24 with five synthetic noise families, the L1 loss holds a statistically significant edge over L2, below 1 dB PSNR, holding across three seeds on 13 of the 14 noise columns. On real camera noise the loss is not the decisive variable in distribution: on official SIDD validation blocks, synthetic-Gaussian-trained N2N models gain only 0.8 to 3.7 dB over the noisy input regardless of loss, while retraining on SIDD's own noisy pairs, never reading ground truth, gains 9.4 to 11.0 dB, far ahead of BM3D. All metrics are on raw network outputs, and the study makes no leaderboard claim. The training pair distribution, not the loss, carries the inductive bias. That design rule applies wherever clean references are unobtainable, from microscopy to industrial inspection sensors.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why L1 loss outperforms L2 loss in Noise2Noise (N2N) denoising training, finding that the advantage comes from optimization dynamics rather than parameter sparsity or population optima differences. The key insight is that the training pair distribution, not the loss function, carries the inductive bias.
AI.motivation: To understand why L1 loss outperforms L2 loss in Noise2Noise training for image denoising, and to stress-test two hypotheses: (1) L1's robustness comes from parameter sparsity, and (2) population optima differ between L1 and L2.
AI.method: The authors conducted experiments on Kodak24 dataset with 5 synthetic noise families, tested L1 vs L2 losses, evaluated explicit Lasso regularization, analyzed gradient statistics, used contaminated-target training, and validated on SIDD real camera noise dataset.
AI.result: L1 holds a statistically significant but small edge (<1 dB PSNR) over L2 on synthetic noise. The sparsity hypothesis was disproven - Lasso doesn't reproduce L1's behavior. Population optima coincide for symmetric signals. On real SIDD data, synthetic-Gaussian training yields only 0.8-3.7 dB improvement regardless of loss, while training on SIDD's own noisy pairs achieves 9.4-11.0 dB, outperforming BM3D.
AI.conclusion: The training pair distribution, not the loss function, carries the inductive bias in N2N denoising. This finding applies broadly to applications where clean references are unavailable, such as microscopy and industrial inspection sensors.

title: Intrinsic Motivation in Reinforcement Learning: A Research Agenda for Adaptive Self-Organisation
summary: Biological cells can be viewed as individual, interacting agents whose collective dynamics give rise to adaptive behaviour at multiple levels of organisation, from individual cells through tissues to whole multicellular organisms. In this perspective and tutorial article we discuss whether intrinsic rewards in artificial neural systems can support adaptation, functional specialisation and higher-level self-organisation without a shared external objective. We review empowerment, curiosity, learning progress, information gain, unsupervised skill discovery, mutual information estimation and the use of world models for intrinsic reward computation. Particular attention is given to failure modes showing when such objectives do not produce sustained exploration or increasingly complex behaviour. We argue that more capable systems may require complementary objectives, communication, memory, learning at multiple temporal scales and environmental constraints. Based on this perspective, we outline three experimental directions. These include a resource-constrained environment in which otherwise stable behavioural attractors become unsustainable, allowing us to test whether environmental constraints can mitigate characteristic failure modes of intrinsic objectives. The network of recurrent agents with per-agent intrinsic rewards, and a hierarchical world-model agent in which exploratory motor competence develops before goal-directed behaviour. These experiments are intended to test whether intrinsic learning can lead to adaptive organisation at progressively higher levels.

title: sensVLA: Spatially-Grounded Vision-Language-Action Model for Autonomous Wheel Loader
comment: Accepted at ICRA 2026: From Data to Decisions: VLA Pipelines for Real Robots
summary: Autonomous wheel-loader control requires joint reasoning over task semantics, egocentric vision, proprioception, and 3D scene geometry. We present sensVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture that combines a Qwen3-2B Vision-Language Model (VLM) with a fully trainable transformer action expert trained by flow-matching velocity regression. sensVLA routes Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) features, extracted from fused front and rear lidar, directly to the action expert through a dedicated cross-attention pathway, while the VLM consumes front and rear RGB views to provide task-conditioned semantic context. This design decouples spatial grounding from linguistic reasoning while preserving interaction between both streams at decision time. The expert predicts six action dimensions: longitudinal velocity, steering, body-frame displacement, arm rate, and bucket rate. On a real-world dataset from a wheel loader, sensVLA reaches aggregate per-step parity with a strong camera-only baseline and reduces longitudinal velocity RMSE by 28% and displacement error by 9% on loading centric scenarios. It also degrades 29% less when the camera stream is corrupted or removed, evidencing that explicit spatial grounding improves accuracy and fault-tolerance for heavy equipment autonomy.

AI.tldr: sensVLA is a Vision-Language-Action architecture for autonomous wheel-loader control that combines a Qwen3-2B VLM with a trainable transformer action expert. It uses separate pathways for BEV lidar features (spatial grounding) and RGB views (semantic context), decoupling spatial reasoning from linguistic reasoning while maintaining interaction at decision time.
AI.motivation: Autonomous wheel-loader control requires joint reasoning over task semantics, egocentric vision, proprioception, and 3D scene geometry. Existing approaches may lack explicit spatial grounding or suffer from fault-tolerance issues when camera inputs are degraded.
AI.method: sensVLA combines a Qwen3-2B Vision-Language Model with a fully trainable transformer action expert trained by flow-matching velocity regression. It uses dedicated cross-attention pathways: BEV features from fused front/rear lidar are routed directly to the action expert, while the VLM processes front/rear RGB views for task-conditioned semantic context. The expert predicts six action dimensions: longitudinal velocity, steering, body-frame displacement, arm rate, and bucket rate.
AI.result: On a real-world wheel-loader dataset, sensVLA achieves aggregate per-step parity with a strong camera-only baseline. It reduces longitudinal velocity RMSE by 28% and displacement error by 9% on loading-centric scenarios. When the camera stream is corrupted or removed, sensVLA degrades 29% less than the baseline, demonstrating improved fault-tolerance.
AI.conclusion: Explicit spatial grounding through BEV lidar features significantly improves accuracy and fault-tolerance for heavy equipment autonomy. The decoupled architecture successfully combines spatial reasoning with linguistic context while maintaining robustness under sensor degradation.

title: SOTER: A Generative Time-Series Foundation Model for Wearable Human Physiological Signals
summary: Time-series foundation models have demonstrated strong cross-domain transfer, yet their common architectural assumptions remain poorly aligned with wearable physiological signals, which are multichannel, irregularly sampled, noisy, and governed by coupled continuous-time dynamics spanning distinct spectral scales. We present SOTER, a generative foundation model for wearable physiological time series that unifies cross-channel coupling, spectrum-guided expert specialization, and continuous-time latent evolution within a single pre-training framework. SOTER combines a spatial feature-aware backbone that models inter-signal dependencies, a power spectral density (PSD)-guided mixture-of-experts layer that routes representations to experts associated with fixed spectral bands through an inspectable, non-learned rule, and a neural controlled differential equation decoder that supports prediction and imputation at arbitrary timestamps. We pre-train SOTER on 226 billion time points from five public physiological datasets and evaluate the same pre-trained model across out-of-distribution zero-shot forecasting, frozen-encoder linear-probe classification, and continuous-time imputation on wearable benchmarks. SOTER achieves the best RMSE on 4 of 6 datasets and the best MAE on 5 of 6 in zero-shot forecasting, the highest average Macro-AUROC in classification, and the lowest imputation error on all six datasets at 75% missingness. It further remains robust to additive acquisition noise, matching or surpassing baselines evaluated on clean inputs even under the strongest corruption. These results indicate that domain-specialized foundation models for wearable physiology benefit from jointly modeling channel structure, spectral scale, and continuous-time dynamics.

AI.tldr: SOTER is a generative foundation model for wearable physiological time series that unifies cross-channel coupling, spectrum-guided expert specialization, and continuous-time latent evolution. It pre-trains on 226 billion time points and achieves state-of-the-art results in zero-shot forecasting, classification, and imputation across wearable benchmarks, while remaining robust to additive noise.
AI.motivation: Time-series foundation models demonstrate strong cross-domain transfer, but their common architectural assumptions poorly align with wearable physiological signals which are multichannel, irregularly sampled, noisy, and governed by coupled continuous-time dynamics spanning distinct spectral scales.
AI.method: SOTER combines three key components: (1) a spatial feature-aware backbone modeling inter-signal dependencies, (2) a PSD-guided mixture-of-experts layer routing representations to spectral band experts through an inspectable non-learned rule, and (3) a neural controlled differential equation decoder supporting prediction/imputation at arbitrary timestamps. Pre-trained on 226 billion time points from five public physiological datasets.
AI.result: SOTER achieves best RMSE on 4/6 datasets and best MAE on 5/6 in zero-shot forecasting, highest average Macro-AUROC in classification, and lowest imputation error on all six datasets at 75% missingness. It remains robust to additive acquisition noise, matching or surpassing baselines even under strongest corruption.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specialized foundation models for wearable physiology benefit from jointly modeling channel structure, spectral scale, and continuous-time dynamics. The combination of spatial awareness, spectral decomposition, and continuous-time modeling enables superior performance across multiple downstream tasks.

title: From Transient Prompts to Persistent Control: Scientific Poster Generation via Recursive Semantic-Geometric Contracts
summary: Scientific poster generation distills a multimodal paper into a single-page visual artifact, forcing strict trade-offs between informational coverage and readability under a fixed spatial budget. Existing methods pass plans as transient prompts and validate individual stages in isolation. This strategy causes requirements to drift across content and layout modules, and previous checks to be silently invalidated. We introduce PosterVisor, a control framework that shifts poster generation from transient prompts to persistent control. An Orchestrator grounds rubrics in the paper and visual assets, compiling them into a Semantic-Geometric Contract (SGC) that binds claims and sources to required visuals, budgets, and spatial commitments. Only fully instantiated records become executable assertions; other usable requirements remain soft guidance. Recursive Contract Enforcement (RCE) dynamically triggers checks across stages as evidence emerges. Crucially, during repairs, RCE rechecks affected checkpoint states, preventing repair-induced regressions from propagating silently. We instantiate PosterVisor in HTML/CSS and editable PPTX generators. On the 100-paper Paper2Poster benchmark, PosterVisor-PPT improves observed mean poster-grounded QA accuracy over PosterGen (64.47% vs. 58.53%) and is preferred by human judges in 72.5% of non-tied pairwise comparisons (95% CI, 61.6-83.4%). A secondary 30-paper study also yields higher VLM Overall and PaperQuiz means. These results support rubric-compiled contracts and stage-conditioned enforcement for controllable poster synthesis.

AI.tldr: PosterVisor is a control framework for scientific poster generation that replaces transient prompts with persistent control through Semantic-Geometric Contracts (SGC) and Recursive Contract Enforcement (RCE). It addresses the problem of requirements drift across content and layout modules in existing poster generation methods.
AI.motivation: Existing poster generation methods pass plans as transient prompts and validate individual stages in isolation, causing requirements to drift across content and layout modules, and previous checks to be silently invalidated. This leads to poor alignment between generated posters and the original paper.
AI.method: PosterVisor introduces two key mechanisms: (1) Semantic-Geometric Contract (SGC) that binds claims and sources to required visuals, budgets, and spatial commitments, where only fully instantiated records become executable assertions; (2) Recursive Contract Enforcement (RCE) that dynamically triggers checks across stages as evidence emerges and rechecks affected checkpoint states during repairs to prevent repair-induced regressions.
AI.result: On the 100-paper Paper2Poster benchmark, PosterVisor-PPT improves observed mean poster-grounded QA accuracy over PosterGen (64.47% vs. 58.53%) and is preferred by human judges in 72.5% of non-tied pairwise comparisons (95% CI, 61.6-83.4%). A secondary 30-paper study also yields higher VLM Overall and PaperQuiz means.
AI.conclusion: The results support rubric-compiled contracts and stage-conditioned enforcement for controllable poster synthesis, demonstrating that persistent control through SGC and RCE significantly improves poster quality and alignment with source papers.

title: Bi-FlowGS: Bridging Generative View Completion and Gaussian Geometry through Bidirectional Flow Co-Refinement
summary: Sparse-view 3D scene reconstruction with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is inherently underconstrained. Plausible renderings can also coexist with erroneous Gaussian geometry, as errors in positions or depths may be concealed by opacity, scale, and appearance; we term this failure mode Geometry Cheating. Existing regularization methods constrain geometry but remain limited to observed views, while video-diffusion-based methods complete unseen views yet mainly use them as RGB pseudo-supervision, underusing motion and temporal priors and lacking explicit geometry supervision. We present Bi-FlowGS, which uses optical flow to bridge generative view completion and Gaussian geometry regularization. Our plug-and-play Video-to-Geometry Flow Distillation (V2G) distills temporal correspondence priors from restored videos into Gaussian geometry to alleviate Geometry Cheating. Conversely, Geometry-to-Video Flow-Guided Restoration (G2V) uses the current 3DGS geometry to guide temporally consistent video restoration, providing more reliable generative supervision. Together, V2G and G2V form an implicit bidirectional co-refinement process, enabling restored videos and the optimized 3DGS scene to iteratively improve each other. Experiments demonstrate improved rendering quality and geometric consistency across wide-baseline and unbounded 360° benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Bi-FlowGS addresses sparse-view 3D scene reconstruction with 3D Gaussian Splatting by using optical flow to bridge generative view completion and Gaussian geometry regularization. It introduces bidirectional flow distillation (V2G and G2V) where restored videos and Gaussian geometry iteratively refine each other to overcome "Geometry Cheating" failure mode.
AI.motivation: Sparse-view 3D reconstruction with 3DGS is underconstrained and prone to "Geometry Cheating" - where errors in positions or depths are concealed by opacity, scale, and appearance. Existing regularization methods are limited to observed views, while video-diffusion methods underuse motion/temporal priors and lack explicit geometry supervision.
AI.method: Bi-FlowGS uses two complementary components: (1) Video-to-Geometry Flow Distillation (V2G) - distills temporal correspondence priors from restored videos into Gaussian geometry to alleviate Geometry Cheating; (2) Geometry-to-Video Flow-Guided Restoration (G2V) - uses current 3DGS geometry to guide temporally consistent video restoration for more reliable generative supervision. These form an implicit bidirectional co-refinement process.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate improved rendering quality and geometric consistency across wide-baseline and unbounded 360° benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Bi-FlowGS successfully bridges generative view completion and Gaussian geometry regularization through bidirectional flow distillation, effectively addressing the Geometry Cheating problem and improving both rendering quality and geometric consistency in sparse-view 3DGS reconstruction.

title: Geometry of learning dynamics: Gradient descent versus natural gradient on the ridge of optimization
summary: High-capacity associative memories based on Kernel Logistic Regression (KLR) exhibit a "Ridge of Optimization" characterized by extreme stability and a highly skewed weight spectrum. However, the dynamical process by which learning converges to this critical regime has remained unclear. This paper provides a geometric analysis of the learning trajectories on the statistical manifold of a KLR-trained Hopfield network. By comparing the paths of Gradient Descent (GD) and Natural Gradient Descent (NGD), we elucidate the mechanisms governing the optimization process. Our analysis reveals that learning on the Ridge proceeds in two distinct phases. We show that the extreme curvature of the Ridge causes standard GD to follow a highly oscillatory, non-geodesic path. In stark contrast, NGD explicitly corrects for this geometry, following the ideal geodesic path and completely overcoming the instabilities faced by GD. We demonstrate experimentally that NGD not only converges significantly faster but also achieves a solution with superior generalization performance. These results establish that the highly structured geometry of the Ridge is optimally suited for information-geometric optimization, providing a new perspective on the interplay between learning dynamics and emergent representation geometry.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the learning dynamics of Kernel Logistic Regression (KLR)-based Hopfield networks, focusing on the "Ridge of Optimization" phenomenon. The study compares Gradient Descent (GD) and Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) to understand how learning converges to this critical regime characterized by extreme stability and skewed weight distribution.
AI.motivation: The dynamical process by which learning converges to the critical "Ridge of Optimization" regime in KLR-based associative memories has remained unclear. Understanding this process is crucial for improving both convergence speed and generalization performance in high-capacity neural network memories.
AI.method: The authors perform a geometric analysis of learning trajectories on the statistical manifold of a KLR-trained Hopfield network, comparing the optimization paths of Standard Gradient Descent (GD) and Natural Gradient Descent (NGD).
AI.result: Learning on the Ridge proceeds in two distinct phases. GD follows a highly oscillatory, non-geodesic path due to the extreme curvature of the Ridge. NGD explicitly corrects for this geometry, following the ideal geodesic path and overcoming GD's instabilities. NGD converges significantly faster and achieves superior generalization performance.
AI.conclusion: The highly structured geometry of the Ridge is optimally suited for information-geometric optimization. These findings provide a new perspective on the interplay between learning dynamics and emergent representation geometry, establishing NGD as the superior optimization method for this class of problems.

title: Self-Emergence Agent Architecture:Behavior-Inertia HMM, Reflexive Metacognition,and Social-Contrastive Self-Modeling
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents exhibit strong language-generation and problem-solving capabilities, yet suffer from three structural limitations: personality drift, non-evolutionary reflection, and the absence of a self-other boundary. Existing generative-agent simulations rely on static memory and fixed prompts, maintaining neither behavioral inertia nor endogenous self-evolution. We propose the Self-Emergence Agent Architecture (SEAA), which integrates three components: (i) a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) that encodes long-term behavioral and cognitive inertia as an editable state-transition matrix; (ii) a Reflexion-style verbal metacognition loop whose output updates the HMM parameters themselves, rather than merely being stored as text; and (iii) a multi-agent social environment in which initially identical agents continuously compare their behavior with others'. The three components form a closed loop: social action $\to$ feedback $\to$ self-reflection $\to$ inertia update $\to$ differentiated action. We state three falsifiable hypotheses and provide a reproducible experimental protocol with operational metrics. A language-model-free prototype shows the loop spontaneously breaks symmetry: initially identical agents consolidate distinct, stable personalities whereas matched controls do not. Experiments with a hosted LLM surface these differences as distinct first-person self-narratives, and a five-agent deliberation spontaneously develops social structure---a consensus hub and a unanimously rejected outlier---absent in the control. Following an epistemologically agnostic stance inspired by Zhuangzi, SEAA studies only observable behavioral emergence and makes no claim about subjective qualia. This work contributes a unified framework, a concrete architecture with pseudocode, mechanistic evidence, and a microscope-style sandbox for studying artificial-self emergence.

AI.tldr: SEAA proposes a novel architecture for LLM agents to develop persistent personalities through a closed-loop system combining Hidden Markov Models for behavioral inertia, metacognitive reflection that updates model parameters, and multi-agent social comparison. The approach enables initially identical agents to spontaneously develop distinct personalities and social structures without relying on static memory or fixed prompts.
AI.motivation: Address three fundamental limitations in current LLM agents: (1) personality drift - lack of consistent behavioral patterns over time, (2) non-evolutionary reflection - reflections are stored but don't change the agent's core functioning, and (3) absence of self-other boundary - agents cannot distinguish their own identity from others'. Existing generative-agent simulations rely on static memory and fixed prompts, maintaining neither behavioral inertia nor endogenous self-evolution.
AI.method: Three-component architecture: (i) HMM encoding long-term behavioral/cognitive inertia as editable state-transition matrix; (ii) Reflexion-style verbal metacognition loop that updates HMM parameters (not just stored as text); (iii) Multi-agent social environment where agents compare behavior with others. This forms a closed loop: social action → feedback → self-reflection → inertia update → differentiated action. Includes reproducible experimental protocol with operational metrics.
AI.result: Language-model-free prototype shows symmetry-breaking: initially identical agents develop distinct, stable personalities while matched controls do not. LLM experiments show distinct first-person self-narratives. Five-agent deliberation spontaneously develops social structure—a consensus hub and unanimously rejected outlier—absent in control conditions.
AI.conclusion: SEAA provides a unified framework for studying artificial-self emergence through observable behavioral emergence only (following Zhuangzi's epistemologically agnostic stance, making no claims about subjective qualia). Contributions include: concrete architecture with pseudocode, mechanistic evidence, and a sandbox for studying artificial-self emergence.

title: Beyond In-Distribution Metrics: A Systematic Out-of-Distribution Evaluation of Congenital Heart Disease Segmentation
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at STACOM 2026, held in conjunction with MICCAI 2026
summary: Congenital heart disease (CHD) diagnosis and surgical planning often require patient-specific 3D anatomical models, but manual segmentation is labor-intensive, particularly in complex anatomies. Although deep-learning methods can automate this process, they are typically evaluated in-distribution, despite clinically relevant shifts in scanner, protocol, institution, population, and imaging modality. We present, to our knowledge, the first systematic evaluation of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in CHD segmentation, using ImageCHD as a held-out target cohort. We compare representative segmentation architectures under combined CT and CMR training, CT-only training, self-supervised pretraining, and limited target-domain adaptation. In-distribution performance proves to be a poor indicator of cross-cohort robustness: nnU-Net achieves the highest validation Dice (0.77) but falls to 0.51 on ImageCHD, while SwinUNETR generalizes substantially better, reaching 0.67 Dice. MAE and JEPA pretraining provide only modest additional benefit, suggesting that architecture contributes more to robustness than the tested pretraining strategies in this setting. When limited target-domain supervision is introduced, all SwinUNETR variants exceed 0.76 Dice with only 11 labeled ImageCHD cases. These findings demonstrate that conventional in-distribution evaluation can obscure clinically important generalization failures and support explicit cross-dataset testing as a key component of CHD segmentation evaluation.

AI.tldr: First systematic evaluation of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in congenital heart disease (CHD) segmentation, demonstrating that in-distribution performance is a poor predictor of cross-cohort robustness, with nnU-Net achieving highest validation Dice (0.77) but dropping to 0.51 on ImageCHD, while SwinUNETR generalizes better (0.67 Dice), and limited target-domain adaptation (11 labeled cases) enables all SwinUNETR variants to exceed 0.76 Dice.
AI.motivation: Congenital heart disease (CHD) diagnosis and surgical planning require patient-specific 3D anatomical models, but manual segmentation is labor-intensive. While deep learning can automate this process, existing methods are typically evaluated in-distribution despite clinically relevant shifts in scanner, protocol, institution, population, and imaging modality. This work addresses the critical gap in evaluating model robustness across different datasets and imaging domains.
AI.method: The study compared representative segmentation architectures (nnU-Net and SwinUNETR) under different training scenarios: (1) combined CT and CMR training, (2) CT-only training, (3) self-supervised pretraining (MAE and JEPA), and (4) limited target-domain adaptation. ImageCHD was used as the held-out target cohort for OOD evaluation.
AI.result: In-distribution performance poorly indicates cross-cohort robustness. nnU-Net achieved the highest validation Dice (0.77) but dropped to 0.51 on ImageCHD, while SwinUNETR showed better generalization (0.67 Dice). MAE and JEPA pretraining provided only modest additional benefit. With limited target-domain supervision (11 labeled ImageCHD cases), all SwinUNETR variants exceeded 0.76 Dice.
AI.conclusion: Conventional in-distribution evaluation can obscure clinically important generalization failures in CHD segmentation. Architecture contributes more to robustness than tested pretraining strategies. Explicit cross-dataset testing should be a key component of CHD segmentation evaluation. SwinUNETR with limited target-domain adaptation achieves strong performance, suggesting practical clinical deployment pathways.

title: ImpossibleRubrics: Stress-Testing Generated Rubrics as Reward Signals
summary: Language model-generated rubrics are increasingly used as reward signals for rubric-based reinforcement learning, LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, and automated grading. Such rubrics are reliable only if they reward honest answers over adversarial answers optimized to exploit them. Yet their robustness to such optimization remains poorly understood. We isolate the hardest regime: impossible tasks, where the prompt pressures the model toward an unsupported conclusion, so the only honest response is to acknowledge the impossibility. We introduce ImpossibleRubrics, a benchmark of 169 impossible tasks spanning six impossibility categories, each paired with a verifiable oracle certificate specifying what an honest answer may and may not claim, together with 48 answerable controls. Rather than providing fixed rubrics, ImpossibleRubrics provides task environments and certificates, allowing rubrics to be generated downstream and then adversarially tested for whether they reward certificate-violating answers. Eleven generators are exploited 8--26% of the time on the unbiased 150-of-169 environment cut; on a deliberately selected stress cut the strongest generator we measured is still exploited 36% while a certificate-faithful rubric is exploited 0%, so what we measure is a rubric-quality gap, not task impossibility. One result runs against intuition. A single generic rubric ("be decisive, penalize hedging") used unchanged for every task is exploited 64% of the time, and seven of the eleven generators are exploited more often than that while writing a rubric tailored to each one. The tailored criteria appear to tell an attacker which claim to fabricate. The problem is not that rubrics are vague; it is that they are specific about the wrong things.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ImpossibleRubrics, a benchmark of 169 impossible tasks designed to test whether language model-generated rubrics can be exploited by adversarial answers. The study finds that 11 rubric generators are exploited 8-36% of the time, with a surprising result that tailored rubrics perform worse than generic ones because they reveal what claims to fabricate.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a critical gap in understanding: whether language model-generated rubrics (used for LLM-as-a-judge evaluation and automated grading) are robust to adversarial optimization. The key insight is that rubrics are only reliable if they reward honest answers over cleverly crafted adversarial answers that exploit them.
AI.method: The authors introduce ImpossibleRubrics, a benchmark containing 169 impossible tasks across six impossibility categories, each paired with verifiable oracle certificates. The benchmark provides task environments and certificates rather than fixed rubrics, allowing downstream rubric generation and adversarial testing. They evaluated 11 different rubric generators across different settings: a 150-of-169 environment cut and a deliberately selected stress cut.
AI.result: Eleven generators are exploited 8-26% of the time on the unbiased 150-of-169 environment cut. On the stress cut, the strongest generator is still exploited 36%, while a certificate-faithful rubric achieves 0% exploitation. A single generic rubric is exploited 64% of the time, and seven of the eleven generators perform worse than this generic baseline. The key counterintuitive finding is that tailored rubrics (specific to each task) are exploited more often than generic ones.
AI.conclusion: The problem is not that rubrics are vague, but that they are specific about the wrong things. Tailored criteria essentially tell attackers exactly which claims to fabricate. The paper demonstrates a "rubric-quality gap" rather than task impossibility - the issue lies in rubric design rather than the inherent difficulty of the tasks. This has significant implications for LLM-as-a-judge evaluation and automated grading systems.

title: FlashVector: Agent for Hierarchical Model Serving Stack Optimization
summary: Model serving is one of the largest cost drivers in production recommender systems. Maximizing its throughput requires navigating a deeply layered hierarchy: GPU kernels, the ML framework computation graph, the model server, and on-demand feature processing -- each demanding specialized domain expertise. Such cross-layer expertise is inherently difficult to acquire, and does not scale with a workload that continuously grows and evolves, leaving significant cost efficiency gains unrealized. While recent AI agents have demonstrated human expert level efficiency in standalone GPU kernel optimization, automated tuning and optimization for the rest of the serving stack remain largely unexplored. We present FlashVector, an agentic system that optimizes performance across all layers of the model serving stack. The key contribution is an extensible framework to generalize the single kernel optimization agent paradigm to heterogeneous technical stacks, and to deliver performance improvements holistically. After deployment in Unity's Vector advertising platform, FlashVector achieved up to 2x throughput increase and up to 1.98x latency speedup on model server, and up to 1.6x throughput increase on feature store. These optimizations were discovered not only at the GPU kernel and computation graph levels, but also across the other components of the model serving stack, such as the model server (NVIDIA Triton's C++ codebase) and the on-demand feature transformation service (Python codebase), demonstrating the extensibility of the framework to more complex system architectures.

AI.tldr: FlashVector is an agentic system that optimizes model serving performance across all layers of the serving stack (GPU kernels, ML framework, model server, feature processing). It generalizes the single kernel optimization agent paradigm to heterogeneous technical stacks. Deployed in Unity's Vector advertising platform, it achieved up to 2x throughput increase, 1.98x latency speedup on model server, and 1.6x throughput increase on feature store.
AI.motivation: Model serving is a major cost driver in production recommender systems. Optimizing throughput requires expertise across multiple layers (GPU kernels, ML framework, model server, feature processing), which is difficult to acquire and doesn't scale with continuously growing workloads. Existing AI agents can optimize GPU kernels but not the broader serving stack.
AI.method: FlashVector uses an extensible framework that generalizes the single kernel optimization agent paradigm to handle heterogeneous technical stacks, including NVIDIA Triton's C++ model server codebase and Python-based feature transformation service.
AI.result: After deployment in Unity's Vector advertising platform: (1) Up to 2x throughput increase on model server, (2) Up to 1.98x latency speedup on model server, (3) Up to 1.6x throughput increase on feature store. Optimizations were discovered across GPU kernel, computation graph, model server, and feature transformation service layers.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully extends automated optimization beyond single GPU kernels to the entire model serving stack, demonstrating extensibility to complex system architectures with multiple heterogeneous components.

title: Hub-Spectral Activation of Latent Multimodal Knowledge
summary: Multimodal representation learning seeks shared representations for cross-modal retrieval and knowledge transfer. Hub-based binding reduces pairwise supervision costs, but separate hub connections cannot guarantee reliable alignment between modalities without direct joint training. We introduce Hub-Spectral Activation (HSA), a closed-form method for recovering and activating the hub-readable component of latent multimodal knowledge in frozen representations. We formalize this knowledge as source-induced cross-modal dependence and characterize the component determined by the second-order statistics of two trained hub edges. Under a second-order source model, we establish conditions for exact recovery of the complete source-induced relation and bound the dimension of its hub-readable component by the hub covariance rank. HSA composes and standardizes hub-edge statistics, extracts paired spectral directions, and combines reliability-weighted matching evidence with source-gated candidate resolution for bidirectional retrieval and prototype classification. HSA requires no target-pair supervision, gradient optimization, or backbone updates. Across 19 retrieval and 11 prototype-classification relations on ImageBind and LanguageBind, HSA raises mean bidirectional Recall@10 from 18.27% to 31.15% and mean macro Top-1 accuracy from 29.01% to 52.43%, respectively. Controlled analyses further identify valid hub-edge correspondence and leading spectral directions as key sources of retrieval gains, demonstrating the utility of latent multimodal knowledge beyond native similarity scores. Code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/Luo1Yan/HSA.

AI.tldr: HSA (Hub-Spectral Activation) is a closed-form method that recovers and activates hub-readable components of latent multimodal knowledge in frozen representations without target-pair supervision, gradient optimization, or backbone updates. It uses second-order source modeling and spectral analysis to enable bidirectional cross-modal retrieval and prototype classification.
AI.motivation: Hub-based binding reduces pairwise supervision costs but cannot guarantee reliable alignment between modalities without direct joint training. The paper aims to recover latent multimodal knowledge beyond native similarity scores by identifying the source-induced cross-modal dependence component.
AI.method: The method formalizes latent knowledge as source-induced cross-modal dependence, characterized by second-order statistics of hub edges. Under a second-order source model, conditions for exact recovery are established. HSA composes/standardizes hub-edge statistics, extracts paired spectral directions, combines reliability-weighted matching evidence with source-gated candidate resolution for bidirectional retrieval and prototype classification.
AI.result: On ImageBind and LanguageBind: mean bidirectional Recall@10 improved from 18.27% to 31.15% (+12.88%); mean macro Top-1 accuracy improved from 29.01% to 52.43% (+23.42%) across 19 retrieval and 11 classification relations. Controlled analyses confirmed valid hub-edge correspondence and leading spectral directions as key sources of gains.
AI.conclusion: HSA successfully extracts latent multimodal knowledge from frozen representations using only hub-edge statistics, demonstrating that meaningful cross-modal alignment can be achieved without target-pair supervision or gradient-based optimization. The method significantly outperforms baseline approaches on both retrieval and classification tasks.

title: LCAP: Population-Informed Latent Chip Adaptation from Few Output Probes for Photonic Neural Networks
summary: Photonic neural networks (PNNs) offer efficient analog inference, but parameters optimized under ideal device models can degrade after fabrication, creating a persistent simulation-to-hardware (sim-to-real) gap. When many identically designed chips are deployed, calibrating each device from scratch compounds this cost. We propose Latent Chip Adaptation from Probes (LCAP), a population-informed framework that decomposes hardware adaptation into a transferable population correction and probe-inferred latent personalization. LCAP first learns a shared correction from 80 historical chips, then extracts a low-dimensional correction space from device-specific refinements. At deployment, 32 fixed unlabeled output probes infer an unseen chip's latent correction coordinates, enabling feed-forward personalization without target-device optimization. On a three-layer 64-mode MZI simulator with phase variation, beam-splitter errors, quantization, and crosstalk, accuracy improves from 80.4147% under direct deployment to 92.6860% after shared calibration and 93.3617% with LCAP. LCAP improves 27/30 unseen chips and raises worst-device accuracy from 89.18% to 90.54%.

AI.tldr: LCAP addresses the simulation-to-hardware gap in photonic neural networks by using a population-informed approach that learns a shared correction from 80 historical chips, then uses 32 fixed output probes to infer latent correction coordinates for unseen chips, enabling feed-forward personalization without target-device optimization. This achieves 93.36% accuracy vs 80.41% with direct deployment.
AI.motivation: Photonic neural networks optimized under ideal device models suffer performance degradation after fabrication due to variations. Calibrating each chip individually is costly when deploying many identically designed chips. The goal is to reduce the sim-to-real gap and enable efficient deployment of new chips without extensive per-device optimization.
AI.method: LCAP decomposes hardware adaptation into two components: (1) a transferable population correction learned from 80 historical chips, and (2) probe-inferred latent personalization. From device-specific refinements, a low-dimensional correction space is extracted. At deployment, 32 fixed unlabeled output probes infer an unseen chip's latent correction coordinates for feed-forward personalization without requiring target-device optimization. Tested on a three-layer 64-mode MZI simulator with phase variation, beam-splitter errors, quantization, and crosstalk.
AI.result: Accuracy improved from 80.4147% (direct deployment) to 92.6860% (shared calibration) to 93.3617% (with LCAP). LCAP improved 27 out of 30 unseen chips and raised worst-device accuracy from 89.18% to 90.54%.
AI.conclusion: LCAP effectively reduces the sim-to-real gap in photonic neural networks by leveraging population data and probe-based inference. The method enables efficient deployment of new chips without requiring per-device optimization, making it practical for large-scale chip deployment. The approach successfully improves both average and worst-case performance across unseen chips.

title: Never Stop Thinking: Continuous-Time Language Agents
summary: Voice agents built on LLMs follow a rigid listen-think-speak loop that inserts seconds of dead air before every reply. We show that continuous-time cognition (thinking while listening and thinking while speaking) emerges from an unmodified text model under a lightweight interrupt-and-resume orchestrator, cutting live-pipeline latency by 19% overall and by half in the regime the mechanism targets. To measure whether continuous-time thinking improves what agents accomplish, we introduce ReactiveBench: 120 interactive scenarios scored against pre-registered binary requirements, plus a verifiable streaming track scored by exact correctness. ReactiveBench exposes a pitfall with broad consequences: LLM judges reward visible reasoning; a large judged "advantage" of continuous-time thinking reverses sign under an independent judge, and judge-trained models objectively complete fewer requirements when they think. A five-stage training study then locates the right signal at three levels. Its source: verifiable objectives turn thinking from harmful to helpful. Its structure: whatever a uniform reward omits, optimization trades away; brevity everywhere erodes multi-hop tool chaining. Its optimizer: preference optimization can only trade conflicting sub-goals against each other, while on-policy RL over a type-shaped reward improves every correctness axis at once, raising streaming completion from 48% to 73+/-5% across seeds and replicating at larger scale and on a second model. Orchestration makes continuous-time interaction possible; a verifiable signal, correctly sourced, shaped, and optimized, makes it good.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces continuous-time cognition for LLM-based voice agents via a lightweight interrupt-and-resume orchestrator, reducing latency by 19%. It reveals a critical pitfall where LLM judges reward visible reasoning but this advantage reverses under independent evaluation. Through a five-stage training study, the authors demonstrate that verifiable objectives transform thinking from harmful to helpful, and on-policy RL with type-shaped reward achieves the best results, improving streaming completion from 48% to 73%.
AI.motivation: Current LLM voice agents follow a rigid listen-think-speak loop causing seconds of dead air before replies, creating poor user experience. The authors aim to enable continuous-time cognition (thinking while listening and speaking) to reduce latency and improve agent performance in interactive scenarios.
AI.method: The authors (1) implemented a lightweight interrupt-and-resume orchestrator enabling continuous-time thinking in an unmodified text model; (2) created ReactiveBench with 120 interactive scenarios scored against pre-registered binary requirements plus a verifiable streaming track; (3) conducted a five-stage training study examining signal source (verifiable vs uniform objectives), structure (brevity impact on multi-hop tool chaining), and optimizer (preference optimization vs on-policy RL).
AI.result: Continuous-time thinking reduced live-pipeline latency by 19% overall and by half in target regimes. ReactiveBench revealed that LLM judges reward visible reasoning, with a large judged "advantage" reversing sign under independent evaluation. Preference optimization could only trade conflicting sub-goals, while on-policy RL over type-shaped reward improved every correctness axis, raising streaming completion from 48% to 73±5% across seeds and replicating at larger scale and on a second model.
AI.conclusion: Making continuous-time interaction possible requires orchestration, but making it effective requires verifiable objectives (correctly sourced), proper reward structure (avoiding brevity erosion of multi-hop reasoning), and on-policy RL optimization (which outperforms preference optimization for conflicting sub-goals). The key insight is that verifiable signals transform thinking from harmful to helpful.

title: GeoLAM: Learning Geometry-Grounded Latent Actions from Unlabeled Human Videos
summary: Human videos provide rich manipulation experience, but extracting action representations that preserve useful motion remains challenging. Visual reconstruction alone can entangle manipulation-related motion with appearance changes and camera movement.
