The method is trained and evaluated on extended synthetic N-HOT3D and the new EEH-R dataset (largest real-world event-based egocentric hand dataset with ~1M annotated frames).
AI.motivation: Conventional cameras struggle in low-light and severe motion blur. Event cameras offer high dynamic range and temporal resolution but face challenges in egocentric settings where camera wearer's motion produces dense background events obscuring hand signals. Prior egocentric event-based approach used binary hand masks that fail to distinguish between left and right hands, lacking instance-level information and leading to incorrect inter-hand relationships and degraded accuracy.
AI.method: The proposed EventEgoHands++ framework incorporates: (1) Hand Detector - estimates instance-level bounding boxes and masks for both left and right hands; (2) Adaptive Attention - dynamically gates attention based on detection results to accurately learn spatial relationships and mutual interactions between hands. The method is trained on extended synthetic N-HOT3D dataset and newly constructed EEH-R dataset (largest real-world event-based egocentric hand dataset with ~1M annotated frames in various environments including low-light).
AI.result: Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that the method consistently outperforms baselines.
AI.conclusion: The proposed EventEgoHands++ successfully addresses the instance-level hand distinction problem in event-based egocentric 3D hand mesh reconstruction. By incorporating hand detection and adaptive attention mechanisms, the method achieves improved reconstruction accuracy with correct inter-hand relationships, particularly in challenging conditions like low-light environments where conventional cameras fail.

title: Structural Negative Transfer in Federated Graph Neural Networks: Diagnosis, Causal Investigation, and the Limits of Divergence-Aware Mitigation
summary: Federated learning lets multiple participants train a shared model without pooling raw data, by exchanging locally trained model updates instead. Federated averaging assumes that averaging local models is a reasonable way to solve one shared problem when participants' data are broadly similar. Work on non-IID federated learning has shown that this assumption can withstand differences in label and feature distributions. We ask whether it survives a different strain specific to graph neural networks, where client graphs differ not in label or feature distribution but in structure itself, requiring the same shared weights to operate over fundamentally different topologies. We call the resulting harm structural negative transfer. In a federation of real citation networks and synthetic structural proxies, a structurally atypical client lost more than half its achievable accuracy simply by joining. In an initial six-client federation, two label-free structural statistics computable before training were strongly associated with this harm. Expanding to twenty clients showed that degree divergence remained associated with harm, although more weakly, and survived removal of domain contrast. Spectral divergence did not replicate, which we trace to a confound caused by the composition of the reference pool used for leave-one-out statistics. A causal intervention isolating topology found no significant effect. A degree-normalization mechanism held across twenty-four seeds but did not explain the harm when corrected. The best of five candidate fixes beat a tuned baseline only until a matched, structurally blind control was applied, after which the gain disappeared. What survives is a modest, partially replicated, degree-specific signal that is not yet a validated predictor at scale.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates structural negative transfer in federated learning with graph neural networks (GNNs), where clients have different graph topologies rather than different label/feature distributions. The authors find that a structurally atypical client can lose over 50% accuracy by joining a federation. While degree divergence shows a modest, partially replicated association with harm, the effect does not survive rigorous validation at scale.
AI.motivation: Federated learning typically assumes that averaging local models works well when participants' data are similar. While prior work addressed non-IID data in terms of label and feature distributions, the authors ask whether this assumption survives when clients have fundamentally different graph topologies - a unique challenge for GNNs where the same shared weights must operate over different topological structures.
AI.method: The authors conducted experiments using: (1) real citation networks and synthetic structural proxies; (2) initial 6-client federation expanded to 20 clients; (3) two label-free structural statistics - degree divergence and spectral divergence; (4) causal intervention isolating topology; (5) degree-normalization mechanism tested across 24 seeds; (6) five candidate fixes compared against tuned baseline and matched structurally blind control.
AI.result: A structurally atypical client lost more than half its achievable accuracy by joining the federation. Degree divergence showed weak association with harm in 20-client setting and survived removal of domain contrast, but spectral divergence did not replicate due to a confound. A causal intervention isolating topology found no significant effect. The degree-normalization mechanism held across seeds but did not explain the harm when corrected. The best of five candidate fixes beat baseline until a matched structurally blind control was applied, after which the gain disappeared.
AI.conclusion: The only surviving finding is a modest, partially replicated, degree-specific signal that is not yet a validated predictor at scale. The paper concludes that structural negative transfer, while observable in specific cases, may not be a robust or scalable problem in federated GNN learning.

title: Probe-VAD: Ordinal Likelihood Probing for Training-Free Video Anomaly Detection
summary: Video anomaly detection (VAD) aims to localize anomalous events in untrimmed videos. Vision-language models (VLMs) provide rich visual understanding for training-free VAD, but existing approaches impose restrictive interfaces between visual understanding and anomaly scoring. Caption-based pipelines compress visual evidence into text, potentially discarding subtle cues, while direct numerical generation forces the model to express its judgment through a small set of predefined scores. Such interfaces can obscure subtle differences in anomaly severity, causing visually distinct clips to receive similar representations or scores and thereby limiting the resolution of anomaly ranking. We propose \textbf{Probe-VAD}, an ordinal binary-probing framework that directly probes severity preferences from a frozen VLM. Given raw video clips, Probe-VAD queries ten ordered severity thresholds and extracts constrained \textit{YES}/\textit{NO} continuation likelihoods. Their normalized preferences form a cumulative severity profile, from which tail evidence is aggregated into a continuous anomaly score, with isotonic projection enforcing ordinal consistency. Experiments on public VAD benchmarks demonstrate superior performance with low computational cost. Probe-VAD provides a simple interface for translating frozen VLM visual understanding into continuous, rank-sensitive anomaly scores without task-specific training or caption-based compression. Code is available at: https://github.com/yvestine/COVAS-VAD.

AI.tldr: Probe-VAD is a training-free video anomaly detection framework that uses ordinal binary probing to extract continuous anomaly scores from frozen Vision-Language Models (VLMs). It queries ten ordered severity thresholds, extracts YES/NO continuation likelihoods, and forms a cumulative severity profile to score anomalies without task-specific training or caption-based compression.
AI.motivation: Existing VLM-based VAD methods have restrictive interfaces that compress visual evidence into text (potentially losing subtle cues) or force judgment through predefined numerical scores. These limitations obscure subtle differences in anomaly severity, causing visually distinct clips to receive similar representations or scores.
AI.method: Probe-VAD uses an ordinal binary-probing framework: (1) Query ten ordered severity thresholds from a frozen VLM, (2) Extract constrained YES/NO continuation likelihoods for each threshold, (3) Form normalized preferences as a cumulative severity profile, (4) Aggregate tail evidence into a continuous anomaly score, (5) Apply isotonic projection to enforce ordinal consistency.
AI.result: Experiments on public VAD benchmarks demonstrate superior performance with low computational cost. The method provides a simple interface for translating frozen VLM visual understanding into continuous, rank-sensitive anomaly scores.
AI.conclusion: Probe-VAD successfully bridges the gap between VLM visual understanding and anomaly scoring through an ordinal probing approach, eliminating the need for task-specific training or caption-based compression while achieving better performance than existing methods.

title: CLARE: Scalable Class-Incremental Continual Learning via a Sparsity-Based Framework
summary: Continual learning must balance the learning of new knowledge with the retention of previously learned knowledge to incrementally learn tasks from a data stream without catastrophic forgetting. While leveraging pretrained models has significantly advanced continual learning, existing methods exhibit a scalability bottleneck when trained sequentially on many tasks, suffering from performance degradation due to inter-task interference and loss of plasticity. Inspired by evidence that sparse fine-tuning achieves performance comparable to full fine-tuning, this paper presents a novel sparsity-driven continual learning framework. Our continual learning method, termed CLARE, operates in two stages: it first identifies a sparse, task-critical parameter mask via a sparsity-inducing objective, then performs mask-constrained fine-tuning by only optimizing parameters selected by the mask. This two-stage sparse adapter mechanism enables all tasks to be accumulated within a shared adapter space while reducing destructive interference across tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate the scalability of CLARE. On the long task-sequence benchmark Omnibenchmark-1k, CLARE outperforms strong baselines in final accuracy by a large margin, e.g, improving EASE by 4.64% and 13.34% after learning 100 tasks, respectively.

AI.tldr: CLARE is a sparsity-driven continual learning framework that addresses catastrophic forgetting and scalability issues when training pretrained models on sequential tasks. It uses a two-stage approach: first identifying task-critical sparse parameter masks, then performing mask-constrained fine-tuning to reduce inter-task interference.
AI.motivation: Existing continual learning methods with pretrained models face a scalability bottleneck when trained sequentially on many tasks, suffering from performance degradation due to inter-task interference and loss of plasticity. The work is inspired by evidence that sparse fine-tuning can achieve performance comparable to full fine-tuning.
AI.method: CLARE operates in two stages: (1) identifies a sparse, task-critical parameter mask via a sparsity-inducing objective, then (2) performs mask-constrained fine-tuning by only optimizing parameters selected by the mask. This two-stage sparse adapter mechanism enables all tasks to be accumulated within a shared adapter space while reducing destructive interference across tasks.
AI.result: On the long task-sequence benchmark Omnibenchmark-1k, CLARE outperforms strong baselines in final accuracy by a large margin, e.g., improving EASE by 4.64% and 13.34% after learning 100 tasks.
AI.conclusion: Sparsity-driven continual learning effectively addresses catastrophic forgetting and scalability issues. The two-stage sparse adapter mechanism enables efficient accumulation of many tasks in a shared adapter space while reducing destructive interference across tasks.

title: InfoTaxa: Information-Calibrated Label-Free Clustering for Fine-Grained Visual Taxonomy
summary: Label-free clustering of frozen pretrained visual embeddings offers a scalable route to biodiversity monitoring, but image-only fine-grained taxonomy exhibits a consistent coarse-to-fine failure mode: clusters recover broad taxonomic structure yet plateau at species level. We study this behaviour on BIOSCAN-5M through an information-calibrated clustering analysis. BioCLIP~2 features with UMAP and HDBSCAN reach $0.79$ AMI at family and $0.67$ at genus, substantially improving over the prior image baseline and remaining competitive with oracle-$K$, graph-based, and learned clustering heads on the same frozen features. To diagnose whether the remaining plateau is method-limited or information-limited, we introduce InfoTaxa, which combines clustering efficiency---the fraction of probe-estimated image information recovered by an unsupervised partition---with paired DNA as an audit signal only, not an inference input. The density pipeline recovers approximately $0.90$ and $0.81$ of the image-available information at order and family, respectively. Held-out late-fusion probes show that adding DNA to the image embedding reduces species-level prediction error by approximately two bits. Robustness analyses cover multiple image encoders, described-species and rare-class subsets, probe diagnostics, and held-out-species coarse-rank generalisation and same-species retrieval. Thus, in the tested setting, species-level label-free clustering is both clustering-limited and representation-limited: improved clustering may recover additional image-exposed structure, but cannot close the DNA-audited information gap alone.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the "coarse-to-fine failure mode" in label-free clustering of frozen pretrained visual embeddings for biodiversity monitoring, where clusters recover broad taxonomic structure but plateau at species level. The authors introduce InfoTaxa, which uses DNA as an audit signal (not inference input) to diagnose whether the limitation is method-limited or information-limited.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand why image-only fine-grained taxonomy fails at species-level clustering despite success at broader taxonomic levels (family, genus). The authors aim to diagnose whether this limitation is due to clustering algorithms or the image representations themselves.
AI.method: 1) BioCLIP visual features with UMAP dimensionality reduction and HDBSCAN clustering; 2) InfoTaxa - combining clustering efficiency (fraction of probe-estimated image information recovered) with paired DNA as an audit signal only; 3) Density pipeline for information recovery estimation; 4) Late-fusion probes adding DNA to image embedding
AI.result: BioCLIP+UMAP+HDBSCAN achieves 0.79 AMI at family and 0.67 at genus, substantially improving over prior image baseline. Density pipeline recovers ~0.90 and 0.81 of image-available information at order and family respectively. Adding DNA reduces species-level prediction error by ~2 bits. Species-level clustering is both clustering-limited and representation-limited.
AI.conclusion: Species-level label-free clustering is both clustering-limited and representation-limited. Improved clustering algorithms may recover additional image-exposed structure, but cannot close the DNA-audited information gap alone. DNA provides complementary information that image embeddings alone cannot capture.

title: Distributed JEPA: A Self-Supervised Framework for Energy Forecasting
summary: Traditional energy forecasting solutions rely on task-specific supervision and energy asset representations, limiting transferability and the ability to capture general temporal dynamics across heterogeneous assets. We address this by proposing a distributed Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for self-supervised learning from heterogeneous energy time-series. The framework predicts latent representations of masked temporal segments while integrating temporal observations and contextual information within a shared embedding space. To prevent representation collapse, training combines a latent-space predictive objective with covariance and temporal variance regularization. The evaluation was conducted on energy consumption and generation datasets under data-degradation scenarios and compared with a Transformer forecasting baseline. The learned representations remained stable (cosine similarity $\approx 0.98$; effective rank 185-235). JEPA achieved performance comparable to a Transformer on building energy data, higher $R^2$ in 3/5 consumer clusters, and outperformed the baseline on 9/10 unseen PVs ($R^2$=0.73-0.88 vs. <0.45), while showing greater robustness to missing data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a distributed Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for self-supervised learning from heterogeneous energy time-series. The framework predicts latent representations of masked temporal segments while integrating temporal observations and contextual information within a shared embedding space. JEPA achieved comparable performance to Transformers on building energy data, higher R² in 3/5 consumer clusters, and outperformed the baseline on 9/10 unseen PVs (R²=0.73-0.88 vs. <0.45), while showing greater robustness to missing data.
AI.motivation: Traditional energy forecasting solutions rely on task-specific supervision and energy asset representations, which limits transferability and the ability to capture general temporal dynamics across heterogeneous assets. This limitation motivates the development of a more通用 and transferable approach.
AI.method: The proposed JEPA framework predicts latent representations of masked temporal segments while integrating temporal observations and contextual information within a shared embedding space. To prevent representation collapse, training combines a latent-space predictive objective with covariance and temporal variance regularization. Evaluation was conducted on energy consumption and generation datasets under data-degradation scenarios and compared with a Transformer forecasting baseline.
AI.result: The learned representations remained stable (cosine similarity ≈ 0.98; effective rank 185-235). JEPA achieved performance comparable to a Transformer on building energy data, higher R² in 3/5 consumer clusters, and outperformed the baseline on 9/10 unseen PVs (R²=0.73-0.88 vs. <0.45), while showing greater robustness to missing data.
AI.conclusion: The proposed JEPA framework demonstrates strong transferability and robustness to missing data in energy forecasting tasks, outperforming Transformer baselines on unseen PV systems while maintaining stable representation learning.

title: FROD: Feature Matching Residual Denoising Oracle Bone Decipher
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at ICONIP 2026
summary: Oracle bone script (OBS), one of the earliest Chinese writing systems, plays an important role in the study of Chinese etymology. Traditional decipherment relies heavily on domain experts who analyze characters through semantic context and structural evolution. To assist this labor-intensive process, we formulate OBS decipherment assistance as a cross-era image translation task and propose FROD (Feature Matching Residual Denoising Oracle Bone Decipher). Although many OBS characters differ substantially from their modern counterparts, they often preserve local topological invariants at the radical level. During training, FROD leverages fast feature matching to provide gated segmentation supervision: paired samples with sufficient matches are processed patch-wise to align fine-grained radicals, whereas low-similarity pairs are trained holistically to avoid mismatched artifacts. In addition, a Residual Denoising Diffusion Model (RDDM) jointly estimates noise and residual signals, thereby reducing the positional drift and stroke disorder commonly observed in standard diffusion models. Finally, a multi-stage font stylization refinement network refines the generated images by eliminating edge noise and stabilizing stroke structures. On our augmented character-disjoint dataset, FROD achieves higher Top-1 recognition accuracy than the evaluated baselines, with a 3.8% absolute gain over OBSD.

AI.tldr: FROD is a deep learning framework that assists Oracle Bone Script (OBS) decipherment by treating it as a cross-era image translation task, using feature matching for gated segmentation supervision, a Residual Denoising Diffusion Model (RDDM), and a multi-stage font stylization refinement network.
AI.motivation: Traditional OBS decipherment relies heavily on domain experts analyzing characters through semantic context and structural evolution, which is labor-intensive. The paper aims to automate this process by leveraging the fact that OBS characters often preserve local topological invariants at the radical level despite substantial differences from modern characters.
AI.method: FROD uses three key components: (1) Fast feature matching to provide gated segmentation supervision - paired samples with sufficient matches are processed patch-wise to align fine-grained radicals, while low-similarity pairs are trained holistically to avoid mismatched artifacts; (2) A Residual Denoising Diffusion Model (RDDM) that jointly estimates noise and residual signals to reduce positional drift and stroke disorder; (3) A multi-stage font stylization refinement network to eliminate edge noise and stabilize stroke structures.
AI.result: On an augmented character-disjoint dataset, FROD achieves higher Top-1 recognition accuracy than evaluated baselines, with a 3.8% absolute gain over OBSD.
AI.conclusion: FROD successfully addresses the challenges of OBS decipherment through its innovative feature matching and residual denoising approach, demonstrating significant improvement over existing methods and providing a valuable tool for assisting experts in Oracle Bone Script decipherment.

title: Learning Options for Compositional Motor Control with Adapter Banks
summary: Learning flexible motor primitives is a hallmark of skilled motor control. Recent neuroscience theory proposes that motor primitives may be implemented as low-rank perturbations of a shared recurrent network, but leaves open how such a system is learned. We translate this principle into a novel architecture for learning motor skills end-to-end: a shared recurrent core modulated by a bank of residual adapters, each selected by a discrete latent code. Trained on closed-loop biomechanical control, the adapters develop emergent low-rank perturbations of the recurrent dynamics despite no architectural rank constraint, placing task representations in disparate subspaces of the shared core network. A simple high-level policy over the learned options, optimized while the whole network is frozen, sequences the low-rank adapters to produce novel out-of-distribution movements. We demonstrate the ability to generalize to novel motor sequences within the closed-loop control setting, improving on the generalization error of a task-input-conditioned multitask baseline by upto order of magnitude.

AI.tldr: A novel architecture for learning motor skills using a shared recurrent core modulated by residual adapters selected via discrete latent codes. The system learns low-rank perturbations of recurrent dynamics without architectural constraints, enabling generalization to novel motor sequences in closed-loop biomechanical control.
AI.motivation: Motor primitives are a hallmark of skilled motor control. Neuroscience theory suggests they may be implemented as low-rank perturbations of shared recurrent networks, but how such a system is learned remained unknown. This work addresses this gap by translating the neuroscience principle into a learnable architecture.
AI.method: The architecture consists of: (1) a shared recurrent core network, (2) a bank of residual adapters, each selected by a discrete latent code, and (3) a high-level policy over learned options. The adapters develop emergent low-rank perturbations of recurrent dynamics without explicit rank constraints. The high-level policy is optimized while the entire network is frozen to sequence the low-rank adapters for novel movements.
AI.result: The method demonstrates generalization to novel motor sequences within closed-loop control settings. It improves generalization error of a task-input-conditioned multitask baseline by up to an order of magnitude, with task representations placed in disparate subspaces of the shared core network.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture successfully translates neuroscience theory into a practical learning system. The emergent low-rank structure enables effective motor skill learning and generalization, suggesting that discrete latent codes combined with residual adapters provide a powerful framework for flexible motor control in robotics and biomechanics.

title: DecoGS: Adaptive Static-Dynamic Decoupling of 3D Gaussians for Free-Viewpoint Video Streaming
summary: Streaming 3D reconstruction demands both speed and temporal fidelity, goals that existing methods undermine by updating every Gaussian every frame, even in static regions. We present DecoGS, a method for efficient online training of 3D Gaussians from streaming videos. Unlike prior methods that update the entire scene indiscriminately, DecoGS introduces an adaptive mechanism that selectively focuses optimization on spatiotemporal regions exhibiting motion or photometric changes. This targeted training strategy eliminates redundant updates that cause flickering and drift in nominally static regions, while enabling fast, high-fidelity scene updates. The pipeline further integrates region-aware Gaussian management through gradient gating and efficient visibility filtering to maintain temporal coherence and a compact memory footprint. On N3DV and MeetRoom, DecoGS achieves 34.55 and 31.60 dB PSNR respectively, outperforming all streaming and offline baselines, while rendering at 261 FPS with $70\times$ lower temporal flicker than the best prior method, requiring no large-scale pretraining.

AI.tldr: DecoGS is a method for efficient online 3D Gaussian reconstruction from streaming videos that uses adaptive optimization to selectively update only regions with motion or photometric changes, achieving state-of-the-art PSNR (34.55 dB on N3DV, 31.60 dB on MeetRoom) at 261 FPS with 70× lower temporal flicker than prior methods, without requiring large-scale pretraining.
AI.motivation: Existing streaming 3D reconstruction methods update every Gaussian every frame, even in static regions, which causes inefficiencies, flickering, and drift. The goal is to achieve both speed and temporal fidelity in online 3D Gaussian training from streaming videos.
AI.method: DecoGS introduces: (1) an adaptive mechanism that selectively focuses optimization on spatiotemporal regions with motion or photometric changes; (2) region-aware Gaussian management through gradient gating; (3) efficient visibility filtering to maintain temporal coherence and compact memory footprint.
AI.result: On N3DV: 34.55 dB PSNR; On MeetRoom: 31.60 dB PSNR; Rendering at 261 FPS; 70× lower temporal flicker than the best prior method; no large-scale pretraining required.
AI.conclusion: DecoGS outperforms all streaming and offline baselines while maintaining high rendering speed and temporal coherence, demonstrating that selective optimization is more effective than full-scene updates for streaming 3D reconstruction.

title: Repurposing Unified Topological Signatures for Graph Representation Learning
summary: Message-passing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) iteratively propagate and aggregate local neighborhood information followed by global readout to learn graph representations. However, their discriminative power is upper-bounded by the Weisfeiler--Lehman (1-WL) graph isomorphism test. This prevents GNNs from distinguishing certain non-isomorphic graphs with identical local neighborhood structures, often leading to similar graph representations. Unified Topological Signatures (UTS) capture compact, multi-scale representation of global graph topology derived from persistent homology. We introduce two complementary UTS signatures: Graph_UTS- a static signature of the input graph topology, and Embedding_UTS- a dynamic signature of the evolving embedding topology. They encode structural information inaccessible to 1-WL-based message-passing GNNs, yet their capabilities are explored solely for post-hoc embedding-space analysis. We integrate UTS into GNN training across three architectural interventions: (i) UTS-Aug: augmenting with standard readout feature that encodes graph's true topology; (ii) UTS-Reg: topological regularizer that constrains representation collapse; (iii) UTS-Pool: topology-guided pooling that retains structurally critical nodes. We further leverage UTS as a layer-wise diagnostic to quantify oversmoothing during GNN training. Theoretically, we show that integrating UTS into GNN optimization strictly extends GNN expressivity beyond the 1-WL hierarchy. Experiments on three graph classification benchmarks show consistent benefits: Graph-UTS, Dual-UTS, and UTS-Pool improve accuracy across all three datasets, Embedding-UTS provides smaller but similarly consistent gains, and UTS-Reg's benefit varies across graph domains. Accuracy improves by up to 5.8% with Graph-UTS augmentation, by up to 1.9% with UTS-Reg, and achieves comparable performance to TOGL with UTS-Pool.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Unified Topological Signatures (UTS) to enhance Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) beyond the 1-WL test limitation. It proposes three architectural interventions (UTS-Aug, UTS-Reg, UTS-Pool) that integrate topological information into GNN training, achieving up to 5.8% accuracy improvement on graph classification benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Message-passing GNNs are limited by the Weisfeiler-Lehman (1-WL) graph isomorphism test, meaning they cannot distinguish certain non-isomorphic graphs with identical local neighborhood structures. This limits their discriminative power and expressivity.
AI.method: The authors propose two UTS signatures: Graph_UTS (static signature of input graph topology) and Embedding_UTS (dynamic signature of evolving embedding topology). They integrate UTS into GNN training through three architectural interventions: (1) UTS-Aug: augmenting standard readout with topological features; (2) UTS-Reg: topological regularizer to prevent representation collapse; (3) UTS-Pool: topology-guided pooling to retain structurally critical nodes. They also use UTS as a layer-wise diagnostic for oversmoothing.
AI.result: Experiments on three graph classification benchmarks show: Graph-UTS improves accuracy by up to 5.8%, UTS-Reg by up to 1.9%, and UTS-Pool achieves comparable performance to TOGL. Embedding-UTS provides smaller but consistent gains, while UTS-Reg's benefit varies across domains.
AI.conclusion: Integrating UTS into GNN optimization strictly extends GNN expressivity beyond the 1-WL hierarchy. The proposed methods consistently improve graph classification accuracy, with Graph-UTS showing the largest gains.

title: Video-HolmesV2: Can MLLMs Reason with Spatio-Temporal Audio-Visual Evidence in Long Videos?
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models have demonstrated impressive video understanding, yet their ability to reason over long-form narratives is often masked by visual-centric evaluations and inefficient context processing. Existing benchmarks over-rely on visual heuristics while marginalizing auditory cues, effectively reducing models to "silent observers" that bypass genuine cross-modal reasoning. Moreover, standard dense sampling creates an evidence-context trade-off: increasing frames to capture evidence inevitably leads to attention distraction and token explosion. To bridge these gaps, we present Video-HolmesV2, a novel benchmark designed for Deep Audio-Visual Coupling. Unlike previous works, it enforces an Evidence-Based Evaluation, requiring models to justify answers with precise spatio-temporal audio-visual evidence, thereby reducing confounding effects of guessing and hallucinated evidence. To support this, we introduce: (1) a Multi-Model Cross-Verification pipeline to ensure task rigor; (2) a Spatio-temporal Evidence-Aware Metric for fine-grained calibration. Furthermore, we propose an Audio-Text Guided Token Compression framework. By fusing task intent with auditory anchors, our method distills high-value reasoning cues to mitigate long-context noise. In our evaluation, even strong proprietary models achieve below 60% accuracy, while our approach outperforms comparable open-source omni-models.

AI.tldr: Video-HolmesV2 is a benchmark for evaluating multimodal LLMs on deep audio-visual reasoning in long-form video narratives, featuring evidence-based evaluation and an audio-text guided token compression method to address limitations in current video understanding benchmarks that over-rely on visual cues and inefficient context processing.
AI.motivation: Current video understanding benchmarks and models have three key limitations: (1) over-reliance on visual heuristics while marginalizing audio cues, effectively treating models as "silent observers"; (2) dense sampling creates an evidence-context trade-off where more frames lead to attention distraction and token explosion; (3) existing evaluations lack rigorous evidence-based assessment, allowing guessing and hallucinated evidence to confound results.
AI.method: The paper proposes three innovations: (1) Video-HolmesV2 benchmark with Evidence-Based Evaluation requiring precise spatio-temporal audio-visual evidence justification; (2) Multi-Model Cross-Verification pipeline for task rigor; (3) Spatio-temporal Evidence-Aware Metric for fine-grained calibration. Additionally, an Audio-Text Guided Token Compression framework is introduced that fuses task intent with auditory anchors to distill high-value reasoning cues and mitigate long-context noise.
AI.result: Evaluation shows that even strong proprietary models achieve below 60% accuracy on the benchmark, while the proposed approach outperforms comparable open-source omni-models.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that current multimodal LLMs have significant limitations in true cross-modal audio-visual reasoning. The proposed benchmark and compression framework provide more rigorous evaluation and improved performance, though substantial room for improvement remains as even leading models fall below 60% accuracy.

title: High-Fidelity Digital Twin Data Models by Randomized Dynamic Mode Decomposition and Deep Learning with Applications in Fluid Dynamics
summary: The purpose of this paper is the identification of high-fidelity digital twin data models from numerical code outputs by non-intrusive techniques (i.e., not requiring Galerkin projection of the governing equations onto the reduced modes basis). In this paper the author defines the concept of the digital twin data model (DTM) as a model of reduced complexity that has the main feature of mirroring the original process behavior. The significant advantage of a DTM is to reproduce the dynamics with high accuracy and reduced costs in CPU time and hardware for settings difficult to explore because of the complexity of the dynamics over time. This paper introduces a new framework for creating efficient digital twin data models by combining two state-of-the-art tools: randomized dynamic mode decomposition and deep learning artificial intelligence. It is shown that the outputs are consistent with the original source data with the advantage of reduced complexity. The DTMs are investigated in the numerical simulation of three shock wave phenomena with increasing complexity. The author performs a thorough assessment of the performance of the new digital twin data models in terms of numerical accuracy and computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a new framework for creating high-fidelity digital twin data models (DTMs) by combining randomized dynamic mode decomposition and deep learning AI. The non-intrusive technique identifies reduced-complexity models that mirror original process behavior while maintaining accuracy and reducing computational costs. The method is validated on three shock wave phenomena with increasing complexity.
AI.motivation: The need for efficient digital twins that can reproduce complex dynamic behaviors with high accuracy while significantly reducing CPU time and hardware requirements. Traditional high-fidelity simulations are computationally expensive for settings with complex dynamics over time.
AI.method: Non-intrusive technique combining randomized dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) with deep learning artificial intelligence. Does not require Galerkin projection of governing equations onto reduced modes basis.
AI.result: The digital twin data models produce outputs consistent with original source data while achieving reduced complexity. The framework was validated through numerical simulations of three shock wave phenomena with increasing complexity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables efficient creation of digital twin data models that achieve good numerical accuracy and computational efficiency for shock wave simulations, offering a promising approach for reduced-order modeling of complex dynamic systems.

title: Exploring 2D backbone effects for indoor semantic occupancy prediction
summary: Semantic occupancy prediction gives an embodied agent a voxel-level account of where space is free, occupied, and semantically meaningful. In RGB-D pipelines such as EmbodiedScan, the image encoder is often left as a default module, even though its features are the visual evidence later sampled into the 3D grid. We study this design choice directly. A central finding is that changing the 2D backbone improves occupancy accuracy more than several carefully designed occupancy architectures or modules. We keep the main RGB-D projection, depth branch, and occupancy head fixed, and replace only the image backbone. The compared encoders are CLIP-ResNet, CLIP-ViT, BLIP2, and DINOv2. Under the controlled setting, the measured mIoU changes substantially: DINOv2 obtains 30.55\%, BLIP2 obtains 29.49\%, CLIP-ViT obtains 24.33\%, and CLIP-ResNet obtains 17.41\%. The stronger encoders also exceed the original EmbodiedScan ResNet-50 baseline without modifying the downstream 3D fusion pipeline. Class-level results give a more detailed picture: DINOv2 is stronger on many layout and structural categories, whereas BLIP2 remains close on several object-centered classes. CLIP-ViT improves clearly over CLIP-ResNet, showing that the way CLIP features are exposed as dense tokens matters for voxel lifting. These results indicate that the image backbone is not a secondary engineering detail in embodied semantic occupancy, but a major source of variation in the final 3D prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the importance of the 2D image backbone in RGB-D pipelines for semantic occupancy prediction in embodied AI. The key finding is that the image encoder is a major source of variation in final 3D predictions, with changing the backbone proving more impactful than several occupancy architecture designs.
AI.motivation: The authors observed that in RGB-D pipelines like EmbodiedScan, the image encoder is often left as a default module, even though its features are later sampled into the 3D grid. They wanted to systematically study whether this design choice is optimal.
AI.method: The authors kept the main RGB-D projection, depth branch, and occupancy head fixed while only replacing the image backbone. They compared four encoders: CLIP-ResNet, CLIP-ViT, BLIP2, and DINOv2 under controlled settings.
AI.result: DINOv2 achieved 30.55% mIoU, BLIP2 achieved 29.49%, CLIP-ViT achieved 24.33%, and CLIP-ResNet achieved 17.41%. DINOv2 performed better on layout and structural categories, while BLIP2 remained competitive on object-centered classes. CLIP-ViT showed significant improvement over CLIP-ResNet, demonstrating that the way CLIP features are exposed as dense tokens matters for voxel lifting.
AI.conclusion: The image backbone is not a secondary engineering detail but a major source of variation in embodied semantic occupancy prediction. Stronger encoders can exceed the original baseline without modifying the downstream 3D fusion pipeline.

title: Neural Field Ensembles for Aerodynamic Surface Prediction: Winning Solution to the ONERA CRM Wall Distribution 2025 Challenge
summary: Machine-learning surrogate models offer a promising alternative to high-fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations for aerodynamic analysis and design. However, constructing accurate surrogates for realistic aircraft configurations remain challenging due to complex geometries, multiple flow regimes, and limited training data. This work presents the methodology that achieved first place in the ONERA CRM Wall Distribution Regression Challenge, which focuses on predicting pressure and skin-friction coefficient distributions over the NASA Common Research Model wing-body-pylon-nacelle configuration under different operating conditions. The proposed approach formulates the problem as a conditional neural field mapping spatial coordinates, surface normals, and operating conditions to aerodynamic wall quantities. Fourier feature encoding, a relative squared error objective aligned with the challenge metric, ensemble learning, and $k$-fold cross-validation are progressively introduced to improve prediction accuracy and exploit the limited training data. Beyond presenting the final methodology, the paper documents the successive model design choices that led to the winning solution through a comprehensive ablation study and discusses several alternative approaches that were investigated but ultimately discarded. On the hidden competition test set, the proposed methodology achieves an overall score of 8.81, outperforming the strongest organizer-provided baseline, which achieved a score of 8.64, while requiring approximately three orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters. These results illustrate that carefully designed coordinate-based neural fields constitute an efficient and robust framework for aerodynamic surrogate modeling on complex geometries under limited-data conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a neural field-based surrogate model that won the ONERA CRM Wall Distribution Regression Challenge for predicting pressure and skin-friction coefficient distributions over a NASA Common Research Model wing-body-pylon-nacelle configuration. The approach uses Fourier feature encoding, ensemble learning, and k-fold cross-validation to achieve superior accuracy with three orders of magnitude fewer parameters than baselines.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity CFD simulations are computationally expensive for aerodynamic analysis. Machine learning surrogates offer an alternative but struggle with complex geometries, multiple flow regimes, and limited training data. This challenge addresses predicting aerodynamic wall quantities for realistic aircraft configurations.
AI.method: The approach formulates the problem as a conditional neural field mapping spatial coordinates, surface normals, and operating conditions to aerodynamic wall quantities. Key techniques include: Fourier feature encoding, relative squared error objective (aligned with challenge metric), ensemble learning, and k-fold cross-validation. A comprehensive ablation study documented the progressive improvements.
AI.result: On the hidden competition test set, the methodology achieves an overall score of 8.81, outperforming the strongest organizer-provided baseline (8.64) while requiring approximately three orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: Carefully designed coordinate-based neural fields constitute an efficient and robust framework for aerodynamic surrogate modeling on complex geometries under limited-data conditions, achieving state-of-the-art performance with significantly reduced model complexity.

title: Semantic-Spatial Agreement Verification for Mitigating Object Hallucination in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal large language models generate natural-language responses from visual inputs, yet may mention objects absent from an image. In medication assistance, accessible perception, and environmental decision-making, such hallucinations can create real-world safety risks. We propose Semantic-Spatial Agreement Verification (SSAV), a training-free method for verifying object claims. A visually grounded claim should remain stable across semantically equivalent queries and repeatedly localize to the same image region. SSAV aggregates multiple prompts to estimate semantic support and reduce sensitivity to query wording. Query-Induced Regional Verification (QIRV) combines cross-query region persistence, spatial overlap, and relative candidate dominance to identify isolated high responses and dispersed localizations. A geometric mean fuses semantic and spatial evidence, lowering the verification score when either branch lacks support. Experiments on three base models and multiple evaluation protocols show that SSAV effectively mitigates object hallucination. On LLaVA-1.5-7B, accuracy averaged across COCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA improves by 1.81 and 3.17 percentage points under POPE Popular and Adversarial, respectively, while CHAIRs decreases from 49.40% to 32.80%. These results show that cross-query semantic stability and regional consistency provide interpretable external visual evidence for object claims.

AI.tldr: SSAV is a training-free method that verifies object claims in multimodal LLM outputs by checking semantic stability across multiple query phrasings and spatial consistency through repeated localization to the same image regions.
AI.motivation: Multimodal large language models can hallucinate non-existent objects in images, creating safety risks in critical applications like medication assistance, accessibility, and environmental decision-making. Existing methods lack interpretable external visual evidence for verification.
AI.method: SSAV aggregates multiple prompts to estimate semantic support and reduce sensitivity to query wording. Query-Induced Regional Verification (QIRV) combines cross-query region persistence, spatial overlap, and relative candidate dominance to identify isolated high responses and dispersed localizations. A geometric mean fuses semantic and spatial evidence.
AI.result: On LLaVA-1.5-7B, accuracy averaged across COCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA improves by 1.81 and 3.17 percentage points under POPE Popular and Adversarial settings, while CHAIRs (hallucination metric) decreases from 49.40% to 32.80%.
AI.conclusion: Cross-query semantic stability and regional consistency provide interpretable external visual evidence for object claims, effectively mitigating object hallucination in multimodal LLMs without requiring additional training.

title: A unified framework for global and local interpretability using adaptive derivative-ordered random explanation
summary: The interpretability of complex machine learning models is of paramount importance, especially in real-world high-stakes domains such as healthcare and finance. However, existing post-hoc interpretability methods suffer from inherent limitations: fragmented analytical processes, inadequate capacity to model nonlinear feature interactions, computational inefficiencies, and over-reliance on specific model architectures. To address these challenges, this paper provides a novel method - Adaptive Derivative-Ordered Random Explanation (ADORE) - that leverages first- and second-order derivatives to accommodate nonlinear model complexities, while enabling effective capture of feature-sample interactions within a unified analytical framework. ADORE integrates global feature importance with local sample contributions, precisely quantifying feature impact by capturing both magnitude and direction, and identifying critical samples influencing model decisions. Furthermore, it achieves computational efficiency through randomized singular value decomposition (SVD) and dynamic sparsity detection, making it scalable to large, high-dimensional datasets. Experiments across three data modalities - tabular, text, and image - demonstrate that ADORE outperforms existing methods such as LIME and SHAP in handling complex interactions and computational efficiency, while providing detailed and reliable explanations. To facilitate adoption and reproducibility, ADORE has been released as an open-source Python package, hosted on GitHub, enabling researchers and practitioners to readily adapt and apply our approach to their specific tasks, models, and datasets.

AI.tldr: ADORE (Adaptive Derivative-Ordered Random Explanation) is a novel post-hoc interpretability method that uses first- and second-order derivatives to explain complex machine learning models, integrating global feature importance with local sample contributions while achieving computational efficiency through randomized SVD and dynamic sparsity detection.
AI.motivation: Existing post-hoc interpretability methods suffer from limitations: fragmented analytical processes, inadequate capacity for nonlinear feature interactions, computational inefficiencies, and over-reliance on specific model architectures. There is a need for a unified, scalable approach that can handle complex models in high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance.
AI.method: ADORE leverages first- and second-order derivatives to capture nonlinear model complexities. It integrates global feature importance with local sample contributions, quantifying feature impact by capturing both magnitude and direction. Critical samples influencing model decisions are identified. Computational efficiency is achieved through randomized singular value decomposition (SVD) and dynamic sparsity detection.
AI.result: Experiments across three data modalities (tabular, text, and image) demonstrate that ADORE outperforms existing methods (LIME and SHAP) in handling complex interactions and computational efficiency, while providing detailed and reliable explanations.
AI.conclusion: ADORE provides a more effective and efficient approach to model interpretability compared to existing methods. It has been released as an open-source Python package on GitHub for adoption and reproducibility.

title: Optical-Flow Wingbeat Counting in MuJoCo: A Comparison of Convolutional, Spiking, and Attention-Based Temporal Models
comment: 12 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Controlled simulation study
summary: Visual monitoring of flapping-wing vehicles requires distinguishing individual wingbeats from motion strength and average frequency. This paper presents a controlled MuJoCo evaluation of wingbeat counting from signed optical flow observed by virtual cameras mounted on Crazyflie vehicles. Three flapping-wing models were recorded at optical distances of 1.5 and 3.0 m, producing 1,440 clips from 240 paired scene configurations with a scene-level 3:1 training-test split. A common spatial convolutional encoder was combined with a causal temporal convolutional network, a recurrent leaky integrate-and-fire spiking network, or causal self-attention. Each model predicted phase and activity, followed by the same directed-crossing event counter. The six existing convolutional models were retained, and all twelve new models were frozen before their test predictions were generated. Exact-count accuracies at 1.5 m were 96.67%, 95.00%, and 96.67%, respectively; at 3.0 m they were 94.44%, 92.22%, and 95.00%. All paired scene-bootstrap intervals for differences in exact-count accuracy included zero. Seven far-distance spiking-model clips had correct totals despite event-timing mismatches, demonstrating why total-count and event-level measurements must be reported together. The results support the feasibility of causal optical-flow counting in the tested setting and identify boundary-sensitive errors. They do not establish an architecture ranking across repeated training, real-flight robustness, or hardware efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates wingbeat counting from signed optical flow in flapping-wing vehicles using MuJoCo simulation. Three encoder-architecture combinations (temporal CNN, spiking network, self-attention) were tested on 1,440 video clips at 1.5m and 3.0m distances, achieving 92-97% exact-count accuracies with no significant architectural differences.
AI.motivation: Visual monitoring of flapping-wing vehicles requires distinguishing individual wingbeats from motion strength and average frequency. This is challenging because wingbeat motion must be isolated from general movement patterns.
AI.method: Controlled MuJoCo evaluation using signed optical flow from virtual cameras on Crazyflie vehicles. Three flapping-wing models were recorded at optical distances of 1.5m and 3.0m, producing 1,440 clips from 240 paired scene configurations (3:1 train-test split). A common spatial convolutional encoder was combined with: (1) causal temporal convolutional network, (2) recurrent leaky integrate-and-fire spiking network, or (3) causal self-attention. Each model predicted phase and activity, followed by a directed-crossing event counter.
AI.result: Exact-count accuracies at 1.5m were 96.67% (CNN), 95.00% (spiking), 96.67% (self-attention); at 3.0m they were 94.44%, 92.22%, and 95.00% respectively. All bootstrap intervals for accuracy differences included zero, indicating no significant architectural differences. Seven far-distance spiking-model clips had correct totals despite event-timing mismatches, highlighting the need to report both total-count and event-level measurements.
AI.conclusion: The results support the feasibility of causal optical-flow counting for wingbeat monitoring in the tested setting and identify boundary-sensitive errors. However, the study does not establish an architecture ranking across repeated training, real-flight robustness, or hardware efficiency. Future work should address these limitations and test in real-world conditions.

title: IRENE: A Convolutional GRU Ensemble Model for Radar Precipitation Nowcasting over Italy
summary: We present IRENE (Italian Radar Ensemble Nowcasting Experiment), a deep learning model for probabilistic short-range precipitation nowcasting over the Italian domain at \SI{1}{km} spatial and 5 min temporal resolution. IRENE adopts an encoder--forecaster architecture built on multi-scale Convolutional Gated Recurrent Units (ConvGRUs), trained on the national radar composite produced by the Italian Civil Protection Department (DPC). An importance-sampling scheme focuses training on precipitation-relevant events, while the almost-fair Continuous Ranked Probability Score (afCRPS) is adopted as the primary probabilistic loss function. Two additional training configurations are proposed: an adversarial (GAN) variant, IRENE-GAN, designed to improve the spatial sharpness of the generated forecasts, and a spectrally constrained variant, IRENE-GAN-RAPSD, in which the adversarial objective is complemented by an explicit penalty on the radially averaged power spectral density. The three configurations are evaluated against the stochastic extrapolation method STEPS and the pre-trained deep learning model DGMR. All IRENE configurations attain a lower Continuous Ranked Probability Score than both benchmarks at every lead time and rank histograms closer to uniformity, indicating better probabilistic skill and ensemble calibration. In terms of ensemble-mean mean absolute error the advantage is confined to the first 90 min, beyond which the strongly damped DGMR fields and, to a lesser extent, STEPS become competitive. Spectral analysis shows that the adversarial training removes the progressive loss of small-scale variance exhibited by IRENE, at the cost of an excess of fine-scale power at long lead times that the spectral penalty only partially controls.

AI.tldr: IRENE is a deep learning model for probabilistic short-range precipitation nowcasting over Italy at 1km/5min resolution, using encoder-forecaster architecture with ConvGRUs. It includes GAN and spectrally-constrained variants, outperforming STEPS and DGMR in probabilistic skill but with advantages limited to first 90 minutes for ensemble-mean MAE.
AI.motivation: Need for accurate probabilistic short-range precipitation nowcasting in Italy, with existing methods (STEPS, DGMR) having limitations in probabilistic skill, ensemble calibration, or maintaining small-scale variance at longer lead times.
AI.method: Encoder-forecaster architecture with multi-scale ConvGRUs trained on Italian radar composite using importance-sampling and afCRPS loss. Two additional variants: IRENE-GAN (adversarial training for spatial sharpness) and IRENE-GAN-RAPSD (spectral penalty on radially averaged power spectral density).
AI.result: All IRENE configurations achieve lower CRPS than benchmarks at every lead time with rank histograms closer to uniformity, indicating better probabilistic skill and ensemble calibration. Ensemble-mean MAE advantage confined to first 90 min. Adversarial training removes progressive small-scale variance loss but causes excess fine-scale power at long lead times, partially controlled by spectral penalty.
AI.conclusion: IRENE outperforms STEPS and DGMR in probabilistic nowcasting, with GAN variant improving spatial sharpness and spectral penalty partially controlling fine-scale power excess. Trade-off exists between probabilistic skill and ensemble-mean accuracy at longer lead times.

title: PanoGS-SLAM: Panoramic 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM
summary: Real-time dense SLAM is a core capability for robotics applications that require robust localization and high- quality mapping in dynamic or fast-changing environments. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based SLAM methods have shown promising performance, but most are designed for narrow-FoV pinhole cameras, where limited angular coverage weakens pose observability and often leads to unstable photo- metric optimization under rapid motion and large viewpoint changes. We present PanoGS-SLAM, the first panoramic dense SLAM system built on 3D Gaussian Splatting. Our method per- forms differentiable rendering and pose optimization directly in the spherical domain, enabling omnidirectional photometric constraints for more stable tracking. To improve geometric consistency and robustness, we introduce (1) a sphere-consistent photometric loss that compensates for the area distortion of equirectangular projection, and (2) a depth-guided Gaussian initialization strategy that stabilizes incremental mapping in newly observed regions. Extensive experiments on both real and synthetic panoramic benchmarks (PALVIO and SynPano) show that PanoGS-SLAM consistently outperforms geometric and GS-based baselines in tracking accuracy and rendering quality, while achieving fast front-end convergence and real-time perfor- mance. In addition, controlled field-of-view experiments reveal a clear monotonic improvement in optimization conditioning and convergence stability as angular coverage increases, high- lighting the fundamental role of sensing geometry in shaping the optimization landscape of differentiable Gaussian-based SLAM. The source code will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: PanoGS-SLAM is the first panoramic dense SLAM system built on 3D Gaussian Splatting, addressing limitations of narrow-FoV cameras by performing differentiable rendering and pose optimization directly in the spherical domain. It introduces a sphere-consistent photometric loss to compensate for equirectangular projection distortion and a depth-guided Gaussian initialization strategy for stable incremental mapping.
AI.motivation: Existing 3DGS-based SLAM methods are designed for narrow-FoV pinhole cameras with limited angular coverage, which weakens pose observability and causes unstable photometric optimization under rapid motion and large viewpoint changes. There was a need for an omnidirectional approach that provides more stable tracking.
AI.method: 1) Performing differentiable rendering and pose optimization directly in the spherical domain; 2) Sphere-consistent photometric loss that compensates for area distortion of equirectangular projection; 3) Depth-guided Gaussian initialization strategy for stabilizing incremental mapping in newly observed regions
AI.result: PanoGS-SLAM consistently outperforms geometric and GS-based baselines in tracking accuracy and rendering quality on PALVIO and SynPano benchmarks, while achieving fast front-end convergence and real-time performance. Controlled FoV experiments demonstrate monotonic improvement in optimization conditioning and convergence stability as angular coverage increases.
AI.conclusion: PanoGS-SLAM successfully enables panoramic dense SLAM using 3D Gaussian Splatting. The work highlights the fundamental role of sensing geometry in shaping the optimization landscape of differentiable Gaussian-based SLAM, showing that wider angular coverage leads to better optimization conditioning and convergence stability.

title: LoopSpec: Pipelined Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
summary: Looped Transformers achieve strong performance with compact parameter sizes by repeatedly applying a shared stack of Transformer blocks across recurrent depths. However, they incur higher decoding latency than standard Transformer models of comparable parameter size because shared weights are accessed at every recurrent depth. To improve decoding efficiency, self-speculative decoding is particularly well suited to Looped Transformers, as their intermediate recurrent states can directly provide draft predictions without an auxiliary draft model. We therefore propose LoopSpec, a training-free self-speculative decoding framework tailored for Looped Transformers. LoopSpec extracts draft tokens from early recurrent states and operates in a pipelined manner, overlapping draft generation of future tokens with target verification of the current token. To improve draft accuracy without excessive compute overhead, we introduce a selective second proposal from deeper recurrent depth while ensuring lossless decoding under both greedy and sampling regimes. Furthermore, we derive the optimal proposal depths in closed form and show the prediction matches measurement. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, LoopSpec achieves up to 6.83$\times$ inference speedup across diverse Looped Transformers.

AI.tldr: LoopSpec is a training-free self-speculative decoding framework designed to improve decoding efficiency of Looped Transformers by using intermediate recurrent states as draft predictions, achieving up to 6.83× inference speedup.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers achieve strong performance with compact parameters by repeatedly applying shared Transformer blocks, but they suffer from higher decoding latency because shared weights must be accessed at every recurrent depth. The authors aim to address this efficiency bottleneck.
AI.method: LoopSpec extracts draft tokens from early recurrent states and operates in a pipelined manner, overlapping draft generation of future tokens with target verification. It introduces a selective second proposal from deeper recurrent depth while ensuring lossless decoding under both greedy and sampling regimes. The optimal proposal depths are derived in closed form.
AI.result: LoopSpec achieves up to 6.83× inference speedup across diverse Looped Transformers on reasoning and coding benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Self-speculative decoding is well-suited to Looped Transformers because their intermediate recurrent states can directly provide draft predictions without an auxiliary draft model. LoopSpec provides a training-free solution that significantly improves decoding efficiency while maintaining accuracy.

title: SSC-Priors: Exploring Semantic and Visibility Priors to Boost Lidar Semantic Scene Completion
summary: This paper investigates easy strategies to boost the performance of existing networks for lidar semantic scene completion (SSC) without requiring complex architectural redesigns. The fact is that, over the last years, SSC methods have mostly pursued architectural innovations, making the models heavier and more complex, e.g., by jointly training a point cloud semantic segmentation branch. In this work, we take a step back and explore two priors used as simple ingredients (possibly noisy) to improve existing approaches: semantic pseudo-labels and sensor visibility information. Concretely, we provide both kinds of information directly as additional inputs to a given SSC network, requiring only a minimal adaptation of the original architecture. We first demonstrate that endowing input point clouds with semantic pseudo-labels from off-the-shelf segmenters significantly improves the performance of existing SSC models. In fact, by evaluating these models against an oracle, we establish that high-quality semantic priors are a primary driver of semantic gains (mIoU), and that the SSC model can be trained just once with ground-truth semantics and then exploited without retraining using any segmenter. Furthermore, we equip the input lidar point cloud with visibility information that distinguishes between empty spaces (between the lidar and a scanned point) and unknown spaces (outside of lines of sight), providing a secondary performance boost across the tested architectures. We study the design space of data for representing visibility information and bound the remaining headroom with a ground-truth oracle on the free-space labels. On SemanticKITTI, these enhancements make older models competitive with state-of-the-art systems across four architectures, in one case even outperforming them. On the SSCBench-nuScenes benchmark, both priors also transfer with the sparser 32-beam sensor.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes two simple strategies to boost performance of existing LiDAR semantic scene completion (SSC) networks without complex architectural redesigns: adding semantic pseudo-labels from off-the-shelf segmenters and incorporating sensor visibility information (distinguishing empty vs. unknown spaces) as additional inputs.
AI.motivation: Over recent years, SSC methods have focused on architectural innovations, making models heavier and more complex. This work takes a step back to explore simple priors that can improve existing approaches with minimal adaptation.
AI.method: The method involves two key enhancements: (1) Endowing input point clouds with semantic pseudo-labels from off-the-shelf segmenters as additional inputs, and (2) Equipping input point clouds with visibility information that distinguishes empty spaces (between lidar and scanned points) from unknown spaces (outside lines of sight). Both require only minimal architectural adaptation.
AI.result: On SemanticKITTI, these enhancements make older models competitive with state-of-the-art systems across four architectures, in one case even outperforming them. Both priors also transfer to SSCBench-nuScenes with sparser 32-beam sensor. The oracle experiments show that high-quality semantic priors are a primary driver of semantic gains (mIoU), and the SSC model can be trained once with ground-truth semantics and then exploited without retraining using any segmenter.
AI.conclusion: Simple priors—semantic pseudo-labels and visibility information—can significantly boost SSC performance with minimal architectural changes, making older models competitive with state-of-the-art systems. The approach transfers well across different sensor configurations.

title: MyoFlow: Anchor-Tied Rectified Flow for HD-sEMG Gesture Recognition Across Sessions and Subjects
summary: High-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG) gesture recognition supports prosthetic control, assistive robotics, and rehabilitation, but electrode re-donning and physiological variability cause distribution shifts that degrade accuracy across sessions and subjects. Generative HD-sEMG models primarily synthesize signals for augmentation; although diffusion models enhance representation learning, prediction still relies on a separate classifier. To tie learned dynamics to the decision rule, we propose MyoFlow, the first discriminative flow-matching framework for HD-sEMG recognition across sessions and subjects. It recasts classification as anchor-tied transport: a domain-conditioned rectified flow moves encoded windows toward gesture anchors that serve as transport targets and define the nearest-anchor decision geometry, enabling zero-shot prediction without an independent head. On the Hyser dataset, MyoFlow improves mean cross-session and cross-subject accuracy over the strongest diffusion-based baseline by 4.24\% and 6.37\%, respectively, and achieves 91.71\% mean zero-shot accuracy and 97.39\% mean few-shot accuracy across multiple days on the CEMHSEY dataset.

AI.tldr: MyoFlow is a novel discriminative flow-matching framework for HD-sEMG gesture recognition that addresses distribution shifts across sessions and subjects. It uses anchor-tied transport where gesture anchors serve as both transport targets and decision geometry, enabling zero-shot prediction without a separate classifier.
AI.motivation: HD-sEMG gesture recognition suffers from distribution shifts due to electrode re-donning and physiological variability, degrading accuracy across sessions and subjects. Existing generative models primarily synthesize signals for augmentation, while diffusion models enhance representation learning but still rely on separate classifiers, failing to tie learned dynamics to decision rules.
AI.method: MyoFlow recasts classification as anchor-tied transport using domain-conditioned rectified flow. It moves encoded HD-sEMG windows toward gesture anchors that serve as transport targets and define nearest-anchor decision geometry, enabling zero-shot prediction without an independent classification head.
AI.result: On Hyser dataset, MyoFlow improves mean cross-session accuracy by 4.24% and cross-subject accuracy by 6.37% over the strongest diffusion-based baseline. On CEMHSEY dataset, it achieves 91.71% mean zero-shot accuracy and 97.39% mean few-shot accuracy across multiple days.
AI.conclusion: MyoFlow successfully addresses distribution shifts in HD-sEMG gesture recognition through its discriminative flow-matching approach. By tying learned dynamics directly to decision geometry via anchor-tied transport, it eliminates the need for a separate classifier and achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-session and cross-subject recognition, with particularly strong zero-shot and few-shot capabilities.

title: SlotDiT: Object-Centric Representations for Diffusion Transformers
comment: Accepted at BMVC 2026. Project page: https://slot-dit.github.io/
summary: Text-conditioned latent diffusion models perform strongly in video generation and are promising backbones for robotic applications. However, existing approaches rely on pixel-level or VAE-based latent representations that lack explicit semantic structure, leaving the impact of the representation space largely unexplored. Slot-based object-centric representations offer a structured alternative by decomposing scenes into object-level latents, or slots. While they have shown success in dynamics modeling and planning, they have not yet been explored for diffusion-based generative modeling. We introduce SlotDiT, a text-guided Diffusion Transformer (DiT) that operates in a slot-based latent space. Given a reference image and a language instruction, SlotDiT decomposes the scene into object-centric slots representing individual entities. Conditioned on the instruction and observed scene context, the model autoregressively denoises future slot trajectories to predict scene dynamics. To systematically investigate latent-space design for diffusion transformers, we compare slot-based representations against VAE-based and semantics-aligned alternatives within a unified DiT framework. Our experiments show that using slots as DiT latents yields competitive video generation quality while consistently improving task-completion rates across four robotic datasets. Furthermore, their compact representation provides a computationally efficient alternative to VAE-based and semantics-aligned latent spaces. Overall, our results demonstrate that object-centric structure is a powerful inductive bias for diffusion-based generative modeling in robotic environments. The project page is available at https://slot-dit.github.io/.

AI.tldr: SlotDiT introduces a text-guided Diffusion Transformer that uses slot-based object-centric representations for video generation in robotic applications, comparing it against VAE-based and semantics-aligned alternatives within a unified framework.
AI.motivation: Existing text-conditioned latent diffusion models for video generation rely on pixel-level or VAE-based representations that lack explicit semantic structure. The impact of representation space design on diffusion transformers for robotic applications remains unexplored.
AI.method: SlotDiT decomposes scenes into object-level slots from reference images, conditioned on language instructions and observed scene context. The model autoregressively denoises future slot trajectories to predict scene dynamics. The study compares slot-based, VAE-based, and semantics-aligned representations within a unified DiT framework across four robotic datasets.
AI.result: Slot-based representations as DiT latents achieve competitive video generation quality while consistently improving task-completion rates across four robotic datasets. They also provide computationally efficient alternatives to VAE-based and semantics-aligned latent spaces.
AI.conclusion: Object-centric structure (slot-based representations) serves as a powerful inductive bias for diffusion-based generative modeling in robotic environments, offering a promising backbone for robotic applications.

title: Memorisation bias in medical AI
summary: Medical AI models hold immense potential to improve patient outcomes, but they are also known to unintentionally memorise individual records from their training datasets. While such memorisation has been linked to targeted privacy attacks, its consequences for clinical deployment, where patients may be assessed by a model that saw their historical data during training, remain poorly understood. Here we show that predictions on a patient's unseen future data can change significantly if a model observed that same patient's anonymised historical data during training, a phenomenon we term "memorisation bias". We demonstrate that this bias exists across diverse data modalities and model architectures, and over prolonged time spans: in some cases, memorisation bias persists on future records acquired decades after the historical records used for training. Moreover, in simulated prospective deployment, memorisation bias has asymmetric effects on the diagnostic accuracy of returning data contributors. When a patient returned with a de novo condition absent from their historical records in the training dataset, diagnostic sensitivity decreased significantly compared to an otherwise identical model not trained on their historical data. Conversely, when their health state was unchanged, both sensitivity and specificity were significantly inflated. Our findings reveal a previously uncharacterised risk in medical AI that arises when a model is deployed on patients who contributed to its training data. This exposes a shortcoming of current model development practice: the de-identification measures designed to protect patients' privacy make it difficult to identify returning contributors and exclude them from the AI-assisted interpretation of their own future data. Mitigating memorisation risks may thus require changes to current model training and deployment protocols.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies "memorisation bias" in medical AI models—when a model trained on a patient's historical data makes different predictions on that patient's future data compared to if the model hadn't seen their history. This bias persists across modalities and architectures, even spanning decades, and asymmetrically affects diagnostic accuracy for returning patients, creating a previously uncharacterized risk in clinical deployment.
AI.motivation: The researchers aimed to address a critical gap: while medical AI models are known to memorize training data (posing privacy risks), the consequences of this memorization for actual clinical deployment—when patients are assessed by models that saw their historical data—were poorly understood. Current de-identification practices make it difficult to identify returning contributors, creating an unaddressed risk.
AI.method: The paper conducted experiments across diverse data modalities and model architectures to demonstrate memorisation bias. They simulated prospective deployment scenarios to test how diagnostic accuracy differs for patients whose data was included vs. excluded from training.
AI.result: Memorisation bias exists across diverse data modalities and model architectures and persists over prolonged time spans (in some cases decades). It has asymmetric effects on diagnostic accuracy: for returning patients with new conditions, sensitivity decreases significantly; for those with unchanged health states, both sensitivity and specificity are inflated.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a previously uncharacterized risk in medical AI deployment—when models are used on patients who contributed to their training data. Current de-identification measures that protect privacy paradoxically make it difficult to identify returning contributors and exclude them from AI-assisted interpretation of their own future data. Mitigating this risk may require changes to model training and deployment protocols.

title: Tracking the Unseen: An Occlusion-Robust Framework for Target Tracking Under Full and Long-Term Occlusion
summary: Real-time multi-object tracking systems remain highly vulnerable to full and long-term occlusion, where targets temporarily or completely disappear from the camera's field of view. Conventional trackers may terminate trajectories prematurely, resulting in identity loss and reduced situational awareness in applications such as defense and surveillance. This work proposes an occlusion-robust target tracking framework that maintains target identity and trajectory continuity through the integration of YOLOv11n object detection, Kalman Filter motion prediction, and occlusion-aware appearance-based re-identification. The framework consists of three stages: object detection, position estimation during occlusion, and identity recovery after target reappearance. Six Re-Identification (Re-ID) architectures were evaluated within the same tracking framework under identical conditions, with the Occlusion-Aware Mask Network (OAMN) achieving the best overall performance and therefore selected for the final pipeline. The framework was benchmarked against OccluTrack on the public OVIS dataset, achieving relative improvements of 18.1 percent in Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA) and 25.1 percent in Identity F1 Score (IDF1), while reducing identity switches by 12.8 percent.
