On a custom military dataset simulating surveillance and battlefield-like environments with long-term occlusion, the framework achieved a MOTA of 0.734 and an IDF1 of 0.729, corresponding to relative improvements of 14.2 percent and 5.8 percent over OccluTrack. The system demonstrated strong tracking continuity, robust identity preservation, and reliable trajectory estimation under challenging occlusion conditions, highlighting its effectiveness for defense-related surveillance applications requiring continuous target tracking during visibility loss.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an occlusion-robust multi-object tracking framework that combines YOLOv11n object detection, Kalman Filter motion prediction, and occlusion-aware appearance-based re-identification to maintain target identity and trajectory continuity during full and long-term occlusion. The framework was evaluated with six Re-ID architectures, with Occlusion-Aware Mask Network (OAMN) performing best. Benchmarking on OVIS dataset showed significant improvements over OccluTrack, and on a custom military dataset, achieved MOTA of 0.734 and IDF1 of 0.729.
AI.motivation: Real-time multi-object tracking systems are highly vulnerable to full and long-term occlusion, where targets temporarily or completely disappear from the camera's field of view. Conventional trackers may terminate trajectories prematurely, resulting in identity loss and reduced situational awareness in defense and surveillance applications.
AI.method: The framework consists of three stages: object detection using YOLOv11n, position estimation during occlusion using Kalman Filter motion prediction, and identity recovery after target reappearance using occlusion-aware appearance-based re-identification. Six Re-Identification (Re-ID) architectures were evaluated within the same tracking framework under identical conditions, with the Occlusion-Aware Mask Network (OAMN) achieving the best overall performance.
AI.result: On the OVIS dataset, the framework achieved relative improvements of 18.1% in MOTA and 25.1% in IDF1, while reducing identity switches by 12.8% compared to OccluTrack. On a custom military dataset simulating surveillance and battlefield-like environments with long-term occlusion, the framework achieved a MOTA of 0.734 and an IDF1 of 0.729, corresponding to relative improvements of 14.2% and 5.8% over OccluTrack.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrated strong tracking continuity, robust identity preservation, and reliable trajectory estimation under challenging occlusion conditions, highlighting its effectiveness for defense-related surveillance applications requiring continuous target tracking during visibility loss.

title: Easy to Catch a Liar, Hard to Clear an Honest One: Language Models Diagnosing a Corrupted Reward Channel from a Verified Record
comment: 15 pages, 9 tables. Code, prompts, answer keys, and every scored output: https://github.com/IamArmanNikkhah/easy-to-catch-a-liar
summary: An agent that learns from rewards has to trust whatever reports those rewards. When the reports suddenly change, either the world changed or the reporter broke. From the reports alone these are indistinguishable, and reinforcement learning theory shows that no amount of further experience separates them. The prescribed escape is richer data about the reporter itself. We ask whether a frozen language model, handed exactly that data, uses it. We build a two-option game in which a payout swap and a lying reporter produce byte-identical histories. Then we add one verified record: an independent check of one round's real result, printed beside what the reporter said about that round. That single line settles the case. We ask three large models, from two families, to answer one question with one letter. Is the reporter honest or lying? They catch a lying reporter almost perfectly. At the 70B class that holds in every condition we tried; the 32B model slips in one wording. They clear an honest reporter far less often, and how often depends on things that should not matter. Averaged over rounds, letters, and wordings, a 72B model calls an honest reporter a liar 38% of the time when nothing has changed at all, and 58% of the time when the payouts moved. A 70B model from a second family calls an honest reporter a liar 26% and 48% of the time. The failure is not one of reading, because in the situation where nothing changed the same models score 0.96 to 1.00 with the answer printed in the prompt. Which surface feature drives it differs by family. For the Qwen models it is which round the record names, and for Llama it is which letter stands for "honest." Adding the record to a prompt that already states the answer makes Llama less likely to give that answer. We had registered a prediction for that 58% before the run: 35%. The failure is larger than we expected.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can detect when a reporter is lying about rewards in a game. The authors create a scenario where a lying reporter and a changed payout produce identical histories, then add one verified record to see if models can detect the lie. They test three large models (70B-72B class) from two families (Qwen and Llama) and find that while models can catch lying reporters almost perfectly, they often falsely accuse honest reporters (38-58% false accusation rates). The failure appears to be driven by surface features like which round the record names or which letter represents "honest."
AI.motivation: The core problem is that an agent learning from rewards cannot distinguish between a changed world and a lying reporter based on reward reports alone. The authors ask whether a frozen language model, given additional verified data about the reporter, can use that information to detect lying.
AI.method: The authors built a two-option game where a payout swap and a lying reporter produce byte-identical histories. They added one verified record—an independent check of one round's real result printed beside what the reporter said. They tested three large models (Qwen2.5-72B, Qwen2.5-32B, and Llama3.1-70B) from two families, asking them to answer one question with one letter: Is the reporter honest or lying?
AI.result: Models catch lying reporters almost perfectly (near 100% at 70B class), but falsely accuse honest reporters 26-38% of the time when nothing changed, and 48-58% when payouts moved. The 32B model slips in one wording. The failure is not reading comprehension (models score 0.96-1.00 when the answer is printed in the prompt). Surface features drive the errors: for Qwen models, it matters which round the record names; for Llama, it matters which letter stands for "honest." Adding the record to a prompt that already states the answer makes Llama less likely to give that answer.
AI.conclusion: Large language models fail to reliably use verified information to detect lying reporters. The failure is larger than expected (predicted 35%, got 58%). The errors are driven by irrelevant surface features rather than logical reasoning, suggesting the models are not truly reasoning about the reporter's honesty but are biased by superficial prompt characteristics.

title: BrainFocus: EEG-Guided ROI Selection for Efficient Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve strong visual question answering (VQA) performance, but processing large cluttered images is computationally expensive when only a small region is relevant. Electroencephalography (EEG) signals, which capture human neural responses to visual stimuli, can provide a human-derived semantic cue about the region of interest (ROI). However, EEG-guided visual category decoding remains imperfect, making direct ROI routing unreliable. In this work, we propose BrainFocus, a reliable EEG-guided efficient VLM framework for VQA. An EEG classifier predicts a target category, and a YOLO detector localizes the matching ROI. The VLM receives the cropped ROI only when both predictions pass confidence thresholds; otherwise, it processes the full image. For evaluation, we build on EEG-ImageNet to construct a 40-class benchmark comprising generated cluttered images and real object-centric images, with target-ROI annotations and 600 English visual question-answer pairs. Across Qwen3.5-VL 2B, 4B, and 9B models, BrainFocus improves VQA accuracy by 4.14-9.87 percentage points (pp) on cluttered scenes while reducing input tokens and total tokens by 23.2%-39.4% and 23.2%-39.3%, and end-to-end floating-point operations (FLOPs) by 23.2%-39.5%. These results demonstrate that EEG can guide efficient VLM inference even when its semantic decoding is imperfect.

AI.tldr: BrainFocus proposes using EEG signals to guide vision-language models (VLMs) to focus on relevant image regions for visual question answering, reducing computational cost while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Processing large cluttered images with VLMs is computationally expensive when only a small region is relevant. EEG signals can provide human-derived semantic cues about regions of interest, but EEG-guided category decoding is imperfect, making direct ROI routing unreliable.
AI.method: BrainFocus uses an EEG classifier to predict target category and a YOLO detector to localize matching ROI. The VLM receives cropped ROI only when both predictions pass confidence thresholds; otherwise it processes the full image. Built benchmark on EEG-ImageNet with 40-class dataset, cluttered images, real object-centric images, ROI annotations, and 600 VQA pairs.
AI.result: Across Qwen3.5-VL 2B, 4B, and 9B models, BrainFocus improved VQA accuracy by 4.14-9.87 percentage points on cluttered scenes while reducing input tokens by 23.2%-39.4%, total tokens by 23.2%-39.3%, and FLOPs by 23.2%-39.5%.
AI.conclusion: EEG signals can guide efficient VLM inference even when semantic decoding is imperfect, demonstrating a promising approach for human-AI collaborative vision systems.

authors: José Mairton Barros da Silva Júnior
title: Personalized Federated Learning through Global Knowledge Distillation and Local Head Adaptation
summary: Statistical heterogeneity limits federated learning when a single global classifier cannot represent client-specific label distributions. In this work, we propose Personalized Federated Knowledge Distillation with Head Adaptation (pFedKDH), which aggregates only the shared backbone, keeps persistent client-specific heads, and uses a recalibrated global head as a teacher during local training. Across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 under class-wise Dirichlet partitions, pFedKDH obtains the best accuracy in most settings, with accuracy gaps up to 37.67\% over the weakest baseline and consistently low standard deviation across repetitions. Component-wise diagnostics and convergence results support the role of persistent heads and distillation-guided local optimization under label-skewed data.

AI.tldr: pFedKDH addresses statistical heterogeneity in federated learning by aggregating only the shared backbone while keeping persistent client-specific heads, using a recalibrated global head as teacher for local training. Achieves best accuracy across multiple datasets under class-wise Dirichlet partitions with up to 37.67% improvement over baselines.
AI.motivation: Statistical heterogeneity in federated learning limits performance when a single global classifier cannot represent client-specific label distributions. The problem is that label skew (non-IID data) across clients causes the global model to perform poorly for clients with different label distributions.
AI.method: pFedKDH uses three key components: (1) Aggregates only the shared backbone across clients, (2) Keeps persistent client-specific heads that remain local, (3) Uses a recalibrated global head as a teacher during local training for knowledge distillation. This approach handles label heterogeneity by maintaining client-specific classification heads while sharing only the feature extraction backbone.
AI.result: pFedKDH achieves the best accuracy across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 under class-wise Dirichlet partitions. Accuracy gaps up to 37.67% over the weakest baseline, with consistently low standard deviation across repetitions.
AI.conclusion: Persistent heads and distillation-guided local optimization are effective under label-skewed data. The approach successfully handles statistical heterogeneity in federated learning by separating backbone aggregation from client-specific head adaptation.

title: ORCA: Occlusion-Aware Refinement and Completion for Novel View Synthesis
summary:
Novel-view synthesis from a single image is a fundamentally ambiguous problem. As the camera moves away from the input viewpoint, previously hidden regions become visible, exposing missing geometry and holes in the reconstructed scene. Existing methods often rely on generative models to complete such regions. However, many of these artifacts are small gaps near depth boundaries and do not require generating new scene content.
  In order to eliminate expensive process of generating image we introduce ORCA, an occlusion-aware method for reconstructing and completing explorable 3D scenes from a single image. ORCA first introduces 3D structure into a Gaussian-anchor representation using monocular depth while preserving the original camera-ray correspondence. During scene exploration, missing regions are handled based on their size and structure. Small disocclusions are repaired using RGB-D information already available in the reconstruction, while generative inpainting is reserved for larger regions that cannot be reliably recovered from the scene. New Gaussian anchors are added and optimized locally without modifying the existing representation. By reducing unnecessary reliance on generative inpainting, ORCA limits generation-induced hallucinations and better preserves the content and structure of the original scene.
  On DIV2K, ORCA improves novel-view quality over VistaDream across all reported metrics, increasing MUSIQ from 61.60 to 68.71 and CLIP-IQA from 0.474 to 0.574. These results show that many novel-view artifacts can be repaired effectively by reusing information already present in the reconstructed scene.

AI.tldr: ORCA is an occlusion-aware method for novel-view synthesis from a single image that uses Gaussian-anchor representation with monocular depth to reconstruct and complete explorable 3D scenes. It handles small disocclusions by reusing existing RGB-D information and reserves generative inpainting only for larger regions that cannot be recovered, reducing hallucinations and preserving original scene content.
AI.motivation: Novel-view synthesis from a single image is fundamentally ambiguous because moving the camera reveals previously hidden regions with missing geometry. Existing methods rely heavily on generative models to complete these regions, but many artifacts are small gaps near depth boundaries that don't require generating new content. The goal is to reduce unnecessary generative inpainting and better preserve the original scene structure.
AI.method: ORCA introduces 3D structure into a Gaussian-anchor representation using monocular depth while preserving camera-ray correspondence. During scene exploration, it handles missing regions based on size and structure: small disocclusions are repaired using RGB-D information already available in the reconstruction, while generative inpainting is reserved only for larger regions. New Gaussian anchors are added and optimized locally without modifying the existing representation.
AI.result: On DIV2K dataset, ORCA improves novel-view quality over VistaDream across all reported metrics, increasing MUSIQ from 61.60 to 68.71 and CLIP-IQA from 0.474 to 0.574.
AI.conclusion: Many novel-view artifacts can be repaired effectively by reusing information already present in the reconstructed scene, rather than relying on generative models. This approach limits generation-induced hallucinations and better preserves the content and structure of the original scene.

title: Same Flow, Different Paths: Variance Reduction in Flow Matching
summary: In flow matching (FM), a velocity model $v_θ$ is trained using a predefined path $g_t$ that connects data and noise samples (e.g., $g_t(x_0, x_1) = (1 - t) x_0 + t x_1$). In this work, we study the choice of this path from an optimization perspective by analyzing the variance of stochastic gradients. We consider the class $G(p_t,v^\star_t)$ of paths that induce the same marginal distributions $p_t$ and marginal velocity field $v^\star_t$, and therefore the same FM objective. Our main finding is that the choice of path $g_t$ can fundamentally change the convergence rate of SGD, even when the FM objective remains exactly the same. (i) For a linear velocity model and one-dimensional Gaussian data, we derive a tight bound on the SGD iteration complexity up to logarithmic factors and find an analytically optimal path that minimizes this bound among linear paths inducing the same FM problem. (ii) We then extend the variance analysis to general FM problems and formulate path selection at a fixed $θ$ as the variance-minimization problem PathOpt$_θ$, constrained to $g_t\in G(p_t,v^\star_t)$. We show that this constraint is essential: reducing variance without it can lead to slower convergence. (iii) Since the constraint $g_t \in G(p_t,v^\star_t)$ cannot generally be verified directly, we derive an equivalent formulation with constraints that can be estimated from samples, allowing paths to be found numerically. Our theoretical results are supported by experiments with Gaussian data, Gaussian mixture models, and real datasets.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how the choice of path in flow matching (FM) affects SGD convergence, even when the FM objective remains identical. The authors show that path selection can fundamentally change convergence rates, derive optimal paths for linear cases, and develop a practical framework (PathOpt_θ) for general cases.
AI.motivation: In flow matching, a velocity model v_θ is trained using a predefined path g_t connecting data and noise samples. While the path is typically chosen heuristically (e.g., linear interpolation), the authors recognize that different paths inducing the same marginal distributions and velocity fields should yield the same FM objective, yet may have different convergence properties due to gradient variance.
AI.method: The authors analyze variance of stochastic gradients across path choices. They consider the class G(p_t, v*_t) of paths that induce the same marginal distributions p_t and marginal velocity field v*_t. They derive: (i) tight bounds on SGD iteration complexity for linear velocity models with 1D Gaussian data, (ii) a general variance-minimization framework PathOpt_θ, and (iii) an equivalent sample-based formulation for numerical optimization.
AI.result: Key findings: (i) Path choice fundamentally affects convergence rate - an analytically optimal path can be derived for linear cases, (ii) the constraint g_t ∈ G(p_t, v*_t) is essential - reducing variance without it can paradoxically slow convergence, (iii) practical numerical methods can find good paths using sample-based estimates. Experiments on Gaussian data, GMMs, and real datasets validate the theory.
AI.conclusion: The choice of path in flow matching is not just a heuristic consideration but a fundamental optimization variable. By selecting paths that minimize gradient variance within the constraint of preserving the FM objective, significant improvements in convergence speed can be achieved. The PathOpt_θ framework provides a practical approach for general cases.

title: Tables Decoded: DELTA for Structure, TARQA for Understanding
comment: Accepted at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision 2026
summary: Table understanding is a core task in document intelligence, encompassing two key subtasks: table reconstruction and table visual question answering (TabVQA). While recent approaches predominantly rely on vision- language models (VLMs) operating on table images, we propose a more scalable and effective alternative based on structured textual representations. These representations are easier to process, align more naturally with LLMs, and eliminate the need for language-specific visual encoders, making them particularly suitable for multilingual documents. We present DELTA, which separates physical structure recognition, logical structure recognition, and OCR to extract both layout and content accurately. DELTA outputs tables in Optimised Table Structure Language (OTSL), a compact and unified format that encodes cell arrangements and textual content. On table structure recognition (TSR), DELTA achieves TEDS- Structure scores comparable with state-of-the-art methods across FinTabNet, PubTabNet, and PubTables-1M. We further establish its robustness on non-English tables through our curated Hindi benchmark, TORQUE. Building on this, we introduce TARQA, an LLM fine-tuned on OTSL sequences. Our approach yields gains of 9.3 p.p. on WTQ (TabQA) and 9.2 p.p. on FinTabNetQA (TabVQA), respectively. On TORQUE, our method ranks second among all VLMs and DELTA + LLM variants. We release our code, models, and benchmark at: https://github.com/Tihiitborg/Tables-Decoded

AI.tldr: The paper presents DELTA, a table understanding system that uses structured textual representations (OTSL) instead of vision-language models, achieving state-of-the-art results on table structure recognition and significant improvements on TabVQA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current approaches rely on VLMs operating on table images, which are less scalable and require language-specific visual encoders. The authors propose a more scalable and effective alternative based on structured textual representations that align better with LLMs and work well for multilingual documents.
AI.method: DELTA separates physical structure recognition, logical structure recognition, and OCR to extract layout and content. It outputs tables in Optimised Table Structure Language (OTSL), a compact format encoding cell arrangements and textual content. TARQA is an LLM fine-tuned on OTSL sequences for TabVQA.
AI.result: DELTA achieves TEDS-Structure scores comparable with state-of-the-art methods on FinTabNet, PubTabNet, and PubTables-1M. TARQA yields gains of 9.3 p.p. on WTQ and 9.2 p.p. on FinTabNetQA. On TORQUE (Hindi benchmark), the method ranks second among all VLMs and DELTA + LLM variants.
AI.conclusion: The proposed textual representation approach (OTSL) is effective for table understanding, achieving competitive results on TSR and significant improvements on TabVQA tasks while being more scalable and suitable for multilingual documents compared to vision-based methods.

title: Hybrid Variational Quantum Circuits for Multivariate Regression and High-Dimensional Data Reconstruction
summary: Variational quantum circuits (VQCs) are parameterized quantum circuits optimized classically. We propose a hybrid variational quantum circuit (HVQC) extending VQCs with a classical affine post-measurement layer, enabling vector-valued regression without the linear overhead of independent scalar circuits. Theoretically, we show that elementary one-and two-qubit circuits can approximate quadratic functions and products via data re-uploading and entanglement, providing the foundations of the full architecture. Experimentally, on two synthetic image reconstruction datasets and the Friedman1 benchmark (40,568 test samples), our HVQC matches Gaussian Process Regression and outperforms XGBoost and Random Forest. An ablation study confirms that both quantum and classical components are essential, and results highlight the central role of the feature map in hybrid quantum-classical models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Hybrid Variational Quantum Circuit (HVQC) that extends traditional VQCs by adding a classical affine post-measurement layer, enabling efficient vector-valued regression without the overhead of independent scalar circuits. The approach achieves performance comparable to Gaussian Process Regression while outperforming XGBoost and Random Forest on benchmark tasks.
AI.motivation: Traditional VQCs require linear overhead when solving multi-output regression problems (independent scalar circuits). This paper aims to develop a more efficient architecture that can handle vector-valued regression with reduced computational overhead while leveraging both quantum and classical computation.
AI.method:
1) Propose HVQC architecture extending VQCs with a classical affine post-measurement layer
2) Theoretical analysis showing elementary one-and two-qubit circuits can approximate quadratic functions and products via data re-uploading and entanglement
3) Experimental validation on synthetic image reconstruction and Friedman1 benchmark (40,568 test samples)
4) Ablation study to verify contribution of both quantum and classical components
AI.result:
1) HVQC matches Gaussian Process Regression performance
2) Outperforms XGBoost and Random Forest on Friedman1 benchmark
3) Ablation study confirms both quantum and classical components are essential
4) Feature map plays a central role in hybrid quantum-classical models
AI.conclusion: The proposed HVQC successfully enables efficient vector-valued regression using hybrid quantum-classical architecture. The combination of quantum circuits (for feature extraction via data re-uploading and entanglement) and classical post-processing (affine transformation) is crucial for performance. The research highlights the importance of feature map design in hybrid quantum-classical machine learning models.

title: Det-LIME: Detector-Aware, Multi-Instance Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations for Automated Marine Mammal Detection
summary:
Despite the rapid uptake of black-box object detectors in marine mammal research and monitoring, explainability techniques are rarely integrated into conservation workflows. Furthermore, most classification-oriented explainability tools are ill-suited to detection tasks involving imagery of social organisms or those with colonial life histories, as they ignore multiple detections within a scene and produce single-instance outputs that blur evidence across individuals. These methods also generate low-resolution, often biologically irrelevant visuals, limiting their utility for debugging, targeted data augmentation, and refined data collection.
  We proposed Det-LIME, a detector-aware, multi-instance adaptation of Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) that produced instance-specific, box-aligned explanations by combining per-detection weighting, a proximity kernel that emphasizes regions near each box, and Intersection-over-Union-based matching to track the same instance across perturbations. We evaluated Det-LIME on aerial drone imagery for harbor seal detection, with an additional seabird case study to assess generality, and compared it with vanilla LIME, Stabilized LIME, Deterministic LIME, and gradient-based attribution methods.
  Using the Attribution Ratio and Max Saliency Hit Rate metrics, we showed that Det-LIME consistently improved multi-instance attribution. In practice, these higher-resolution, instance-aware explanations provide insight into model outputs and support post-processing, debugging, and actionable improvements in modeling and data collection or augmentation.

AI.tldr: Det-LIME is a novel detector-aware explainability method that adapts LIME for multi-instance object detection in marine mammal imagery, producing instance-specific, box-aligned explanations that address limitations of classification-oriented explainability tools when applied to detection tasks involving social organisms.
AI.motivation: The rapid adoption of black-box object detectors in marine mammal research lacks integrated explainability techniques. Existing classification-oriented explainability tools fail for detection tasks with social organisms because they ignore multiple detections, produce single-instance outputs that blur evidence across individuals, and generate low-resolution, biologically irrelevant visuals that limit utility for debugging and data augmentation.
AI.method: Det-LIME combines three key mechanisms: (1) per-detection weighting to handle multiple instances, (2) a proximity kernel emphasizing regions near each detection box, and (3) Intersection-over-Union (IoU)-based matching to track the same instance across perturbations. Evaluated on aerial drone imagery for harbor seal detection and a seabird case study, compared against vanilla LIME, Stabilized LIME, Deterministic LIME, and gradient-based attribution methods.
AI.result: Using Attribution Ratio and Max Saliency Hit Rate metrics, Det-LIME consistently improved multi-instance attribution over baseline methods, producing higher-resolution, instance-aware explanations.
AI.conclusion: Det-LIME provides actionable insights for post-processing, debugging, and improving modeling and data collection/augmentation in marine mammal conservation workflows. The approach addresses a critical gap between advancing computer vision techniques and conservation implementation needs.

title: Large Language Models Develop Belief State Geometry In-Context
summary: Large language models (LLMs) trained on next-token prediction exhibit remarkable in-context learning (ICL) abilities, yet the representations that support ICL remain poorly understood. We consider such representations in a controlled setting: prompting LLMs with data emitted from hidden Markov models (HMMs) and probing for the corresponding belief state -- the posterior distribution over the HMM's hidden states given the observed token history. Across six open-source LLMs prompted with data from 40 HMMs selected for non-trivial belief structure, we find that belief states are linearly decodable from residual stream activations, with peak probe $R^2$-values from 0.83-0.99 across HMM and LLM combinations, ranging from early to late layers. To establish functional relevance, we intervene directly on the probe-identified subspace via patching and steering, resulting in downstream prediction quality on the order of the untampered model, while controls degrade performance substantially. Together, these results provide representation-level evidence that ICL in open-source LLMs approximates optimal Bayesian prediction over a context-inferred generative model. More broadly, our findings extend prior results linking input-distribution structure to activation geometry: from toy networks trained explicitly on HMM data to production-scale LLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether representations supporting in-context learning (ICL) in large language models correspond to Bayesian belief states. Using hidden Markov models (HMMs) as a controlled setting, the authors probe LLM activations and find that belief states are linearly decodable from residual stream activations (R² = 0.83-0.99). Intervening on the identified subspace allows manipulation of downstream predictions, suggesting ICL approximates optimal Bayesian prediction.
AI.motivation: Large language models show remarkable in-context learning abilities, yet the underlying representations that enable ICL remain poorly understood. The authors seek to establish whether ICL representations correspond to Bayesian belief states over latent generative model parameters.
AI.method: The authors probe six open-source LLMs with data from 40 HMMs selected for non-trivial belief structure. They examine residual stream activations and test linear decodability of belief states. They also perform intervention experiments via patching and steering on the probe-identified subspace.
AI.result: Belief states are linearly decodable from residual stream activations with peak probe R²-values ranging from 0.83-0.99 across different HMM and LLM combinations, across early to late layers. Intervention on the identified subspace yields downstream prediction quality comparable to untampered models, while control interventions degrade performance substantially.
AI.conclusion: ICL in open-source LLMs approximates optimal Bayesian prediction over a context-inferred generative model. The findings extend prior results linking input-distribution structure to activation geometry from toy networks to production-scale LLMs.

title: OPEN-1B: A Fully Auditable Training Run
summary:
Open-source language models have a reproducibility problem. Despite releasing weights, training data, and recipes, none of them are provably reproducible due to the non-associativity of floating-point arithmetic. Deep learning frameworks often offer a deterministic execution mode, allowing reproducible operations on the same machines. Unfortunately, this determinism does not carry across hardware such that a user can verify that a released checkpoint was actually produced using the declared training recipe. This leaves room for undisclosed data, injected biases, or backdoors that existing techniques such as proof-of-learning or proof-of-training-data cannot rule out.
  We introduce a new tier of model transparency, fully auditable, in which every operation on every data sample during training is independently reproducible on heterogeneous commodity hardware with bitwise certainty. By imposing a definite order on the sources of training nondeterminism, GPU kernel reductions, data batch ordering across a data-parallel cluster, and inter/intra-node collective communication, we make it possible to replay any individual step of a large, distributed training run on a single piece of commodity hardware and check it against the published trajectory.
  Because replaying an entire run on one machine is infeasible, we support this with a collective verification scheme in which many independent auditors each certify individual steps, together covering the whole run. We release Open-1B, a model trained under this regime, together with its full pretraining dataset, every intermediate checkpoint, the training codebase, and the audit harness needed to reproduce and verify any step of its training.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the reproducibility problem in open-source language models by introducing a "fully auditable" tier of model transparency, enabling bitwise-reproducible training on heterogeneous commodity hardware through deterministic ordering of nondeterministic operations, with a collective verification scheme for large-scale distributed training.
AI.motivation: Open-source language models claim reproducibility but cannot be provably verified due to floating-point non-associativity and cross-hardware nondeterminism. This leaves room for undisclosed data, injected biases, or backdoors that existing techniques cannot detect.
AI.method: The authors impose a definite order on sources of training nondeterminism: GPU kernel reductions, data batch ordering across data-parallel clusters, and inter/intra-node collective communication. They enable replay of any training step on a single commodity machine and support this with a collective verification scheme where multiple independent auditors certify individual steps covering the whole run.
AI.result: The authors release Open-1B, a model trained under this fully auditable regime, together with its full pretraining dataset, every intermediate checkpoint, the training codebase, and the audit harness needed to reproduce and verify any step of its training.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a new tier of model transparency that enables complete verification of LLM training on commodity hardware, addressing concerns about undisclosed training data, biases, or backdoors in open-source models.

title: Bridging the Confidence Gap: Temperature Scaling for Calibrating Test-Time Prompt Tuning
summary: Test-time prompt tuning (TPT) enables adaptation on a single test instance, achieving improved accuracy but often sacrificing calibration performance. Most existing calibration methods introduce additional regularization terms to promote dispersion across text embeddings and reduce calibration error, yet these methods often suffer from a drop in accuracy. Motivated by the well-calibrated nature of zero-shot predictions, we propose CoTS, a simple yet effective post-hoc calibration method that preserves accuracy. Specifically, CoTS applies temperature scaling to minimize the confidence gap between adapted and zero-shot predictions. To fully exploit the potential of multiple augmentations during adaptation, we introduce a weak-strong ensemble strategy that further boosts accuracy. We then apply CoTS to this ensemble, termed E-CoTS, to maintain its well-calibrated property. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets and backbones show that our approaches effectively mitigate miscalibration without compromising primary accuracy. For instance, E-CoTS reduces the average expected calibration error of TPT from 11.90% to 5.38% on ImageNet variants, while even increasing accuracy from 60.74% to 62.95%. Moreover, when integrated with existing calibration methods, E-CoTS usually enhances both accuracy and calibration simultaneously.

AI.tldr: CoTS is a post-hoc calibration method that preserves accuracy while mitigating miscalibration in test-time prompt tuning (TPT). It applies temperature scaling to minimize the confidence gap between adapted and zero-shot predictions. E-CoTS extends this with a weak-strong ensemble strategy, reducing ECE from 11.90% to 5.38% on ImageNet variants while increasing accuracy from 60.74% to 62.95%.
AI.motivation: Test-time prompt tuning (TPT) achieves improved accuracy but often sacrifices calibration performance. Existing calibration methods introduce regularization terms that promote dispersion across text embeddings and reduce calibration error, but suffer from accuracy drop. The well-calibrated nature of zero-shot predictions motivates this approach.
AI.method: CoTS applies temperature scaling to minimize the confidence gap between adapted and zero-shot predictions. E-CoTS introduces a weak-strong ensemble strategy to exploit multiple augmentations during adaptation, then applies CoTS to maintain well-calibrated property.
AI.result: E-CoTS reduces average expected calibration error (ECE) of TPT from 11.90% to 5.38% on ImageNet variants, while increasing accuracy from 60.74% to 62.95%. When integrated with existing calibration methods, E-CoTS usually enhances both accuracy and calibration simultaneously.
AI.conclusion: CoTS and E-CoTS effectively mitigate miscalibration without compromising primary accuracy. The weak-strong ensemble combined with temperature scaling provides a simple yet effective solution that can work with existing calibration methods to enhance both accuracy and calibration.

title: Knowledge as Orbit: Finite Collections as Phases of an Exactly Periodic Latent Generator
summary: Finite knowledge is usually stored extensionally, one code or vector per item. We ask whether a finite collection can instead be stored intensionally, as the decoded orbit of one compact law that returns exactly to its start. For X objects, we encode item i as the i-th phase of a fixed rotation in a learned latent space and decode all phases with a shared network; the latent advances through a bank of rotations at integer harmonics of the cycle, a real discrete Fourier operator, so that R^X equals the identity and exact closure is guaranteed rather than learned. Images are a controlled carrier; looping video is the case where the phase order is the content's own temporal structure. Holding the decoder fixed and varying only the operator, a general learned operator diverges, a norm-preserving but non-periodic one degrades around the loop, and the exactly periodic operator is flat; on real images the gap widens. Capacity is then the decoder's budget: dense decoders carry a structural overhead per crisp image that no size reconciles with compression, while a small convolutional decoder on objects that share a manifold reaches crisp and compressed. A codebook control shows the generative law is free in reconstruction terms while multiplying the latent store many-fold. On seven benchmark clips, against a matched frame-index baseline, the cycle reaches equal or better fidelity at equal parameters while wrapping at machine precision, where the baseline leaves a visible seam; pinning the baseline's frequencies to loop harmonics closes its seam too, confirming that exact periodicity is the operative constraint. Finite cyclic knowledge can be stored as dynamics rather than independent instances, with exact recurrence supplied by algebra and content by a shared decoder.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes storing finite knowledge (like image sequences or video clips) intensionally as the decoded orbit of one compact law with exact periodicity, rather than extensionally as independent instances. By encoding items as phases of a rotation in latent space and using a discrete Fourier operator where R^X equals identity, exact closure is guaranteed. The decoder architecture critically affects performance - dense decoders carry structural overhead unsuitable for compression, while small convolutional decoders work well for objects sharing a manifold. On seven benchmark clips, this approach matches or exceeds baseline fidelity at equal parameters while achieving machine-precision looping.
AI.motivation: The authors question whether finite knowledge collections can be stored intensionally (as a compact law) rather than extensionally (one code per item). They aim to achieve exact periodicity/closure rather than approximate looping, which is particularly important for video compression where visible seams at loop boundaries are a common problem.
AI.method: The approach encodes item i as the i-th phase of a fixed rotation in a learned latent space, decoded by a shared network. The latent advances through a bank of rotations at integer harmonics of the cycle using a real discrete Fourier operator where R^X equals identity. This guarantees exact closure. They compare: (1) general learned operator, (2) norm-preserving but non-periodic operator, and (3) exactly periodic operator. They also test pinning baseline frequencies to loop harmonics.
AI.result: The exactly periodic operator achieves flat performance; general learned operators diverge; norm-preserving non-periodic operators degrade around the loop. On real images, the gap widens. Dense decoders carry structural overhead per crisp image that cannot reconcile with compression. Small convolutional decoders on objects sharing a manifold achieve both crisp and compressed results. On seven benchmark clips against a matched frame-index baseline, the cycle achieves equal or better fidelity at equal parameters while wrapping at machine precision (no visible seam). Pinning baseline frequencies to loop harmonics closes its seam, confirming exact periodicity as the operative constraint.
AI.conclusion: Finite cyclic knowledge can be stored as dynamics rather than independent instances, with exact recurrence supplied by algebra and content by a shared decoder. This approach enables compression of sequential data (like video) by storing only the generative law and decoder parameters, rather than storing each frame independently.

title: Learning-Guided Planning in Large Dynamic Action Spaces: Budgeted Tree Search for One-to-Many Mobile Charging
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures. Learning-guided planning, budgeted tree search, PUCT, and sequential decision-making in large dynamic action spaces
summary: Many learned sequential decision systems map the current state directly to an action. That shortcut becomes brittle when candidate actions are numerous, geometrically structured, and rebuilt with the state. One-to-many mobile charging makes this setting concrete: with N=250 sensors, the initial state induces about 1,125 candidate charging-stop actions; each chosen stop simultaneously serves its in-range sensors, and the action universe changes as sensors die. LP-BTS is a learning-guided planning architecture: a graph proposal policy concentrates a small candidate support, a learned value critic evaluates leaves, and edge-budgeted PUCT compares short simulated futures before committing an action. Because the policy scores this set without a fixed output head, a single frozen checkpoint covers every evaluated setting, spanning action universes from 736 to 2,813 stops. Matched ablations reveal complementary effects: uniform sampling costs 8.8 survival percentage points, while, with targeted support fixed, PUCT jointly retains 1.4 points (about 3.5 of 250 sensors) and direct policy selection travels 23% farther. On a prospectively specified, sealed 30-scenario confirmatory bank evaluated once, LP-BTS attains the highest observed survival (0.4545) and alive-AUC (0.8031). Its estimated survival advantage over the strongest domain-engineered comparator is +0.0066 (95% CI [-0.0037, +0.0184]), an unresolved difference, while it exceeds a deadline heuristic and two source-derived direct-policy reconstructions on every paired scenario. Both learned rows are trained, source-derived reconstructions of variants reported by Gong et al. In this setting, the results provide controlled evidence about learning-guided planning in a large, dynamic action space.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses sequential decision-making in large, dynamic action spaces, specifically for a one-to-many mobile charging problem with 250 sensors and ~1,125 candidate charging-stop actions. The proposed LP-BTS architecture combines a graph proposal policy, learned value critic, and edge-budgeted PUCT for action selection. It achieves the highest survival (0.4545) and alive-AUC (0.8031) on a 30-scenario test bank, providing controlled evidence for learning-guided planning in this domain.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that standard learned decision systems map states directly to actions, which becomes brittle when: (1) candidate actions are numerous, (2) geometrically structured, and (3) rebuilt with the state. The mobile charging scenario exemplifies this—the action universe changes as sensors die, with action spaces ranging from 736 to 2,813 stops. The authors seek to demonstrate that learning-guided planning can handle this large, dynamic action space better than direct policy or heuristic approaches.
AI.method: LP-BTS is a learning-guided planning architecture with three components: (1) Graph proposal policy that concentrates a small candidate support set; (2) Learned value critic that evaluates leaf nodes; (3) Edge-budgeted PUCT that compares short simulated futures before committing an action. The key innovation is that the policy scores candidate sets without a fixed output head, allowing a single frozen checkpoint to cover varying action universes.
AI.result: On a sealed 30-scenario confirmatory bank, LP-BTS achieves the highest observed survival (0.4545) and alive-AUC (0.8031). The estimated survival advantage over the strongest domain-engineered comparator is +0.0066 (95% CI [-0.0037, +0.0184]), an unresolved difference. LP-BTS exceeds a deadline heuristic and two source-derived direct-policy reconstructions on every paired scenario. Ablations show: uniform sampling costs 8.8 survival percentage points; with targeted support, PUCT retains 1.4 points (3.5 of 250 sensors); direct policy selection travels 23% farther.
AI.conclusion: The results provide controlled evidence that learning-guided planning (combining graph proposal policy, value critic, and PUCT search) outperforms direct policy selection and heuristic approaches in large, dynamic action spaces. The complementary effects of the components reveal that targeted support selection and PUCT search each contribute meaningful improvements, while the fixed checkpoint design enables generalization across varying action universes.

title: Reduced-Space Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization of Process Simulation Models
comment: Accepted at the 20th Learning and Intelligent Optimization Conference (LION 20), 2026. Corrected author version. This version corrects a typo in the mathematical description of the multi-fidelity covariance kernel in Section 3.2
summary: Optimizing industrial process flowsheets is often computationally prohibitive due to the high cost of rigorous simulations and the curse of dimensionality inherent in complex design spaces. To address these challenges, we present a reduced-space multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (RS-MFBO) framework designed for high-dimensional, expensive black-box functions. The approach integrates Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA) for dimensionality reduction with a fidelity-augmented Gaussian process that captures correlations between low-cost approximations and expensive high-fidelity evaluations. A cost-aware acquisition strategy, augmented with cooldown and promotion mechanisms, adaptively guides the allocation of samples across fidelities. The framework is validated on two distinct industrial process simulators: a plasmid DNA bioprocess in SuperPro Designer and a green fuel synthesis plant in Aspen HYSYS. Results across diverse economic and physical objectives demonstrate that the proposed method substantially reduces the number of high-fidelity simulator evaluations while maintaining competitive optimization performance compared to single-fidelity baselines. These results highlight RS-MFBO as a scalable, simulator-agnostic approach for cost-constrained black-box optimization.

AI.tldr: A reduced-space multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (RS-MFBO) framework for high-dimensional, expensive black-box optimization in industrial process flowsheets, integrating Global Sensitivity Analysis for dimensionality reduction with a fidelity-augmented Gaussian process and cost-aware acquisition strategy.
AI.motivation: Industrial process flowsheet optimization is computationally prohibitive due to high cost of rigorous simulations and curse of dimensionality in complex design spaces.
AI.method: The framework combines: (1) Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA) for dimensionality reduction, (2) a fidelity-augmented Gaussian process capturing correlations between low-cost approximations and expensive high-fidelity evaluations, and (3) a cost-aware acquisition strategy with cooldown and promotion mechanisms for adaptive sample allocation across fidelities.
AI.result: Validated on two industrial process simulators (plasmid DNA bioprocess in SuperPro Designer and green fuel synthesis plant in Aspen HYSYS). The method substantially reduces high-fidelity simulator evaluations while maintaining competitive optimization performance compared to single-fidelity baselines.
AI.conclusion: RS-MFBO provides a scalable, simulator-agnostic approach for cost-constrained black-box optimization in industrial processes.

title: Coupled Calibration and Learning: Mitigating Teacher Bias in LLM Distillation without Target-Domain Reward Feedback
summary: Large language model (LLM) distillation aims to transfer the capabilities of a powerful teacher to a smaller student. Direct imitation, however, can also transfer the teacher's systematic bias and errors. This challenge is particularly pronounced under covariate shift, when the teacher's reliability on target questions is uncertain and target-domain reward feedback is unavailable. We propose Coupled Calibration and Learning (CCL), an LLM distillation algorithm that couples teacher calibration with student updates through token-level branching, using reward feedback only on source questions. Each iteration calibrates the teacher using source feedback and then uses the calibrated teacher to train the student on target questions. The updated student, in turn, informs subsequent calibration. In an autoregressive policy framework, we prove that the output student's expected average Kullback-Leibler divergence to the oracle student converges to zero at a polynomial rate in the number of iterations. The oracle maximizes the true reference-regularized target reward within the student class, which need not represent the unrestricted optimal policy. Our analysis quantifies the progress of projected student gradient updates while controlling the error in teacher calibration. We further establish a separation from regularized direct matching: its error relative to the oracle student can remain bounded away from zero even when the teacher achieves higher regularized target reward than every student policy. These results demonstrate that LLM distillation can overcome persistent teacher bias and recover the optimal student through coupled calibration and learning, without target-domain reward feedback.

AI.tldr: CCL is an LLM distillation algorithm that iteratively couples teacher calibration with student updates through token-level branching, using only source-domain reward feedback. It theoretically guarantees convergence to the optimal student (oracle) at polynomial rates, overcoming persistent teacher bias without requiring target-domain feedback.
AI.motivation: Direct LLM imitation learning transfers teacher capabilities but also propagates systematic bias and errors. This is especially problematic under covariate shift when teacher's reliability on target questions is uncertain and target-domain reward feedback is unavailable. Current methods fail to address the teacher's inherent bias in distillation.
AI.method: Coupled Calibration and Learning (CCL) uses token-level branching to couple teacher calibration with student updates. Each iteration: (1) calibrates the teacher using source feedback, then (2) uses the calibrated teacher to train the student on target questions. The updated student then informs subsequent calibration. Analysis uses autoregressive policy framework with projected student gradient updates.
AI.result: Proven theoretical guarantees: (1) Output student's expected average KL divergence to oracle student converges to zero at polynomial rate in iterations. (2) Oracle maximizes true reference-regularized target reward within student class. (3) Separated from regularized direct matching - its error can remain bounded away from zero even when teacher achieves higher regularized target reward than every student policy.
AI.conclusion: LLM distillation can overcome persistent teacher bias and recover the optimal student through coupled calibration and learning, without requiring target-domain reward feedback. This provides a theoretically grounded solution for effective knowledge transfer from powerful teachers to smaller students under covariate shift.

title: FreqSpaNet: Frequency and Spatial Learning of SFPF for Physical Layer Hardware Integrity Detection
summary: Unauthorized hardware replacement can preserve a wireless device's logical identity while altering its physical implementation, posing a challenge to hardware integrity verification. Spatio-frequency polarization fingerprints (SFPFs) capture device-dependent responses across multiple frequencies and directions, but their frequency and spatial dimensions exhibit different structural dependencies. We propose FreqSpaNet, an SFPF representation learning network for open set hardware anomaly detection. A frequency branch captures local variations among neighboring frequencies, while a geometry-aware spatial branch models directional relationships using angular information. The two representations are combined through adaptive fusion, and complementary pretraining further captures shared information while preserving the distinct characteristics of the frequency and spatial representations. Experiments show that FreqSpaNet achieves a mean AUROC of 96.31\%, 9.05 points above the baseline. Results under seven hardware replacement scenarios further verify the effectiveness of FreqSpaNet.

AI.tldr: FreqSpaNet is a deep learning network for detecting unauthorized hardware replacement in wireless devices by learning spatio-frequency polarization fingerprint (SFPF) representations. It uses dual branches (frequency and spatial) with adaptive fusion and complementary pretraining to achieve 96.31% mean AUROC in hardware anomaly detection.
AI.motivation: Unauthorized hardware replacement can preserve a wireless device's logical identity while altering its physical implementation, posing a significant challenge to hardware integrity verification. Traditional methods struggle because existing spatio-frequency polarization fingerprints (SFPFs) have frequency and spatial dimensions with different structural dependencies that are not properly captured.
AI.method: The proposed FreqSpaNet employs two specialized branches: (1) A frequency branch that captures local variations among neighboring frequencies, and (2) A geometry-aware spatial branch that models directional relationships using angular information. These two representations are combined through adaptive fusion, and complementary pretraining is used to capture shared information while preserving the distinct characteristics of both representations.
AI.result: FreqSpaNet achieves a mean AUROC of 96.31%, which is 9.05 percentage points above the baseline. The method was validated under seven different hardware replacement scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The dual-branch architecture with adaptive fusion and complementary pretraining effectively addresses the challenge of hardware integrity verification by properly capturing the different structural dependencies in frequency and spatial dimensions of SFPFs, enabling accurate detection of unauthorized hardware replacements.

title: ENCP: Episode-Normalized Conformal Prediction for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Uncertainty estimation for Vision-Language-Navigation (VLN) models is a critical task since it can help identify ambiguous and unreliable predictions, enabling agents to make safer navigation decisions. As one of the most advanced uncertainty estimation frameworks, conformal prediction (CP) offers a promising approach for uncertainty estimation in VLN. However, given that VLN agent requires a sequence of steps, standard calibration in conformal prediction fails to provide coverage guarantee it promises over a dependent, variable-length VLN episode. To this end, we propose Episode-Normalized Conformal Prediction (ENCP), which rescales a nonconformity score by the policy's residual confidence and calibrates one maximum score per episode. Under exchangeable calibration and test episodes, this construction covers the ground truth at every step with probability at least $1 - α$, while allowing dependence among steps within an episode. Across four VLN policies and three nonconformity scores on R2R and REVERIE dataset, ENCP meets all reported empirical step-coverage targets on the seen-to-unseen evaluation. These results demonstrate that ENCP can provide model-agnostic uncertainty estimates, which might be useful for determining when a VLN agent should defer to a more capable predictor, including human assistance.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses uncertainty estimation for Vision-Language-Navigation (VLN) agents by proposing Episode-Normalized Conformal Prediction (ENCP), which handles the challenge of variable-length dependent episodes in VLN tasks. The method rescales nonconformity scores by policy's residual confidence and calibrates one maximum score per episode to provide coverage guarantees.
AI.motivation: Standard conformal prediction fails to provide coverage guarantees over dependent, variable-length VLN episodes because VLN requires a sequence of steps with dependencies among steps. There was a need for an uncertainty estimation framework that can handle these dependencies while still guaranteeing coverage at every step.
AI.method: The proposed ENCP method rescales a nonconformity score by the policy's residual confidence and calibrates one maximum score per episode. This construction allows dependence among steps within an episode while maintaining coverage guarantees under exchangeable calibration and test episodes.
AI.result: ENCP meets all reported empirical step-coverage targets on the seen-to-unseen evaluation across four VLN policies and three nonconformity scores on R2R and REVERIE datasets. The method provides model-agnostic uncertainty estimates that can identify when a VLN agent should defer to more capable predictors, including human assistance.
AI.conclusion: ENCP successfully provides reliable uncertainty estimates for VLN agents, enabling safer navigation decisions by identifying ambiguous and unreliable predictions. This approach can be useful for determining when to defer to human assistance or more capable predictors.
